text.english: O lord, ruler of Pytho, Far-shooter, prophet, who by lot attained the Parnassian crag of the sun-bathed peak, your excellence I hymn; and do you grant me noble fame; send upon my breast a truth-declaring voice, that to far-scattered mortals I may proclaim a clear-voiced song at the Muse’s behests and with the close-strung pectis.
text.greek: Ὦναξ Πυθῶνος μεδέων, ἑκατηβόλε, μάντι, ὃς λάχες ἠλιβάτου κορυφῆς Παρνασσίδα πέτρην σὴν ἀρετὴν ὑμνῶ· σὺ δέ μοι κλέος ἐσθλὸν ὀπάσσαις· πέμπε δ' ἐπὶ πραπίδεσσιν ἐμαῖς ἐτυμηγόρον αὐδήν ὄφρα πολυσπερέεσσι βρότοις λιγύφωνον ἀοιδήν ἠπύσω Μούσης ἐφετμαῖς καὶ πηκτίδι πυκνῇ.

line_details.english: O lord, ruler of Pytho, Far-shooter, prophet,
line_details.greek: Ὦναξ Πυθῶνος μεδέων, ἑκατηβόλε, μάντι,
line_details.note: Invocation is to Apollo, identified by epithets: Pytho = Delphi; hekatēbolos = “Far-shooter”; mantis = “prophet/seer.”

line_details.english: who by lot attained the Parnassian crag of the sun-bathed peak,
line_details.greek: ὃς λάχες ἠλιβάτου κορυφῆς Παρνασσίδα πέτρην
line_details.note: laches = “you obtained (by lot),” echoing divine allotments; ēlibatos = “sun-bathed/sun-blest”; “Parnassian rock” is the crag at Delphi on Mt. Parnassus.

line_details.english: your excellence I hymn; and do you grant me noble fame;
line_details.greek: σὴν ἀρετὴν ὑμνῶ· σὺ δέ μοι κλέος ἐσθλὸν ὀπάσσαις·
line_details.note: aretē = “excellence” (divine prowess); kleos esthlon = “goodly/noble fame.”

line_details.english: send upon my breast a truth-declaring voice,
line_details.greek: πέμπε δ' ἐπὶ πραπίδεσσιν ἐμαῖς ἐτυμηγόρον αὐδήν
line_details.note: prapides = “midriff/breast,” seat of thought; etymēgoros = “truth-declaring, truth-speaking.”

line_details.english: that to far-scattered mortals I may proclaim a clear-voiced song
line_details.greek: ὄφρα πολυσπερέεσσι βρότοις λιγύφωνον ἀοιδήν
line_details.note: polysperes = “much-sown,” used metaphorically of mankind as widely scattered over the earth; ligyphōnos = “clear-voiced”; ēpysō = “I cry aloud/proclaim.”

line_details.english: at the Muse’s behests and with the close-strung pectis.
line_details.greek: ἠπύσω Μούσης ἐφετμαῖς καὶ πηκτίδι πυκνῇ.
line_details.note: ephetmai = “behests/commands”; pectis (πηκτίς) is a stringed instrument akin to the lyre; pyknē = “close-set/closely strung.”

text.english: For now, to you, lyre‑working one, as I sing the beloved lay, my spirit urges me to tell the very things which never before I declared when I proclaimed the deeds of Bakchos and of lord Apollon.
text.greek: - Νῦν γάρ σοι, λυροεργὲ, φίλον μέλος ἀείδοντι θυμὸς ἐποτρύνει λέξαι τάπερ οὔποτε πρόσθεν ἔφρασ' ὅταν Βακχοῖο καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος ἄνακτος

line_details.english: For now, to you, lyre‑working one, as I sing the beloved lay,
line_details.greek: - Νῦν γάρ σοι, λυροεργὲ, φίλον μέλος ἀείδοντι
line_details.note: λυροεργέ (“lyre‑working”) is an elevated epithet, likely addressing either Hermes (inventor of the lyre) or, by self‑address, the poet as master of the lyre; σοι … ἀείδοντι “to you … as I sing” frames the invocation.

line_details.english: my spirit urges me to tell the very things which never before
line_details.greek: θυμὸς ἐποτρύνει λέξαι τάπερ οὔποτε πρόσθεν
line_details.note: τὰ περ (“the very things”) uses περ as an intensifier; λέξαι is the aorist infinitive “to tell, relate.”

line_details.english: I declared when I proclaimed the deeds of Bakchos and of lord Apollon.
line_details.greek: ἔφρασ' ὅταν Βακχοῖο καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος ἄνακτος
line_details.note: ἔφρασ’ “I declared”; ὅταν here functions as “when” (epic/poetic usage), and an object such as ἔργα (“deeds”) is understood with φράζω; Βακχοῖο is the epic genitive of Bakchos; ἄνακτος “lord” preserves the epic epithet for Apollon.

text.english: Driven on by the goad, I was bringing to light dread afflictions, remedies for mortal men—and thereafter oaths for initiates; first of all the implacable Anankē of ancient Chaos.
text.greek: κέντρῳ ἐλαυνόμενος, φρικώδεα κῆλ' ἐπίφαυσκον θνητοῖς ἀνθρώποισιν ἄκη· μετὰ δ' ὅρκια μύσταις· ἀρχαίου μὲν πρῶτα χάους ἀμέγαρτον ἀνάγκην

line_details.english: Driven on by the goad, I was bringing to light dread afflictions,
line_details.greek: κέντρῳ ἐλαυνόμενος, φρικώδεα κῆλ' ἐπίφαυσκον
line_details.note: κέντρῳ ἐλαυνόμενος is a vivid metaphor of compulsion/inspiration. ἐπίφαυσκον (imperfect with -σκ-) = “kept revealing/was bringing to light.” φρικώδεα κῆλ’: κῆλα can literally be “arrows,” but here likely “afflictions/ills,” pairing with ἄκη (“remedies”). Some take κῆλα as “spells,” but the medical antithesis favors “ills.”

line_details.english: remedies for mortal men—and thereafter oaths for initiates;
line_details.greek: θνητοῖς ἀνθρώποισιν ἄκη· μετὰ δ' ὅρκια μύσταις·
line_details.note: ἄκη is the poetic plural of ἄκος (“remedy”). ὅρκια μύσταις refers to the vows/bindings of initiates in Orphic rites, indicating Orpheus’ role as mystagogue.

line_details.english: first of all the implacable Anankē of ancient Chaos.
line_details.greek: ἀρχαίου μὲν πρῶτα χάους ἀμέγαρτον ἀνάγκην
line_details.note: ἀμέγαρτον is rare and debated; here rendered “implacable/inexorable.” The phrase presents personified Anankē associated with primordial Chaos (ἀρχαίου χάους). Some have proposed nuances like “unsociable” or “unwedded,” but “implacable” suits Anankē’s force.

text.english: and Kronos, who engendered beneath boundless birth‑pangs Aither and the two‑formed, far‑seen, glorious Eros, renowned father of ever‑born Nyx; whom indeed they call Phanes, The later‑born mortals call him Phanes; for he first shone forth; and the child of Brimo of exceeding might, and the baleful deeds of the Earth‑born, who from Heaven dripped the woeful blood.
text.greek: καὶ Κρόνον ὃς ἐλόχευσεν ἀπειρεσίοισιν ὑφ' ὁλκοῖς Αἰθέρα καὶ διφυῆ περιωπέα κυδρὸν Ἔρωτα Νυκτὸς ἀειγνήτης πατέρα κλυτόν· ὃν ῥα Φάνητα ὁπλότεροι καλέουσι βροτοί· πρῶτος γὰρ ἐφάνθη· Βριμοῦς τ' εὐδυνάτοιο γονὰς, ἠδ' ἔργ' ἀΐδηλα Γηγενέων, οἳ λυγρὸν ἀπ' οὐρανοῦ ἐστάξαντο

line_details.english: and Kronos, who engendered beneath boundless birth‑pangs
line_details.greek: καὶ Κρόνον ὃς ἐλόχευσεν ἀπειρεσίοισιν ὑφ' ὁλκοῖς
line_details.note: Κρόνον in Orphic cosmogony is best understood as Chronos (Time), not the Titan Cronus. ἐλόχευσεν (“engendered/bring to birth”) suits cosmogonic begetting. The phrase ἀπειρεσίοισιν ὑφ’ ὁλκοῖς is difficult; many emend ὁλκοῖς to ὠδῖσι(ν) (“birth‑pangs”), which the translation reflects.

line_details.english: Aither and the two‑formed, far‑seen, glorious Eros,
line_details.greek: Αἰθέρα καὶ διφυῆ περιωπέα κυδρὸν Ἔρωτα
line_details.note: διφυῆ (“two‑formed”) is an Orphic epithet of Eros/Phanes, indicating androgyny; περιωπέα can mean “far‑seen” (conspicuous from afar) or “all‑seeing,” both fitting the luminous, manifest nature of Phanes.

line_details.english: renowned father of ever‑born Nyx; whom indeed they call Phanes,
line_details.greek: Νυκτὸς ἀειγνήτης πατέρα κλυτόν· ὃν ῥα Φάνητα
line_details.note: ἀειγνήτης is problematic in case and form; it is often taken as an epithet of Nyx meaning “ever‑born/everlasting,” and some editors emend to ἀειγενής. ὃν ῥα Φάνητα is elliptic for “whom indeed they call Phanes,” a common epic idiom. The line reflects the Orphic notion that Eros/Phanes is father of Nyx.

line_details.english: The later‑born mortals call him Phanes; for he first shone forth;
line_details.greek: ὁπλότεροι καλέουσι βροτοί· πρῶτος γὰρ ἐφάνθη·
line_details.note: “Hoplóteroi” = “later(-born)” or “younger.” The referent (supplied from context) is Protogonos/Phanes; πρῶτος γὰρ ἐφάνθη (“for he appeared/shone forth first”) etymologically explains the name Phanes. I supply “Phanes” in translation though the name is implicit in this line.

line_details.english: and the child of Brimo of exceeding might, and the baleful deeds
line_details.greek: Βριμοῦς τ' εὐδυνάτοιο γονὰς, ἠδ' ἔργ' ἀΐδηλα
line_details.note: Brimo is an epithet (often of Persephone, sometimes Hekate); “the child of Brimo” in Orphic myth is Zagreus-Dionysos. γονάς (plural) functions as “offspring/child”; εὐδυνάτοιο = “of mighty power.”

line_details.english: of the Earth‑born, who from Heaven dripped the woeful blood.
line_details.greek: Γηγενέων, οἳ λυγρὸν ἀπ' οὐρανοῦ ἐστάξαντο
line_details.note: Γηγενέων (“Earth‑born”) refers to the Giants. ἐστάξαντο is used intransitively/middle, with ellipsis of the noun “blood”; λυγρόν qualifies the omitted αἷμα. The line compresses the myth of Ouranos’ blood dripping from Heaven, from which the Earth‑born arose.

text.english: the seed of generation, whence aforetime the race sprang forth of mortals, who ever abide throughout the boundless earth; and the service of Zeus, and the worship of the Mountain-roaming One.
text.greek: σπέρμα γονῆς, τὸ πρόσθεν ὅθεν γένος ἐξεγένοντο θνητῶν, οἳ κατὰ γαῖαν ἀπείριτον αἰὲν ἔασι· θητείαν τε Ζηνὸς, ὀρεσσιδρόμου τε λατρείαν

line_details.english: the seed of generation, whence aforetime the race sprang forth
line_details.greek: σπέρμα γονῆς, τὸ πρόσθεν ὅθεν γένος ἐξεγένοντο
line_details.note: σπέρμα γονῆς = “seed of begetting/procreation.” The plural verb ἐξεγένοντο with γένος (sg.) is awkward; many editors emend to γένε᾽ (pl.), “races,” to match the verb: “whence aforetime the races of mortals sprang forth.”

line_details.english: of mortals, who ever abide throughout the boundless earth;
line_details.greek: θνητῶν, οἳ κατὰ γαῖαν ἀπείριτον αἰὲν ἔασι·
line_details.note: Error: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'translations'

line_details.english: and the service of Zeus, and the worship of the Mountain-roaming One.
line_details.greek: θητείαν τε Ζηνὸς, ὀρεσσιδρόμου τε λατρείαν
line_details.note: θητεία and λατρεία are both cultic ‘service,’ here rendered as “service” and “worship” for nuance. ὀρεσσιδρόμου (“mountain‑roaming,” fem. gen. sg.) is a substantive epithet; the referent is debated (often taken as the Mother of the Gods, Rhea/Cybele, though Artemis is also possible).

text.english: as in the Kybelian mountains he contrived the Mother’s maiden, Persephone, in regard to her father, the resistless Kronion; and the far‑famed wounding by Heracles at the fair‑fruited [garden].
text.greek: μητρὸς ἅτ' ἐν Κυβέλοις ὄρεσιν μητίσατο κούρην Φερσεφόνην περὶ πατρὸς ἀμαιμακέτου Κρονίωνος· εὐμήλου θ' Ἡρακλῆος περίφημον ἄμυξιν·

line_details.english: as in the Kybelian mountains he contrived the Mother’s maiden,
line_details.greek: μητρὸς ἅτ' ἐν Κυβέλοις ὄρεσιν μητίσατο κούρην
line_details.note: Κυβέλοις ὄρεσιν = the mountains sacred to Kybele (the Phrygian/Rhean “Mother”); μητρὸς … κούρην = “the Mother’s maiden (daughter)”; μητίσατο (“contrived/devised”) has an understood subject from the prior context. The ‘Mother’ here is likely Demeter, syncretized with Kybele.

line_details.english: Persephone, in regard to her father, the resistless Kronion;
line_details.greek: Φερσεφόνην περὶ πατρὸς ἀμαιμακέτου Κρονίωνος·
line_details.note: Κρονίων (“Kronion”) is Zeus; ἀμαιμακέτος means “irresistible, unyielding.” The phrase περὶ πατρὸς indicates “with respect to (her) father,” reflecting the Orphic genealogy in which Zeus is Persephone’s father.

line_details.english: and the far‑famed wounding by Heracles at the fair‑fruited [garden].
line_details.greek: εὐμήλου θ' Ἡρακλῆος περίφημον ἄμυξιν·
line_details.note: εὐμήλου = “fair‑fruited,” commonly of the Hesperides’ garden (κῆπος understood elliptically); ἄμυξις = “gash, wounding,” here of Heracles’ blow against the guardian serpent (Ladon) when taking the apples.

text.english: and the oaths of the Idaeans, and the boundless might of the Korybantes.
text.greek: ὅρκιά τ' Ἰδαίων, Κορυβάντων τ' ἄπλετον ἰσχύν.

line_details.english: and the oaths of the Idaeans, and the boundless might of the Korybantes.
line_details.greek: ὅρκιά τ' Ἰδαίων, Κορυβάντων τ' ἄπλετον ἰσχύν.
line_details.note: “Idaeans” probably means the Idaean Dactyls/Curetes, attendants of Rhea; ὅρκια can denote solemn, oath-bound rites; “Korybantes” are divine dancers/guardians; ἄπλετον = “boundless, measureless.”

text.english: Demeter’s wandering, and Persephone’s great grief, and how she was Thesmophoros; and the splendid gifts of the Kabeiroi, and the ineffable oracles of Nyx concerning lord Bakchos, and holy Lemnos and sea‑girt Samothrace, and steep Cyprus, and Adonaean Aphrodite, the orgies of Praxidikē, and of warlike Night‑Athena, and the laments of the Egyptians and the sacred pots of Osiris.
text.greek: Δήμητρός τε πλάνην, καὶ Φερσεφόνης μέγα πένθος, θεσμοφόρος θ' ὡς ἦν· ἠδ' ἀγλαὰ δῶρα Καβείρων, χρησμούς τ' ἀρρήτους Νυκτὸς περὶ Βάκχου ἄνακτος, Λῆμνόν τε ζαθέην ἠδ' εἰναλίην Σαμοθράκην, αἰπεινήν τε Κύπρον, καὶ Ἀδωναίην Ἀφροδίτην ὄργια Πραξιδίκης, καὶ ἀρείνης νυκτὸς Ἀθήνης θρήνους τ' Αἰγυπτίων καὶ Ὀσίριδος ἱερὰ χύτλα.

line_details.english: Demeter’s wandering, and Persephone’s great grief,
line_details.greek: Δήμητρός τε πλάνην, καὶ Φερσεφόνης μέγα πένθος,
line_details.note: πλάνην alludes to Demeter’s search for Persephone; the “great grief” evokes Persephone’s abduction.

line_details.english: and how she was Thesmophoros; and the splendid gifts of the Kabeiroi,
line_details.greek: θεσμοφόρος θ' ὡς ἦν· ἠδ' ἀγλαὰ δῶρα Καβείρων,
line_details.note: Thesmophoros is Demeter’s epithet and the name of her festival; the Kabeiroi are Samothracian mystery deities.

line_details.english: and the ineffable oracles of Nyx concerning lord Bakchos,
line_details.greek: χρησμούς τ' ἀρρήτους Νυκτὸς περὶ Βάκχου ἄνακτος,
line_details.note: ἀρρήτους = “unspeakable,” i.e., esoteric; Nyx (Night) is linked with Bacchic mysteries; Bakchos = Dionysos.

line_details.english: and holy Lemnos and sea‑girt Samothrace,
line_details.greek: Λῆμνόν τε ζαθέην ἠδ' εἰναλίην Σαμοθράκην,
line_details.note: ζαθέην = “very holy”; εἰναλίην = “sea‑girt”; both islands were famed for mystery cults.

line_details.english: and steep Cyprus, and Adonaean Aphrodite,
line_details.greek: αἰπεινήν τε Κύπρον, καὶ Ἀδωναίην Ἀφροδίτην
line_details.note: Adonaean Aphrodite = Aphrodite in connection with Adonis; αἰπεινή is an epic epithet meaning “steep/lofty.”

line_details.english: the orgies of Praxidikē, and of warlike Night‑Athena,
line_details.greek: ὄργια Πραξιδίκης, καὶ ἀρείνης νυκτὸς Ἀθήνης
line_details.note: ὄργια = sacred rites; Praxidikē is a chthonic justice/avenger figure (or one of the Praxidikai). The phrase ἀρείνης νυκτὸς Ἀθήνης is textually uncertain; “Night‑Athena” is an obscure cult‑title, and ἀρείνης is often taken as “warlike.”

line_details.english: and the laments of the Egyptians and the sacred pots of Osiris.
line_details.greek: θρήνους τ' Αἰγυπτίων καὶ Ὀσίριδος ἱερὰ χύτλα.
line_details.note: θρῆνοι = ritual laments; ἱερὰ χύτλα (rare plural of χύτρα) are sacred earthen pots used in Osirian rites.

text.english: And of divination you learned the much-tried pathways, of wild beasts and of birds, and that which is the disposition of the entrails; and whatever they foretell on the dream-ways, the souls of mortal men, their heart smitten by sleep; the unravellings of signs and portents, and the courses of the stars; and the pure-working purification, a great boon to those upon the earth; and propitiations of the gods, and the gifts poured over the dead.
text.greek: Ἀμφὶ δὲ μαντείης ἐδάης πολυπείρονας οἴμους θηρῶν οἰωνῶν τε καὶ ἣ σπλάγχνων θέσις ἐστίν· ἠδ' ὅσα θεσπίζουσιν ὀνειροπόλοισιν ἀταρποῖς ψυχαὶ ἐφημερίων, ὕπνῳ βεβολημέναι ἦτορ· σημείων τεράτων τε λύσεις, ἄστρων τε πορείας· ἁγνοπόλον τε καθαρμὸν ἐπιχθονίοις μέγ' ὄνειαρ· ἱλασμούς τε θεῶν, φθιμένων τ' ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα.

line_details.english: And of divination you learned the much-tried pathways,
line_details.greek: Ἀμφὶ δὲ μαντείης ἐδάης πολυπείρονας οἴμους

line_details.english: of wild beasts and of birds, and that which is the disposition of the entrails;
line_details.greek: θηρῶν οἰωνῶν τε καὶ ἣ σπλάγχνων θέσις ἐστίν·
line_details.note: θήσις σπλάγχνων: the “setting/arrangement of the entrails,” i.e., extispicy; θηρῶν οἰωνῶν distinguishes omens from beasts and from birds.

line_details.english: and whatever they foretell on the dream-ways,
line_details.greek: ἠδ' ὅσα θεσπίζουσιν ὀνειροπόλοισιν ἀταρποῖς
line_details.note: ὀνειροπόλοισιν ἀταρποῖς: literally “on dream-plying paths,” an instrumental dative for the channel/medium of revelation (“on the dream-ways”).

line_details.english: the souls of mortal men, their heart smitten by sleep;
line_details.greek: ψυχαὶ ἐφημερίων, ὕπνῳ βεβολημέναι ἦτορ·
line_details.note: ἐφήμεροι (“men of a day”) = mortals; ὕπνῳ βεβολημέναι ἦτορ “their heart struck by sleep” is an epic idiom for trance-like receptivity in dreams.

line_details.english: the unravellings of signs and portents, and the courses of the stars;
line_details.greek: σημείων τεράτων τε λύσεις, ἄστρων τε πορείας·
line_details.note: λύσεις (“untyings”) = interpretations/explanations; τέρατα = prodigies/portents.

line_details.english: and the pure-working purification, a great boon to those upon the earth;
line_details.greek: ἁγνοπόλον τε καθαρμὸν ἐπιχθονίοις μέγ' ὄνειαρ·
line_details.note: ἁγνοπόλος (rare) = “pure-working” as epithet of καθαρμός (purificatory rite); ἐπιχθόνιοι “earth-dwellers” = the living.

line_details.english: and propitiations of the gods, and the gifts poured over the dead.
line_details.greek: ἱλασμούς τε θεῶν, φθιμένων τ' ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα.
line_details.note: ἱλασμοί = propitiatory rites; ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα “gifts poured over,” i.e., libations/offerings for the dead (funerary choai).

text.english: Moreover, I have recounted to you the things I saw and understood, when I went to Taenarum, the shadowy path within Aïdos, trusting in my own kithara, for love of my wife; and how much of the Egyptians’ sacred lore I ferreted out, having crossed to glorious Memphis and the holy cities of Apis, which the loud‑rushing Neilos has wreathed about; all these things you have learned most exactly from my breast.
text.greek: Ἄλλα δέ σοι κατέλεξ' ἅπερ εἴσιδον ἠδ' ἐνόησα, Ταίναρον ἡνίκ' ἔβην σκοτίην ὁδὸν, Ἄϊδος εἴσω, ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ δι' ἔρωτ' ἀλόχοιο· ἠδ' ὅσον Αἰγυπτίων ἰερὸν λόγον ἐξελόχευσα, Μέμφιν ἐς ἠγαθέην περάσας, ἱεράς τε πόληας Ἄπιδος ἃς πέρι Νεῖλος ἀγάρροος ἐστεφάνωται· πάντα μάλ' ἀτρεκέως ἀπ' ἐμῶν στέρνων δεδάηκας.

line_details.english: Moreover, I have recounted to you the things I saw and understood,
line_details.greek: Ἄλλα δέ σοι κατέλεξ' ἅπερ εἴσιδον ἠδ' ἐνόησα,

line_details.english: when I went to Taenarum, the shadowy path within Aïdos,
line_details.greek: Ταίναρον ἡνίκ' ἔβην σκοτίην ὁδὸν, Ἄϊδος εἴσω,
line_details.note: Taenarum (Cape Tainaron) was famed as an entrance to the Underworld; Aïdos (genitive) here denotes the realm of Hades. “Shadowy path” renders the conventional epic σκοτίη ὁδός.

line_details.english: trusting in my own kithara, for love of my wife;
line_details.greek: ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ δι' ἔρωτ' ἀλόχοιο·
line_details.note: πίσυνος with the dative means “trusting in.” “For love of my wife” alludes to Orpheus’ descent for Eurydice.

line_details.english: and how much of the Egyptians’ sacred lore I ferreted out,
line_details.greek: ἠδ' ὅσον Αἰγυπτίων ἰερὸν λόγον ἐξελόχευσα,
line_details.note: ἐξελόχευσα is a rare verb meaning “to spy out, ferret out, eavesdrop,” fitting the notion of esoteric Egyptian lore.

line_details.english: having crossed to glorious Memphis and the holy cities
line_details.greek: Μέμφιν ἐς ἠγαθέην περάσας, ἱεράς τε πόληας
line_details.note: ἠγαθέην is an epic epithet; “glorious”/“august” suits Memphis’ sacral prestige. πέρασας is aorist participle, “having crossed/after crossing.”

line_details.english: of Apis, which the loud‑rushing Neilos has wreathed about;
line_details.greek: Ἄπιδος ἃς πέρι Νεῖλος ἀγάρροος ἐστεφάνωται·
line_details.note: Ἄπις is the Egyptian bull‑god; “cities of Apis” points to cult‑centers around Memphis. ἀγάρροος = “loud‑rushing”; ἐστεφάνωται (“is wreathed”) metaphorically of Neilos encircling them.

line_details.english: all these things you have learned most exactly from my breast.
line_details.greek: πάντα μάλ' ἀτρεκέως ἀπ' ἐμῶν στέρνων δεδάηκας.
line_details.note: “From my breast” is a formula for “from my inmost understanding,” underscoring the accuracy of the report (μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως).

text.english: Now, since the baneful gadfly, air-roving, has flown off, leaving our body behind and betaking itself to the broad heaven, you shall learn from our voice all that before I kept concealed.
text.greek: - Νῦν δ' ἐπεὶ ἀερόφοιτος ἀπέπτατο δήϊος οἶστρος, ἡμέτερον δέμας ἐκπρολιπὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν, πεύσῃ ἀφ' ἡμετέρης ἐνοπῆς ὅσσα πρὶν ἔκευθον.

line_details.english: Now, since the baneful gadfly, air-roving, has flown off,
line_details.greek: - Νῦν δ' ἐπεὶ ἀερόφοιτος ἀπέπτατο δήϊος οἶστρος,
line_details.note: “δήϊος οἶστρος” is literally the “destructive/baleful gadfly”; οἶστρος can denote both the literal insect (cf. Io) and a god-sent frenzy or goad. “ἀερόφοιτος” (“air-roving”) underscores its wandering, inspired character.

line_details.english: leaving our body behind and betaking itself to the broad heaven,
line_details.greek: ἡμέτερον δέμας ἐκπρολιπὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν,
line_details.note: “ἡμέτερον δέμας” (“our body/frame”) uses the poetic first-person plural for a single speaker. “ἐκπρολιπών” intensifies “leaving utterly.” The phrase indicates the frenzy has departed the poet and gone heavenward.

line_details.english: you shall learn from our voice all that before I kept concealed.
line_details.greek: πεύσῃ ἀφ' ἡμετέρης ἐνοπῆς ὅσσα πρὶν ἔκευθον.
line_details.note: “ἐνοπή” means “sound, voice” (often of battle or song); here “voice/utterance.” “ὅσσα” = “all that.” “ἔκευθον” is epic imperfect 1sg of κεύθω, “I kept concealed,” fitting Orphic motifs of prior silence/secrecy.

text.english: Thus once he traversed Pieria and the towering peaks of Libethra, (foremost among heroes and demigods, he crossed over), beseeching me to become an ally of his homecoming, with a sea‑faring ship toward the inhospitable tribes of men, to a wealthy and reckless nation, wherein ruled Aeëtes, son of Helios, light‑bringer to mortals.
text.greek: Ὥς ποτε Πιερίην Λειβήθρων τ' ἄκρα κάρηνα (ἡρώωντε καὶ ἡμιθέων πρόμος ἐξεπέρησε) λισσόμενός μ' ἐπίκουρον ἑοῦ νόστοιο γενέσθαι ποντοπόρῳ σὺν νηῒ πρὸς ἄξενα φῦλ' ἀνθρώπων, ἔθνος ἐς ἀφνειὸν καὶ ἀτάσθαλον ᾧ ἐνὶ κραῖνεν Αἰήτης υἱὸς φαεσιμβρότου ἠελίοιο.

line_details.english: Thus once he traversed Pieria and the towering peaks of Libethra,
line_details.greek: Ὥς ποτε Πιερίην Λειβήθρων τ' ἄκρα κάρηνα
line_details.note: Pieria and Libethra are Thracian/Macedonian haunts of the Muses; ἄκρα κάρηνα = “lofty peaks.”

line_details.english: (foremost among heroes and demigods, he crossed over),
line_details.greek: (ἡρώωντε καὶ ἡμιθέων πρόμος ἐξεπέρησε)
line_details.note: πρόμος = “foremost, champion, leader.” The verb ἐξεπέρασε supplies the motion for line 50; the referent is Jason as leader of the Argonauts.

line_details.english: beseeching me to become an ally of his homecoming,
line_details.greek: λισσόμενός μ' ἐπίκουρον ἑοῦ νόστοιο γενέσθαι
line_details.note: νόστος is the technical epic term for “homecoming.” ἐπίκουρος = “ally/helper.”

line_details.english: with a sea‑faring ship toward the inhospitable tribes of men,
line_details.greek: ποντοπόρῳ σὺν νηῒ πρὸς ἄξενα φῦλ' ἀνθρώπων,
line_details.note: ἄξενα (“inhospitable”) alludes to the Pontos Axeinos (later Euxinos), i.e., the Black Sea region.

line_details.english: to a wealthy and reckless nation, wherein ruled
line_details.greek: ἔθνος ἐς ἀφνειὸν καὶ ἀτάσθαλον ᾧ ἐνὶ κραῖνεν
line_details.note: ἀφνειός = “wealthy, rich”; ἀτάσθαλος = “reckless, overweening.” κραίνειν in epic can mean “to rule, hold sway.”

line_details.english: Aeëtes, son of Helios, light‑bringer to mortals.
line_details.greek: Αἰήτης υἱὸς φαεσιμβρότου ἠελίοιο.
line_details.note: φαεσιμβρότου = “light‑bringing to mortals,” an epithet of Helios; Aeëtes is the Colchian king, son of Helios.

text.english: For Pelias quailed before the oracular decrees, lest hereafter the Aisonid by his hand should cast down his kingly rule.
text.greek: - Θέσφατα γὰρ Πελίας δειδίσσετο μή οἱ ὄπισθεν χειρὸς ὕπ' Αἰσονίδα καθέλῃ βασιλήϊον ἀρχήν.

line_details.english: For Pelias quailed before the oracular decrees, lest hereafter
line_details.greek: - Θέσφατα γὰρ Πελίας δειδίσσετο μή οἱ ὄπισθεν
line_details.note: - θέσφατα: “oracular decrees.” δειδίσσετο: iterative/imperfective ‘was in dread.’ ὄπισθεν here is adverbial = ‘in future, hereafter,’ not strictly spatial ‘from behind.’

line_details.english: the Aisonid by his hand should cast down his kingly rule.
line_details.greek: χειρὸς ὕπ' Αἰσονίδα καθέλῃ βασιλήϊον ἀρχήν.
line_details.note: - Αἰσονίδα = “the Aisonid,” i.e., Jason. The phrase χειρὸς ὑπ’ Αἰσονίδα is taken as ‘by the hand of the Aisonid’; the construction is slightly compressed (some would expect a genitive with ὑπό). βασίληϊον is the epic adjective ‘royal’; καθέλῃ ‘cast down, depose’ suits ἀρχή ‘rule, sovereignty.’

text.english: And within his heart she was plying the track of guile; for she was enjoining him to bring from the Kolchians the Golden Fleece to horse-rich Thessaly. And when he heard an out-of-measure voice, stretching forth his hands he called upon Lady Hērē; for among the Blessed he was wont to glorify her beyond the rest.
text.greek: Καί οἱ ὑπὸ πραπίδεσσι δόλου τρίβον ἠπερόπευε· τάσσε γὰρ ἐκ Κόλχων χρύσειον κῶας ἐνεῖκαι Θεσσαλίην εὔπωλον. Ὁ δ' ὡς κλύεν ἔκνομον αὐδήν χεῖρας ἐπαντείνας ἐπεκέκλετο πότνιαν Ἥρην· τήνδε γὰρ ἐκ μακάρων περιώσια κυδαίνεσκεν.

line_details.english: And within his heart she was plying the track of guile;
line_details.greek: Καί οἱ ὑπὸ πραπίδεσσι δόλου τρίβον ἠπερόπευε·
line_details.note: prapídes (“midriff, heart”) is epic for the seat of thought; dólou tríbon (“track/path of guile”) is a cognate-accusative phrase with ἠπερόπευε “was practising deception/beguilement,” here of the goddess instilling crafty counsel.

line_details.english: for she was enjoining him to bring from the Kolchians the Golden Fleece
line_details.greek: τάσσε γὰρ ἐκ Κόλχων χρύσειον κῶας ἐνεῖκαι
line_details.note: tásse (“array, set in order”) commonly = “enjoin, order” in epic; eneîkai is the aorist infinitive of enenkein “to bring/carry off.”

line_details.english: to horse-rich Thessaly. And when he heard an out-of-measure voice,
line_details.greek: Θεσσαλίην εὔπωλον. Ὁ δ' ὡς κλύεν ἔκνομον αὐδήν
line_details.note: éknomon (“out of rule/mode,” esp. of music) conveys a strange, unearthly quality to the voice—i.e., a divine manifestation.

line_details.english: stretching forth his hands he called upon Lady Hērē;
line_details.greek: χεῖρας ἐπαντείνας ἐπεκέκλετο πότνιαν Ἥρην·
line_details.note: pótniā “Lady” is a reverential epithet regularly used of goddesses; Hērē is transliterated.

line_details.english: for among the Blessed he was wont to glorify her beyond the rest.
line_details.greek: τήνδε γὰρ ἐκ μακάρων περιώσια κυδαίνεσκεν.
line_details.note: makárōn (“the Blessed”) = the gods; periósia “beyond the rest, especially”; the -sk- of kudaínasken marks customary/repeated action (“used to honor”).

text.english: But she attended upon the vows, being indeed full of care; for above all mortals she admired and was wont to love the dread-in-might hero, the far-famed son of Aison, and, having called him, Tritogeneia gave her command.
text.greek: Ἡ δὲ παρ' εὐχωλῇσιν ἐφέσπετο κηδομένη περ· ἔξοχα γὰρ μερόπων ἠγάζετο καὶ φιλέεσκεν δεινοβίην ἥρωα, περικλυτὸν Αἴσονος υἷα, καί ῥα καλεσσαμένη ἐπετέλλετο Τριτογενείη.

line_details.english: But she attended upon the vows, being indeed full of care;
line_details.greek: Ἡ δὲ παρ' εὐχωλῇσιν ἐφέσπετο κηδομένη περ·
line_details.note: παρ’ εὐχωλῇσιν = “amid/along with (their) prayers/vows.” ἐφέσπετο here means “attended (to), was at hand for.” The pronoun “she” is Athena, anticipated and then named in line 66.

line_details.english: for above all mortals she admired and was wont to love
line_details.greek: ἔξοχα γὰρ μερόπων ἠγάζετο καὶ φιλέεσκεν
line_details.note: μερόπων = “mortals (men),” the Homeric term for articulate-speaking humans. ἠγάζετο conveys “admired/held in awe”; φιλέεσκεν (iterative) = “used to love/was wont to love.”

line_details.english: the dread-in-might hero, the far-famed son of Aison,
line_details.greek: δεινοβίην ἥρωα, περικλυτὸν Αἴσονος υἷα,
line_details.note: δεινοβίην (epic compound) ≈ “terrible/formidable in might,” modifying ἥρωα. περικλυτός = “far-famed.” Αἴσονος υἷα identifies Jason by his patronymic.

line_details.english: and, having called him, Tritogeneia gave her command.
line_details.greek: καί ῥα καλεσσαμένη ἐπετέλλετο Τριτογενείη.
line_details.note: Τριτογενείη is Athena’s epithet. καλεσσαμένη (“having called/summoned”) has an implicit object, naturally understood as the hero just mentioned; ἐπετέλλετο (middle) = “gave her command/charge.”

text.english: And for him she first fashioned an oak‑built ship, which also, beneath fir‑wood oars, the briny depths was first to traverse, and made a track upon the sea.
text.greek: Καί οἱ φηγινέην πρῶτον τεκτήνατο νῆα, ἣ καὶ ὑπ' εἰλατίνοις ἐρετμοῖς ἁλιμυρέα βένθη πρώτην ἐξεπέρησε, τρίβον δ' ἤνυσσε θαλάσσης.

line_details.english: And for him she first fashioned an oak‑built ship,
line_details.greek: Καί οἱ φηγινέην πρῶτον τεκτήνατο νῆα,
line_details.note: φηγινέην from φηγός: in epic commonly ‘oak’ (not ‘beech’); τεκτήνατο (middle) with the dative οἱ = ‘she fashioned for him’; the subject (implied from context) is Pallas Athena.

line_details.english: which also, beneath fir‑wood oars, the briny depths
line_details.greek: ἣ καὶ ὑπ' εἰλατίνοις ἐρετμοῖς ἁλιμυρέα βένθη
line_details.note: εἰλατίνιος = ‘of fir’; hence ‘fir‑wood oars’. The phrase ὑπ’ … ἐρετμοῖς ‘under … oars’ is a standard epic way to mark propulsion by rowing; ἁλιμυρέα βένθη = ‘briny depths’ is formulaic.

line_details.english: was first to traverse, and made a track upon the sea.
line_details.greek: πρώτην ἐξεπέρησε, τρίβον δ' ἤνυσσε θαλάσσης.
line_details.note: πρῶτην ἐξεπέρασε = ‘was first to cross/traverse’; τρῖβον ἤνυσσε ‘made/achieved a track (path)’, i.e., opened a sea‑lane, stressing the ship’s pioneering voyage.

text.english: But when indeed he had gathered the illustrious kings together, to horse-rich Thrace hastened godlike Iason, and he came upon me as I was preparing the cunning-wrought kithara, so that, singing, I might pour forth for you a honey-voiced song, and enchant wild beasts, and creeping things, and winged creatures.
text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ συνάγειρεν ἀγακλειτοὺς βασιλῆας, Θρῄκην εἰς εὔπωλον ἐπείγετο δῖος Ἰήσων, καί μ' ἔκιχεν κιθάρην πολυδαίδαλον ἐντύνοντα, ὄφρα κέ σοι μέλπων προχέω μελίγηρυν ἀοιδήν, κηλήσω δέ τε θῆρας ἰδ' ἑρπετὰ καὶ πετεηνά.

line_details.english: But when indeed he had gathered the illustrious kings together,
line_details.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ συνάγειρεν ἀγακλειτοὺς βασιλῆας,
line_details.note: συνάγειρεν is epic aorist “gathered together”; ἀγακλειτούς = “very famed, illustrious,” an epic epithet.

line_details.english: to horse-rich Thrace hastened godlike Iason,
line_details.greek: Θρῄκην εἰς εὔπωλον ἐπείγετο δῖος Ἰήσων,
line_details.note: εὔπωλον = “rich in horses”; δῖος = “godlike” (Homeric epithet); ἐπείγετο imperfect middle “was hastening/pressed on.”

line_details.english: and he came upon me as I was preparing the cunning-wrought kithara,
line_details.greek: καί μ' ἔκιχεν κιθάρην πολυδαίδαλον ἐντύνοντα,
line_details.note: μ’ ἔκιχεν = “he came upon me” (aorist of κιχάνω); πολυδαίδαλον = “cunningly wrought, much-wrought”; ἐντύνω of instruments can imply “stringing/tuning.”

line_details.english: so that, singing, I might pour forth for you a honey-voiced song,
line_details.greek: ὄφρα κέ σοι μέλπων προχέω μελίγηρυν ἀοιδήν,
line_details.note: ὄφρα κέ introduces a purpose clause (“so that I might”); προχέω “pour forth” is idiomatic of song; μελίγηρυν = “honey-voiced.”

line_details.english: and enchant wild beasts, and creeping things, and winged creatures.
line_details.greek: κηλήσω δέ τε θῆρας ἰδ' ἑρπετὰ καὶ πετεηνά.
line_details.note: κηλέω = “enchant, bewitch (by song)”; θῆρας = “wild beasts”; ἑρπετά = “creeping things, reptiles”; πετεηνά = “winged creatures,” i.e., birds.

text.english: But when he entered a much‑loved cavern, he lifted up a honey‑sweet voice from his shaggy breast; - "Orpheus, dear son of Kalliope and Oiagros, ruling in Bistonia over the Ciconians rich in flocks, hail, since for the first time I arrive at the Haemonian watercourses, and the Strymonian streams, and toward the sheer glens of Rhodope." And I, among the Minyans, have inherited blood preeminent above all.
text.greek: Ἡνίκα δ' εἰς ἄντρον πολυήρατον εἰσεπέρησε, μείλιχον ἐκ λασίων στέρνων ἀνενείκατο φωνήν· - "Ὀρφεῦ Καλλιόπης τε καὶ Οἰάγρου φίλε κοῦρε, Βιστονίῃ Κικόνεσσι πολυρρήνοισιν ἀνάσσων χαῖρ' ἐπεὶ Αἱμονίους ὀχεὰς πρώτιστον ἱκάνω, Στρυμονίους τε ῥοὰς, Ῥοδόπης τ' αἰπεινὰ πρὸς ἄγκη. Εἰμὶ δ' ἐγὼ Μινύαισι πανέξοχον αἷμα λελογχώς

line_details.english: But when he entered a much‑loved cavern,
line_details.greek: Ἡνίκα δ' εἰς ἄντρον πολυήρατον εἰσεπέρησε,

line_details.english: he lifted up a honey‑sweet voice from his shaggy breast;
line_details.greek: μείλιχον ἐκ λασίων στέρνων ἀνενείκατο φωνήν·
line_details.note: Lasion sternon is a poetic plural (“shaggy breasts”); rendered as singular “breast” in English idiom. Meilichos means “gentle, honey‑sweet.”

line_details.english: - "Orpheus, dear son of Kalliope and Oiagros,
line_details.greek: - "Ὀρφεῦ Καλλιόπης τε καὶ Οἰάγρου φίλε κοῦρε,
line_details.note: Kalliope and Oiagros are Orpheus’ parents; phile koure is “dear son/child.”

line_details.english: ruling in Bistonia over the Ciconians rich in flocks,
line_details.greek: Βιστονίῃ Κικόνεσσι πολυρρήνοισιν ἀνάσσων
line_details.note: Bistonia is a Thracian district; the Kikones (Ciconians) are a Thracian people. Polyrrhēnoisin means “rich in flocks (many‑sheep).”

line_details.english: hail, since for the first time I arrive at the Haemonian watercourses,
line_details.greek: χαῖρ' ἐπεὶ Αἱμονίους ὀχεὰς πρώτιστον ἱκάνω,
line_details.note: Haemonian here refers to Mt. Haemus (Aimos) in Thrace, not Thessaly; ocheai are “channels, watercourses.” Prōtiston = “for the first time.”

line_details.english: and the Strymonian streams, and toward the sheer glens of Rhodope."
line_details.greek: Στρυμονίους τε ῥοὰς, Ῥοδόπης τ' αἰπεινὰ πρὸς ἄγκη.
line_details.note: Strymon is the Thracian river; Rhodope is the neighboring mountain range. Ankē are “glens,” aipeina “steep, sheer.”

line_details.english: And I, among the Minyans, have inherited blood preeminent above all.
line_details.greek: Εἰμὶ δ' ἐγὼ Μινύαισι πανέξοχον αἷμα λελογχώς
line_details.note: Minyans: the Minyan people/Argonauts. “Blood” (haima) = lineage; πανέξοχον “preeminent above all”; λελογχώς is the perfect participle of λαγχάνω, “to obtain by lot, inherit,” conveying inherited nobility.

text.english: A Thessalian, Aisonides; and I declare myself your guest‑friend.
text.greek: Θεσσαλὸς Αἰσονίδης· ξεῖνος δέ τοι εὔχομαι εἶναι.

line_details.english: A Thessalian, Aisonides; and I declare myself your guest‑friend.
line_details.greek: Θεσσαλὸς Αἰσονίδης· ξεῖνος δέ τοι εὔχομαι εἶναι.
line_details.note: Aisonides = “son of Aison” (Jason). εὔχομαι here means “profess/avow,” not “pray”; ξένος denotes a formal guest‑friendship; τοι is the ethical dative “to you.”

text.english: But, friend, receive me with ready heart and hearken to my word with gentle ears, and, as I entreat, give heed, to draw near the inmost recesses of Axenos Pontos and the stout Phasis with the ship Argo, and to point out the maiden paths of the sea, dear to the heroes, who indeed await your chelys-lyre and god-ordained voice, hoping for common succor in their labors upon the sea.
text.greek: Ἀλλὰ, φίλος, πρόφρων μ' ὑποδέχνυσο καὶ κλύε μῦθον μειλιχίαις ἀκοαῖς, καὶ λισσομένῳ ὑπάκουσον Ἀξείνου Πόντοιο μυχοὺς καὶ Φᾶσιν ἐρυμνόν νηῒ σὺν Ἀργῴῃ πελάσαι δεῖξαί τε θαλάσσης παρθενίης ἀτραποὺς, ἐπιήρατον ἡρώεσσιν, οἵ ῥα τεὴν μίμνουσι χέλυν καὶ θέσφατον ὀμφήν ἐλπόμενοι ξυνὸν πελάγει ἐπαρηγόνα μόχθων.

line_details.english: But, friend, receive me with ready heart and hearken to my word
line_details.greek: Ἀλλὰ, φίλος, πρόφρων μ' ὑποδέχνυσο καὶ κλύε μῦθον
line_details.note: ὑποδέχνυσο is likely an epic/morphological variant for ὑποδέξαι/ὑποδέχου “receive”; many editors print a form of ὑποδέχομαι. κλύε μῦθον is a conventional epic formula “listen to my word.”

line_details.english: with gentle ears, and, as I entreat, give heed,
line_details.greek: μειλιχίαις ἀκοαῖς, καὶ λισσομένῳ ὑπάκουσον

line_details.english: to draw near the inmost recesses of Axenos Pontos and the stout Phasis
line_details.greek: Ἀξείνου Πόντοιο μυχοὺς καὶ Φᾶσιν ἐρυμνόν
line_details.note: Axenos Pontos is the “Inhospitable Sea” (older name of the Black Sea). μυχοί = “innermost recesses.” ἐρυμνός (“stout, well-defended”) is applied unusually to Phasis (river/region), conveying strength or fortified character.

line_details.english: with the ship Argo, and to point out the maiden paths of the sea,
line_details.greek: νηῒ σὺν Ἀργῴῃ πελάσαι δεῖξαί τε θαλάσσης
line_details.note: “maiden paths” (παρθενίης ἀτραπούς) = untraveled, virgin sea-ways.

line_details.english: dear to the heroes,
line_details.greek: παρθενίης ἀτραποὺς, ἐπιήρατον ἡρώεσσιν,

line_details.english: who indeed await your chelys-lyre and god-ordained voice,
line_details.greek: οἵ ῥα τεὴν μίμνουσι χέλυν καὶ θέσφατον ὀμφήν
line_details.note: χελύς here denotes the tortoise-shell lyre (chelys-lyre). θέσφατος ὀμφή = “god-ordained/prophetic voice,” of inspired song.

line_details.english: hoping for common succor in their labors upon the sea.
line_details.greek: ἐλπόμενοι ξυνὸν πελάγει ἐπαρηγόνα μόχθων.
line_details.note: ξυνὸν … ἐπαρήγονα = “common aid/helper,” i.e., a shared succor to all the heroes; πελάγει is a dative of sphere (“upon the sea”).

text.english: For indeed they do not purpose to sail toward barbarian peoples apart from you; for even toward the misty gloom into the nethermost recess, by supplication to the very base of the earth, to draw near, alone among men, and to discover a return; for which cause he undertook a shared distress to gratify the Minyae.
text.greek: Οὐ γὰρ δὴ πλῶσαι πρὸς βάρβαρα φῦλα μέδονται νόσφι σέθεν· καὶ γάρ ῥα ποτὶ ζόφον ἠερόεντα νείατον εἰς κευθμῶνα, λιτῆς εἰς πυθμένα γαίης, μοῦνον ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων πελάσαι καὶ νόστον ἀνευρεῖν· ὧν ἕνεκεν ξυνήν τε δύην Μινύαισιν ἀρέσθαι

line_details.english: For indeed they do not purpose to sail toward barbarian peoples
line_details.greek: Οὐ γὰρ δὴ πλῶσαι πρὸς βάρβαρα φῦλα μέδονται
line_details.note: “Barbarian peoples” = non-Greek nations, here likely the Colchians; μέδονται = “intend, have in mind”; πλῶσαι = “to set sail.”

line_details.english: apart from you; for even toward the misty gloom
line_details.greek: νόσφι σέθεν· καὶ γάρ ῥα ποτὶ ζόφον ἠερόεντα
line_details.note: νόσφι σέθεν = “apart from you [singular],” probably addressed to Jason; ζόφον ἠερόεντα is a Homeric formula for “misty gloom” (often of the underworld or far west); the thought is enjambed into the next line.

line_details.english: into the nethermost recess, by supplication to the very base of the earth,
line_details.greek: νείατον εἰς κευθμῶνα, λιτῆς εἰς πυθμένα γαίης,
line_details.note: λιτῆς is best taken as a genitive of means (“by supplication/prayer”); νείατον κευθμῶνα and πυθμένα γαίης evoke the underworld as the earth’s lowest hidden place and very foundation.

line_details.english: to draw near, alone among men, and to discover a return;
line_details.greek: μοῦνον ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων πελάσαι καὶ νόστον ἀνευρεῖν·
line_details.note: νόστος here implies a return from the underworld; μοῦνον ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπων = “alone among mortals,” stressing uniqueness.

line_details.english: for which cause he undertook a shared distress to gratify the Minyae.
line_details.greek: ὧν ἕνεκεν ξυνήν τε δύην Μινύαισιν ἀρέσθαι
line_details.note: ξυνήν τε δύην = “a common/shared woe” (ξυνήν ‘shared’ + δύη ‘woe, distress’). ἀρέσθαι can be understood either as ‘to choose/undertake (for oneself)’ or ‘to please/propitiate’ with the dative; the translation renders a mediating sense (“undertook … to gratify”). Μινύαισιν = the Minyae, i.e., the Argonauts.

text.english: and that renown may be heard among men in generations yet to come.
text.greek: καὶ κλέος ἀνθρώποισιν ἐπ' ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι."

line_details.english: and that renown may be heard among men in generations yet to come.
line_details.greek: καὶ κλέος ἀνθρώποισιν ἐπ' ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι."
line_details.note: κλέος = “renown, fame”; πυθέσθαι (aor. mid.) = “to learn, hear of”; ἐπ’ ἐσσομένοισι (dat. pl.) = “among/for those yet to come,” i.e., future generations.

text.english: Him then I, answering with words, addressed: “Aisonides, why, coaxing me, do you ask me these things?” so that I might come to the Colchians, well-pleasing to the Minyans, sailing in the well-benched ship over the wine-dark sea? for already for me there is enough of toils, enough there has been of hardships, to whose boundless land and cities I came, in Egypt and in Libya, revealing to mortals the divine oracles.
text.greek: Τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον· - "Αἰσονίδη, τί με ταῦτα παραιφάμενος ἐρεείνεις, ὄφρα κεν ἐς Κόλχους Μινύαις ἐπιήρανος ἔλθω, νηῒ σὺν εὐσέλμῳ πλεύσας ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον; ἤδη γάρ μοι ἅλις καμάτων, ἅλις ἔπλετο μόχθων, ὧν ἱκόμην ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἀπείριτον ἠδὲ πόληας Αἰγύπτῳ Λιβύῃ τε βροτοῖς ἀνὰ θέσφατα φαίνων.

line_details.english: Him then I, answering with words, addressed:
line_details.greek: Τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
line_details.note: Epic formula: μύθοισιν … προσέειπον “addressed with words”; ἀμειβόμενος = “in reply.”

line_details.english: “Aisonides, why, coaxing me, do you ask me these things?”
line_details.greek: - "Αἰσονίδη, τί με ταῦτα παραιφάμενος ἐρεείνεις,
line_details.note: Αἰσονίδη (voc.) = “son of Aison,” i.e., Iason/Jason. παραιφάμενος carries the nuance “coaxing, trying to draw me out” (also “beguile” in Homeric usage). ἐρεείνεις is Homeric for “you question/ask closely.”

line_details.english: so that I might come to the Colchians, well-pleasing to the Minyans,
line_details.greek: ὄφρα κεν ἐς Κόλχους Μινύαις ἐπιήρανος ἔλθω,
line_details.note: ὄφρα κεν with subjunctive expresses purpose (“so that I might”). ἐπιήρανος = “well-pleasing/propitious, serviceable.” Μινύαις (“the Minyans”) is a poetic designation for the Argonauts.

line_details.english: sailing in the well-benched ship over the wine-dark sea?
line_details.greek: νηῒ σὺν εὐσέλμῳ πλεύσας ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον;
line_details.note: νηῒ σὺν εὐσέλμῳ = “in/with the well-benched ship” (epic formula for a well-rowed vessel). οἴνοπα πόντον = “wine-dark sea.” The transmitted punctuation makes this a rhetorical question.

line_details.english: for already for me there is enough of toils, enough there has been of hardships,
line_details.greek: ἤδη γάρ μοι ἅλις καμάτων, ἅλις ἔπλετο μόχθων,
line_details.note: ἅλις + genitive = “enough, in plenty.” ἔπλετο functions existentially (“has proved to be/has been”). The pairing καμάτοι/μόχθοι is a traditional hendiadys for “toils/hardships.”

line_details.english: to whose boundless land and cities I came,
line_details.greek: ὧν ἱκόμην ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἀπείριτον ἠδὲ πόληας
line_details.note: ὧν (gen. pl.) picks up an antecedent from the broader context (“those” among whom/whose), yielding “to whose land and cities.” ἀπείριτον = “boundless, limitless”; ἐπὶ + acc. with ἱκόμην expresses motion “to/upon.”

line_details.english: in Egypt and in Libya, revealing to mortals the divine oracles.
line_details.greek: Αἰγύπτῳ Λιβύῃ τε βροτοῖς ἀνὰ θέσφατα φαίνων.
line_details.note: ἀνὰ with θέσφατα is adverbial/intensive (“abroad, all around”), here best rendered simply as “revealing” or “showing forth.” θέσφατα = “divine oracles/utterances.” The datives Αἰγύπτῳ Λιβύῃ function locatively (“in Egypt and Libya”), while βροτοῖς is the indirect object (“to mortals”).

text.english: And she delivered me both from wandering and from the gadfly’s goad, my mother; and then she led me into another house, so that I might attain the term of death amid grievous old age.
text.greek: Καί με ἀλητείης τε καὶ ἐξ οἴστρου ἐσάωσε μήτηρ ἡμετέρη καί ῥ' εἰς δόμον ἤγαγεν ἄλλον ὄφρα τέλος θανάτοιο κίχω μετὰ γήραϊ λυγρῷ.

line_details.english: And she delivered me both from wandering and from the gadfly’s goad,
line_details.greek: Καί με ἀλητείης τε καὶ ἐξ οἴστρου ἐσάωσε
line_details.note: οἶστρος literally “gadfly,” emblematic of maddening goad (cf. Io), hence also “frenzy”; ἐσάωσε is an epic form meaning “saved/delivered.”

line_details.english: my mother; and then she led me into another house,
line_details.greek: μήτηρ ἡμετέρη καί ῥ' εἰς δόμον ἤγαγεν ἄλλον
line_details.note: εἰς δόμον ἄλλον = “into another house/household”; the object “me” is supplied from the previous line; καί ῥ’ conveys “and then.”

line_details.english: so that I might attain the term of death amid grievous old age.
line_details.greek: ὄφρα τέλος θανάτοιο κίχω μετὰ γήραϊ λυγρῷ.
line_details.note: τέλος θανάτοιο (“the end/term of death”) is a formula for life’s end; κίχω = “reach/attain” (epic); μετὰ with dative = “amid/with”; λυγρός = “grievous, baleful.”

text.english: But there is no escaping what indeed lies appointed by fate.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔσθ' ὑπαλύξαι ἃ δὴ πεπρωμένα κεῖται.

line_details.english: But there is no escaping what indeed lies appointed by fate.
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔσθ' ὑπαλύξαι ἃ δὴ πεπρωμένα κεῖται.
line_details.note: ὑπαλύξαι = aorist infinitive ‘to escape’ (Homeric); πεπρωμένα = ‘things fated/appointed’ (perf. part. of the verb underlying πέπρωται); κεῖται adds the sense of being fixed/established; δὴ is an intensifier (‘indeed’).

text.english: I hasten under the promptings of the Moirai; for not dishonored are the Litai, maidens of Zeus Hikesios; I shall now come as one numbered among the younger kings and the demigods.
text.greek: Μοιρῶν ἐννεσίῃσιν ἐπείγομαι· οὐ γὰρ ἄτιμοι ἱκεσίου Ζηνὸς κοῦραι Λιταί· ἵξομαι ἤδη ὁπλοτέροις βασιλεῦσι καὶ ἡμιθέοις ἐνάριθμος."

line_details.english: I hasten under the promptings of the Moirai; for not dishonored
line_details.greek: Μοιρῶν ἐννεσίῃσιν ἐπείγομαι· οὐ γὰρ ἄτιμοι
line_details.note: ἐννεσίῃσιν = “promptings/instigations”; Moirai = the Fates. The litotes “not dishonored” preserves the elevated tone.

line_details.english: are the Litai, maidens of Zeus Hikesios; I shall now come
line_details.greek: ἱκεσίου Ζηνὸς κοῦραι Λιταί· ἵξομαι ἤδη
line_details.note: Litai (“Prayers”), personified daughters of Zeus; “Zeus Hikesios” = Zeus of Suppliants. The phrasing recalls Il. 9.502–12.

line_details.english: as one numbered among the younger kings and the demigods.
line_details.greek: ὁπλοτέροις βασιλεῦσι καὶ ἡμιθέοις ἐνάριθμος."
line_details.note: ὁπλοτέροις = “younger,” i.e., of a later generation; ἐνάριθμος = “counted among, reckoned with.” The younger “kings and demigods” are the Argonautic cohort.

text.english: And then indeed I left the lovely cave and crossed beyond, with my very phorminx, and I came to the Minyae with nimble feet, over the Pagasaean strands.
text.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ λίπον ἄντρον ἐπήρατον ἠδ' ἐπέρησα αὐτῇ σὺν φόρμιγγι καὶ εἰς Μινύας ἀφίκανον λαιψηροῖσι πόδεσσιν, ὑπὲρ Παγασηΐδας ἀκτάς.

line_details.english: And then indeed I left the lovely cave and crossed beyond,
line_details.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ λίπον ἄντρον ἐπήρατον ἠδ' ἐπέρησα
line_details.note: τότε δὴ marks a narrative transition; ἄντρον ἐπήρατον = a conventional epic epithet “lovely cave.”

line_details.english: with my very phorminx, and I came to the Minyae
line_details.greek: αὐτῇ σὺν φόρμιγγι καὶ εἰς Μινύας ἀφίκανον
line_details.note: φόρμιγξ (phorminx) is the epic lyre; αὐτῇ emphasizes “the very” instrument. ἀφίκανον is an epic 1st-sing. aorist (“I came”).

line_details.english: with nimble feet, over the Pagasaean strands.
line_details.greek: λαιψηροῖσι πόδεσσιν, ὑπὲρ Παγασηΐδας ἀκτάς.
line_details.note: ὑπέρ with the accusative here = “over/along.” “Pagasaean” refers to Pagasae, the harbor of Iolkos, point of Argonautic departure.

text.english: There then the band of the best of the Minyans assembled, upon the narrow sands with a roar, and at the surf of Anauros.
text.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἀριστήων Μινυῶν λόχος ἠγερέθοντο στεῖνον δὴ ψαμάθους ὁμάδῳ, ῥηγμῖνα τ' Ἀναύρου.

line_details.english: There then the band of the best of the Minyans assembled,
line_details.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἀριστήων Μινυῶν λόχος ἠγερέθοντο
line_details.note: λόχος “band, company”; ἀριστήων is a partitive genitive “of the best.” The plural verb ἠγερέθοντο with the collective singular λόχος is an epic synesis (“the company assembled”).

line_details.english: upon the narrow sands with a roar, and at the surf of Anauros.
line_details.greek: στεῖνον δὴ ψαμάθους ὁμάδῳ, ῥηγμῖνα τ' Ἀναύρου.
line_details.note: στεῖνον is a substantivized adjective “narrow (strip),” here best taken with the following accusatives as an accusative of place attained with ἠγερέθοντο (“they assembled to the narrow sands … and to the surf”). ὁμάδῳ is instrumental dative “with a din/roar.” ῥηγμῖνα (acc. sg.) is “surf, breaker”; Ἀναύρου is the Thessalian river Anauros near Iolkos.

text.english: But when indeed they perceived me making my way by a trackless path, they rose gladly, and the heart in each rejoiced; but I spoke, questioning the noblest men.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δή μ' ἐνόησαν ἀταρπιτὸν ἐξανύοντα, ἀσπασίως ἤγερθεν· ἐγήθεε δ' ἦτορ ἑκάστῳ· αὐτὰρ ἐμυθεόμην, ἐρεείνων ἄνδρας ἀρίστους.

line_details.english: But when indeed they perceived me making my way by a trackless path,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δή μ' ἐνόησαν ἀταρπιτὸν ἐξανύοντα,
line_details.note: ἀταρπιτὸν (“trackless”) is used substantively/adverbially; ἐξανύω here = “to make good, win through (a route).” Hence “making my way by a trackless path.”

line_details.english: they rose gladly, and the heart in each rejoiced;
line_details.greek: ἀσπασίως ἤγερθεν· ἐγήθεε δ' ἦτορ ἑκάστῳ·
line_details.note: ἀσπασίως = “gladly, with welcome”; ἤγερθεν is intransitive aorist passive “rose up.”

line_details.english: but I spoke, questioning the noblest men.
line_details.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐμυθεόμην, ἐρεείνων ἄνδρας ἀρίστους.
line_details.note: ἐμυθεόμην is the formal epic “I spoke/uttered words”; ἐρεείνων = “inquiring closely, questioning.” ἄνδρας ἀρίστους can mean “the chiefs/leading men.”

text.english: First I beheld the might of divine Herakles, whom Alkmene bore to Zeus Kronion, having mingled with him, when Helios was leaving the threefold blaze of Seirios, and long darkness was creeping on from every side; and Tiphys Agniades, steersman of the long ship; who then was upon the Thespian waters of Telmissos, traversing the shore-hugging current among the Siphaean folk; who, amid choppy seas and gleaming squalls, knew to set the ship straight by resourceful craft; and I beheld horse‑taming Kastor and Polydeukes, and Mopsos from Titarēssos, whom, once wedded to Ampyx, Arēgonis bore beneath a Chaonian oak; and Peleus the Aiakid, glorious son of Aigina, who ruled the Dolopes in much‑nourishing Phthia.
text.greek: - Πρῶτα δὲ εἶδα βίην Ἡρακλῆος θείοιο ὃν τέκεν Ἀλκμήνη Ζηνὶ Κρονίωνι μιγεῖσα ἦμος ὅτε τρισσὴν μὲν ἐλείπετο Σείριος αἴγλην Ἠέλιος, δολιχὴ δ' ἐπεμαίετο πάντοθεν ὄρφνη· Τῖφύν τ' Ἀγνιάδην, δολιχῆς ἰθύντορα νηός· Θεσπιέων δ' ὅγε τῆμος ἐφ' ὕδασι Τελμισσοῖο ἄγχουρος λαοῖς Σιφάεσι ῥεῖθρον ἄμειβεν· ὃς περὶ μὲν βύκταισι καὶ ἀργήεσσιν ἀέλλαις νῆα κατιθύνειν δέδαεν πολυμήτιδι τέχνῃ· Κάστορά θ' ἱππόδαμον Πολυδεύκεά τ' εἰσενόησα καὶ Μόψον Τιταρῆθεν, ὃν Ἄμπυκι νυμφευθεῖσα Χαονίην ὑπὸ φηγὸν Ἀρηγονὶς ἐξελόχευσε· Πηλέα τ' Αἰακίδην, Αἰγίνης ἀγλαὸν υἱόν ὃς Δολόπεσσιν ἄνασσεν ἐνὶ Φθίῃ ἐριβώλῳ.

line_details.english: First I beheld the might of divine Herakles,
line_details.greek: - Πρῶτα δὲ εἶδα βίην Ἡρακλῆος θείοιο

line_details.english: whom Alkmene bore to Zeus Kronion, having mingled with him,
line_details.greek: ὃν τέκεν Ἀλκμήνη Ζηνὶ Κρονίωνι μιγεῖσα

line_details.english: when Helios was leaving the threefold blaze of Seirios,
line_details.greek: ἦμος ὅτε τρισσὴν μὲν ἐλείπετο Σείριος αἴγλην
line_details.note: Seirios is the Dog‑star; “threefold blaze” (trissēn aiglēn) is obscure—often taken as an intensive for the dog‑day glare; the juxtaposition with night “creeping” marks the onset of evening.

line_details.english: and long darkness was creeping on from every side;
line_details.greek: Ἠέλιος, δολιχὴ δ' ἐπεμαίετο πάντοθεν ὄρφνη·

line_details.english: and Tiphys Agniades, steersman of the long ship;
line_details.greek: Τῖφύν τ' Ἀγνιάδην, δολιχῆς ἰθύντορα νηός·
line_details.note: Agniades = “son of Agnias” (often transmitted as Hagnias); ithyntōr = technical term for “steersman.”

line_details.english: who then was upon the Thespian waters of Telmissos,
line_details.greek: Θεσπιέων δ' ὅγε τῆμος ἐφ' ὕδασι Τελμισσοῖο
line_details.note: Θεσπιέων … Σιφάεσι places the scene in Boeotia (Siphae was the port of Thespiae). Τελμισσοῖο is problematic; many emend to Τιλφυσσοῖο (of Tilphousa) or posit a local Telmissos. Translation retains the transmitted reading.

line_details.english: traversing the shore-hugging current among the Siphaean folk;
line_details.greek: ἄγχουρος λαοῖς Σιφάεσι ῥεῖθρον ἄμειβεν·
line_details.note: ἄγχουρος = “near‑shore, coast‑hugging”; ῥεῖθρον here “current/stream” of the harbor.

line_details.english: who, amid choppy seas and gleaming squalls,
line_details.greek: ὃς περὶ μὲν βύκταισι καὶ ἀργήεσσιν ἀέλλαις
line_details.note: βύκταισι is rare; likely “short, steep seas/choppy billows.” ἀργήεσσ(ι) ἀέλλαις = “gleaming/bright squalls,” i.e., spray‑flashing gusts.

line_details.english: knew to set the ship straight by resourceful craft;
line_details.greek: νῆα κατιθύνειν δέδαεν πολυμήτιδι τέχνῃ·

line_details.english: and I beheld horse‑taming Kastor and Polydeukes,
line_details.greek: Κάστορά θ' ἱππόδαμον Πολυδεύκεά τ' εἰσενόησα

line_details.english: and Mopsos from Titarēssos, whom, once wedded to Ampyx,
line_details.greek: καὶ Μόψον Τιταρῆθεν, ὃν Ἄμπυκι νυμφευθεῖσα
line_details.note: Τιταρῆθεν = “from Titarēssos,” the Thessalian river (cf. Il. 2.751–5).

line_details.english: Arēgonis bore beneath a Chaonian oak;
line_details.greek: Χαονίην ὑπὸ φηγὸν Ἀρηγονὶς ἐξελόχευσε·
line_details.note: “Chaonian oak” evokes the sacred oaks of Dodona in Epirus; ἐξελόχευσε is epic for “bore (in childbirth).”

line_details.english: and Peleus the Aiakid, glorious son of Aigina,
line_details.greek: Πηλέα τ' Αἰακίδην, Αἰγίνης ἀγλαὸν υἱόν
line_details.note: Aiakid = descendant of Aiakos; Aigina is mother of Aiakos, hence Peleus is his son.

line_details.english: who ruled the Dolopes in much‑nourishing Phthia.
line_details.greek: ὃς Δολόπεσσιν ἄνασσεν ἐνὶ Φθίῃ ἐριβώλῳ.

text.english: And thrice have I seated on board the illustrious stock of Hermes, Aithalides, whom far-famed Eupolemeia bore, daughter of Myrmidon, in rocky Alope; and Erytos, and fair Echion, whom once lying beside the Nymph Laothoë, daughter of Menetos, he fathered, the golden‑wanded Argeiphontes, lord of Kyllene.
text.greek: Τρισσὴν δ' Ἑρμείαο κλυτὴν εἰσέδρακα γένναν, Αἰθαλίδην, ὃν ἔτικτε περικλυτὴ Εὐπολέμεια, Μυρμιδόνος θυγάτηρ, Ἀλόπῃ ἐνὶ πετρηέσσῃ ἠδ' Ἔρυτον, καὶ καλὸν Ἐχίονα, τούς ποτε Νύμφῃ Λαοθόῃ Μενετοῖο παρευνηθεὶς ἐλόχευσε Κυλλήνης μεδέων χρυσόρραπις Ἀργειφόντης.

line_details.english: And thrice have I seated on board the illustrious stock of Hermes,
line_details.greek: Τρισσὴν δ' Ἑρμείαο κλυτὴν εἰσέδρακα γένναν,
line_details.note: εἰσέδρακα (“I have seated [on board]”) is a cataloguing formula in this poem; τρισσὴν … γένναν indicates that three sons of Hermes are among the crew.

line_details.english: Aithalides, whom far-famed Eupolemeia bore,
line_details.greek: Αἰθαλίδην, ὃν ἔτικτε περικλυτὴ Εὐπολέμεια,
line_details.note: Eupolemeia (otherwise obscure) is here the mother of Aithalides; her parentage is specified in the next line.

line_details.english: daughter of Myrmidon, in rocky Alope;
line_details.greek: Μυρμιδόνος θυγάτηρ, Ἀλόπῃ ἐνὶ πετρηέσσῃ
line_details.note: Alope (Ἀλόπη) is a rocky locale, likely the Thessalian/Phthiotian Alope; πετρηέσσῃ = “rocky.”

line_details.english: and Erytos, and fair Echion, whom once
line_details.greek: ἠδ' Ἔρυτον, καὶ καλὸν Ἐχίονα, τούς ποτε Νύμφῃ
line_details.note: τούς refers specifically to Erytos and Echion (not to Aithalides). The name Ἔρυτον here is often elsewhere Εὔρυτον (Eurytos).

line_details.english: lying beside the Nymph Laothoë, daughter of Menetos, he fathered,
line_details.greek: Λαοθόῃ Μενετοῖο παρευνηθεὶς ἐλόχευσε
line_details.note: παρευνηθείς ἐλόχευσε: with a male subject (Hermes), “to bring to birth” = “to beget/father” after lying with; Laothoë is styled a Nymph and daughter of Menetos.

line_details.english: the golden‑wanded Argeiphontes, lord of Kyllene.
line_details.greek: Κυλλήνης μεδέων χρυσόρραπις Ἀργειφόντης.
line_details.note: Κυλλήνης μεδέων = “lord of Kyllene,” a standard Hermes title; χρυσόρραπις = “golden‑wanded”; Ἀργειφόντης is the epithet “Argeiphontes.”

text.english: Straightway came the Aktorides and ox‑devouring Koronos.
text.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' Ἀκτορίδης καὶ βουφάγος ἦλθε Κόρωνος.

line_details.english: Straightway came the Aktorides and ox‑devouring Koronos.
line_details.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' Ἀκτορίδης καὶ βουφάγος ἦλθε Κόρωνος.
line_details.note: Aktorides is a patronymic, ‘son of Aktor’ (often taken to refer to Menoetius of Opus in Argonautic catalogues). The syntax is awkward: the singular ἦλθε with two apparent nominatives (Ἀκτορίδης and Κόρωνος) suggests that Ἀκτορίδης and βουφάγος may function as appositive epithets to Κόρωνος; alternatively some emend ἦλθε to plural ἦλθον. βουφάγος literally means ‘ox‑devouring.’

text.english: Iphiklos too, illustrious scion of Phylakos, stepped forth in turn.
text.greek: Ἴφικλος αὖ Φυλάκου δῖον γένος ἀντετόρησεν

line_details.english: Iphiklos too, illustrious scion of Phylakos, stepped forth in turn.
line_details.greek: Ἴφικλος αὖ Φυλάκου δῖον γένος ἀντετόρησεν
line_details.note: The verb ἀντετόρησεν is rare; likely built on τορέω (“to bore; to set forth distinctly”). In this catalogic context it is best taken as “answered/stepped forth in turn.” Some editors suspect a corruption and have proposed verbs like ἀντεβόλησεν (“met, came forward to meet”). “δῖον γένος” preserves the epic formula “illustrious/divine-born.”

text.english: And Boutes, son of Aineias, like unto gold-sworded Phoibos.
text.greek: Βούτης τ' Αἰνειάδης, ἴκελος χρυσάορι Φοίβῳ.

line_details.english: And Boutes, son of Aineias, like unto gold-sworded Phoibos.
line_details.greek: Βούτης τ' Αἰνειάδης, ἴκελος χρυσάορι Φοίβῳ.
line_details.note: Αἰνειάδης is a patronymic; Orphic Argonautica differs from Apollonius (who makes Boutes son of Teleon). Whether the patronymic points to Aineias (chronologically problematic) or a figure Aineus is debated. ἴκελος governs the dative (“like unto”), and χρυσάωρ is the traditional epithet of Phoibos (“gold-sworded”).

text.english: But Canthus, Abantiades, sailed across from Euboea.
text.greek: Κάνθος δ' Εὐβοίηθεν Ἀβαντιάδης ἐπέρησεν

line_details.english: But Canthus, Abantiades, sailed across from Euboea.
line_details.greek: Κάνθος δ' Εὐβοίηθεν Ἀβαντιάδης ἐπέρησεν
line_details.note: “Abantiades” = ‘son of Abas’; the Euboeans were called Abantes. ἐπέρησεν means ‘sailed across/crossed by sea’.

text.english: whom indeed Moira subdued, and Ananke imposed his doom.
text.greek: ὃν δὴ μοῖρ' ἐδάμασσε, τέλος δ' ἐπέθηκεν ἀνάγκη

line_details.english: whom indeed Moira subdued, and Ananke imposed his doom.
line_details.greek: ὃν δὴ μοῖρ' ἐδάμασσε, τέλος δ' ἐπέθηκεν ἀνάγκη
line_details.note: Moira and Ananke are personified Fate and Necessity; τέλος ἐπέθηκεν = ‘imposed/appointed his end (doom)’.

text.english: to perish off Libya, and to be bereft of the homecoming to his house.
text.greek: φθίσθαι ὑπὲρ Λιβύης, νόστον δ' οἴκοιο λαθέσθαι.

line_details.english: to perish off Libya, and to be bereft of the homecoming to his house.
line_details.greek: φθίσθαι ὑπὲρ Λιβύης, νόστον δ' οἴκοιο λαθέσθαι.
line_details.note: ὑπὲρ Λιβύης = ‘off (the coast of) Libya’; νόστον … λαθέσθαι means ‘to miss/lose the homecoming,’ not mere mental ‘forgetting.’

text.english: And Phaleros, son of Alkon, from the streams of Aisepos, came, who founded the sea-crowned city of Gyrton.
text.greek: Ἄλκωνος δὲ Φάληρος ἀπ' Αἰσήποιο ῥοάων ἤλυθεν, ὃς Γύρτωνος ἁλιστεφὲς ἔκτισεν ἄστυ.

line_details.english: And Phaleros, son of Alkon, from the streams of Aisepos,
line_details.greek: Ἄλκωνος δὲ Φάληρος ἀπ' Αἰσήποιο ῥοάων
line_details.note: Aisepos is the river in the Troad/Mysia; ῥοάων (“streams”) is a poetic genitive plural. The Orphic poet here departs from the common Athenian origin of Phaleros attested elsewhere.

line_details.english: came, who founded the sea-crowned city of Gyrton.
line_details.greek: ἤλυθεν, ὃς Γύρτωνος ἁλιστεφὲς ἔκτισεν ἄστυ.
line_details.note: ἁλιστεφές (“sea-crowned”) is a conventional epic epithet for coastal places; its application to Gyrton (usually the inland Thessalian city, Γυρτών/Γυρτώνη) is problematic and may be formulaic or reflect a different/local Gyrton-tradition. ἔκτισεν ἄστυ is the standard “founded a city” formula.

text.english: Iphitus in turn followed with them, the son of Naubolus.
text.greek: Ἴφιτος αὖ μετὰ τοῖσιν ἐφέσπετο Ναυβόλου υἱός

line_details.english: Iphitus in turn followed with them, the son of Naubolus.
line_details.greek: Ἴφιτος αὖ μετὰ τοῖσιν ἐφέσπετο Ναυβόλου υἱός
line_details.note: ἐφέσπετο (middle) “followed in their train”; the phrase μετὰ τοῖσιν is Homeric/formulaic.

text.english: who was lord over Phocis and well‑towered Tanagra.
text.greek: Φωκίδος ὅς ῥ' ἤνασσε καὶ εὐπύργοιο Τανάγρης.

line_details.english: who was lord over Phocis and well‑towered Tanagra.
line_details.greek: Φωκίδος ὅς ῥ' ἤνασσε καὶ εὐπύργοιο Τανάγρης.
line_details.note: ἤνασσε (“was lord over”) governs the genitive (Φωκίδος, Τανάγρης). Tanagra is Boeotian; the poet credits Iphitus with rule over both Phocis and well‑towered Tanagra, reflecting fluid regional attributions in epic geography. εὐπύργοιο is a stock epithet for fortified cities.

text.english: Laodokos, Talaos, and Areios, blameless sons, came, the renowned Abantiads, whom Pêrô bore.
text.greek: Λαοδόκος, Ταλαὸς καὶ Ἀρήϊος, υἱοὶ ἄμωμοι ἦλθον Ἀβαντιάδαι περιώνυμοι οὓς τέκε Πηρώ.

line_details.english: Laodokos, Talaos, and Areios, blameless sons,
line_details.greek: Λαοδόκος, Ταλαὸς καὶ Ἀρήϊος, υἱοὶ ἄμωμοι
line_details.note: The three are presented as the blameless sons of Pêrô (by Bias); Areios (Ἀρήϊος, with diaeresis marking hiatus) is a lesser‑attested brother alongside Talaos (well known as Adrastos’ father). The epithet “blameless” (ἄμωμος) is a standard epic honorific.

line_details.english: came, the renowned Abantiads, whom Pêrô bore.
line_details.greek: ἦλθον Ἀβαντιάδαι περιώνυμοι οὓς τέκε Πηρώ.
line_details.note: “Abantiads” (Ἀβαντιάδαι) is a patronymic/ethnic for Argives, i.e., descendants of Abas; thus the phrase marks them as Argive nobles. Pêrô is the daughter of Neleus, traditionally the wife of Bias and mother of these sons.

text.english: And Iphidamas, son of Aleus, came; for his stalwart sire sent him forth after leaving the bounds of Tegea.
text.greek: Ἰφιδάμας δ' Ἀλέου παῖς ἤλυθε· πέμψε γὰρ αὐτόν ἴφθιμος γενέτης, Τεγέης ὅρια προλιπόντα.

line_details.english: And Iphidamas, son of Aleus, came; for his stalwart sire sent him forth
line_details.greek: Ἰφιδάμας δ' Ἀλέου παῖς ἤλυθε· πέμψε γὰρ αὐτόν
line_details.note: ἴφθιμος is a Homeric epithet (“stalwart, mighty”); γενέτης = “begetter, father.” Aleus is the Arcadian king of Tegea; naming Iphidamas as his son is a distinctive Orphic genealogy (elsewhere Aleus is chiefly father of Ancaeus and Cepheus).

line_details.english: after leaving the bounds of Tegea.
line_details.greek: ἴφθιμος γενέτης, Τεγέης ὅρια προλιπόντα.
line_details.note: ὅρια = “bounds, borders” of the land; προλιπόντα (acc. masc. sg.) modifies αὐτόν and is temporal: “after leaving/when he had left.”

text.english: And Erginus came, leaving the grain‑rich ploughland of Branchus, and the turreted citadel of well‑fortified Miletus, where the streams of much‑wandering Maeander wash about.
text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Ἐργῖνος, Βράγχου πολύπυρον ἄρουραν ἐκπρολιπὼν καὶ τύρσιν ἐρυμνῆς Μιλήτοιο, ἔνθα ῥοαὶ κλύζουσι πολυπλανέος Μαιάνδρου.

line_details.english: And Erginus came, leaving the grain‑rich ploughland of Branchus,
line_details.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Ἐργῖνος, Βράγχου πολύπυρον ἄρουραν
line_details.note: Branchus is the eponymous hero of the Branchidae, the prophetic clan at Didyma near Miletus; aroura = cultivated/ploughland, here “grain‑rich” (polypyros). The passage marks Erginus’ origin in the Milesian territory.

line_details.english: and the turreted citadel of well‑fortified Miletus,
line_details.greek: ἐκπρολιπὼν καὶ τύρσιν ἐρυμνῆς Μιλήτοιο,
line_details.note: Tyrsis is an archaic epic word for “citadel, towered town”; erymnos means “strong, well‑fortified.” The phrase denotes the city of Miletus.

line_details.english: where the streams of much‑wandering Maeander wash about.
line_details.greek: ἔνθα ῥοαὶ κλύζουσι πολυπλανέος Μαιάνδρου.
line_details.note: Polyplanes (“much‑wandering”) is the traditional epithet of the winding river Maeander. Rhoai klyzousi literally “the streams wash/surge,” i.e., around the site of Miletus at the Maeander’s mouth.

text.english: And among them Neleïan Periklymenos arrived, close by Pellene and well-watered Lipaxos, having left the wealthy city and the mountain‑pastured Kolonai.
text.greek: Ἐν δὲ Περικλύμενος Νηλήϊος εἰσαφίκανεν, ἀγχόθι Πελλήνης τε καὶ εὐύδροιο Λιπάξου ἄστυ λιπὼν ἀφνειὸν ὀρειονόμους τε Κολώνας.

line_details.english: And among them Neleïan Periklymenos arrived,
line_details.greek: Ἐν δὲ Περικλύμενος Νηλήϊος εἰσαφίκανεν,
line_details.note: “Neleïan” (Nēlēïos) = son/descendant of Neleus; Periklymenos is the famed Pylian hero. The verb “arrived” renders eisa-phíkanen, the standard epic verb for coming to the muster/ship.

line_details.english: close by Pellene and well-watered Lipaxos,
line_details.greek: ἀγχόθι Πελλήνης τε καὶ εὐύδροιο Λιπάξου
line_details.note: ἀγχόθι governs the genitive (“near to”). Pellene is the Achaean city; Lipaxos is otherwise obscure—likely a local river or site—here marked by the epic epithet “well‑watered.”

line_details.english: having left the wealthy city and the mountain‑pastured Kolonai.
line_details.greek: ἄστυ λιπὼν ἀφνειὸν ὀρειονόμους τε Κολώνας.
line_details.note: ὀρειονόμους (“mountain‑pastured”) is a rare compound qualifying Kolonai (acc. pl.). The phrase “near Pellene and Lipaxos” most naturally modifies “the wealthy city,” with Kolonai as an additional locality left behind. Identification of Kolonai in this context is uncertain.

text.english: And, leaving Kalydon, swift Meleagros set out.
text.greek: Ἐκ δὲ λιπὼν Καλυδῶνα θοὸς Μελέαγρος ἔβαινεν.

line_details.english: And, leaving Kalydon, swift Meleagros set out.
line_details.greek: Ἐκ δὲ λιπὼν Καλυδῶνα θοὸς Μελέαγρος ἔβαινεν.
line_details.note: θόος is a stock epic epithet (“swift”); Kalydon is Meleagros’ Aitolian city. The imperfect ἔβαινεν (“was going”) in catalog style conveys the action of setting out; in some epic contexts βαίνω can imply “go aboard,” but here it is general ‘set out/went.’

text.english: Oineus was his sire, and Althaia, rosy‑armed, bore him.
text.greek: Οἰνεὺς τόν ῥ' ἐλόχευσε καὶ Ἀλθαίη ῥοδόπηχυς.

line_details.english: Oineus was his sire, and Althaia, rosy‑armed, bore him.
line_details.greek: Οἰνεὺς τόν ῥ' ἐλόχευσε καὶ Ἀλθαίη ῥοδόπηχυς.
line_details.note: ἐλόχευσε (“bore”) is a Homeric/epic genealogical formula used of the mother; the father’s name is coordinated in the nominative though the singular verb agrees notionally with the mother. Hence the idiomatic rendering supplies “was his sire” for Oineus. ῥοδόπηχυς = “rosy‑armed,” an ornamental epithet. The pronoun τόν refers to the hero named in the preceding line (traditionally Meleager).

text.english: Iphiklos in turn crossed over, leaving the Atracian lake, a kinsman of Althaia; and he honored, above all others, the fair‑formed Meleagros, and he taught him glorious deeds.
text.greek: Ἴφικλος αὖτ' ἐπέρησε λιπὼν Ἀτρακηίδα λίμνην, σύγγονος Ἀλθαίης· περὶ δ' αὖ τίεν ἔξοχα πάντων εὐειδῆ Μελέαγρον, ἰδ' ἀγλαὰ ἔργ' ἐδίδασκεν.

line_details.english: Iphiklos in turn crossed over, leaving the Atracian lake,
line_details.greek: Ἴφικλος αὖτ' ἐπέρησε λιπὼν Ἀτρακηίδα λίμνην,
line_details.note: “Atracian lake” likely refers to the Thessalian region around Atrax (cf. the Boebeian lake near Iolkos); the exact hydronym is debated. ἐπέρασε with the participle λιπών conveys departure (“crossed over, having left…”).

line_details.english: a kinsman of Althaia; and he honored, above all others, the fair‑formed Meleagros,
line_details.greek: σύγγονος Ἀλθαίης· περὶ δ' αὖ τίεν ἔξοχα πάντων
line_details.note: σύγγονος Ἀλθαίης identifies this Iphiklos as Althaia’s brother (a Thestiad), hence Meleagros’ maternal uncle—distinct from the Thessalian Iphiklos son of Phylakos found elsewhere. The intensifying περὶ … ἔξοχα πάντων underscores the superlative honor.

line_details.english: and he taught him glorious deeds.
line_details.greek: εὐειδῆ Μελέαγρον, ἰδ' ἀγλαὰ ἔργ' ἐδίδασκεν.
line_details.note: ἰδ’ = ἠδέ (“and”). ἀγλαὰ ἔργα is a formula for “glorious exploits,” especially martial prowess. The imperfects τίεν and ἐδιδάσκεν suggest habitual action (“he used to honor/teach”).

text.english: And Asterion crossed over, the son of renowned Komētus, who dwelt in Peiresiae by the streams of the Apidanus; Peneus, mingling them, bears their common current into the sea.
text.greek: Ἀστερίων δ' ἐπέρησε πάϊς κλεινοῖο Κομήτου, Πειρεσίην ὃς ἔναιεν ἐπ' Ἀπιδανοῖο ῥεέθροις· Πηνειὸς μίσγων ξυνὸν ῥόον εἰς ἅλα πέμπει.

line_details.english: And Asterion crossed over, the son of renowned Komētus,
line_details.greek: Ἀστερίων δ' ἐπέρησε πάϊς κλεινοῖο Κομήτου,
line_details.note: ἐπέρησε (“crossed over”) is the conventional epic verb for setting out across the sea; παῖς here = “son.”

line_details.english: who dwelt in Peiresiae by the streams of the Apidanus;
line_details.greek: Πειρεσίην ὃς ἔναιεν ἐπ' Ἀπιδανοῖο ῥεέθροις·
line_details.note: Πειρεσίην is a poetic accusative of place for “in Peiresiae”; the Apidanus is a tributary in Thessaly.

line_details.english: Peneus, mingling them, bears their common current into the sea.
line_details.greek: Πηνειὸς μίσγων ξυνὸν ῥόον εἰς ἅλα πέμπει.
line_details.note: ξυνὸν (“common”) is the older form of κοινόν; the line describes the confluence of Apidanus with Peneus, which then carries the joined waters to the sea.

text.english: And Eurydamas set forth, leaving Lake Boibeïs, near the Peneios and fair‑open‑sea’d Meliboia.
text.greek: Εὐρυδάμας δ' ἐπόρευσε λιπὼν Βοιβηΐδα λίμνην, ἀγχόθι Πηνειοῖο καὶ εὐπελαγέος Μελιβοίης.

line_details.english: And Eurydamas set forth, leaving Lake Boibeïs,
line_details.greek: Εὐρυδάμας δ' ἐπόρευσε λιπὼν Βοιβηΐδα λίμνην,
line_details.note: Boibeïs (Lake Boebeis) is the Thessalian lake near Pherae; ἐπόρευσε is epic active used intransitively, “went/advanced.”

line_details.english: near the Peneios and fair‑open‑sea’d Meliboia.
line_details.greek: ἀγχόθι Πηνειοῖο καὶ εὐπελαγέος Μελιβοίης.
line_details.note: ἀγχόθι governs both genitives (Πηνειοῖο, Μελιβοίης). εὐπελαγέος literally “of good/open sea,” here marking Meliboia’s exposure to the open Aegean; hence “fair‑open‑sea’d.”

text.english: But then the son of Elatos, Polyphemos, arrived, who among the Heroes was preeminent in manly prowess; Aineios, son of Kaineus, arrived, whom they say when he joined with the Lapiths, was subdued by the Centaurs, being struck with pines and with long‑needled firs, and that he endured and planted his unbending knees, and, alive among the dead, went down beneath the depths of the earth.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ' Ἐλάτοιο πάϊς Πολύφημος ἵκανεν ὅς σφιν ἐν ἠνορέῃσι μετέπρεπεν Ἡρώεσσιν· Ἠνειὸς Καινῆος ἀφίκετο, τόν ῥά τε φασί μισγόμενον Λαπίθαις ὑπὸ Κενταύροισι δαμῆναι, θεινόμενον πεύκαισι τανυφλοίοις τ' ἐλάτῃσι, καὶ οἱ ἀνατλῆναι καὶ ἀκαμπέα γούνατ' ἐρεῖσαι ζῳόν τ' ἐν φθιμένοισι μολεῖν ὑπὸ κεύθεα γαίης.

line_details.english: But then the son of Elatos, Polyphemos, arrived,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ' Ἐλάτοιο πάϊς Πολύφημος ἵκανεν

line_details.english: who among the Heroes was preeminent in manly prowess;
line_details.greek: ὅς σφιν ἐν ἠνορέῃσι μετέπρεπεν Ἡρώεσσιν·
line_details.note: “manly prowess” renders ἠνορέαι, the epic term for valor/virility.

line_details.english: Aineios, son of Kaineus, arrived, whom they say
line_details.greek: Ἠνειὸς Καινῆος ἀφίκετο, τόν ῥά τε φασί
line_details.note: Ἠνειὸς Καινῆος is problematic: the relative clause that follows gives the famous fate of Kaineus, not of a son. Many emend to read the nominative ‘Kaineus’ himself, or replace Ἠνειός with ‘Koronos, son of Kaineus’ (cf. Apollonius Rhodios 1.57). I translate the transmitted text as ‘Aineios, son of Kaineus,’ while the following clauses refer to Kaineus’s myth.

line_details.english: when he joined with the Lapiths, was subdued by the Centaurs,
line_details.greek: μισγόμενον Λαπίθαις ὑπὸ Κενταύροισι δαμῆναι,
line_details.note: μισγόμενον with the dative “Lapiths” means “joining battle with,” not “mingling” in a general sense.

line_details.english: being struck with pines and with long‑needled firs,
line_details.greek: θεινόμενον πεύκαισι τανυφλοίοις τ' ἐλάτῃσι,
line_details.note: τανυφλόιος = “long‑leafed/long‑needled,” of conifers (fir ἐλάτη; pine πεύκη).

line_details.english: and that he endured and planted his unbending knees,
line_details.greek: καὶ οἱ ἀνατλῆναι καὶ ἀκαμπέα γούνατ' ἐρεῖσαι
line_details.note: ἀκαμπέα “unyielding, inflexible,” highlighting Kaineus’s invulnerability and immovability.

line_details.english: and, alive among the dead, went down beneath the depths of the earth.
line_details.greek: ζῳόν τ' ἐν φθιμένοισι μολεῖν ὑπὸ κεύθεα γαίης.
line_details.note: “alive among the dead” (ζῳόν τ’ ἐν φθιμένοισι) alludes to Kaineus’s peculiar end: crushed and pressed into the earth alive, he descends beneath the hidden depths (κεύθεα) of the earth.

text.english: And Admetos came from Pherai, to whom once Paian —serving for hire—stooped; and he was shunning the wrath of Zeus, because indeed the Kyklopes with irresistible arrows he smote among mortals, on account of the wrong done to Asklepios.
text.greek: Ἄδμητος δ' ἀφίκανε Φεραιόθεν, ᾧ ποτε Παιὰν θητεύων ὑπόεικε· Διὸς δ' ἠλεύατο μῆνιν οὕνεκά τοι Κύκλωπας ἀμαιμακέτοισιν ὀϊστοῖς ἐν φθιτοῖσιν ἔτευξ' Ἀσκληπιοῦ εἵνεκα λώβης.

line_details.english: And Admetos came from Pherai, to whom once Paian
line_details.greek: Ἄδμητος δ' ἀφίκανε Φεραιόθεν, ᾧ ποτε Παιὰν
line_details.note: ἀφίκανε is an epic/poetic 3rd sg aorist for ἀφίκετο; Paian is Apollo under his healing epithet.

line_details.english: —serving for hire—stooped; and he was shunning the wrath of Zeus,
line_details.greek: θητεύων ὑπόεικε· Διὸς δ' ἠλεύατο μῆνιν
line_details.note: θητεύων ὑπόεικε literally “yielded while serving (for hire)”; the subject is Paian (Apollo), who condescends to serve Admetos.

line_details.english: because indeed the Kyklopes with irresistible arrows
line_details.greek: οὕνεκά τοι Κύκλωπας ἀμαιμακέτοισιν ὀϊστοῖς
line_details.note: ἀμαιμακέτοισιν is a stereotyped epic epithet meaning “irresistible, unrelenting”; enclitic τοι adds emphasis (“indeed”).

line_details.english: he smote among mortals, on account of the wrong done to Asklepios.
line_details.greek: ἐν φθιτοῖσιν ἔτευξ' Ἀσκληπιοῦ εἵνεκα λώβης.
line_details.note: ἐν φθιτοῖσιν = “among mortals”; ἔτευξ’ (aor. of τεύχω) here has the sense “smote/struck.” The phrase Ἀσκληπιοῦ λώβης means “because of the outrage done to Asklepios” (i.e., Apollo avenged Zeus’ slaying of Asklepios by killing the Kyklopes).

text.english: And there came Eurytion, son of Iros, son of Aktor, leaving rugged Opoeis; and with him came Idas and Lynkeus, who beyond all through the aether and the sea the depths, and the streams of chthonic Ploutes, he alone among men with dread eyes could behold.
text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Εὐρυτίων Ἴρου παῖς Ἀκτορίωνος τρηχείην Ὀπόεντα λιπὼν, σὺν δ' ἤλυθεν Ἴδας Λυγκεύς θ', ὃς τήλιστα δι' αἰθέρος ἠδὲ θαλάσσης βένθεα, καὶ Πλουτῆος ὑποχθονίοιο ῥέεθρα μοῦνος ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων δεινοῖσιν ὀπώπεεν ὄσσοις.

line_details.english: And there came Eurytion, son of Iros, son of Aktor,
line_details.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Εὐρυτίων Ἴρου παῖς Ἀκτορίωνος
line_details.note: Ἀκτορίωνος is a patronymic (“Aktorion”), here appositive to Ἴρου: Iros is the son of Aktor; thus Eurytion is Aktor’s grandson.

line_details.english: leaving rugged Opoeis; and with him came Idas
line_details.greek: τρηχείην Ὀπόεντα λιπὼν, σὺν δ' ἤλυθεν Ἴδας
line_details.note: Ὀπόεντα is the accusative of Opoeis (Opous), the Opuntian Locrian city; τρηχείην “rugged” is a conventional epithet of that terrain.

line_details.english: and Lynkeus, who beyond all through the aether and the sea
line_details.greek: Λυγκεύς θ', ὃς τήλιστα δι' αἰθέρος ἠδὲ θαλάσσης
line_details.note: τήλιστα means “to the greatest extent, surpassingly”; αἰθήρ is the upper air (“aether”).

line_details.english: the depths, and the streams of chthonic Ploutes,
line_details.greek: βένθεα, καὶ Πλουτῆος ὑποχθονίοιο ῥέεθρα
line_details.note: Πλουτῆος ὑποχθονίοιο = “of chthonic Ploutes (Pluto),” i.e., the Underworld; ῥέεθρα “streams” refers to the rivers of Hades.

line_details.english: he alone among men with dread eyes could behold.
line_details.greek: μοῦνος ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων δεινοῖσιν ὀπώπεεν ὄσσοις.
line_details.note: ὀπώπεεν (a perfect-form in epic usage) conveys Lynkeus’ extraordinary capacity: “he could behold.” δεινοῖσιν ὄσσοις “with dread (i.e., formidable, piercing) eyes.”

text.english: But when Telamon had joined the company, him she bore to Aiakos the unwearied, the maiden of famed Asopos, Aegina, amid the pebbles of sea‑wreathed Salamis.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Τελαμὼν συνεφέσπετο, τόν ῥ' ἐλόχευσεν Αἰακῷ ἀτρύτῳ κούρη κλυτοῦ Ἀσωποῖο Αἴγιν' ἐν κροκάλῃσιν ἀλιστεφέος Σαλαμῖνος.

line_details.english: But when Telamon had joined the company, him she bore
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Τελαμὼν συνεφέσπετο, τόν ῥ' ἐλόχευσεν
line_details.note: συνεφέσπετο = “joined/followed in company” (epic of ἕπομαι); τόν refers to Telamon; ἐλόχευσεν = “bore in childbirth.”

line_details.english: to Aiakos the unwearied, the maiden of famed Asopos,
line_details.greek: Αἰακῷ ἀτρύτῳ κούρη κλυτοῦ Ἀσωποῖο
line_details.note: Aegina is the daughter of Asopos. Orphic genealogy here makes Aegina the mother of Telamon by Aiakos, differing from the more common tradition that Endeis was his mother; ἀτρύτος = “unwearied.”

line_details.english: Aegina, amid the pebbles of sea‑wreathed Salamis.
line_details.greek: Αἴγιν' ἐν κροκάλῃσιν ἀλιστεφέος Σαλαμῖνος.
line_details.note: κροκάλαι = rounded beach‑pebbles; ἀλιστέφεος = “sea‑wreathed/sea‑girt.” The phrase locates the birth on Salamis, fitting Telamon’s later kingship there. Αἴγιν’ shows elision of final -α before ἐν (nom. Αἴγινα).

text.english: Then indeed came the stalwart Idmon, bastard son of Abas, whom, having conceived, she bore to lord Apollon beside the stream of Amphrysus—Pheretian Antianeira.
text.greek: Δὴ τότ' Ἄβαντος παῖς νόθος ἤλυθε καρτερὸς Ἴδμων, τόν ῥ' ὑποκυσσαμένη τέκεν Ἀπόλλωνι ἄνακτι Ἀμφρύσου παρὰ χεῦμα Φερητιὰς Ἀντιάνειρα.

line_details.english: Then indeed came the stalwart Idmon, bastard son of Abas,
line_details.greek: Δὴ τότ' Ἄβαντος παῖς νόθος ἤλυθε καρτερὸς Ἴδμων,
line_details.note: “nothos” (bastard) reconciles two traditions: Idmon is publicly reckoned son of Abas yet truly begotten by Apollon; “karteros” preserves the epic epithet. The scene is the heroes’ muster.

line_details.english: whom, having conceived, she bore to lord Apollon
line_details.greek: τόν ῥ' ὑποκυσσαμένη τέκεν Ἀπόλλωνι ἄνακτι
