line_details.note: “hypokyssamenē” means “having conceived (by),” and the dative “Apolloni anakti” expresses paternity (“to/for lord Apollon”).

line_details.english: beside the stream of Amphrysus—Pheretian Antianeira.
line_details.greek: Ἀμφρύσου παρὰ χεῦμα Φερητιὰς Ἀντιάνειρα.
line_details.note: “para cheuma Amphrysou” = “beside the stream/flow of Amphrysus,” a Thessalian river associated with Apollon; “Pheretias” marks Antianeira as of Pherae. This line completes the syntax of the preceding.

text.english: To him also Phoibos bestowed prophetic skill and a heaven‑ordained oracular voice, so that he might speak to men words well‑fitted.
text.greek: Τῷ καὶ μαντοσύνην ἔπορεν καὶ θέσφατον ὀμφήν Φοῖβος, ἵν' ἀνθρώποισιν ἀρηρότα μυθίζοιτο.

line_details.english: To him also Phoibos bestowed prophetic skill and a heaven‑ordained oracular voice,
line_details.greek: Τῷ καὶ μαντοσύνην ἔπορεν καὶ θέσφατον ὀμφήν
line_details.note: θέσφατον ὀμφήν: literally “heaven‑ordained voice,” with ὀμφή denoting an oracular utterance; Φοῖβος = Apollo; μαντοσύνη = prophetic craft/skill.

line_details.english: so that he might speak to men words well‑fitted.
line_details.greek: Φοῖβος, ἵν' ἀνθρώποισιν ἀρηρότα μυθίζοιτο.
line_details.note: ἀρηρότα is the neuter plural perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω (“fit, join”), used substantively/adverbially = “(things) fitted, apt,” supplying an implied object such as “words”; μυθίζοιτο (deponent) “to utter/speak,” optative in a final clause after a secondary tense (ἔπορεν).

text.english: And in turn there came among them Menoetius from Opus, a comrade of the Minyae; and after him came godlike Oïleus.
text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' αὖ μετὰ τοῖσι Μενοίτιος ἐξ Ὀπόεντος, σύγχορτος Μινύαις· ἐπὶ δ' ἤλυθε δῖος Ὀϊλεύς.

line_details.english: And in turn there came among them Menoetius from Opus, a comrade of the Minyae;
line_details.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' αὖ μετὰ τοῖσι Μενοίτιος ἐξ Ὀπόεντος,
line_details.note: μετὰ τοῖσι = “among them,” continuing the catalogue; Ὀπόεντος is the poetic genitive of Ὀπόεις, i.e., Opus (Opountian Locris); σύγχορτος lit. “pasturing together,” used metaphorically of comradeship (“comrade of the Minyae”).

line_details.english: and after him came godlike Oïleus.
line_details.greek: σύγχορτος Μινύαις· ἐπὶ δ' ἤλυθε δῖος Ὀϊλεύς.
line_details.note: δῖος is the standard Homeric epithet “godlike”; ἐπὶ δ’ ἤλυθε is a sequencing formula (“and then/after him came”). Oïleus is the Locrian hero, better known as the father of Aias the Lesser, but included among Argonauts in some traditions.

text.english: And far-famed Phlias came, whom once to Bakkhos a Nymph, yielding herself by the streams of Asopos, bore, possessing an unblemished frame and prudent counsel.
text.greek: Φλίας δ' ἐξίκανε περικλυτός ὅν ποτε Βάκχῳ νύμφη ὑποκλινθεῖσα παρ' Ἀσωποῖο ῥοῇσι τίκτεν, ἄμωμον ἔχοντα δέμας καὶ ἐπίφρονα μῆτιν.

line_details.english: And far-famed Phlias came, whom once to Bakkhos
line_details.greek: Φλίας δ' ἐξίκανε περικλυτός ὅν ποτε Βάκχῳ
line_details.note: ἐξίκανε = “came, arrived.” The relative ὅν refers forward to the description of Phlias’ birth; Bakkhos is Dionysos.

line_details.english: a Nymph, yielding herself by the streams of Asopos, bore,
line_details.greek: νύμφη ὑποκλινθεῖσα παρ' Ἀσωποῖο ῥοῇσι
line_details.note: ὑποκλινθεῖσα is an erotic euphemism (“yielding herself”). Asopos is the river-god; other traditions name the mother (e.g., Chthonophyle), but here she is an unnamed Nymph by Asopos’ streams.

line_details.english: possessing an unblemished frame and prudent counsel.
line_details.greek: τίκτεν, ἄμωμον ἔχοντα δέμας καὶ ἐπίφρονα μῆτιν.
line_details.note: ἄμωμον δέμας = “unblemished body/form”; μῆτις with ἐπίφρων denotes sagacious, practical intelligence, pairing physical and mental excellence.

text.english: And Cepheus too, from Arkadia, came among the heroes.
text.greek: Κηφεύς τ' Ἀρκαδίηθε μεθ' ἡρώεσσι πελάσθη.

line_details.english: And Cepheus too, from Arkadia, came among the heroes.
line_details.greek: Κηφεύς τ' Ἀρκαδίηθε μεθ' ἡρώεσσι πελάσθη.
line_details.note: Ἀρκαδίηθε is an epic adverb meaning “from Arkadia” (suffix -θε ≈ -θεν). πελάσθη is an aorist passive used intransitively, “came near/approached.” Cepheus is the Arcadian hero (son of Aleus) known from Argonaut lists.

text.english: But Alcaeus, into the band, from sheep‑abounding Arcadia, his aged father sent him forth for the voyage to the Axenos; he never cast a cloak upon his sturdy shoulders, but about his breast he wrapped the shaggy hide of a bear.
text.greek: Ἀλκαῖον δ' ἄν' ὅμιλον ἀπ' Ἀρκαδίης πολυμήλου πέμψε πατὴρ γηραιὸς ἐπὶ πλόον Ἀξείνοιο· οὗτος δ' οὔποτε χλαῖναν ἐπὶ στιβαροῖς βάλεν ὤμοις, ἀλλ' ἄρκτου λάσιον στέρνοις ἀμπίσχετο δέρμα.

line_details.english: But Alcaeus, into the band, from sheep‑abounding Arcadia,
line_details.greek: Ἀλκαῖον δ' ἄν' ὅμιλον ἀπ' Ἀρκαδίης πολυμήλου
line_details.note: The reading Alcaeus (Alkaios) is likely corrupt; many emend to Ancaeus (Agkaios), the Arcadian Argonaut. πολυμήλου = “rich in flocks.”

line_details.english: his aged father sent him forth for the voyage to the Axenos;
line_details.greek: πέμψε πατὴρ γηραιὸς ἐπὶ πλόον Ἀξείνοιο·
line_details.note: Axenos = the “Inhospitable” Sea, i.e., the Black Sea (later Euxeinos Pontos).

line_details.english: he never cast a cloak upon his sturdy shoulders,
line_details.greek: οὗτος δ' οὔποτε χλαῖναν ἐπὶ στιβαροῖς βάλεν ὤμοις,

line_details.english: but about his breast he wrapped the shaggy hide of a bear.
line_details.greek: ἀλλ' ἄρκτου λάσιον στέρνοις ἀμπίσχετο δέρμα.

text.english: Nauplius in turn came, the beloved son of Amymone, whom she bore after sharing the bed with far-famed Ennosigaios, glorious in manly prowess, his form like unto the immortals.
text.greek: Ναύπλιος αὖθ' ἵκανεν, Ἀμυμώνης φίλος υἱός, ὃν τέκεν εὐνηθεῖσα περικλυτῷ Ἐννοσιγαίῳ ἀγλαὸν ἠνορέην δέμας εἴκελον ἀθανάτοισι.

line_details.english: Nauplius in turn came, the beloved son of Amymone,
line_details.greek: Ναύπλιος αὖθ' ἵκανεν, Ἀμυμώνης φίλος υἱός,
line_details.note: philos huios can mean “beloved” or “one’s own” son; Amymone is the Danaid mother of Nauplius. ἵκανεν = “came, arrived.”

line_details.english: whom she bore after sharing the bed with far-famed Ennosigaios,
line_details.greek: ὃν τέκεν εὐνηθεῖσα περικλυτῷ Ἐννοσιγαίῳ
line_details.note: Ennosigaios is the epithet-name of Poseidon, here transliterated; periklutos = “far-famed.” εὐνηθεῖσα is literally “having been bedded (by),” with the dative Ἐννοσιγαίῳ marking the agent; rendered idiomatically.

line_details.english: glorious in manly prowess, his form like unto the immortals.
line_details.greek: ἀγλαὸν ἠνορέην δέμας εἴκελον ἀθανάτοισι.
line_details.note: ἀγλαὸν ἠνορέην is an accusative phrase; ἀγλαόν functions adverbially (“gloriously”) with ἠνορέην (“manly prowess”). δέμας εἴκελον ἀθανατοῖσι is formulaic: “in body like to the immortals,” with δέμας as accusative of respect and ἀθανατοῖσι as the dative after εἴκελος.

text.english: And Tainarian Euphemus went forth from the headland of Malea, having left behind the glens and the sea‑surge‑washed precincts.
text.greek: Ταιναρίευς δ' Εὔφημος ἔβη Μαλεάτιδος ἄκρης ἐκπρολιπὼν αὐλῶνας, ἁλικλύστους τε θεράπνας.

line_details.english: And Tainarian Euphemus went forth from the headland of Malea,
line_details.greek: Ταιναρίευς δ' Εὔφημος ἔβη Μαλεάτιδος ἄκρης
line_details.note: “Tainarian” (Tainarieus) = of Tainaron (Cape Matapan) in Laconia; “the headland of Malea” is Cape Malea. Epic ἔβη = “went/set out.”

line_details.english: having left behind the glens and the sea‑surge‑washed precincts.
line_details.greek: ἐκπρολιπὼν αὐλῶνας, ἁλικλύστους τε θεράπνας.
line_details.note: αὐλῶνες = “glens, hollows” (of the coastal landscape). θεράπνας = “abodes/precincts”; some take it as the toponym Therapnai in Laconia, but the epithet ἁλικλύστους (“sea‑washed”) better suits a generic sense of sea‑beaten districts than inland Therapne. ἐκπρολιπών = “having left behind.”

text.english: Ankaios too came, the Pleuronian, who indeed had learned the heavenly courses of the stars, and the wandering circuits.
text.greek: Ἀγκαῖός τ' ἔμολε Πλευρώνιος, ὅς ῥα πορείας οὐρανίας ἄστρων ἐδάη, κύκλους τε πλάνητας.

line_details.english: Ankaios too came, the Pleuronian, who indeed had learned the heavenly courses of the stars,
line_details.greek: Ἀγκαῖός τ' ἔμολε Πλευρώνιος, ὅς ῥα πορείας
line_details.note: Pleuronios = from Pleuron (Aetolia). ἔμολε is epic for “came,” and ἐδάη means “knew well/was versed in.” The line highlights Ankaios’ expertise in celestial navigation.

line_details.english: and the wandering circuits.
line_details.greek: οὐρανίας ἄστρων ἐδάη, κύκλους τε πλάνητας.
line_details.note: “Wandering circuits” (kykloi planētai) refers to the orbits of the planets, “wanderers” in contrast to the fixed stars.

text.english: For he was inquiring into both the things that are and the things that shall be for mortals.
text.greek: Δίζετο γὰρ τά τ' ἐόντα τά τ' ἐσσόμεν' ἀνθρώποισιν.

line_details.english: For he was inquiring into both the things that are and the things that shall be for mortals.
line_details.greek: Δίζετο γὰρ τά τ' ἐόντα τά τ' ἐσσόμεν' ἀνθρώποισιν.
line_details.note: δίζετο is the middle of δίζημαι “seek, inquire”; τὰ τ᾽ ἐόντα τὰ τ᾽ ἐσσόμεν(α) is a Homeric formula (“what is and what will be”), here lacking the usual πρό τ᾽ ἐόντα (“what was before”; cf. Il. 1.70); ἐσσόμεν' = ἐσσόμενα by elision; ἀνθρώποισιν is the epic dative plural, “for mortals.”

text.english: And among them came Palaimonius, the illegitimate son of Lernos; and his two ankle-bones were afflicted, and his feet were not well set; for this cause all were wont to call him the offspring of Hephaistos.
text.greek: Ἐν δὲ Παλαιμόνιος Λέρνου νόθος ἤλυθεν υἱός· σίνετο δὲ σφυρὰ δισσὰ πόδας δ' οὐκ ἦεν ἀρηρώς· τοὔνεκεν Ἡφαίστοιο γόνον καλέεσκον ἅπαντες.

line_details.english: And among them came Palaimonius, the illegitimate son of Lernos;
line_details.greek: Ἐν δὲ Παλαιμόνιος Λέρνου νόθος ἤλυθεν υἱός·
line_details.note: Παλαιμόνιος (Palaimonius) and Λέρνος (Lernos) are obscure; Λέρνου (genitive) is likely a personal name, not the toponym Lerna (which would be Λέρνης). Νόθος = “illegitimate.”

line_details.english: and his two ankle-bones were afflicted, and his feet were not well set;
line_details.greek: σίνετο δὲ σφυρὰ δισσὰ πόδας δ' οὐκ ἦεν ἀρηρώς·
line_details.note: σφυρά = “ankle(-bones), malleoli”; σίνετο = “was afflicted/maimed”; ἀρηρώς (perf. of ἀραρίσκω) = “well-fitted, sound,” here negated of the feet, indicating lameness.

line_details.english: for this cause all were wont to call him the offspring of Hephaistos.
line_details.greek: τοὔνεκεν Ἡφαίστοιο γόνον καλέεσκον ἅπαντες.
line_details.note: Hephaistos is proverbially lame; hence the nickname. καλέεσκον is an iterative/imperfective “they used/were wont to call.”

text.english: And Augeias came, leaving the Pisatid banks of Alpheios, the son of fire-bright Helios.
text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Ἀλφειοῖο λιπὼν Πισάτιδας ὄχθας Αὐγείης, υἱὸς πυριφεγγέος Ἠελίοιο.

line_details.english: And Augeias came, leaving the Pisatid banks of Alpheios,
line_details.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Ἀλφειοῖο λιπὼν Πισάτιδας ὄχθας
line_details.note: Pisatid: the district of Pisatis in Elis by the river Alpheios; Augeias is the subject (epic nominative in -ēs); λιπών is a circumstantial participle “having left.”

line_details.english: the son of fire-bright Helios.
line_details.greek: Αὐγείης, υἱὸς πυριφεγγέος Ἠελίοιο.
line_details.note: πυριφεγγέος means “fire-bright”; Ἠελίοιο is the epic genitive of Helios. Augeias is here explicitly the son of Helios (elsewhere sometimes Poseidon).

text.english: Aye, indeed, two blameless scions came as well, Amphion, famed-of-report, and Asterios, staunch in battle, after leaving Pellene and the haunts of their native land.
text.greek: Ναὶ μὴν καὶ δίσσοι ὅρπηκες ἀμύμονες ἧκον, Ἀμφίων κλυτόφημος ἰδ' Ἀστέριος μενεχάρμης Πελλήνην προλιπόντ' ἠδ' ἤθεα πατρίδος αἴης.

line_details.english: Aye, indeed, two blameless scions came as well,
line_details.greek: Ναὶ μὴν καὶ δίσσοι ὅρπηκες ἀμύμονες ἧκον,
line_details.note: horpēkes (‘young shoots; saplings’) used metaphorically of noble youths or scions; amymones is the conventional epic ‘blameless’.

line_details.english: Amphion, famed-of-report, and Asterios, staunch in battle,
line_details.greek: Ἀμφίων κλυτόφημος ἰδ' Ἀστέριος μενεχάρμης
line_details.note: klytophēmos = ‘renowned, of far-famed report’; menecharmēs = ‘steadfast/staunch in battle’.

line_details.english: after leaving Pellene and the haunts of their native land.
line_details.greek: Πελλήνην προλιπόντ' ἠδ' ἤθεα πατρίδος αἴης.
line_details.note: Pellene is the Achaean city; ēthea here means ‘haunts, accustomed abodes’ of the fatherland (not ‘customs’).

text.english: And again I espied the fair twin ear of Boreas, whom renowned Oreithyia, daughter of divine Erechtheus, bore, having mingled in love beside the flow of the god Ilissos; who indeed had taken to flight with winglets at their ankles, Zetes and Kalais, in form like unto the immortals.
text.greek: Δισσὸν δ' αὖ Βορέου καλὸν στάχυν εἰσενόησα, οὓς τέκ' Ἐρεχθῆος θείου κλυτὴ Ὠρείθυια Ἰλισσοῦ παρὰ χεῦμα θεοῦ φιλότητι μιγεῖσα· οἳ δὴ καὶ ταρσοῖσιν ὑπουατίοις πεπότηντο, Ζήτης καὶ Κάλαϊς δέμας εἴκελοι ἀθανάτοισιν.

line_details.english: And again I espied the fair twin ear of Boreas,
line_details.greek: Δισσὸν δ' αὖ Βορέου καλὸν στάχυν εἰσενόησα,
line_details.note: στάχυς (“ear of grain”) is a poetic metaphor for offspring; the “twin ear” refers to Boreas’ pair of sons.

line_details.english: whom renowned Oreithyia, daughter of divine Erechtheus, bore,
line_details.greek: οὓς τέκ' Ἐρεχθῆος θείου κλυτὴ Ὠρείθυια
line_details.note: ἐκ + genitive is understood: Oreithyia is the daughter of Erechtheus; hence “of divine Erechtheus.”

line_details.english: having mingled in love beside the flow of the god Ilissos;
line_details.greek: Ἰλισσοῦ παρὰ χεῦμα θεοῦ φιλότητι μιγεῖσα·
line_details.note: θεοῦ is appositive to Ἰλισσοῦ: Ilissos is treated as a river-god; φιλότητι μιγεῖσα is the standard euphemism for sexual union (with Boreas, implied).

line_details.english: who indeed had taken to flight with winglets at their ankles,
line_details.greek: οἳ δὴ καὶ ταρσοῖσιν ὑπουατίοις πεπότηντο,
line_details.note: ταρσοῖσιν = “at the insteps/ankles.” The adjective ὑπουατίοις is obscure; most take it to mean something like “with ear-like appendages beneath,” i.e., small winglets at the ankles. Some have suspected emendation (e.g., to ὑποπτεροῖς, “under-winged”). πεπότηντο (perf. of πέτομαι) conveys a stative sense, “were winged/ready to fly.”

line_details.english: Zetes and Kalais, in form like unto the immortals.
line_details.greek: Ζήτης καὶ Κάλαϊς δέμας εἴκελοι ἀθανάτοισιν.

text.english: But then there came from Pherae a kinsman of lord Pelias; for he had come to be on board the ship Argo, to drive across the Axeinos toward Phasis together with the heroes.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ δὴ Πελίαο Φεραιόθεν ἤλυθ' ἄνακτος ἀγχιστεύς· νηὸς γὰρ ἐπ' Ἀργῴας γεγένητο ἄξεινον ποτὶ Φᾶσιν ἅμ' ἡρώεσσιν ἐλάσσαι.

line_details.english: But then there came from Pherae a kinsman of lord Pelias;
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ δὴ Πελίαο Φεραιόθεν ἤλυθ' ἄνακτος
line_details.note: ἀγχιστεύς = “near-kin, kinsman.” Φεραιόθεν = “from Pherae” (Thessaly). The person implied is Admetus, nephew of Pelias.

line_details.english: for he had come to be on board the ship Argo,
line_details.greek: ἀγχιστεύς· νηὸς γὰρ ἐπ' Ἀργῴας γεγένητο
line_details.note: νηὸς is the Homeric genitive of ναῦς “ship” (not “temple”); ἐπ’ Ἀργῴας = “on [board] the Argo.” γεγένητο (perfect) indicates having been enrolled/appointed as part of the crew.

line_details.english: to drive across the Axeinos toward Phasis together with the heroes.
line_details.greek: ἄξεινον ποτὶ Φᾶσιν ἅμ' ἡρώεσσιν ἐλάσσαι.
line_details.note: ἄξεινον = the Axeinos (“Inhospitable” [Sea], i.e., the Black Sea), with understood πόντον; ἐλᾶσαι/ἐλάσσαι “to drive” is the epic verb for sailing; ποτὶ Φᾶσιν = “toward the Phasis” (the river in Colchis).

text.english: And with him there came a comrade of divine Herakles.
text.greek: Σὺν δέ οἱ ἦλθ' ἕταρος Ἡρακλέεος θείοιο

line_details.english: And with him there came a comrade of divine Herakles.
line_details.greek: Σὺν δέ οἱ ἦλθ' ἕταρος Ἡρακλέεος θείοιο
line_details.note: “theios” (divine/godlike) is a conventional epic epithet; “hetairos” = comrade, here identifying Hylas as the companion of Herakles.

text.english: the fair Hylas; over his dewy chin not yet had the soft first-down reddened his bright cheeks, but he was still a boy, and he greatly pleased Herakles.
text.greek: καλὸς Ὕλας· τὸν δ' οὔπω ὑπὲρ δροσεροῖο γενείου ἀργεννὰς ἐρύθηνε παρηίδας ἁβρὸς ἴουλος, ἀλλ' ἔτι κοῦρος ἔην, πολὺ δ' ἤνδανεν Ἡρακλῆϊ.

line_details.english: the fair Hylas; over his dewy chin not yet
line_details.greek: καλὸς Ὕλας· τὸν δ' οὔπω ὑπὲρ δροσεροῖο γενείου
line_details.note: “droseros” (dewy) evokes the youthful bloom; “geneion” = chin.

line_details.english: had the soft first-down reddened his bright cheeks,
line_details.greek: ἀργεννὰς ἐρύθηνε παρηίδας ἁβρὸς ἴουλος,
line_details.note: “ioulos” is the first growth of beard (soft down); “argennas” means bright/silvery-white; the verb “eruthēne” (‘reddened’) takes the down as subject reddening the cheeks.

line_details.english: but he was still a boy, and he greatly pleased Herakles.
line_details.greek: ἀλλ' ἔτι κοῦρος ἔην, πολὺ δ' ἤνδανεν Ἡρακλῆϊ.
line_details.note: “kouros” denotes a youth/adolescent; “ēndanen” means ‘pleased, delighted.’

text.english: These men, for their part, assembled at the ship and went into ambush.
text.greek: - Οὗτοι μὲν ποτὶ νῆα καὶ ἐς λόχον ἠγερέθοντο.

line_details.english: These men, for their part, assembled at the ship and went into ambush.
line_details.greek: - Οὗτοι μὲν ποτὶ νῆα καὶ ἐς λόχον ἠγερέθοντο.
line_details.note: λόχος here is the epic ‘ambush’/‘hiding-place’ (not ‘childbirth’); ἠγερέθοντο is an intransitive/middle aorist ‘gathered/assembled (themselves)’; ποτὶ = epic πρός ‘toward/at’. The single verb governs both prepositional phrases, indicating they mustered by the ship and took up a concealed position.

text.english: And then from every side one after another would call to him and speak.
text.greek: Καί ῥά οἱ ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος ἐκέκλετο ἠδ' ἀγόρευε.

line_details.english: And then from every side one after another would call to him and speak.
line_details.greek: Καί ῥά οἱ ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος ἐκέκλετο ἠδ' ἀγόρευε.
line_details.note: ῥά marks transition (“and then”); ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is a distributive idiom (“from one side and another,” hence “from every side”), with the singular implying successive speakers. ἐκέκλετο is the imperfect middle of κέλομαι (“call upon, bid, exhort”) used with the dative οἱ (“to him”); ἀγόρευε (impf. of ἀγορεύω) conveys formal public speaking. The imperfects suggest repeated or continued action: men addressed him in turn.

text.english: And they were preparing the feasts of the all‑hospitable board, But when the heart had had its fill of food and of drink, sitting in order, each man longed for the great enterprise.
text.greek: Δεῖπνα δ' ἐπορσύνοντο πολυξείνοιο τραπέζης, Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σίτοιο ποτοῦ θ' ἅλις ἔπλετο θυμός, ἥμενοι ἑξείης πόθεεν μέγα ἔργον ἕκαστος.

line_details.english: And they were preparing the feasts of the all‑hospitable board,
line_details.greek: Δεῖπνα δ' ἐπορσύνοντο πολυξείνοιο τραπέζης,
line_details.note: πολυξείνιος (“much-guesting, all-hospitable”) marks the epic tone of generous reception; τραπέζης in the genitive is descriptive (“of the board”). ἐπορσύνω (mid.) = “make ready, set out.”

line_details.english: But when the heart had had its fill of food and of drink,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σίτοιο ποτοῦ θ' ἅλις ἔπλετο θυμός,
line_details.note: θυμός ἅλις ἔπλετο is a Homeric idiom for being satisfied; σῖτος = staple food, ποτός = drink (not necessarily specifically wine).

line_details.english: sitting in order, each man longed for the great enterprise.
line_details.greek: ἥμενοι ἑξείης πόθεεν μέγα ἔργον ἕκαστος.
line_details.note: ἑξείης = “in order, in a row.” πόθεεν (imperfect) conveys sustained yearning. μέγα ἔργον (“great work/deed”) refers to the Argonautic enterprise.

text.english: And rising up all together from the deep sand, they went to where the sea-faring ship was waiting upon the sand, which, as they gazed upon it, they marveled at; but thereafter Argos, with counsels of his mind, made ready the heaving, with wooden rollers and well-twisted cables, having made them fast from the stern. And he called on them to come to the toil, honoring them all. They eagerly obeyed; they stripped off their armor and about their breasts they fastened a rope-thong harness. And each leaned his weight straightway to haul the swift, well-voiced Argō toward the wave.
text.greek: Ἀνστάντες δ' ἅμα πάντες ἀπὸ ψαμάθοιο βαθείης ἤϊον, ἔνθά τ' ἔμιμνεν ὑπὲρ ψαμάθου ἁλίη ναῦς, τήν ῥά ποτ' εἰσορόωντες ἐθάμβεον· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα Ἄργος ἐφημοσύναισι νόου πόρσυνεν ὀχλίζειν, δουρατέαισι φάλαγξι καὶ εὐστρέπτοισι κάλωσι πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσας. Κάλεεν δ' ἐπὶ μόχθον ἱκάνειν πάντας κυδαίνων. Οἱ δ' ἐσσυμένως ὑπάκουσαν· τεύχεα δ' ἐκδύνοντο, περὶ στέρνοισι δ' ἀνῆπτον σειραίην μήρινθον. Ἐπέβριθεν δ' ἄρ' ἕκαστος αἶψα θοὸν ποτὶ κῦμα κατειρύσαι εὔλαλον Ἀργώ.

line_details.english: And rising up all together from the deep sand,
line_details.greek: Ἀνστάντες δ' ἅμα πάντες ἀπὸ ψαμάθοιο βαθείης
line_details.note: ἀνστάντες is an epic/orthographic variant of ἀναστάντες; ψαμάθοιο βαθείης = “deep beach-sand.”

line_details.english: they went to where the sea-faring ship was waiting upon the sand,
line_details.greek: ἤϊον, ἔνθά τ' ἔμιμνεν ὑπὲρ ψαμάθου ἁλίη ναῦς,
line_details.note: ἤϊον is the epic imperfect of εἶμι (“went”); ἁλίη ναῦς “sea-faring ship”; ὑπὲρ ψαμάθου indicates the ship is beached.

line_details.english: which, as they gazed upon it, they marveled at; but thereafter
line_details.greek: τήν ῥά ποτ' εἰσορόωντες ἐθάμβεον· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
line_details.note: τήν refers to the ship; ποτ’ can suggest “at times/once”; the imperfect ἐθάμβεον gives an iterative sense (“as they looked, they would marvel”).

line_details.english: Argos, with counsels of his mind, made ready the heaving,
line_details.greek: Ἄργος ἐφημοσύναισι νόου πόρσυνεν ὀχλίζειν,
line_details.note: Ἄργος is the builder of the ship; ἐφημοσύναις νόου = “by instructions/counsels of his mind”; ὀχλίζειν is a technical term for “heave” (set in motion with levers).

line_details.english: with wooden rollers and well-twisted cables,
line_details.greek: δουρατέαισι φάλαγξι καὶ εὐστρέπτοισι κάλωσι
line_details.note: δουρατέαισι φάλαγξι are wooden rollers; εὐστρέπτοις κάλωσι are well-twisted cables/ropes.

line_details.english: having made them fast from the stern. And he called on them to come to the toil,
line_details.greek: πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσας. Κάλεεν δ' ἐπὶ μόχθον ἱκάνειν
line_details.note: πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσας = “having made (the gear) fast from the stern,” i.e., attaching ropes/cables at the stern before the launch.

line_details.english: honoring them all. They eagerly obeyed;
line_details.greek: πάντας κυδαίνων. Οἱ δ' ἐσσυμένως ὑπάκουσαν·
line_details.note: κυδαίνων literally “honoring, exalting,” here “encouraging with praise.”

line_details.english: they stripped off their armor and about their breasts they fastened
line_details.greek: τεύχεα δ' ἐκδύνοντο, περὶ στέρνοισι δ' ἀνῆπτον

line_details.english: a rope-thong harness. And each leaned his weight
line_details.greek: σειραίην μήρινθον. Ἐπέβριθεν δ' ἄρ' ἕκαστος
line_details.note: σειραίην μήρινθον is a rare phrase for a rope-thong harness used for hauling; ἐπέβριθεν = “leaned/bore his weight (on it).”

line_details.english: straightway to haul the swift, well-voiced Argō toward the wave.
line_details.greek: αἶψα θοὸν ποτὶ κῦμα κατειρύσαι εὔλαλον Ἀργώ.
line_details.note: εὔλαλος (“well-voiced”) alludes to Argō’s speaking timber from Dodona; κατειρύσαι = “to draw/haul down” toward the sea.

text.english: But she, wedged into the sand, had grown heavy for him, being held fast toward the dry land by withered sea‑wrack, unyielding beneath the sturdy palms of the heroes.
text.greek: Ἣ δέ οἱ ἐγχριφθεῖσα ποτὶ ψαμάθῳ βεβάρητο, αὐαλέοις φυκέεσσιν ἐρυκομένη ποτὶ χέρσῳ ἡρώων παλάμῃσιν ὑπὸ στιβαρῇσιν ἀπειθής.

line_details.english: But she, wedged into the sand, had grown heavy for him,
line_details.greek: Ἣ δέ οἱ ἐγχριφθεῖσα ποτὶ ψαμάθῳ βεβάρητο,
line_details.note: ἐγχριφθεῖσα is a rare/passive aorist participle (manuscripts vary: ἐγχριφθεῖσα/ἐγκριφθεῖσα) probably from ἐγκρῖπτω “to jam/wedge in”; hence “wedged.” The enclitic οἱ is a dative of interest (“for him”), likely referring to the leader (Jason). The subject “she” is the ship (Argo).

line_details.english: being held fast toward the dry land by withered sea‑wrack,
line_details.greek: αὐαλέοις φυκέεσσιν ἐρυκομένη ποτὶ χέρσῳ
line_details.note: αὐαλέοις = “dry, withered”; φυκέεσσιν = “seaweeds/sea‑wrack.” ποτὶ χέρσῳ is the epic preposition ποτί with χέρσος “dry land,” here “toward/against the shore.” ἐρυκομένη = “being held back/restrained.”

line_details.english: unyielding beneath the sturdy palms of the heroes.
line_details.greek: ἡρώων παλάμῃσιν ὑπὸ στιβαρῇσιν ἀπειθής.
line_details.note: ἀπειθής here means “unyielding, stubborn” rather than moral “disobedient.” ὑπό with the dative (παλάμῃσιν… στιβαρῇσιν) conveys resistance “beneath/under” their strong hands.

text.english: And Jason’s spirit grew chill again; but to me, indeed, he nodded, casting a glance at me, that for him courage and might I might ever rouse by my song in the wearied.
text.greek: Παχνώθη δ' αὖ θυμὸς Ἰάσονος· αὐτὰρ ἔμοιγε νεῦσεν ὀπιπτεύων ἵνα οἱ θάρσος τε βίην τε μολπῇ ὑφ' ἡμετέρῃ κεκμηόσιν αἰὲν ὁρίνω.

line_details.english: And Jason’s spirit grew chill again; but to me, indeed,
line_details.greek: Παχνώθη δ' αὖ θυμὸς Ἰάσονος· αὐτὰρ ἔμοιγε
line_details.note: Παχνώθη (“was frosted, grew chill”) is a vivid metaphor of fear or discouragement; ἔμοιγε is an emphatic dative (“to me indeed”).

line_details.english: he nodded, casting a glance at me, that for him courage and might
line_details.greek: νεῦσεν ὀπιπτεύων ἵνα οἱ θάρσος τε βίην τε
line_details.note: ὀπιπτεύων = “watching closely, glancing toward”; νεῦσεν “he nodded” as a signal; ἵνα introduces a purpose clause.

line_details.english: I might ever rouse by my song in the wearied.
line_details.greek: μολπῇ ὑφ' ἡμετέρῃ κεκμηόσιν αἰὲν ὁρίνω.
line_details.note: μολπῇ ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃ = “by my song,” with ἡμετέρῃ the poetic plural for “my”; ὁρίνω governs accusatives (θάρσος, βίην) with a dative of the persons affected (κεκμηόσιν “the wearied [men]”); οἱ is an ethical dative “for him (Jason).”

text.english: But I, shaking the phorminx in my hands, blended in my mother’s delightful adornment of song, and from my breast I brought forth for them a lily-like voice; “Illustrious Minyan blood of the Heroes’ lineage, come now, set the hawsers beneath your firm breasts bear down in unison, and brace your footprints in the earth, with your soles, stretching far out the extremity of the foot; and, rejoicing, haul the ship toward the gleaming surge.” Argo, pegged with pines and oaks, hearken to my voice; for even before you hearkened, when I was bewitching the trees on a wooded knoll and the pathless rocks, and for my sake you went over the sea, leaving the mountains far behind, and again you followed the virgin tracks of the sea; make haste to reach the Phasis, trusting in my kithara and my god-wrought utterance.” Then the Tomarian oak, booming aloft, obeyed the call, the one which Argos set as the keelson for the black ship, at Pallas’ instigation; and she was very quickly lifted up, lightening her timbers, and swift she slid upon the sea; and as she pressed on she scattered the close-packed rollers which lay beneath her keel, held taut by a single rope.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ φόρμιγγα τιτηνάμενος μετὰ χερσί, μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἐκέρασσ' εὐτερπέα κόσμον ἀοιδῆς, καί οἱ ἀπὸ στηθέων ὄπα λείριον ἐξελόχευσα· - "Ἔξοχον Ἡρώων Μινυήιον αἷμα γενέθλης, εἰ δ' ἄγε νῦν στερροῖσιν ὑπὸ στέρνοισι κάλωας βρίσαθ' ὁμορροθέοντες, ἐρείσατε δ' ἴχνια γαίῃ ταρσοῖσιν ποδὸς ἄκρον ὑπερβλήδην τανύσαντες· καὶ χαροπὸν ποτὶ χεῦμα γεγηθότες ἕλξατε νῆα. - Ἀργὼ πεύκῃσιν τ' ἠδὲ δρυσὶ γομφωθεῖσα ἄι' ἐμῆς ἐνοπῆς καὶ γὰρ πάρος ἔκλυες ἤδη ἡνίκα δένδρε' ἔθελγον ἐν ὑλήεντι κολώνῃ πέτρας τ' ἠλιβάτους, καί μοι κατὰ πόντον ἔβαινες οὔρε' ἀποπρολιποῦσα, ἐπέσπεο δ' αὖτε θαλάσσης παρθενίης ἀτραπούς· σπέρχου δ' ἐπὶ Φᾶσιν ἀμείβειν, ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ καὶ θεσκέλῳ ὀμφῇ." - Δὴ τότ' ἐπιβρομέουσα Τομαριὰς ἔκλυε φηγός ἥν οἱ ὑποτροπίην Ἄργος θέτο νηῒ μελαίνῃ Παλλάδος ἐννεσίῃσιν· ἀνηέρθη δὲ μάλ' ὦκα δούρατ' ἐλαφρίζουσα, θοὴ δ' ὠλίσθανε πόντῳ· καί οἱ ἐπειγομένη θαμινὰς ἐκέδασσε φάλαγγας

line_details.english: But I, shaking the phorminx in my hands,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ φόρμιγγα τιτηνάμενος μετὰ χερσί,
line_details.note: phorminx: the epic lyre; τιτηνάμενος = “brandishing, vibrating.”

line_details.english: blended in my mother’s delightful adornment of song,
line_details.greek: μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἐκέρασσ' εὐτερπέα κόσμον ἀοιδῆς,
line_details.note: ἐκέρασσ’ (from κεράννυμι) “I mixed/tempered”; κόσμον ἀοιδῆς = the “order/adornment of song.” “My mother” is Kalliope, implying Orpheus’ Muse-taught craft.

line_details.english: and from my breast I brought forth for them a lily-like voice;
line_details.greek: καί οἱ ἀπὸ στηθέων ὄπα λείριον ἐξελόχευσα·
line_details.note: λείριον “lily-like” marks delicacy; ἐξελόχευσα (from λοχεύω) literally “I brought to birth,” i.e., “I delivered” a voice; οἱ = “for them,” the Argonauts.

line_details.english: “Illustrious Minyan blood of the Heroes’ lineage,
line_details.greek: - "Ἔξοχον Ἡρώων Μινυήιον αἷμα γενέθλης,
line_details.note: Μινυήιον “Minyan” (the Argonauts as Minyae); Ἡρώων “of Heroes”; αἷμα γενέθλης = “blood of birth/lineage”; ἔξοχον = “preeminent, illustrious.”

line_details.english: come now, set the hawsers beneath your firm breasts
line_details.greek: εἰ δ' ἄγε νῦν στερροῖσιν ὑπὸ στέρνοισι κάλωας
line_details.note: κάλωας = ship’s cables/hawsers; στερροῖσιν στέρνοισι “firm/stout breasts” reflects the hauling technique of passing the rope under the chest; εἶ δ’ ἄγε = idiomatic “come now.”

line_details.english: bear down in unison, and brace your footprints in the earth,
line_details.greek: βρίσαθ' ὁμορροθέοντες, ἐρείσατε δ' ἴχνια γαίῃ
line_details.note: βρίσαθ’ (aor. mid. imper.) = “bear/press down”; ὁμορροθέοντες = “moving/straining in concert”; ἐρείσατε = “brace, set firm.”

line_details.english: with your soles, stretching far out the extremity of the foot;
line_details.greek: ταρσοῖσιν ποδὸς ἄκρον ὑπερβλήδην τανύσαντες·
line_details.note: ταρσοῖσιν = “with the soles (of the feet)”; ποδὸς ἄκρον = “the extremity of the foot,” i.e., the toes; ὑπερβλήδην = “exceedingly, far out,” describing the hauling stance.

line_details.english: and, rejoicing, haul the ship toward the gleaming surge.”
line_details.greek: καὶ χαροπὸν ποτὶ χεῦμα γεγηθότες ἕλξατε νῆα.
line_details.note: χαροπὸν χεῦμα = “gleaming/bright surge (of the sea)”; ἕλξατε = “haul, drag”; γεγηθότες = “rejoicing.”

line_details.english: Argo, pegged with pines and oaks,
line_details.greek: - Ἀργὼ πεύκῃσιν τ' ἠδὲ δρυσὶ γομφωθεῖσα
line_details.note: “gomphōtheisa” = ‘pegged/dowelled together,’ i.e., mortise-and-tenon joinery; peukai/dryes are the ship’s pine and oak timbers.

line_details.english: hearken to my voice; for even before you hearkened,
line_details.greek: ἄι' ἐμῆς ἐνοπῆς καὶ γὰρ πάρος ἔκλυες ἤδη
line_details.note: “ἄι’” is the imperative of ἀίω, ‘hear!’; ἔκλυες can imply ‘heard and obeyed.’

line_details.english: when I was bewitching the trees on a wooded knoll
line_details.greek: ἡνίκα δένδρε' ἔθελγον ἐν ὑλήεντι κολώνῃ
line_details.note: “ἔθελγον” (θέλγω) ‘enchant/bewitch’; “κολώνη” = low wooded hill/knoll—Orphic topos of trees moved by song.

line_details.english: and the pathless rocks, and for my sake you went over the sea,
line_details.greek: πέτρας τ' ἠλιβάτους, καί μοι κατὰ πόντον ἔβαινες
line_details.note: “ἠλιβάτους” = ‘untraversable/steep, pathless’; “κατὰ πόντον ἔβαινες” ‘you went over/onto the sea.’

line_details.english: leaving the mountains far behind, and again you followed the
line_details.greek: οὔρε' ἀποπρολιποῦσα, ἐπέσπεο δ' αὖτε θαλάσσης
line_details.note: “ἀποπρολιποῦσα” intensifies ‘leaving far behind’; Argo is personified as responding to the singer.

line_details.english: virgin tracks of the sea; make haste to reach the Phasis,
line_details.greek: παρθενίης ἀτραπούς· σπέρχου δ' ἐπὶ Φᾶσιν ἀμείβειν,
line_details.note: “παρθενίης ἀτραπούς” ‘virgin paths,’ i.e., unsailed sea-routes; “Φᾶσιν” = the Colchian river Phasis.

line_details.english: trusting in my kithara and my god-wrought utterance.”
line_details.greek: ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ καὶ θεσκέλῳ ὀμφῇ."
line_details.note: “πίσυνος” = ‘trusting, relying on’; “θεσκέλῳ ὀμφῇ” = ‘marvellous/divine (or oracular) voice/utterance’ (ὀμφή often has an oracular nuance).

line_details.english: Then the Tomarian oak, booming aloft, obeyed the call,
line_details.greek: - Δὴ τότ' ἐπιβρομέουσα Τομαριὰς ἔκλυε φηγός
line_details.note: “Τομαριὰς φηγός” = the oak of Tomaros, i.e., the Dodonaean oak; “ἐπιβρομέουσα” ‘booming/rumbling,’ echoing Zeus’ thunder; “ἤκλυε” = ‘hearkened/obeyed.’

line_details.english: the one which Argos set as the keelson for the black ship, at Pallas’ instigation;
line_details.greek: ἥν οἱ ὑποτροπίην Ἄργος θέτο νηῒ μελαίνῃ
line_details.note: “ὑποτροπίην” is a debated shipbuilding term; here taken as ‘keelson’ (an internal longitudinal timber), though some take it as an ‘under-keel’ fitting; Argos installs it by Pallas’ counsel.

line_details.english: and she was very quickly lifted up, lightening her timbers, and swift she slid upon the sea;
line_details.greek: Παλλάδος ἐννεσίῃσιν· ἀνηέρθη δὲ μάλ' ὦκα
line_details.note: “ἀνηέρθη” ‘was lifted (for launch)’; “δούρατ’ ἐλαφρίζουσα” ‘making her timbers light,’ i.e., buoyed as she takes the water.

line_details.english: and as she pressed on she scattered the close-packed rollers
line_details.greek: δούρατ' ἐλαφρίζουσα, θοὴ δ' ὠλίσθανε πόντῳ·
line_details.note: “φάλαγγες” here most plausibly ‘rollers’ (or ‘chocks’) used under the hull during launching; “ἐκέδασσε” ‘scattered, broke apart.’

line_details.english: which lay beneath her keel, held taut by a single rope.
line_details.greek: καί οἱ ἐπειγομένη θαμινὰς ἐκέδασσε φάλαγγας
line_details.note: “ὑπὸ τρόπι” = ‘beneath the keel’; “μιᾶς σχοίνιοιο ταθεῖσαι” ‘stretched/held taut by a single rope,’ i.e., lashings binding the rollers/chocks together.

text.english: [Translation missing] And in she went, and the grim wave of the harbor recoiled.
text.greek: αἵ οἱ ὑπὸ τρόπι κεῖντο μιᾶς σχοίνοιο ταθεῖσαι. Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἔβη, λιμένος χαροπὸν δ' ἀνεχάσσατο κῦμα·

line_details.english: [Translation missing]
line_details.greek: αἵ οἱ ὑπὸ τρόπι κεῖντο μιᾶς σχοίνοιο ταθεῖσαι.

line_details.english: And in she went, and the grim wave of the harbor recoiled.
line_details.greek: Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἔβη, λιμένος χαροπὸν δ' ἀνεχάσσατο κῦμα·
line_details.note: “She” = the ship (neōs). “χαροπὸν” is rendered “grim,” a common epic epithet; the wave is personified as it “drew back” (ἀνεχάσσατο).

text.english: And the sandbanks were washed all around; and Jason’s heart rejoiced.
text.greek: Θῖνες δ' ἀμφέκλυσθεν· ἐγήθει δὲ φρέν' Ἰήσων,

line_details.english: And the sandbanks were washed all around; and Jason’s heart rejoiced.
line_details.greek: Θῖνες δ' ἀμφέκλυσθεν· ἐγήθει δὲ φρέν' Ἰήσων,
line_details.note: Θῖνες are shore‑sands/sandbanks; ἀμφέκλυσθεν (“were washed all around”) evokes the surge on both sides as the ship enters.

text.english: And he leapt inside the ship Argo, and Tiphys followed close at hand.
text.greek: ἆλτο δ' ἔσω νεὸς Ἄργος, ἐφέσπετο δ' ἀγχόθι Τῖφυς

line_details.english: And he leapt inside the ship Argo, and Tiphys followed close at hand.
line_details.greek: ἆλτο δ' ἔσω νεὸς Ἄργος, ἐφέσπετο δ' ἀγχόθι Τῖφυς
line_details.note: Subject of ἆλτο is Jason from the preceding hemistich; νεὸς Ἄργος = “the ship Argo” (not Argus the builder).

text.english: And for him they set the well‑fitted tackle, making all things ready, the mast and the sail‑cloths; and thereon they bound the sheets, fastening them from the stern, and they tightened them with thongs.
text.greek: καί οἱ ἐπάρτια θῆκαν ἀρηρότα πορσύνοντες, ἱστόν τ' ἠδ' ὀθόνας· ἐπὶ δ' αὖτ' οἴηκας ἔδησαν, πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσαντες, ἐπεσφίγξαντο δ' ἱμᾶσιν.

line_details.english: And for him they set the well‑fitted tackle, making all things ready,
line_details.greek: καί οἱ ἐπάρτια θῆκαν ἀρηρότα πορσύνοντες,
line_details.note: ἐπάρτια = “tackle/rigging”; ἀρηρότα (from ἀραρίσκω) = “well‑fitted”; πορσύνειν = “to get things ready, equip.”

line_details.english: the mast and the sail‑cloths; and thereon they bound the sheets,
line_details.greek: ἱστόν τ' ἠδ' ὀθόνας· ἐπὶ δ' αὖτ' οἴηκας ἔδησαν,
line_details.note: ὀθόνες are the sail‑cloths. οἴηκες is best taken as “sheets/braces” (sail‑ropes); some manuscripts read οἴακες (“tiller‑handles”), but the context favors sheets.

line_details.english: fastening them from the stern, and they tightened them with thongs.
line_details.greek: πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσαντες, ἐπεσφίγξαντο δ' ἱμᾶσιν.
line_details.note: πρυμνόθεν (“from the stern”) suits sheets led aft; ἐπεσφίγξαντο (“they tightened fast”) with ἱμᾶσιν (“thongs/straps”) describes the lashings.

text.english: But then they ran out the oars on either side, and they bade the Minyae to embark in eager haste.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔπειθ' ἑκάτερθεν ἐρετμοὺς ἡπλώσαντο, εἰσβαίνειν δ' ἐκέλευον ἐπειγομένους Μινύηας.

line_details.english: But then they ran out the oars on either side,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔπειθ' ἑκάτερθεν ἐρετμοὺς ἡπλώσαντο,
line_details.note: ἡπλώσαντο (aor. mid. of ἁπλόω) has a nautical sense: “to run out/lay out” the oars into rowing position; ἑκάτερθεν = “on both sides (of the ship).”

line_details.english: and they bade the Minyae to embark in eager haste.
line_details.greek: εἰσβαίνειν δ' ἐκέλευον ἐπειγομένους Μινύηας.
line_details.note: Μινύηας (“Minyae”) is an epic designation for the Argonauts (descendants of Minyas); ἐπειγομένους is a circumstantial participle, “in haste/eagerly.”

text.english: Then to them Aisonides spoke winged words: “Hear me, blameless kings; for to me indeed it does not please my heart to lord it over my betters.” But you, whomever your heart and spirit may desire, appoint as leader; and it shall be his to care for all things, to indicate what is to be done, in word and in deed, to those who will sail over the sea and to those who will come to the land, whether to the Colchians or to alien men.
text.greek: τοῖσιν δ' Αἰσονίδης ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα· - "Κέκλυτέ μευ, βασιλῆες ἀμύμονες, οὐ γὰρ ἔμοιγε ἁνδάνει ἐν πραπίδεσσιν ἀρειοτέροισιν ἀνάσσειν. Ὑμεῖς δ', ὅντιν' ἄρα κραδίη θυμὸς τε μενοινᾷ ἡγεμόνα στήσασθε· καὶ ᾧ περὶ πάντα μελήσει σημανέειν ὅ τι κεν ῥέξαι ἔπος ἠδὲ καὶ ἔργον πόντον ἐπιπλώσουσιν ἀφιξομένοις τ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν, εἴτε καὶ ἐς Κόλχους καὶ ἐς ἀλλοδαποὺς ἀνθρώπους.

line_details.english: Then to them Aisonides spoke winged words:
line_details.greek: τοῖσιν δ' Αἰσονίδης ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
line_details.note: “Aisonides” = Jason; “winged words” is the traditional epic formula for swift speech.

line_details.english: “Hear me, blameless kings; for to me indeed
line_details.greek: - "Κέκλυτέ μευ, βασιλῆες ἀμύμονες, οὐ γὰρ ἔμοιγε
line_details.note: Keklyte meu: meu (“of me”) is idiomatic for “hear me”; amymones (“blameless”) is a standard epic epithet of nobles/kings.

line_details.english: it does not please my heart to lord it over my betters.”
line_details.greek: ἁνδάνει ἐν πραπίδεσσιν ἀρειοτέροισιν ἀνάσσειν.
line_details.note: Prapides (“midriff, heart”) denotes the seat of thought; areioterosin is “better, nobler, stronger” (dative plural). Anassein usually governs the genitive “rule over,” but epic also shows a dative; sense: Jason declines to rule over those superior to him.

line_details.english: But you, whomever your heart and spirit may desire,
line_details.greek: Ὑμεῖς δ', ὅντιν' ἄρα κραδίη θυμὸς τε μενοινᾷ
line_details.note: κραδίη θυμὸς τε (“heart and spirit”) forms a paired subject treated as a unit; μενοινᾷ is the optative (“may desire”), expressing potentiality in this exhortation. The particle ἄρα is inferential and not translated.

line_details.english: appoint as leader; and it shall be his to care for all things,
line_details.greek: ἡγεμόνα στήσασθε· καὶ ᾧ περὶ πάντα μελήσει
line_details.note: ᾧ … μελήσει: dative with (impersonal) μέλει, “it will be a care to him,” hence “it shall be his to care for all things.”

line_details.english: to indicate what is to be done, in word and in deed,
line_details.greek: σημανέειν ὅ τι κεν ῥέξαι ἔπος ἠδὲ καὶ ἔργον
line_details.note: σημανέειν is the epic/Ionic infinitive of σημαίνω, “to indicate, give the signal.” ῥέξαι (“to do, perform”) with the formula ἔπος ἠδὲ καὶ ἔργον yields the idiom “in word and in deed.”

line_details.english: to those who will sail over the sea and to those who will come to the land,
line_details.greek: πόντον ἐπιπλώσουσιν ἀφιξομένοις τ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν,
line_details.note: πόντον ἐπιπλώσουσιν and ἀφιξομένοις are dative plural future participles dependent on σημανέειν, indicating the recipients: “to those who will sail … and to those who will come …,” not finite verbs.

line_details.english: whether to the Colchians or to alien men.
line_details.greek: εἴτε καὶ ἐς Κόλχους καὶ ἐς ἀλλοδαποὺς ἀνθρώπους.
line_details.note: εἴτε καὶ … καὶ here has the sense of “whether … or …”; ἀλλοδαπούς = “foreign, alien.” “Colchians” names the specific destination of the voyage.

text.english: For indeed you alone, with me, both many and noble, who even boast yourselves a race from an immortal root, take up the common toil, that you may win glory.
text.greek: Καὶ γὰρ δὴ μοῦνοι σὺν ἐμοὶ πόλεες τε καὶ ἐσθλοί, οἵ ῥα καὶ ἀθανάτου ῥίζης γένος εὐχετάασθε, ξυνὸν ἀνηρείψασθε πόνον, κλέος ὄφρ' ἂν ἄροισθε.

line_details.english: For indeed you alone, with me, both many and noble,
line_details.greek: Καὶ γὰρ δὴ μοῦνοι σὺν ἐμοὶ πόλεες τε καὶ ἐσθλοί,
line_details.note: πόλεες is the Homeric form for “many”; the nominative can function vocatively in epic. μοῦνοι σὺν ἐμοί = “you alone together with me,” marking exclusivity; the finite verb is supplied by the following relative clause.

line_details.english: who even boast yourselves a race from an immortal root,
line_details.greek: οἵ ῥα καὶ ἀθανάτου ῥίζης γένος εὐχετάασθε,
line_details.note: εὐχετάασθε is a deponent “to boast/claim.” ῥίζης (“root”) is a genealogical metaphor; ἀθανάτου ῥίζης = divine/immortal descent.

line_details.english: take up the common toil, that you may win glory.
line_details.greek: ξυνὸν ἀνηρείψασθε πόνον, κλέος ὄφρ' ἂν ἄροισθε.
line_details.note: ξυνόν is the epic form of κοινόν (“common, shared”). ἀνηρείψασθε means “lift up/undertake.” ὄφρ’ ἄν with the aorist subjunctive ἄροισθε (of ἀρνύμαι, “win, gain for yourselves”) expresses purpose: “so that you may win.”

text.english: But surely I do not suppose it possible to become mightier and more warlike— —than lord Herakles; you yourselves know it as well.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐ δὴ κάρτιστον ἀρειότερόν τε γενέσθαι Ἡρακλῆος ἄνακτος ὀΐομαι· ἴστε καὶ αὐτοί."

line_details.english: But surely I do not suppose it possible to become mightier and more warlike—
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐ δὴ κάρτιστον ἀρειότερόν τε γενέσθαι
line_details.note: κάρτιστον ἀρειότερον τε γενέσθαι: neuter adjectives used predicatively with the infinitive; understood subject ‘anyone.’ The comparison is completed by the genitive in the next line.

line_details.english: —than lord Herakles; you yourselves know it as well.
line_details.greek: Ἡρακλῆος ἄνακτος ὀΐομαι· ἴστε καὶ αὐτοί."
line_details.note: Ἡρακλῆος ἄνακτος: genitive of comparison with ἀρειότερον; ἄναξ ‘lord’ in epic style.

text.english: Thus he spoke, and they all approved; and with one voice the people roared aloud, that there be an overlord over the Minyai, Alkeidēs, who was by far preeminent among all the comrades.
text.greek: - Ὣς ἔφαθ', οἱ δ' ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον· ἐν δ' ἄρα φωνῇ λαὸς ἐπερρόθεεν, Μινύαις ἐπικοίρανον εἶναι Ἀλκείδην, ὃς πᾶσι μέγ' ἔξοχος ἦεν ἑταίροις.

line_details.english: Thus he spoke, and they all approved; and with one voice
line_details.greek: - Ὣς ἔφαθ', οἱ δ' ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον· ἐν δ' ἄρα φωνῇ
line_details.note: ἐν δ’ ἄρα φωνῇ is an idiom meaning ‘with one voice/in a single shout.’

line_details.english: the people roared aloud, that there be an overlord over the Minyai,
line_details.greek: λαὸς ἐπερρόθεεν, Μινύαις ἐπικοίρανον εἶναι
line_details.note: ἐπερρόθεεν ‘roared, thundered’ (onomatopoetic). ἐπίκοιρανος ‘one set in command, overlord’; here with infinitive εἶναι, the subject supplied in the next line.

line_details.english: Alkeidēs, who was by far preeminent among all the comrades.
line_details.greek: Ἀλκείδην, ὃς πᾶσι μέγ' ἔξοχος ἦεν ἑταίροις.
line_details.note: Ἀλκείδης is the patronymic of Herakles (‘descendant of Alkeus’). μέγ’ ἔξοχος = ‘by far preeminent’ (μέγα intensifies the adjective).

text.english: But they did not persuade the prudent lord, who indeed knew the son of Aison to be honored by Hera’s counsels, inasmuch as she was bestowing on him noble renown among those yet to come; for he himself declared that Iason should be commander of the fifty oarsmen, over the dry and the wet.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐ πεῖθον ἄνακτα πεπνυμένον, ὅς ῥά οἱ ᾔδη Ἥρης ἐννεσίῃσι τετιμένον Αἴσονος υἱόν, ὥς δή οἱ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἐπεσσομένοισιν ὄπαζεν· ὡς ῥά οἱ αὐτὸς ἔνισπεν, Ἰήσονα κοίρανον εἶναι πεντήκοντ' ἐρέταισιν, ἀνὰ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν.

line_details.english: But they did not persuade the prudent lord, who indeed knew
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐ πεῖθον ἄνακτα πεπνυμένον, ὅς ῥά οἱ ᾔδη
line_details.note: “the prudent lord” is likely Herakles in context (the crew urge him to lead, but he refuses). The enclitic oi here functions as an ethical dative (“for his part”).

line_details.english: the son of Aison to be honored by Hera’s counsels,
line_details.greek: Ἥρης ἐννεσίῃσι τετιμένον Αἴσονος υἱόν,
line_details.note: ennesiēsi (“counsels, instigations, inspirations”) denotes divine prompting; “the son of Aison” is Jason.

line_details.english: inasmuch as she was bestowing on him noble renown among those yet to come;
line_details.greek: ὥς δή οἱ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἐπεσσομένοισιν ὄπαζεν·
line_details.note: epessomenois (“those who will come after”) is a Homeric formula for posterity; “bestowing … noble renown” renders kleos esthlon … opazen (imperfect, ongoing).

line_details.english: for he himself declared that Iason should be commander
line_details.greek: ὡς ῥά οἱ αὐτὸς ἔνισπεν, Ἰήσονα κοίρανον εἶναι
line_details.note: enispen (“declared, told”); the subject remains the same “lord” (Herakles), who proclaims Jason leader. The dative oi may be merely ethical.

line_details.english: of the fifty oarsmen, over the dry and the wet.
line_details.greek: πεντήκοντ' ἐρέταισιν, ἀνὰ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν.
line_details.note: “over the dry and the wet” is an epic periphrasis for “by land and by sea” (elliptic for “earth and sea”); pentēkont’ eretaisin = “fifty oarsmen,” i.e., the Argonauts.

text.english: And then indeed all greatly approved, as Herakles bade, and they appointed Iason to be commander.
text.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ μάλα πάντες ἐπῄνεον, ὡς ἐκέλευεν Ἡρακλέης, καὶ θῆκαν Ἰήσονα κοίρανον εἶναι.

line_details.english: And then indeed all greatly approved, as Herakles bade,
line_details.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ μάλα πάντες ἐπῄνεον, ὡς ἐκέλευεν
line_details.note: ἐπῄνεον (“approved, endorsed”) is an imperfect used narratively; ὡς ἐκέλευεν Ἡρακλέης means “in accordance with the bidding of Herakles.”

line_details.english: and they appointed Iason to be commander.
line_details.greek: Ἡρακλέης, καὶ θῆκαν Ἰήσονα κοίρανον εἶναι.
line_details.note: θῆκαν … εἶναι is a formula for appointment (“they set X to be Y”); κοίρανος is Homeric for “chieftain/commander.” Ἰήσονα is an epic/Ionic form of Ἰάσονα (Iason).

text.english: But when Helios, cleaving the boundless aether, with his swift-footed horses was bringing on black Night, then in his breast the son of Aison was devising to establish a pledge among the heroes and oaths of compacts, so that, guarding them, they might trust that all would stand fast; and then, Musaeus, dear child of Antiophemus, he bade me swiftly make ready goodly victims.
text.greek: - Ἦμος δ' ἠέλιος τὸν ἀπείριτον αἰθέρα τέμνων ἵπποις ὠκυπόδεσσι κελαινὴν ἔντυε νύκτα, τῆμος ἐνὶ πραπίδεσσιν ἐμήτιεν Αἴσονος υἱός πίστιν ἐφ' ἡρώεσσι καὶ ὅρκια συνθεσιάων θέσθαι ὄφρ' ἔμπεδα πάντα φυλασσόμενοι πεπίθοιντο· καὶ τότε τοι, Μουσαῖε, φίλον τέκος Ἀντιοφήμου, πορσύναι μ' ἐκέλευε θοῶς ἱερήϊα καλά.

line_details.english: But when Helios, cleaving the boundless aether,
line_details.greek: - Ἦμος δ' ἠέλιος τὸν ἀπείριτον αἰθέρα τέμνων

line_details.english: with his swift-footed horses was bringing on black Night,
line_details.greek: ἵπποις ὠκυπόδεσσι κελαινὴν ἔντυε νύκτα,
line_details.note: ἔντυε with νύκτα is rendered “was bringing on [Night]”; the dative ἵπποις marks the instrumental means (“with his swift‑footed horses”).

line_details.english: then in his breast the son of Aison was devising
line_details.greek: τῆμος ἐνὶ πραπίδεσσιν ἐμήτιεν Αἴσονος υἱός
line_details.note: πραπίδες = “breast, mind”; ἐμήτιεν conveys ongoing deliberation (“was devising”).

line_details.english: to establish a pledge among the heroes and oaths of compacts,
line_details.greek: πίστιν ἐφ' ἡρώεσσι καὶ ὅρκια συνθεσιάων
line_details.note: πίστιν here is a formal “pledge/assurance”; ἐπ’ ἡρώεσσι = “among/before the heroes.” συνθεσιάων (gen. pl.) = “of compacts/agreements.”

line_details.english: so that, guarding them, they might trust that all would stand fast;
line_details.greek: θέσθαι ὄφρ' ἔμπεδα πάντα φυλασσόμενοι πεπίθοιντο·
line_details.note: ἔμπεδα = “steadfast, secure.” ὄφρ’ with the optative (πεπίθοιντο) expresses purpose/result: “so that they might be assured.” The subject of πεπίθοιντο is the heroes; φυλασσόμενοι refers to keeping the pledge and oaths.

line_details.english: and then, Musaeus, dear child of Antiophemus,
line_details.greek: καὶ τότε τοι, Μουσαῖε, φίλον τέκος Ἀντιοφήμου,
line_details.note: Apostrophe to Musaeus situates the narration; Antiophemus supplies the traditional patronymic.

line_details.english: he bade me swiftly make ready goodly victims.
line_details.greek: πορσύναι μ' ἐκέλευε θοῶς ἱερήϊα καλά.
line_details.note: πορσύναι = “to get ready/provide.” ἱερήϊα are specifically sacrificial victims (not merely rites).

text.english: But I brought to the pebbly strands the timbers, those from the life‑bearing oak; and on top I set in place upon a peplos sea‑washed gifts for the gods.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ ψαφαραῖσιν ἐπ' ἠϊόνεσσιν ἐνεῖκα κᾶλα, τά τ' ἐκ δρυός ἐστι φερεσβίου· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ὕπερθε πέπλῳ παρκατέθηκα θεοῖς ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα.

line_details.english: But I brought to the pebbly strands
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ ψαφαραῖσιν ἐπ' ἠϊόνεσσιν ἐνεῖκα
line_details.note: ψαφαραῖσιν ἐπ᾽ ἠϊόνεσσιν = “on pebbly shores/strands,” a conventional epic collocation for a beach of small stones.

line_details.english: the timbers, those from the life‑bearing oak; and on top
line_details.greek: κᾶλα, τά τ' ἐκ δρυός ἐστι φερεσβίου· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ὕπερθε
line_details.note: κᾶλα = “timbers” (pl. of κᾶλον, any piece of wood; can mean logs, spars, or oars); φερέσβιος is the traditional epithet “life‑bearing/life‑supporting” of the oak (notably of Zeus’ oak at Dodona). “On top” (ἐν δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ὕπερθε) anticipates the action of the next line.

line_details.english: I set in place upon a peplos sea‑washed gifts for the gods.
line_details.greek: πέπλῳ παρκατέθηκα θεοῖς ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα.
line_details.note: παρκατέθηκα = “I set/laid down (beside/in addition),” a compound of παρά + κατατίθημι; ἐπινήχυτα = “sea‑washed,” likely indicating ritual lustration of offerings with seawater; πέπλος (peplos) is a cloth/robe used here as the offering cloth.

text.english: And then indeed a very large krater for the cattle— they slaughtered the bull, having tilted back its head toward the bright aether, while still alive; and around the fire they were pouring the blood, here and there.
text.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ κραντῆρα βοῶν περιμηκέα ταῦρον σφάζον, ἀνακλίνας κεφαλὴν εἰς αἰθέρα δῖαν, ζωόταμον· περὶ δ' αἷμα πυρῇ χέον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.

line_details.english: And then indeed a very large krater for the cattle—
line_details.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ κραντῆρα βοῶν περιμηκέα ταῦρον
line_details.note: κραντῆρα is almost certainly a form of κρατῆρα “krater; mixing-bowl.” The syntax is compressed/anacoluthic: the vessel is introduced without an explicit verb (sc. “they set out/placed”), before the action of slaughter is narrated. Some editors emend the spelling to κρατῆρα. The placement of περιμηκέα most naturally modifies the krater here (“very large”).

line_details.english: they slaughtered the bull, having tilted back its head toward the bright aether,
line_details.greek: σφάζον, ἀνακλίνας κεφαλὴν εἰς αἰθέρα δῖαν,
line_details.note: σφάζον denotes ritual slaughter by cutting the throat; hence the detail “tilting back the head.”

line_details.english: while still alive; and around the fire they were pouring the blood, here and there.
line_details.greek: ζωόταμον· περὶ δ' αἷμα πυρῇ χέον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
line_details.note: ζωόταμον “cut while alive” emphasizes the immediacy of the sacrificial killing; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “hither and thither,” i.e., “on both sides/round about,” describing the distribution of blood around the fire.

text.english: But when, having crushed the heart, I placed it with popanoi, having poured liquid oil, and thereon the rennet of a lamb.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κραδίην θραύσας ποπάνοισιν ἔθηκα, λείψας ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον, ἐπ' αὐτῷ δὲ γλάγος ἄμνης.

line_details.english: But when, having crushed the heart, I placed it with popanoi,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κραδίην θραύσας ποπάνοισιν ἔθηκα,
line_details.note: κραδίην θραύσας: literally “having broken/crushed the heart,” i.e., the victim’s heart prepared for the rite; θραύω can mean to break up into pieces. ποπάνοισιν: popanoi are small sacrificial cakes (instrumental dative), a technical ritual term.

line_details.english: having poured liquid oil, and thereon the rennet of a lamb.
line_details.greek: λείψας ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον, ἐπ' αὐτῷ δὲ γλάγος ἄμνης.
line_details.note: λείψας: aorist participle of λείβω “to pour (as a libation),” not of λείπω “to leave.” γλάγος ἄμνης: γλάγος is rare, ‘curdled milk/rennet’; with ἄμνης (‘of a lamb’) this denotes lamb’s rennet. ἐπ’ αὐτῷ refers back to the item just placed (sc. the offering/heart).

text.english: And I bade the heroes, thronging on every side, to plant their spears and their hilted swords, with the hide and the entrails braced in their hands.
text.greek: Ἥρωας δ' ἐκέλευσα περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντας δούρατ' ἐπαμπήξασθαι ἰδ' ἄορα κωπήεντα, βύρσῃ τε σπλάγχνοισι τ' ἐρειδομέναις παλάμῃσι.

line_details.english: And I bade the heroes, thronging on every side,
line_details.greek: Ἥρωας δ' ἐκέλευσα περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντας
line_details.note: περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντας: a pleonastic combination; ἀμφιχύνω is used figuratively of ‘thronging’ or ‘swarming’ around.

line_details.english: to plant their spears and their hilted swords,
line_details.greek: δούρατ' ἐπαμπήξασθαι ἰδ' ἄορα κωπήεντα,
line_details.note: δούρατα here are ‘spears’ (not ‘timbers’); ἐπαμπήγνυσθαι = ‘to fix/plant (in the ground)’. ἄορα κωπήεντα is the standard epic phrase ‘hilted swords’. The line envisions the warriors planting their weapons as they prepare the rite.

line_details.english: with the hide and the entrails braced in their hands.
line_details.greek: βύρσῃ τε σπλάγχνοισι τ' ἐρειδομέναις παλάμῃσι.
line_details.note: βύρσῃ (‘hide’) and σπλάγχνοισι (‘entrails’) are instrumental/manner datives, referring to sacrificial handling; ἐρειδομέναις παλάμῃσι = ‘with hands braced/supporting’. The participle is fem. dat. pl., agreeing with implied παλάμαι; many take the phrase adverbially of manner (some emend to ἐρειδομένοις). The sense is ‘while handling the victim’s hide and entrails.’

text.english: Then I set in the midst a vessel for kykeon, having set it firm, earthenware, wherein all things had been carefully mixed, first, Demeter’s life-bringing barley-groats, and, upon it, the blood of a bull, and the briny water of the sea.
text.greek: Θῆκα δ' ἄρ' ἐν μέσσῳ τεῦχος κυκεῶνος ἐρείσας ὀστράκεον, τῷ πάντα περιφραδέως ἐμέμικτο, Δήμητρος μὲν πρῶτα φερέσβιος ἀλφίτου ἀκτή, αἷμα δ' ἐπὶ ταύροιο, θαλάσσης θ' ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ.

line_details.english: Then I set in the midst a vessel for kykeon, having set it firm,
line_details.greek: Θῆκα δ' ἄρ' ἐν μέσσῳ τεῦχος κυκεῶνος ἐρείσας
line_details.note: Θῆκα is first-person aorist (“I set”); some read θῆκε (“he set”). τεῦχος = “vessel, implement”; ἐρείσας = “having set/propped it firmly.” Κυκεών (kykeon) is the ritual drink.

line_details.english: earthenware, wherein all things had been carefully mixed,
line_details.greek: ὀστράκεον, τῷ πάντα περιφραδέως ἐμέμικτο,
line_details.note: ὀστράκεον = “earthenware.” τῷ is a dative of respect/means (“in which”); περιφραδέως = “very carefully”; ἐμέμικτο (perf. mid.) implies prior thorough mixing.

line_details.english: first, Demeter’s life-bringing barley-groats,
line_details.greek: Δήμητρος μὲν πρῶτα φερέσβιος ἀλφίτου ἀκτή,
line_details.note: Δήμητρος (Demeter) in the genitive as metonym for grain; φερέσβιος = “life-bringing.” ἀκτή of ἀλφίτον denotes coarse meal/groats, not “shore.”

line_details.english: and, upon it, the blood of a bull, and the briny water of the sea.
line_details.greek: αἷμα δ' ἐπὶ ταύροιο, θαλάσσης θ' ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ.
line_details.note: ἐπὶ marks addition/overlay (“upon it”). The inclusion of bull’s blood and sea-water signals a ritual kykeon distinct from the Homeric culinary mixture; ἁλμυρόν = “briny.”

text.english: And I bade them wreathe themselves with circles of sacred olive.
text.greek: Στέψασθαι δ' ἐκέλευσα κύκλους ἐρόεντας ἐλαίης·

line_details.english: And I bade them wreathe themselves with circles of sacred olive.
line_details.greek: Στέψασθαι δ' ἐκέλευσα κύκλους ἐρόεντας ἐλαίης·
line_details.note: ἐρόεντας is likely for ἱερόεντας (“sacred”); κύκλους here means wreaths (circular garlands) of olive. The middle στεψάσθαι means “to wreathe oneself.”

text.english: Then, taking a golden bowl in my own hands, and filling it with kykeon, I apportioned it in succession, for each man among the very-mighty kings to taste.
text.greek: καὶ τότε χρυσείην φιάλην χείρεσσιν ἐμαῖσιν ἀμπλήσας κυκεῶνος, ἐφεξείης ἐπένειμον γεύειν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ἐρισθενέων βασιλήων.

line_details.english: Then, taking a golden bowl in my own hands,
line_details.greek: καὶ τότε χρυσείην φιάλην χείρεσσιν ἐμαῖσιν
line_details.note: φιάλη is a phiale, a shallow libation-bowl; translated here as “bowl.”

line_details.english: and filling it with kykeon, I apportioned it in succession,
line_details.greek: ἀμπλήσας κυκεῶνος, ἐφεξείης ἐπένειμον
line_details.note: κυκεών (kykeon) is a ritual drink (typically a barley-based mixture); ἐφεξείης means “in succession, one after another.”

line_details.english: for each man among the very-mighty kings to taste.
line_details.greek: γεύειν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ἐρισθενέων βασιλήων.
line_details.note: ἐπένειμον with an infinitive (“to taste”) expresses the allotment/purpose; ἐρισθενέων is an epic intensive (“very-mighty”). “Kings” refers to the Argonaut leaders.

text.english: And at the beacon-fire they bade Jason set a torch of dry pine.
text.greek: Πυρκαϊῇ δ' ἐκέλευον Ἰήσονα λαμπάδα θέσθαι

line_details.english: And at the beacon-fire they bade Jason set a torch of dry pine.
line_details.greek: Πυρκαϊῇ δ' ἐκέλευον Ἰήσονα λαμπάδα θέσθαι
line_details.note: πυρκαϊῇ (dat.) = “at/on the beacon/bonfire” (not necessarily a funerary pyre here). πεύκης ἀζαλέης is a genitive of material, “of dry/parched pine,” well-suited for kindling.

text.english: And under it there ran a wondrous flame.
text.greek: πεύκης ἀζαλέης· ὑπὸ δ' ἔδραμε θεσπεσίη φλόξ.

line_details.english: And under it there ran a wondrous flame.
line_details.greek: πεύκης ἀζαλέης· ὑπὸ δ' ἔδραμε θεσπεσίη φλόξ.
line_details.note: ὑπὸ … ἔδραμε is epic for a flame’s swift spread “from beneath.” θεσπεσίη = “wondrous, divinely-sent”; “wondrous” preserves the epic ambiguity.

text.english: Then indeed I, toward the surge of the loud-roaring sea, stretching out my hands, uttered these words from my tongue, “Guardians of Okeanos and of the brine-swollen sea, deep-dwelling blessed ones, and all you who dwell along the sandy shores, sea-pebbled, and upon Tethys’ utmost water.” Nereus first of all I invoke, the eldest of them all, together with all his fifty lovely maidens; and the glaucous, fish‑swarming sea, and boundless Amphitritê, Proteus and Phorkys, and Triton of broad might, and the nimble winds, together with the golden‑ankled Aurai, and the far‑shining stars, and the mist of murky Night, and the beam of Hêlios, the guide that runs before the feet of his horses, and the sea‑daimones who mingle with heroes, and the shore‑dwelling gods, and the briny streams of the rivers; and himself, the Kronidês, the Earth‑shaker, dark‑haired, to come, leaping forth from the wave, as a helper of oaths.
text.greek: Δὴ τότ' ἐγὼ πρὸς χεῦμα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης, χεῖρας ἐπαντείνας, τάδ' ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα, - "Ὠκεανοῦ μεδέοντες ἁλικλύστοιό τε πόντου ἐμβύθιοι μάκαρες, καὶ ὅσοι ψαμμώδεας ἀκτάς ναίεθ' ἁλικροκάλους, καὶ Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ. Νηρέα μὲν πρώτιστα καλῶ πρέσβυστον ἁπάντων, ἄμμιγα πεντήκοντα κόραις πάσαισιν ἐρανναῖς· Γλαυκὴν δ' ἰχθυόεσσαν, ἀπείριτον Ἀμφιτρίτην, Πρωτέα καὶ Φόρκυνα, καὶ εὐρυβίην Τρίτωνα, λαιψηρούς τ' ἀνέμους, αὔραις μίγα χρυσεοτάρσαις, ἄστρα τε τηλεσίφαντα, καὶ ἀχλύα νυκτὸς ἐρεμνῆς αὐγήν τ' ἠελίοιο ποδῶν προποδηγέτιν ἵππων δαίμονας εἰναλίους τε μιγαζομένους ἥρωσιν, ἀκταίους τε θεοὺς, ποταμῶν θ' ἁλιμυρέα ῥεῖθρα· αὐτόν τε Κρονίδην σεισίχθονα κυανοχαίτην, κύματος ἐκπροθορόντα μολεῖν ἐπιτάρροθον ὅρκων.

line_details.english: Then indeed I, toward the surge of the loud-roaring sea,
line_details.greek: Δὴ τότ' ἐγὼ πρὸς χεῦμα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης,
line_details.note: χεῦμα = “surge/outpouring”; πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης is the traditional epic epithet “loud-roaring sea.”

line_details.english: stretching out my hands, uttered these words from my tongue,
line_details.greek: χεῖρας ἐπαντείνας, τάδ' ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα,
line_details.note: ἀγόρευσα has formal/solemn force (“declared, addressed”); ἀπὸ γλώσσης is a formulaic epic expression for speaking.

line_details.english: “Guardians of Okeanos and of the brine-swollen sea, deep-dwelling blessed ones,
line_details.greek: - "Ὠκεανοῦ μεδέοντες ἁλικλύστοιό τε πόντου
line_details.note: μεδέοντες = “guardians/holders of sway”; ἁλικλύστος literally “washed/beaten by brine” (hence “brine‑swollen”); ἐμβύθιοι = “in the depths, deep‑dwelling.” Okeanos is the world-encircling stream, distinct from the open sea (pontos).

line_details.english: and all you who dwell along the sandy shores, sea-pebbled,
line_details.greek: ἐμβύθιοι μάκαρες, καὶ ὅσοι ψαμμώδεας ἀκτάς
line_details.note: ἁλικροκάλους is a rare compound from ἅλς (sea, brine) + κρόκαλος (rounded pebble), meaning “sea‑pebbled” or “shingled by sea‑worn stones.”

line_details.english: and upon Tethys’ utmost water.”
line_details.greek: ναίεθ' ἁλικροκάλους, καὶ Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ.
line_details.note: Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ = “the outermost/farthest water of Tethys,” i.e., the world’s rim-waters; the object is governed elliptically by ναίεθ’ (“dwell”) from the previous line.

line_details.english: Nereus first of all I invoke, the eldest of them all,
line_details.greek: Νηρέα μὲν πρώτιστα καλῶ πρέσβυστον ἁπάντων,

line_details.english: together with all his fifty lovely maidens;
line_details.greek: ἄμμιγα πεντήκοντα κόραις πάσαισιν ἐρανναῖς·
line_details.note: ἄμμιγα = “together with,” an epic/ionic adverb; the fifty “maidens” are the Nereids.

line_details.english: and the glaucous, fish‑swarming sea, and boundless Amphitritê,
line_details.greek: Γλαυκὴν δ' ἰχθυόεσσαν, ἀπείριτον Ἀμφιτρίτην,
line_details.note: “Glaukên … ichthyoessan” functions substantively for “the sea” (Θάλασσα) without the noun expressed; “boundless” (ἀπείριτος) is a conventional maritime epithet of Amphitritê.

line_details.english: Proteus and Phorkys, and Triton of broad might,
line_details.greek: Πρωτέα καὶ Φόρκυνα, καὶ εὐρυβίην Τρίτωνα,
line_details.note: “εὐρυβίης” = “of broad might,” a set epithet of Triton.

line_details.english: and the nimble winds, together with the golden‑ankled Aurai,
line_details.greek: λαιψηρούς τ' ἀνέμους, αὔραις μίγα χρυσεοτάρσαις,
line_details.note: The Aurai are personified breezes; “golden‑ankled” (χρυσεοτάρσαις) is a nymph‑epithet.

line_details.english: and the far‑shining stars, and the mist of murky Night,
line_details.greek: ἄστρα τε τηλεσίφαντα, καὶ ἀχλύα νυκτὸς ἐρεμνῆς
line_details.note: “ τηλεσίφαντα” is a rare compound, here “far‑shining” of the stars; ἐρεμνός = “murky, dark.”

line_details.english: and the beam of Hêlios, the guide that runs before the feet of his horses,
line_details.greek: αὐγήν τ' ἠελίοιο ποδῶν προποδηγέτιν ἵππων
line_details.note: “προποδηγέτιν” literally “leading on before the feet,” i.e., the first light that precedes Helios’ chariot; hence the sun’s fore‑gleam.

line_details.english: and the sea‑daimones who mingle with heroes,
line_details.greek: δαίμονας εἰναλίους τε μιγαζομένους ἥρωσιν,
line_details.note: “δαίμονες εἰναλίοι” are marine spirits; “mingling with heroes” evokes their intercourse or companionship with heroic figures (e.g., Glaukos, Thetis, etc.).

line_details.english: and the shore‑dwelling gods, and the briny streams of the rivers;
line_details.greek: ἀκταίους τε θεοὺς, ποταμῶν θ' ἁλιμυρέα ῥεῖθρα·
line_details.note: “ἀκταῖοι θεοί” = deities of the shore/coast; “briny streams of the rivers” (ἁλιμυρέα ῥεῖθρα) points to river‑mouths mixing with the sea.

line_details.english: and himself, the Kronidês, the Earth‑shaker, dark‑haired,
line_details.greek: αὐτόν τε Κρονίδην σεισίχθονα κυανοχαίτην,
line_details.note: “Kronidês” (son of Kronos) here denotes Poseidon; “Earth‑shaker” (σεισίχθων) and “dark‑haired/blue‑haired” (κυανοχαίτης) are his fixed epithets.

line_details.english: to come, leaping forth from the wave, as a helper of oaths.
line_details.greek: κύματος ἐκπροθορόντα μολεῖν ἐπιτάρροθον ὅρκων.
line_details.note: “ἐπιτάρροθον ὅρκων” = “as ally/helper of oaths,” i.e., called as witness and enforcer of sworn pledges; “leaping forth from the wave” marks his sea‑epiphany.

text.english: So then, as helpers of Iason, ever steadfast, let us remain willingly, aid-bringers to our shared labors, and let each return alive to his own halls; but whoever shall harm the compact, recking not, by overstepping the oath—of this let witnesses be straight-steering Dike and the dread-giving Erinyes.” Thus I spoke; and they in turn nodded with one mind, fearing the oaths, and signaled with their hands.
text.greek: Τόφρα μὲν οὖν ἐπίκουροι Ἰάσονος ἔμπεδον αἰεί μίμνωμεν προφρόνως ξυνῶν ἐπαρηγόνες ἄθλων, ζῳοὶ νοστήσωμεν ἑὰ πρὸς δώμαθ' ἕκαστος· ὃς δέ κε συνθεσίης δηλήσεται οὐκ ἀλεγίζων ὅρκον ὑπερβάσιον, τούτου δ' ἐπιμάρτυροι ἔστων ἰθύντειρα Δίκη καὶ Ἐριννύες αἰνοδότειραι." Ὣς ἐφάμην· οἱ δ' αὖτις ὁμοφροσύνῃ κατένευσαν ὅρκια δειμαίνοντες, ἐσημήναντο δὲ χερσίν.

line_details.english: So then, as helpers of Iason, ever steadfast,
line_details.greek: Τόφρα μὲν οὖν ἐπίκουροι Ἰάσονος ἔμπεδον αἰεί
line_details.note: Τόφρα is a transitional adverb (“so then,” “meanwhile”). ἔμπεδον is adverbial (“steadfast[ly]”). ἐπίκουροι governs the genitive (“helpers of Iason”).

line_details.english: let us remain willingly, aid-bringers to our shared labors,
line_details.greek: μίμνωμεν προφρόνως ξυνῶν ἐπαρηγόνες ἄθλων,
line_details.note: ξυνῶν is the epic form of κοινῶν (“shared, common”). ἐπαρηγόνες = “aid-bringing, succoring,” used predicatively of the subject; προφρόνως = “willingly, zealously.”

line_details.english: and let each return alive to his own halls;
line_details.greek: ζῳοὶ νοστήσωμεν ἑὰ πρὸς δώμαθ' ἕκαστος·
line_details.note: ζῳοί is emphatic, highlighting safe return; δώματα = “halls, house” in epic diction.

line_details.english: but whoever shall harm the compact, recking not,
line_details.greek: ὃς δέ κε συνθεσίης δηλήσεται οὐκ ἀλεγίζων
line_details.note: δηλέομαι takes the genitive (συνθεσίης) of the thing harmed; οὐκ ἀλεγίζων = “not caring, recking not.”

line_details.english: by overstepping the oath—of this let witnesses be
line_details.greek: ὅρκον ὑπερβάσιον, τούτου δ' ἐπιμάρτυροι ἔστων
line_details.note: ὑπερβάσιος (“overstepping, transgressive”) modifies ὅρκον; sense: “by transgressing the oath.” ἐπιμάρτυροι ἔστων is 3rd-pl imperative: “let X be witnesses.”

line_details.english: straight-steering Dike and the dread-giving Erinyes.”
line_details.greek: ἰθύντειρα Δίκη καὶ Ἐριννύες αἰνοδότειραι."
line_details.note: ἰθύντειρα (lit. “straight-guiding, straight-steering”) is an epithet of Dike; αἰνοδότειραι (“dread-giving”) of the Erinyes (spelled Ἐριννύες in some traditions).

line_details.english: Thus I spoke; and they in turn nodded with one mind,
line_details.greek: Ὣς ἐφάμην· οἱ δ' αὖτις ὁμοφροσύνῃ κατένευσαν
line_details.note: ὁμοφροσύνῃ = “with one mind, in unanimity”; κατένευσαν = “they nodded [assent],” a formulaic gesture of agreement.

line_details.english: fearing the oaths, and signaled with their hands.
line_details.greek: ὅρκια δειμαίνοντες, ἐσημήναντο δὲ χερσίν.
line_details.note: ἐσημήναντο χερσί(ν) = “they made a sign with their hands,” a gesture of assent/ratification; ὅρκια δειμαίνοντες = “fearing the (sanctity of the) oaths.”

text.english: But when indeed they had sworn and brought the oath to its fulfillment, then at that very time they passed into the hollow hull of their own ship, one after another, and beneath the benches they stowed their gear, setting their hands to the oars; and thereupon Tiphys called out to make fast with the outspread tackle along the long ladder, to unfurl the sails, and to cast off the moorings from the harbor.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ' ὄμοσάν τε τελεύτησαν τε τὸν ὅρκον, δὴ τότε νηὸς ἑῆς κοῖλον κύτος εἰσεπέρησαν πάντες ἐφεξείης, ὑπὸ δὲ ζυγὰ τεύχε' ἔθεντο, χεῖρας ἐρετμώσαντες· ἐκέκλετο δ' αὐτόθι Τῖφυς ἐκταδίοις ὅπλοις δῆσαι παρὰ κλίμακα μακρήν ἱστία δ' ἁπλῶσαι, λιμένος δ' ἐκ πείσματα θέσθαι.

line_details.english: But when indeed they had sworn and brought the oath to its fulfillment,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ' ὄμοσάν τε τελεύτησαν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
line_details.note: “To complete the oath” (τελεῦν τὸν ὅρκον) is a traditional formula, implying the full rite of swearing has been performed.

line_details.english: then at that very time they passed into the hollow hull of their own ship,
line_details.greek: δὴ τότε νηὸς ἑῆς κοῖλον κύτος εἰσεπέρησαν
line_details.note: κοῖλον κῦτος, literally “hollow belly,” is a conventional epic expression for the ship’s hull/hold.

line_details.english: one after another, and beneath the benches they stowed their gear,
line_details.greek: πάντες ἐφεξείης, ὑπὸ δὲ ζυγὰ τεύχε' ἔθεντο,
line_details.note: ζυγά are the thwarts or rowing-benches; τεύχεα here means ship’s gear/equipment (not martial arms).

line_details.english: setting their hands to the oars; and thereupon Tiphys called out
line_details.greek: χεῖρας ἐρετμώσαντες· ἐκέκλετο δ' αὐτόθι Τῖφυς
line_details.note: χεῖρας ἐρετμώσαντες is an idiom, “to set one’s hands to the oars”; ἐκέκλετο here conveys “gave the word/command.”

line_details.english: to make fast with the outspread tackle along the long ladder,
line_details.greek: ἐκταδίοις ὅπλοις δῆσαι παρὰ κλίμακα μακρήν
line_details.note: ἐκταδίοις ὅπλοις (“with outspread/spreading tackle”) is nautical; παρὰ κλίμακα μακρήν likely refers to the long shroud or rope-ladder used to ascend the mast/rigging; hence “make fast with the spread-out rigging along the long ladder.”

line_details.english: to unfurl the sails, and to cast off the moorings from the harbor.
line_details.greek: ἱστία δ' ἁπλῶσαι, λιμένος δ' ἐκ πείσματα θέσθαι.
line_details.note: λιμένος ἐκ πείσματα θέσθαι means “to cast off the harbor-moorings”; πείσματα are mooring cables/fastenings, with θέσθαι (middle) conveying removal/casting off.

text.english: And then indeed she sent forth a fair, whistling breeze for sailing.
text.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ λίγυν οὖρον ἐπιπροέηκε νέεσθαι

line_details.english: And then indeed she sent forth a fair, whistling breeze for sailing.
line_details.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ λίγυν οὖρον ἐπιπροέηκε νέεσθαι
line_details.note: λιγύν οὖρον: literally “clear-/shrill-sounding wind,” an epic epithet applied to a favorable breeze; hence “fair, whistling.” νέεσθαι here = “to sail,” not “to return.” ἐπιπροέηκε = “sent forth to speed onward,” aorist sense in context.

text.english: Hera, consort of Zeus; and Argo hastened to the voyage.
text.greek: Ἥρη, Ζηνὸς ἄκοιτις, ἐπείγετο δ' ἐς πλόον Ἀργώ.

line_details.english: Hera, consort of Zeus; and Argo hastened to the voyage.
line_details.greek: Ἥρη, Ζηνὸς ἄκοιτις, ἐπείγετο δ' ἐς πλόον Ἀργώ.
line_details.note: Ἥρη, Ζηνὸς ἄκοιτις appositionally identifies the subject of the previous line. ἐπείγετο (mid.) ἐς πλόον = “pressed on/hastened to the voyage.” Ἀργώ is the ship personified as the grammatical subject.

text.english: Then they kept both hands and mind upon the rowing, the unwearied kings, and the measureless brine was being cloven, as the foam swelled beneath the keel, on this side and on that.
text.greek: Οἱ δ' ἄρ' ἐπ' εἰρεσίην ἔπεχον χεῖράς τε νόον τε ἄκμητοι βασιλῆες, ἐτέτμετο δ' ἄσπετος ἅλμη, ἀφροῦ ἅμ' οἰδαίνοντος ὑπὸ τρόπιν ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.

line_details.english: Then they kept both hands and mind upon the rowing,
line_details.greek: Οἱ δ' ἄρ' ἐπ' εἰρεσίην ἔπεχον χεῖράς τε νόον τε
line_details.note: εἰρεσίη = “rowing, oarage”; the collocation “hands and mind” marks full concentration on the task.

line_details.english: the unwearied kings, and the measureless brine was being cloven,
line_details.greek: ἄκμητοι βασιλῆες, ἐτέτμετο δ' ἄσπετος ἅλμη,
line_details.note: ἄκμητοι = “unwearied” (also “in their prime”); ἐτέτμετο is an epic (plu)perfect used with imperfect force, hence “was being cloven”; ἄσπετος = “immeasurable, boundless.”

line_details.english: as the foam swelled beneath the keel, on this side and on that.
line_details.greek: ἀφροῦ ἅμ' οἰδαίνοντος ὑπὸ τρόπιν ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
line_details.note: Genitive absolute: ἀφροῦ ἅμ’ οἰδαίνοντος = “as the foam swelled”; τρόπις = “keel”; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “on this side and on that.”

text.english: Then holy dawn from the streams of Okeanos was opening the East, and Erigeneia attended, bringing sweet light to mortals and immortals; and then indeed the lookout-heights and the wind‑swept hill from the strand of woody Pelion came into view.
text.greek: Τῆμος δ' ἱερὸς ὄρθρος ἀπ' Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων ἀντολίας ἤνοιγεν, ἐπέσπετο δ' Ἠριγένεια ἡδὺ φάος θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι φέρουσα· καὶ τότε δὴ σκοπιαί τε καὶ ἠνεμόεσσα κολώνη Πηλίου ὑλήεντος ἀπ' ἠϊόνος κατέφαινε.

line_details.english: Then holy dawn from the streams of Okeanos
line_details.greek: Τῆμος δ' ἱερὸς ὄρθρος ἀπ' Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων
line_details.note: Τῆμος = “then, at that time,” an epic-temporal adverb; ἱερὸς ὄρθρος (“holy dawn”) is a formulaic epithet; Ὠκεανός is the world-encircling river.

line_details.english: was opening the East, and Erigeneia attended,
line_details.greek: ἀντολίας ἤνοιγεν, ἐπέσπετο δ' Ἠριγένεια
line_details.note: ἀντολίαι (pl.) = “the East, the risings (of the sun)”; ἐπέσπετο = “attended, followed hard upon.” Ἠριγένεια is the Dawn-goddess (Eos), “Early-born,” here transliterated.

line_details.english: bringing sweet light to mortals and immortals;
line_details.greek: ἡδὺ φάος θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι φέρουσα·
line_details.note: φάος is a poetic synonym for φῶς (“light”); ἡδύ = “sweet, pleasant,” suited to epic diction.

line_details.english: and then indeed the lookout-heights and the wind‑swept hill
line_details.greek: καὶ τότε δὴ σκοπιαί τε καὶ ἠνεμόεσσα κολώνη
line_details.note: σκοπιαί = “lookout-places, watch-heights”; κολώνη = “mound, hill,” here with the Homeric epithet ἠνεμόεσσα (“wind-swept”).

line_details.english: from the strand of woody Pelion came into view.
line_details.greek: Πηλίου ὑλήεντος ἀπ' ἠϊόνος κατέφαινε.
line_details.note: ἀπ’ ἠϊόνος = “from the strand/shore.” κατέφαινε can be taken intransitively (“came into view,” as translated) though the singular verb with two subjects is epic; alternatively, it may be construed transitively with Dawn as the subject (“she made visible the lookout-heights and the wind-swept hill from the shore of woody Pelion”).

text.english: But Tiphys, taking his two hands off the steering-ropes, called for them to furrow the wave a little with under-strokes; and swiftly they ran in under the shores; and from the ship they lowered a wooden ladder within the haven.
text.greek: Τῖφυς δ' ἀμπαύσας δισσῆς οἰήια χειρός τυτθὸν ὑπειρεσίῃσιν ἐκέκλετο κῦμα χαράσσειν· καί ῥα θοῶς ἀκτῇσιν ὑπέδραμον· ἐκ δ' ἄρα νηός κλίμακα δαυρατέην λιμένων ἔντοσθε χάλασσαν.

line_details.english: But Tiphys, taking his two hands off the steering-ropes,
line_details.greek: Τῖφυς δ' ἀμπαύσας δισσῆς οἰήια χειρός
line_details.note: οἰήια = the steering-ropes (from οἴαξ, tiller/helm); δισσῆς χειρός is genitive “of both hands.” ἀμπαύσας is effectively “ceasing/letting go” (either transitive of the ropes or with genitive of separation).

line_details.english: called for them to furrow the wave a little with under-strokes;
line_details.greek: τυτθὸν ὑπειρεσίῃσιν ἐκέκλετο κῦμα χαράσσειν·
line_details.note: κέκλετο is the Homeric middle “he called/urged.” ὑπειρεσίῃσιν (dat. pl.) = “with under-strokes” (of the oars), i.e., gentle or checking strokes; κῦμα χαράσσειν = “to furrow/score the wave.”

line_details.english: and swiftly they ran in under the shores;
line_details.greek: καί ῥα θοῶς ἀκτῇσιν ὑπέδραμον· ἐκ δ' ἄρα νηός
line_details.note: ὑπέδραμον ἀκτῇσιν is a nautical idiom: “they ran in under the shores,” i.e., made landfall quickly; subject = the crew/ship collectively.

line_details.english: and from the ship they lowered a wooden ladder within the haven.
line_details.greek: κλίμακα δαυρατέην λιμένων ἔντοσθε χάλασσαν.
line_details.note: δαυρατέην = “wooden, timbered” (from δαῦρα, timbers). κλίμαξ here is the boarding ladder/gangway; λιμένων (pl.) is generic for the harbor-basin; hence “within the haven.”

text.english: Forth went the Minyan heroes, and they ceased from toil.
text.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἔβαν ἥρωες Μινύαι, παύσαντο δὲ μόχθου·

line_details.english: Forth went the Minyan heroes, and they ceased from toil.
line_details.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἔβαν ἥρωες Μινύαι, παύσαντο δὲ μόχθου·

text.english: And among them, in assembly, Peleus the horseman began to speak words: “Friends, look upon the projecting hill of the lookout, shaded in the midst of the headland; here Cheiron dwells in a cave, the most righteous of the Centaurs who were reared on Pholoē and the lofty crests of Pindos, who indeed is devoted to civic justice and to remedies for diseases; and at other times again, striking in his hands the kithara of Phoibos, or the clear‑toned tortoise‑shell phorminx of Hermes, he makes manifest to all the dwellers round about the ordinances of civic justice.” Meanwhile too, silver-footed Thetis our boy, an infant, newly born, took in her arms, went to leaf-shaking Pelion and gave him to Cheiron, to cherish well and skilfully and to rear.
