text.greek: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχεν ὁμιλαδὸν ἱππότα Πηλεύς· - "Ὦ φίλοι, ἀθρεῖτε σκοπιῆς προὔχοντα κολωνόν, μέσσῳ ἐνὶ πρηῶνι κατάσκιον, ἐνθάδε Χείρων ναίει ἐνὶ σπήλυγγι, δικαιότατος Κενταύρων οἳ τράφεν ἐν Φολόῃ, Πίνδου τ' αἰπεινὰ κάρηνα, ὅς ῥα δικασπολίῃ μέλεται καὶ ἀκεύμασι νούσων· ἄλλοτε δ' αὖ Φοίβου κιθάρην μετὰ χερσὶν ἀράσσων, ἢ λιγυρὴν φόρμιγγα χελυκλόνον Ἑρμάωνος, πᾶσι περικτιόνεσσι δικασπολίας ἀναφαίνει. Τόφρα καὶ ἡμέτερον κοῦρον Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα νήπιον, ἀρτιγένεθλον, ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσι λαβοῦσα, Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον ἔβη, Χείρωνί τ' ἔδωκεν εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως ἀγαπαζέμεν ἠδ' ἀτιτάλλειν.

line_details.english: And among them, in assembly, Peleus the horseman began to speak words:
line_details.greek: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχεν ὁμιλαδὸν ἱππότα Πηλεύς·
line_details.note: ὁμιλαδόν: adverb “in company, in assembly.”

line_details.english: “Friends, look upon the projecting hill of the lookout,
line_details.greek: - "Ὦ φίλοι, ἀθρεῖτε σκοπιῆς προὔχοντα κολωνόν,
line_details.note: σκοπιῆς προὔχοντα κολωνόν: literally “the hill projecting from/of the lookout”; κολωνός is a knoll or mound used here of a promontory feature.

line_details.english: shaded in the midst of the headland; here Cheiron
line_details.greek: μέσσῳ ἐνὶ πρηῶνι κατάσκιον, ἐνθάδε Χείρων
line_details.note: πρηών: a slope or headland/promontory; κατάσκιον “shaded.”

line_details.english: dwells in a cave, the most righteous of the Centaurs
line_details.greek: ναίει ἐνὶ σπήλυγγι, δικαιότατος Κενταύρων

line_details.english: who were reared on Pholoē and the lofty crests of Pindos,
line_details.greek: οἳ τράφεν ἐν Φολόῃ, Πίνδου τ' αἰπεινὰ κάρηνα,
line_details.note: Pholoē (in Arcadia/Elis) and Pindos (the mountain range in Thessaly/Epirus) are traditional haunts of Centaurs.

line_details.english: who indeed is devoted to civic justice and to remedies for diseases;
line_details.greek: ὅς ῥα δικασπολίῃ μέλεται καὶ ἀκεύμασι νούσων·
line_details.note: δικασπολίη: rare compound, “city-justice, civic jurisprudence”; ἀκεύματα “remedies, cures.”

line_details.english: and at other times again, striking in his hands the kithara of Phoibos,
line_details.greek: ἄλλοτε δ' αὖ Φοίβου κιθάρην μετὰ χερσὶν ἀράσσων,

line_details.english: or the clear‑toned tortoise‑shell phorminx of Hermes,
line_details.greek: ἢ λιγυρὴν φόρμιγγα χελυκλόνον Ἑρμάωνος,
line_details.note: Ἑρμάωνος is an epic genitive for Hermes; χελυκλόνον “tortoise‑sounding,” i.e., of a tortoise‑shell lyre (phorminx).

line_details.english: he makes manifest to all the dwellers round about the ordinances of civic justice.”
line_details.greek: πᾶσι περικτιόνεσσι δικασπολίας ἀναφαίνει.
line_details.note: περικτίονες: “neighbors, dwellers round about”; ἀναφαίνει “makes manifest, proclaims.”

line_details.english: Meanwhile too, silver-footed Thetis our boy,
line_details.greek: Τόφρα καὶ ἡμέτερον κοῦρον Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα
line_details.note: Argyropedza (“silver-footed”) is the fixed Homeric epithet of Thetis. Hēmeteron (“our”) is a parental plural, referring to the child of Thetis and Peleus—Achilles.

line_details.english: an infant, newly born, took in her arms,
line_details.greek: νήπιον, ἀρτιγένεθλον, ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσι λαβοῦσα,
line_details.note: Nēpion means “infant” (literally “uncomprehending”); artigenethlon “newly born.” En agkalidesi is “in [her] arms,” an epic plural. The participle labousa supplies the sense “having taken [him].”

line_details.english: went to leaf-shaking Pelion and gave him to Cheiron,
line_details.greek: Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον ἔβη, Χείρωνί τ' ἔδωκεν
line_details.note: Einosiphyllon (“leaf-shaking”) is an epic compound applied to wind-tossed wooded mountains; Pelion is the Thessalian mountain of Cheiron, the wise Centaur.

line_details.english: to cherish well and skilfully and to rear.
line_details.greek: εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως ἀγαπαζέμεν ἠδ' ἀτιτάλλειν.
line_details.note: Agapazemen “to cherish, treat with affection”; epistamenōs “knowingly, skilfully”; atitallein “to rear, nurse.” The paired infinitives express purpose: Thetis entrusts the child to Cheiron to be lovingly and expertly reared.

text.english: Whom indeed a longing is upon my heart to behold in wonder.
text.greek: Ὃν δή μοι πόθος ἐστὶ περὶ φρένα θηήσασθαι.

line_details.english: Whom indeed a longing is upon my heart to behold in wonder.
line_details.greek: Ὃν δή μοι πόθος ἐστὶ περὶ φρένα θηήσασθαι.
line_details.note: περὶ φρένα: literally “around/about the heart,” an epic idiom meaning “at/in my heart, in my mind.”

text.english: But, friends, let us draw near to the cave, that I may behold the condition of my own child, and the dispositions wherein he excels.” So speaking he reached the pathless track; and we followed him; and then we entered into the misty courtyard, and there, reclining upon an earthen couch, lay the great Kentauros, propped against a rock, having stretched out his swift horse-limbs.
text.greek: Ἀλλὰ, φίλοι, πελάσωμεν ἐπὶ σπέος, ὄφρα ἴδωμαι ἕξιν παιδὸς ἐμοῖο, καὶ ἤθεσιν οἷσι κέκασται." - Ὣς εἰπὼν ἐξῖκεν ἀταρπιτόν· οἷ δ' ἑπόμεσθα· Αὐτὰρ ἐπ' εἰς αὐλὴν εἰσήλθομεν ἠεροειδῆ καὶ προσκεκλιμένος μὲν ἐπ' οὐδαίοιο χαμεύνης κεῖτο μέγας Κένταυρος, ἀπηρήρειστο δὲ πέτρῃ ἱππείαισιν ὁπλαῖσι τανυσσάμενος θοὰ κῶλα.

line_details.english: But, friends, let us draw near to the cave, that I may behold
line_details.greek: Ἀλλὰ, φίλοι, πελάσωμεν ἐπὶ σπέος, ὄφρα ἴδωμαι
line_details.note: σπέος = “cave,” here the grotto of Cheiron; the speaker in context is Peleus addressing his comrades.

line_details.english: the condition of my own child, and the dispositions wherein he excels.”
line_details.greek: ἕξιν παιδὸς ἐμοῖο, καὶ ἤθεσιν οἷσι κέκασται."
line_details.note: ἕξις can mean “state, condition,” also “training”; ἤθεα = “habits, dispositions”; κέκασται = “is preeminent/excels.”

line_details.english: So speaking he reached the pathless track; and we followed him;
line_details.greek: - Ὣς εἰπὼν ἐξῖκεν ἀταρπιτόν· οἷ δ' ἑπόμεσθα·
line_details.note: ἀταρπιτόν = “pathless/untrodden (way).” Formulaic epic diction.

line_details.english: and then we entered into the misty courtyard,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπ' εἰς αὐλὴν εἰσήλθομεν ἠεροειδῆ
line_details.note: αὐλή here denotes the forecourt/yard before a dwelling; ἠεροειδής = “misty.” The sequence ἐπ’ εἰς is metrically driven and effectively means “then/thereupon into.”

line_details.english: and there, reclining upon an earthen couch,
line_details.greek: καὶ προσκεκλιμένος μὲν ἐπ' οὐδαίοιο χαμεύνης
line_details.note: οὐδαῖος = “of the ground, earthen”; χαμευνή = “couch on the ground”; προσκεκλιμένος = “reclining, leaning upon.”

line_details.english: lay the great Kentauros, propped against a rock,
line_details.greek: κεῖτο μέγας Κένταυρος, ἀπηρήρειστο δὲ πέτρῃ
line_details.note: ἀπηρήρειστο (perf. mid./pass.) = “was propped/leaning against,” conveying a settled posture.

line_details.english: having stretched out his swift horse-limbs.
line_details.greek: ἱππείαισιν ὁπλαῖσι τανυσσάμενος θοὰ κῶλα.
line_details.note: ἱππείαισιν ὁπλαῖσι is poetic for the centaur’s equine limbs (ὅπλα can denote an animal’s ‘equipment’ for motion, as wings for birds); hence “horse-limbs.”

text.english: And close at hand stood the son of Thetis and Peleus, with his hand he kept striking the lyre, and Cheiron rejoiced in his heart.
text.greek: Ἀγχοῦ δ' ἱστάμενος Θέτιδος καὶ Πηλέος υἱός χειρὶ λύραν ἤρασσε, φρένας δ' ἐπετέρπετο Χείρων.

line_details.english: And close at hand stood the son of Thetis and Peleus,
line_details.greek: Ἀγχοῦ δ' ἱστάμενος Θέτιδος καὶ Πηλέος υἱός
line_details.note: “The son of Thetis and Peleus” identifies Achilles; ἄγχοῦ = ‘near, close by’; the participle ἱστάμενος is rendered idiomatically as a finite verb for smoothness.

line_details.english: with his hand he kept striking the lyre, and Cheiron rejoiced in his heart.
line_details.greek: χειρὶ λύραν ἤρασσε, φρένας δ' ἐπετέρπετο Χείρων.
line_details.note: ἤρασσε (iterative/imperfect of ἀράσσω) = ‘kept striking’; φρένας ἐπετέρπετο is a Homeric idiom ‘he took delight in his heart/mind,’ with middle voice marking personal pleasure; subject shifts from Achilles (striking) to Cheiron (delighting).

text.english: But when indeed he beheld the illustrious kings, gladly he sprang up, and he kissed each man; he made ready a feast, and brought wine in amphorae, and he strewed leaves beneath the rough pallets; and he bade them recline beneath unadorned planks, and he set forth in heaps the meats of swine and of swift deer; and thereafter he apportioned the draught of honey-sweet wine.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δή ῥ' ἄθρησεν ἀγακλειτοὺς βασιλῆας ἀσπασίως ἀνόρουσε, κύσεν δ' ἄρα φῶτα ἕκαστον· δαῖτά τ' ἐπόρσυνεν· μέθυ δ' ἀμφιφορεῦσι κόμισσεν, ῥωγαλέαις τ' ἔστρωσεν ὑπὸ στιβάδεσσι πέτηλα· κλινθῆναι δ' ἐκέλευσεν, ἀδαιδάλτοις δ' ὑπὸ πλακταῖς κρεῖα χύδην προὔθηκε συῶν ἐλάφων τε ταχειῶν· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ' ἐπένειμε ποτὸν μελιηδέος οἴνου.

line_details.english: But when indeed he beheld the illustrious kings,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δή ῥ' ἄθρησεν ἀγακλειτοὺς βασιλῆας
line_details.note: ἄθρησεν = “beheld, gazed upon” (from ἀθρέω), not “gathered” (cf. ἀθροίζω).

line_details.english: gladly he sprang up, and he kissed each man;
line_details.greek: ἀσπασίως ἀνόρουσε, κύσεν δ' ἄρα φῶτα ἕκαστον·
line_details.note: φῶτα = “man, mortal” in epic diction.

line_details.english: he made ready a feast, and brought wine in amphorae,
line_details.greek: δαῖτά τ' ἐπόρσυνεν· μέθυ δ' ἀμφιφορεῦσι κόμισσεν,
line_details.note: μέθυ here denotes wine (not mead); the amphorae and the explicit οἶνος in 405 confirm the sense.

line_details.english: and he strewed leaves beneath the rough pallets;
line_details.greek: ῥωγαλέαις τ' ἔστρωσεν ὑπὸ στιβάδεσσι πέτηλα·
line_details.note: ῥωγαλέαις = “coarse, rough”; στιβάδες are leaf-beds; πέτηλα = “leaves” (poetic form of πέταλα).

line_details.english: and he bade them recline beneath unadorned planks,
line_details.greek: κλινθῆναι δ' ἐκέλευσεν, ἀδαιδάλτοις δ' ὑπὸ πλακταῖς
line_details.note: ἀδαιδάλτοις … πλακταῖς = “unadorned planks,” i.e., the plain roof/ceiling; ὑπό with the dative means “beneath.” Some have taken πλακταί as platters, but ὑπό would then be awkward.

line_details.english: and he set forth in heaps the meats of swine and of swift deer;
line_details.greek: κρεῖα χύδην προὔθηκε συῶν ἐλάφων τε ταχειῶν·
line_details.note: χύδην = “in heaps, en masse”; κρέα = “cuts/meats.”

line_details.english: and thereafter he apportioned the draught of honey-sweet wine.
line_details.greek: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ' ἐπένειμε ποτὸν μελιηδέος οἴνου.
line_details.note: ἐπένειμε = “dealt out, apportioned,” commonly of distributing portions or drink.

text.english: But when at last their spirit was sated with supper and with drink, clapping with their hands they shouted in unison, until I myself should vie with Cheiron, playing the kithara in a most clamorous strain.
text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ δόρποιο ποτοῦ θ' ἅλις ἔπλετο θυμός χερσὶν ἐπικροτέοντες ὁμόκλεον, ὄφρ' ἂν ἔγωγε δηρίσω Χείρωνι διωλύγιον κιθαρίζων.

line_details.english: But when at last their spirit was sated with supper and with drink,
line_details.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ δόρποιο ποτοῦ θ' ἅλις ἔπλετο θυμός

line_details.english: clapping with their hands they shouted in unison, until I myself
line_details.greek: χερσὶν ἐπικροτέοντες ὁμόκλεον, ὄφρ' ἂν ἔγωγε
line_details.note: ὁμόκλεον usually means “to rebuke/threaten” in early epic, but here it denotes a collective shout or outcry; ἐπικροτέοντες is “clapping” to mark time or encourage the performer.

line_details.english: should vie with Cheiron, playing the kithara in a most clamorous strain.
line_details.greek: δηρίσω Χείρωνι διωλύγιον κιθαρίζων.
line_details.note: δηρίσω is aorist subjunctive with ὄφρ’ ἄν (“until I should contend”). διωλύγιον is obscure (a rare/hapax formation), probably related to ὀλολυγή (“ritual ululation”); taken adverbially with κιθαρίζων, it conveys “very loudly/clamorously.” The “contest with Cheiron” is a friendly musical rivalry with the Centaur.

text.english: But I did not obey; for a reverent shame came over me, at, being the younger, matching myself as an equal with an elder; even Cheiron himself kept earnestly entreating me, and, though I was unwilling, he bade me, as he sang, to engage in rivalry for the sake of song.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ οὐ πιθόμην· περὶ γάρ με ἐπήλυθεν αἰδώς, ὁπλότερον γεγαῶτα γεραιτέρῳ ἰσοφαρίζειν· μέσφ' αὐτὸς Χείρων ἐλιλαίετο καί μ' ἀέκοντα ἠνώγει ᾄδων ἐριδαινέμεν εἵνεκα μολπῆς.

line_details.english: But I did not obey; for a reverent shame came over me,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ οὐ πιθόμην· περὶ γάρ με ἐπήλυθεν αἰδώς,
line_details.note: αἰδώς conveys reverential modesty or shame; περὶ μὲ ἐπήλυθεν is an epic idiom “came over me.”

line_details.english: at, being the younger, matching myself as an equal with an elder;
line_details.greek: ὁπλότερον γεγαῶτα γεραιτέρῳ ἰσοφαρίζειν·
line_details.note: ὁπλότερον γεγαῶτα = “being born the younger”; γεραιτέρῳ = “to an elder.” ἰσοφαρίζειν “to match as an equal, rival” explains the cause of the αἰδώς.

line_details.english: even Cheiron himself kept earnestly entreating me, and, though I was unwilling,
line_details.greek: μέσφ' αὐτὸς Χείρων ἐλιλαίετο καί μ' ἀέκοντα
line_details.note: μέσφ’ is a contracted form (likely μέν σφ’), giving concessive/emphatic force (“even indeed”); ἐλιλαίετο (from λιλαιόμαι) “kept beseeching/longing for.” ἀέκοντα is the accusative with ἠνώγει (“bade [me], though unwilling”).

line_details.english: he bade me, as he sang, to engage in rivalry for the sake of song.
line_details.greek: ἠνώγει ᾄδων ἐριδαινέμεν εἵνεκα μολπῆς.
line_details.note: ᾄδων (nominative participle) most naturally modifies Cheiron: “as he sang.” ἐριδαινέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἐριδαίνω “to contend,” and εἵνεκα μολπῆς indicates a singing-contest.

text.english: First then the Centaur took up the fair pektis, which Achilles then, bearing it in his hands, held forth.
text.greek: Πρῶτος δ' αὖ Κένταυρος ἀείρατο πηκτίδα καλήν ἥν ῥα τότ' ἐν χείρεσσι φέρων ὤρεξεν Ἀχιλλεύς.

line_details.english: First then the Centaur took up the fair pektis,
line_details.greek: Πρῶτος δ' αὖ Κένταυρος ἀείρατο πηκτίδα καλήν
line_details.note: πηκτίς (pektis) is a Lydian/Anatolian stringed instrument (harp- or lyre-like). “The Centaur” is almost certainly Cheiron, Achilles’ tutor; αείρατο (middle) suggests “took up” or “raised for himself.” Some have proposed πληκτίδα (“plectrum”), but πήκτιδα is generally preferred as the instrument itself.

line_details.english: which Achilles then, bearing it in his hands, held forth.
line_details.greek: ἥν ῥα τότ' ἐν χείρεσσι φέρων ὤρεξεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
line_details.note: ὤρεξεν (from ὀρέγω) means “stretched/held out,” not “played”; the line depicts Achilles presenting or extending the instrument he carries in his hands.

text.english: Who then sang of the battle of the storm‑spirited Centaurs, whom the Lapiths slew on account of their own recklessness, and how, raging against Herakles, they fought in Pholoë, since the might of wine had roused them.
text.greek: Ὅς δ' ἄρ' ἄειδε μάχην Κενταύρων ὀμβριμοθύμων, οὓς Λαπίθαι κατέπεφνον ἀτασθαλίης ἕνεκα σφῶν ἠδ' ὥς Ἡρακλῆϊ καταντία μαιμώοντες ἐν Φολόῃ δήρισαν· ἐπεὶ μένος οἴνου ἔγειρεν.

line_details.english: Who then sang of the battle of the storm‑spirited Centaurs,
line_details.greek: Ὅς δ' ἄρ' ἄειδε μάχην Κενταύρων ὀμβριμοθύμων,
line_details.note: Ὅς δ’ ἄρ’ ἄειδε is a relative to prior context (“who then sang”); ὀμβριμοθύμων = “storm‑spirited/impetuous,” an epic epithet of violent temper.

line_details.english: whom the Lapiths slew on account of their own recklessness,
line_details.greek: οὓς Λαπίθαι κατέπεφνον ἀτασθαλίης ἕνεκα σφῶν
line_details.note: σφῶν (“their own”) is ambiguous in reference; context favors the Centaurs’ recklessness (ἀτασθαλία) as the cause, matching the traditional myth.

line_details.english: and how, raging against Herakles, they fought in Pholoë,
line_details.greek: ἠδ' ὥς Ἡρακλῆϊ καταντία μαιμώοντες
line_details.note: καταντίa with the dative = “against, facing”; μαιμώοντες = “raging, frenzied.” Φολόη (Pholoë) is the mountain connected with the Centaur Pholos and Herakles’ encounter.

line_details.english: since the might of wine had roused them.
line_details.greek: ἐν Φολόῃ δήρισαν· ἐπεὶ μένος οἴνου ἔγειρεν.
line_details.note: μένος οἴνου (“the might/fury of wine”) personifies wine’s inciting power; ἐπεί is causal (“since”).

text.english: But I myself, after him, taking up the clear-toned phorminx, launching from my mouth honey-sweet song, I sent it up, First, a dark-voiced hymn of primordial Chaos, how it transmuted the natures, and how heaven came to its bound; and the birth of broad‑bosomed Earth, and the sea’s foundations; and Eros, eldest and self‑complete, of much counsel, all that he brought to be, and how he set one apart from another; and Kronos the dread‑destroyer, and how unto Zeus the Thunder‑delighter came the kingly rule of the blessed immortals.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε μετ' αὐτὸν ἑλὼν φόρμιγγα λιγεῖαν, ἐκ στόματος μελίγηρυν ἱεὶς ἀνέπεμπον ἀοιδήν· Πρῶτα μὲν ἀρχαίου χάεος μελανήφατον ὕμνον, ὡς ἐπάμειψε φύσεις, ὥς τ' οὐρανὸς ἐς πέρας ἦλθε· γῆς τ' εὐρυστέρνου γένεσιν, πυθμένας τε θαλάσσης· πρεσβύτατόν τε καὶ αὐτοτελῆ πολύμητιν Ἔρωτα, ὅσσα τ' ἔφυσεν ἅπαντα, διέκρινε δ' ἄλλον ἀπ' ἄλλου· καὶ Κρόνον αἰνολέτην, ὥς τ' ἐς Δία τερπικέραυνον ἤλυθεν ἀθανάτων μακάρων βασιλήϊος ἀρχή.

line_details.english: But I myself, after him, taking up the clear-toned phorminx,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε μετ' αὐτὸν ἑλὼν φόρμιγγα λιγεῖαν,
line_details.note: met’ auton can mean “after him” (temporal succession) or “in turn”; the context favors temporal succession in performance.

line_details.english: launching from my mouth honey-sweet song, I sent it up,
line_details.greek: ἐκ στόματος μελίγηρυν ἱεὶς ἀνέπεμπον ἀοιδήν·
line_details.note: The verb pair ἱεὶς … ἀνέπεμπον (“launching/sending up”) suits hymnic diction, implying an upward-directed song/prayer.

line_details.english: First, a dark-voiced hymn of primordial Chaos,
line_details.greek: Πρῶτα μὲν ἀρχαίου χάεος μελανήφατον ὕμνον,
line_details.note: μελανήφατος (“dark-voiced/dark-uttered”) modifies ὕμνον, not Χάος; hence “a dark-voiced hymn of primordial Chaos.”

line_details.english: how it transmuted the natures, and how heaven came to its bound;
line_details.greek: ὡς ἐπάμειψε φύσεις, ὥς τ' οὐρανὸς ἐς πέρας ἦλθε·
line_details.note: ἐπάμειψε φύσεις is cosmogonic: “changed/transmuted the natures” (i.e., primordial elements or states). οὐρανὸς ἐς πέρας ἦλθε = the delimitation of heaven; Ouranos may be cosmic “heaven,” not necessarily the theonym here.

line_details.english: and the birth of broad‑bosomed Earth, and the sea’s foundations;
line_details.greek: γῆς τ' εὐρυστέρνου γένεσιν, πυθμένας τε θαλάσσης·
line_details.note: εὐρυστέρνος is the traditional epithet “broad‑bosomed” for Earth; πυθμένες θαλάσσης are the sea’s “foundations/bases,” i.e., its deeps or structural roots.

line_details.english: and Eros, eldest and self‑complete, of much counsel,
line_details.greek: πρεσβύτατόν τε καὶ αὐτοτελῆ πολύμητιν Ἔρωτα,
line_details.note: αὐτοτελής (“self‑complete, self-sufficient”) is a technical Orphic attribute of Eros; πολύμητις (“of much counsel”) is striking for Eros, marking creative intelligence.

line_details.english: all that he brought to be, and how he set one apart from another;
line_details.greek: ὅσσα τ' ἔφυσεν ἅπαντα, διέκρινε δ' ἄλλον ἀπ' ἄλλου·
line_details.note: Subject understood as Eros: ἔφυσεν “brought forth/generated”; διέκρινε “separated, distinguished” the elements—an Orphic theme of cosmogonic differentiation.

line_details.english: and Kronos the dread‑destroyer, and how unto Zeus the Thunder‑delighter
line_details.greek: καὶ Κρόνον αἰνολέτην, ὥς τ' ἐς Δία τερπικέραυνον
line_details.note: αἰνολέτης is rare/uncertain; rendered “dread‑destroyer” (alternatively “grim‑slayer”), apt for Kronos’ violent myth. τερπικέραυνος is the set epithet “Thunder‑delighter” of Zeus.

line_details.english: came the kingly rule of the blessed immortals.
line_details.greek: ἤλυθεν ἀθανάτων μακάρων βασιλήϊος ἀρχή.
line_details.note: ἤλυθεν … βασιλήϊος ἀρχή = “the kingly rule came.” μακάρων ἀθανάτων = “of the blessed immortals,” a standard epic periphrasis for the gods.

text.english: Celebrating the birth and the judgment of the younger Blessed Ones; and the baleful deeds of Brimo, of Bakchos, and of the Giants, and the many‑nationed stock of men of feeble might, they sang; and through the strait cave the voice went forth, as our shell was uttering a honey‑sweet voice.
text.greek: Μέλπον θ' ὁπλοτέρων μακάρων γένεσίν τε κρίσιν τε· καὶ Βριμοῦς, Βάκχοιο, Γιγάντων τ' ἔργ' ἀΐδηλα, ἀνθρώπων τ' ὀλιγοδρανέων πολυεθνέα φύτλην ἤειδον· στεινὸν δὲ διὰ σπέος ἤλυθεν αὐδή, ἡμετέρης χέλυος μελιχρὴν ὄπα γηρυούσης.

line_details.english: Celebrating the birth and the judgment of the younger Blessed Ones;
line_details.greek: Μέλπον θ' ὁπλοτέρων μακάρων γένεσίν τε κρίσιν τε·
line_details.note: ὁπλοτέρων μακάρων = the younger generation of gods (as opposed to the elder/Titans). κρίσις may mean “judgment/decision” or the “apportionment” of honors after the succession conflict; translation keeps the ambiguity.

line_details.english: and the baleful deeds of Brimo, of Bakchos, and of the Giants,
line_details.greek: καὶ Βριμοῦς, Βάκχοιο, Γιγάντων τ' ἔργ' ἀΐδηλα,
line_details.note: Brimo is a dread epithet (often of Persephone or Hekate); Bakchos = Dionysos. ἀΐδηλα here means “baleful, ruinous,” not “invisible.”

line_details.english: and the many‑nationed stock of men of feeble might,
line_details.greek: ἀνθρώπων τ' ὀλιγοδρανέων πολυεθνέα φύτλην
line_details.note: ὀλιγοδρανής = “feeble in might.” πολυεθνής = “of many peoples/tribes.” φύτλη is a poetic form for “stock, race” (cf. φύτλον/φῦλον).

line_details.english: they sang; and through the strait cave the voice went forth,
line_details.greek: ἤειδον· στεινὸν δὲ διὰ σπέος ἤλυθεν αὐδή,
line_details.note: σπέος = “cave, grotto.” στεινόν = “narrow, strait.” ἤλυθεν is an epic form of “came (forth).”

line_details.english: as our shell was uttering a honey‑sweet voice.
line_details.greek: ἡμετέρης χέλυος μελιχρὴν ὄπα γηρυούσης.
line_details.note: χελύς is the tortoise‑shell lyre; the genitive absolute (“of our shell uttering…”) indicates accompaniment. The first‑person ἡμετέρης points to the narrator’s own lyre (Orpheus).

text.english: And the uttermost summits and the tree-clad glens stood still of Pelion, and amid the lofty oaks went the sound.
text.greek: Ἔστατο δ' ἄκρα κάρηνα καὶ ἄγκεα δενδρήεντα Πηλίου, ὑψηλάς τε μετὰ δρύας ἤλυθε γῆρυς.

line_details.english: And the uttermost summits and the tree-clad glens stood still
line_details.greek: Ἔστατο δ' ἄκρα κάρηνα καὶ ἄγκεα δενδρήεντα
line_details.note: Neuter plural subjects (ἄκρα κάρηνα, ἄγκεα) take a singular verb (ἔστατο). Πηλίου, though enjambed, governs “the tree-clad glens” and the whole landscape phrase.

line_details.english: of Pelion, and amid the lofty oaks went the sound.
line_details.greek: Πηλίου, ὑψηλάς τε μετὰ δρύας ἤλυθε γῆρυς.
line_details.note: γῆρυς can mean “voice,” “cry,” or more generally “sound”; I render it neutrally as “the sound.” μετά with the accusative (μετὰ ὑψηλὰς δρῦας) = “amid/among the tall oaks.”

text.english: And then the trees, root and all, were leaping toward the fold, and the rocks were ringing; and the beasts, hearing the song, remained before the cavern, shying away; and the birds were circling the Centaur’s cattle-stalls, with their feet worn out, and they forgot their own nest.
text.greek: Καί ῥ' αἱ μὲν πρόρριζοι ἐπ' αὔλιον ἐθρώσκοντο πέτραι τ' ἐσμαράγουν· Θῆρες δ' ἀΐοντες ἀοιδῆς, σπήλυγγος προπάροιθεν ἀλυσκάζοντες ἔμιμνον· οἰωνοί τ' ἐκυκλοῦντο βοαύλια Κενταύροιο ταρσοῖς κεκμηῶσιν, ἑῆς δ' ἐλάθοντο καλιῆς.

line_details.english: And then the trees, root and all, were leaping toward the fold,
line_details.greek: Καί ῥ' αἱ μὲν πρόρριζοι ἐπ' αὔλιον ἐθρώσκοντο
line_details.note: πρόρριζοι (“root-and-all”) implies trees as the subject (supplied from context); ἐθρώσκοντο (“were leaping”) evokes the topos of trees moving to song.

line_details.english: and the rocks were ringing; and the beasts, hearing the song,
line_details.greek: πέτραι τ' ἐσμαράγουν· Θῆρες δ' ἀΐοντες ἀοιδῆς,
line_details.note: ἐσμαράγουν = “were resounding, crashing”; Θῆρες = wild beasts.

line_details.english: remained before the cavern, shying away;
line_details.greek: σπήλυγγος προπάροιθεν ἀλυσκάζοντες ἔμιμνον·
line_details.note: ἀλυσκάζοντες = “shying, shrinking back”; σπήλυγξ = “cavern,” here Cheiron’s cave.

line_details.english: and the birds were circling the Centaur’s cattle-stalls,
line_details.greek: οἰωνοί τ' ἐκυκλοῦντο βοαύλια Κενταύροιο
line_details.note: βοαύλια = “cattle-stalls, byres” (rare); οἰωνοί = “birds (of omen)”; Κενταύροιο refers to Cheiron.

line_details.english: with their feet worn out, and they forgot their own nest.
line_details.greek: ταρσοῖς κεκμηῶσιν, ἑῆς δ' ἐλάθοντο καλιῆς.
line_details.note: ταρσοῖς = “tarsi, feet” (of birds); καλιά = “hut,” by extension “nest”; ἐλάθοντο + gen. = “forgot” (lit. “failed to remember”) their own nest.

text.english: But when he saw it, the Centaur was astonished, brandishing hand upon wrist thick and fast, and with his hooves he smote the earth.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ὁρῶν Κένταυρος ἐθάμβεε, χεῖρ' ἐπὶ καρπῷ πυκνὸν ἐπισσείων, οὖδας δ' ἤρασσεν ὁπλῇσι.

line_details.english: But when he saw it, the Centaur was astonished, brandishing hand upon wrist thick and fast,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ὁρῶν Κένταυρος ἐθάμβεε, χεῖρ' ἐπὶ καρπῷ
line_details.note: “χειρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ πυκνὸν ἐπισσείων”: the phrase depicts an emphatic, repeated hand-gesture—literally “shaking/brandishing the hand upon the wrist.” πυκνόν functions adverbially (“in rapid succession”); ἐπισσείων (from ἐπισείω) conveys vigorous, repeated motion.

line_details.english: and with his hooves he smote the earth.
line_details.greek: πυκνὸν ἐπισσείων, οὖδας δ' ἤρασσεν ὁπλῇσι.
line_details.note: οὖδας is a poetic term for “ground/earth.” ἤρασσεν (impf.) suggests iterative action (“kept striking”). ὁπλῇσι is “with his hooves” (dative plural of ὁπλή), not “with arms” (ὅπλα).

text.english: But Tiphys came in from the ship and straightway gave the word, to cross swiftly, for the Minyans; and I broke off my song, and they quickly sprang up, and each donned his gear.
text.greek: Τῖφυς δ' εἰσεπέρησε νεὼς ἄπο, καί ῥ' ἐκέλευσεν ὦκα περᾶν Μινύαισιν· ἐγὼ δ' ἄμπαυον ἀοιδῆς, οἳ δὲ θοῶς ἤγερθεν, ἔδυνε δὲ τεύχε' ἕκαστος.

line_details.english: But Tiphys came in from the ship and straightway gave the word,
line_details.greek: Τῖφυς δ' εἰσεπέρησε νεὼς ἄπο, καί ῥ' ἐκέλευσεν
line_details.note: νεὼς is the Homeric genitive of ναῦς (“ship”). The combination εἰσεπέρησε … ἄπο (“came in … from”) is idiomatic; sense: “came ashore/into the company from the ship.” Tiphys is the helmsman.

line_details.english: to cross swiftly, for the Minyans; and I broke off my song,
line_details.greek: ὦκα περᾶν Μινύαισιν· ἐγὼ δ' ἄμπαυον ἀοιδῆς,
line_details.note: περᾶν here means “to cross (the sea), make the passage.” Μινύαισιν is a dative of the persons commanded (“bade the Minyans”).

line_details.english: and they quickly sprang up, and each donned his gear.
line_details.greek: οἳ δὲ θοῶς ἤγερθεν, ἔδυνε δὲ τεύχε' ἕκαστος.
line_details.note: ἤγερθεν is intransitive (“they roused themselves”). τεύχεα denotes “gear,” typically “arms/armor”; δύειν τεύχεα is the epic idiom “to don armor.”

text.english: And the horseman Peleus raised the child in his arms, and he kissed his head and both fair eyes, laughing with tears; and Achilleus’ heart was enchanted.
text.greek: Παῖδα δ' ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσιν ἀνίσχανεν ἱππότα Πηλεύς, καί ῥ' ἔκυσεν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ἄμφω φώεα καλά, δακρυόεν γελόων· κηλήθη δὲ φρέν' Ἀχιλλεύς.

line_details.english: And the horseman Peleus raised the child in his arms,
line_details.greek: Παῖδα δ' ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσιν ἀνίσχανεν ἱππότα Πηλεύς,

line_details.english: and he kissed his head and both fair eyes,
line_details.greek: καί ῥ' ἔκυσεν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ἄμφω φώεα καλά,
line_details.note: φώεα (often printed φάεα, “lights”) is epic for the eyes; with ἄμφω it means “both eyes.”

line_details.english: laughing with tears; and Achilleus’ heart was enchanted.
line_details.greek: δακρυόεν γελόων· κηλήθη δὲ φρέν' Ἀχιλλεύς.
line_details.note: δακρυόεν γελόων conveys simultaneous weeping and laughter. κηλήθη (aorist passive of κηλέω) means “was charmed/enchanted”; the subject is the infant Achilleus (φρέν’ = φρήν, ‘heart/mind’).

text.english: But to me the Centaur, with his own hand, bestowed an honor‑gift, a shaggy‑edged fawnskin, a guest‑gift, that I might bear it.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ Κένταυρος ἑῇ γέρας ὤπασε χειρί, νεβρὴν παραλέην ξεινήιον ὄφρα φέροιμι.

line_details.english: But to me the Centaur, with his own hand, bestowed an honor‑gift,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ Κένταυρος ἑῇ γέρας ὤπασε χειρί,
line_details.note: Κένταυρος here almost certainly refers to Cheiron; γέρας is the epic “honor‑gift,” emphasizing the prestige of the bestowal, and ἑῇ χειρί underscores the personal act of giving.

line_details.english: a shaggy‑edged fawnskin, a guest‑gift, that I might bear it.
line_details.greek: νεβρὴν παραλέην ξεινήιον ὄφρα φέροιμι.
line_details.note: νεβρίς is the Bacchic fawnskin; παραλέην is difficult, commonly taken as “rough/shaggy (at the edges), untrimmed.” ξεινήιον is a “guest‑gift,” and φέροιμι (“bear”) can imply “wear” in epic diction.

text.english: But when at length, leaping forth from the cavern, we set out, from the top of the watch-peak the old man, upraising his hands, Philyridēs prayed, and he called upon all the gods, for a homecoming for the Minyae, and that they might win noble renown for the younger kings and for mortals yet to come.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ σπήλυγγος ἄπο προθορόντες ἔβημεν ἄκρης ἐκ σκοπιῆς ὁ γέρων ἀνὰ χεῖρας ἀείρων Φιλλυρίδης ἠρᾶτο, θεοὺς δ' ἐπεκέκλετο πάντας νόστον μὲν Μινύαισιν, ἰδὲ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἀρέσθαι ὁπλοτέροις βασιλεῦσι καὶ ἐσσομένοις μερόπεσσιν.

line_details.english: But when at length, leaping forth from the cavern, we set out,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ σπήλυγγος ἄπο προθορόντες ἔβημεν

line_details.english: from the top of the watch-peak the old man, upraising his hands,
line_details.greek: ἄκρης ἐκ σκοπιῆς ὁ γέρων ἀνὰ χεῖρας ἀείρων
line_details.note: σκοπιή = “watch-peak, lookout”; ἀνὰ χεῖρας ἀείρων describes the conventional Homeric prayer-gesture (“raising his hands upward”).

line_details.english: Philyridēs prayed, and he called upon all the gods,
line_details.greek: Φιλλυρίδης ἠρᾶτο, θεοὺς δ' ἐπεκέκλετο πάντας
line_details.note: Φιλλυρίδης (“son of Philyra”) is the patronymic of Cheiron, used as his name.

line_details.english: for a homecoming for the Minyae, and that they might win noble renown
line_details.greek: νόστον μὲν Μινύαισιν, ἰδὲ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἀρέσθαι
line_details.note: ἀρέσθαι (middle) = “to win/obtain for oneself,” taking the accusative of the thing (renown) and, as here, the dative of advantage (continued in the next line). “Minyae” designates the Argonauts.

line_details.english: for the younger kings and for mortals yet to come.
line_details.greek: ὁπλοτέροις βασιλεῦσι καὶ ἐσσομένοις μερόπεσσιν.
line_details.note: The datives (“for the younger kings … for mortals yet to come”) express advantage; “younger kings” refers to the youthful leaders of the expedition. μερόπες is an epic term for “mortals” (lit. “articulate-speaking men”).

text.english: But when they had come to the strand and all had gone aboard the ship, they took their seats upon the forward thwarts; and then upon the oars stretching out their hands, each smote the brine, having stood off from Pelion; over the great trough of the sea the foam, seething up, whitened the gleaming sea.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τ' ἐπὶ θῖνα καὶ ἐς νέα πάντες ἔβησαν, ἐν προτέροις θώκοισι καθίζανον· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἐρετμοῖς χεῖρας ἐφαπλώσαντες, ἐπί ῥ' ἅλα τύπτον ἕκαστος, Πήλιον ἐκνεύσαντες· ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμά τε πόντου ἀφρὸς ἐπιζείων χαροπὴν λεύκαινε θάλασσαν.

line_details.english: But when they had come to the strand and all had gone aboard the ship,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τ' ἐπὶ θῖνα καὶ ἐς νέα πάντες ἔβησαν,

line_details.english: they took their seats upon the forward thwarts; and then upon the oars
line_details.greek: ἐν προτέροις θώκοισι καθίζανον· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἐρετμοῖς
line_details.note: θῶκοι are the rowers’ benches or “thwarts”; προτέροις marks the forward benches. The imperfect καθίζανον conveys the settling of the crew into their places.

line_details.english: stretching out their hands, each smote the brine,
line_details.greek: χεῖρας ἐφαπλώσαντες, ἐπί ῥ' ἅλα τύπτον ἕκαστος,

line_details.english: having stood off from Pelion; over the great trough of the sea
line_details.greek: Πήλιον ἐκνεύσαντες· ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμά τε πόντου
line_details.note: ἐκνεύσαντες is nautical: “to stand off/clear from” (the shore or landmark); Pelion locates the Pagasaean launch. λαῖτμα denotes the open “trough/deep” of the sea.

line_details.english: the foam, seething up, whitened the gleaming sea.
line_details.greek: ἀφρὸς ἐπιζείων χαροπὴν λεύκαινε θάλασσαν.
line_details.note: χαροπὴν is an epic epithet meaning “gleaming/bright”; ἐπιζείων (“seething up”) modifies ἀφρός (“foam”). λεύκαινε (imperfect) = “was whitening/whitened.”

text.english: And the Pissaean headland was hidden from view, and the Sepias shore, and Skiathos showed itself, and the tomb of Dolops rose into sight, and Homole hard by the sea, and the briny current of Enavlos, which through a great stretch of land sends forth loud-roaring water.
text.greek: Πισσαίη δ' ἀπέκρυφθεν ἄκρη καὶ Σηπιὰς ἀκτή, φάνθη δὲ Σκίαθος, Δολοπός τ' ἀνεφαίνετο σῆμα, ἀγχίαλός θ' Ὁμόλη, ῥεῖθρόν θ' ἁλιμυρὲς ἐναύλου ὃς διὰ πολλὴν γαῖαν ἱεῖ μεγαλόβρομον ὕδωρ.

line_details.english: And the Pissaean headland was hidden from view, and the Sepias shore,
line_details.greek: Πισσαίη δ' ἀπέκρυφθεν ἄκρη καὶ Σηπιὰς ἀκτή,
line_details.note: Πισσαίη ἄκρη: a promontory on the Magnesian/Thessalian coast; exact identification is debated. Σηπιὰς ἀκτή is Cape Sepias, famed in later tradition for shipwrecks (e.g., Xerxes’ fleet).

line_details.english: and Skiathos showed itself, and the tomb of Dolops rose into sight,
line_details.greek: φάνθη δὲ Σκίαθος, Δολοπός τ' ἀνεφαίνετο σῆμα,
line_details.note: Δολοπός σῆμα: sēma usually “tomb” but also “seamark”; in Apollonius (Arg. 1.587) it is a well-known tumulus used by sailors near Skiathos. The eponym “Dolops” is uncertain; the line likely refers to a local hero’s mound rather than the Dolopian ethnos.

line_details.english: and Homole hard by the sea, and the briny current of Enavlos,
line_details.greek: ἀγχίαλός θ' Ὁμόλη, ῥεῖθρόν θ' ἁλιμυρὲς ἐναύλου
line_details.note: ἀγχίαλός (“close to the sea”) modifies Homole; though Homole is a Thessalian mountain, the name can denote the coastal region at its foothills. ῥεῖθρον ἁλιμυρές ἐναύλου: taken as “the briny stream of Enavlos,” Enavlos being a hydronym; some have suspected a reference to the torrent Anauros and propose emendation to Ἀναύρου.

line_details.english: which through a great stretch of land sends forth loud-roaring water.
line_details.greek: ὃς διὰ πολλὴν γαῖαν ἱεῖ μεγαλόβρομον ὕδωρ.
line_details.note: ὃς refers to the stream just mentioned; μεγαλόβρομον (“loud-roaring”) is a traditional epic compound.

text.english: and the rugged forelands of deep-gazing Olympus, the Minyae beheld, and they rounded woody Athos, and broad Pellene; and most holy Samothrace, where too the dread oaths of the gods, unbreakable for mortals, the heroes, at my counsels, gladly passed within, for great to them—aye, to mortal men—is the benefit of this sacrificial rite, unfailing for each seafarer.
text.greek: Οὐλύμπου δὲ βαθυσκοπέλου πρηῶνας ἐρυμνούς εἰσέδρακον Μινύαι, καὶ Ἄθω δενδρώδεα κάμψαν, Πελλήνην τ' εὐρεῖαν· ἰδὲ ζαθέην Σαμοθρῄκην, ἔνθα καὶ ὅρκια φρικτὰ θεῶν ἄρρηκτα βροτοῖσιν, ἄσμενοι εἰσεπέρησαν ἐμῇς ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν ἥρωες· μέγα γάρ σφιν ὀφέλσιμον ἀνθρώποισι τῆσδε θυηπολίης, ἄμοτον πλωτῆρσιν ἑκάστοις.

line_details.english: and the rugged forelands of deep-gazing Olympus,
line_details.greek: Οὐλύμπου δὲ βαθυσκοπέλου πρηῶνας ἐρυμνούς
line_details.note: βαθυσκοπέλου is an elevated epithet; here taken as “deep-gazing” (i.e., far-seen or looking out over the deep). πρηῶνας (“forelands, brows”) can denote jutting spurs or headlands; ἐρυμνούς = “rugged/steep.”

line_details.english: the Minyae beheld, and they rounded woody Athos,
line_details.greek: εἰσέδρακον Μινύαι, καὶ Ἄθω δενδρώδεα κάμψαν,
line_details.note: εἰσέδρακον is an aorist of εἰσοράω, “beheld.” κάμψαν is nautical, “rounded (a headland/cape).”

line_details.english: and broad Pellene; and most holy Samothrace,
line_details.greek: Πελλήνην τ' εὐρεῖαν· ἰδὲ ζαθέην Σαμοθρῄκην,
line_details.note: The transmitted Πελλήνη (Pellene, in Achaea) is likely a corruption for Παλήνη (Pallene, the Chalcidic peninsula), which fits the northern Aegean itinerary with Athos and Samothrace; many editors emend accordingly. ζαθέην = “most holy.”

line_details.english: where too the dread oaths of the gods, unbreakable for mortals,
line_details.greek: ἔνθα καὶ ὅρκια φρικτὰ θεῶν ἄρρηκτα βροτοῖσιν,
line_details.note: Refers to the Samothracian Mysteries; “dread oaths of the gods” suggests solemn, inviolable oaths connected with the cult. ἄρρηκτα = “unbreakable” (not to be confused with ἄρρητα, “unspeakable”).

line_details.english: the heroes, at my counsels, gladly passed within,
line_details.greek: ἄσμενοι εἰσεπέρησαν ἐμῇς ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν
line_details.note: εἰσεπέρασαν literally “passed within/entered,” here understood of entering/undergoing the Samothracian rites, done “at my counsels” (Orpheus as narrator-guide).

line_details.english: for great to them—aye, to mortal men—is the benefit
line_details.greek: ἥρωες· μέγα γάρ σφιν ὀφέλσιμον ἀνθρώποισι
line_details.note: σφιν ἀνθρώποισι is a double dative: “for them—indeed, for mortal men (generally).” ὀφέλσιμον = “beneficial, of great avail.”

line_details.english: of this sacrificial rite, unfailing for each seafarer.
line_details.greek: τῆσδε θυηπολίης, ἄμοτον πλωτῆρσιν ἑκάστοις.
line_details.note: θυηπολίη denotes sacrificial service/rite (here the Samothracian cult); ἄμοτον means “without stint, unfailing,” i.e., a benefit continually available to each mariner (πλωτῆρσιν ἑκάστοις).

text.english: To the Sintian headlands we urged the sea-swift ship, in goodly Lemnos; there indeed evil deeds preoccupied the women, for they had annihilated their bed-mates by their own recklessness, and she, famed Hypsipyle, would satisfy the longing of the women, best in form among women.
text.greek: Σιντιακαῖς δ' ὀφρῦσιν ἐκέλσαμεν ὠκύαλον ναῦν Λήμνῳ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ· τόθι περ κακὰ ἔργα μεμήλει θηλυτέραις· αἳ γάρ κεν ἀϊστώσαντο συνεύνους σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσι, καὶ ἡ κλυτὴ Ὑψιπύλεια ἐλδομέναις κραίνεσκε, γυναικῶν εἶδος ἀρίστη.

line_details.english: To the Sintian headlands we urged the sea-swift ship,
line_details.greek: Σιντιακαῖς δ' ὀφρῦσιν ἐκέλσαμεν ὠκύαλον ναῦν
line_details.note: “Sintian brows” (Σιντιακαῖς ὀφρῦσιν): ὀφρῦς (‘brow’) is used metaphorically of cliffs/headlands; the Sintians are the early inhabitants of Lemnos. ἐκέλσαμεν = ‘we urged/impelled’; ὠκύαλος = ‘sea‑swift’.

line_details.english: in goodly Lemnos; there indeed evil deeds preoccupied the women,
line_details.greek: Λήμνῳ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ· τόθι περ κακὰ ἔργα μεμήλει
line_details.note: ἠγαθέῃ = ‘goodly, noble’ (epic). μεμήλει with dative (‘is a care to’) yields ‘preoccupied’.

line_details.english: for they had annihilated their bed-mates by their own recklessness,
line_details.greek: θηλυτέραις· αἳ γάρ κεν ἀϊστώσαντο συνεύνους
line_details.note: ἀϊστόω = ‘make unseen,’ hence ‘annihilate/kill’; συνεύνους = ‘bed‑mates.’ κεν + optative has potential/gnomic force; in context it reports the notorious Lemnian massacre as effectively realized. ἀτασθαλίαι = ‘reckless wickedness.’

line_details.english: and she, famed Hypsipyle,
line_details.greek: σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσι, καὶ ἡ κλυτὴ Ὑψιπύλεια
line_details.note: κλυτὴ Ὑψιπύλεια = ‘famed Hypsipyle’ (queen of Lemnos). The form Ὑψιπύλεια is an epic variant of Hypsipyle.

line_details.english: would satisfy the longing of the women, best in form among women.
line_details.greek: ἐλδομέναις κραίνεσκε, γυναικῶν εἶδος ἀρίστη.
line_details.note: ἐλδομέναις (dat. fem. pl.) = ‘for the longing women’; κραίνεσκε (iterative imperf.) = ‘used to fulfill/bring to pass,’ with the implicit object ‘their desire (for union with the Argonauts).’ γυναικῶν εἶδος ἀρίστη = ‘best in form among women’ (epic formula for outstanding beauty).

text.english: But why should I speak to you at length, and plainly, of these things, how great a longing Kypris, nurse of love, stirred in the proud Lemnian women to mingle in bed with the Minyae? With lovely philtres Jason subdued Hypsipyle; one man mingled with one woman, another with another; and they quite forgot the voyage, had it not been that, with apotropaic strains, with our mind-bewitching heart, enchanted, they went toward the black ship, yearning for the oar, and they called the toil to mind.
text.greek: Ἀλλὰ τί σοι περὶ τῶνδε πόλυν λόγον ἀμφαδὸν εἰπεῖν, ὅσσον ἐφ' ἵμερον ὦρσεν ἀγαυαῖς Λημνιάδεσσι Κύπρις ἐρωτοτρόφος, Μινύαις εἰς λέκτρα μιγῆναι; φίλτροις Ὑψιπύλην ἐρατοῖς ἐδάμασσεν Ἰήσων· ἄλλῃ δ' ἄλλος ἔμικτο· καὶ ἐκλελάθοντο πορείης, εἰ μὴ ἀποτροπίοις ἐνοπαῖς θελξίφρονι θυμῷ ἡμετέρῳ θελχθέντες ἔβαν ποτὶ νῆα μέλαιναν, εἰρεσίην ποθέοντες ἐπεμνήσαντο δὲ μόχθου.

line_details.english: But why should I speak to you at length, and plainly, of these things,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλὰ τί σοι περὶ τῶνδε πόλυν λόγον ἀμφαδὸν εἰπεῖν,
line_details.note: Line 476: ἀμφαδόν = “openly, plainly.” The line is a rhetorical aporia (“why recount at length...”).

line_details.english: how great a longing Kypris, nurse of love, stirred in the proud Lemnian women
line_details.greek: ὅσσον ἐφ' ἵμερον ὦρσεν ἀγαυαῖς Λημνιάδεσσι
line_details.note: Lines 477–478: Kypris (Aphrodite) is called ἐρωτοτρόφος, “nurse/rearer of love.” ἀγαυαῖς conveys epic “proud/illustrious.” Μινύαι are the Minyae (Argonauts). μιγῆναι is sexual “to mingle” in beds.

line_details.english: to mingle in bed with the Minyae?
line_details.greek: Κύπρις ἐρωτοτρόφος, Μινύαις εἰς λέκτρα μιγῆναι;
line_details.note: Line 479: φίλτροις = “love-philtres/charms,” not necessarily a literal potion; ἐδάμασσεν (“tamed, subdued”) is a conventional erotic metaphor. Hypsipyle is the Lemnian queen.

line_details.english: With lovely philtres Jason subdued Hypsipyle;
line_details.greek: φίλτροις Ὑψιπύλην ἐρατοῖς ἐδάμασσεν Ἰήσων·
line_details.note: Line 480: ἄλλῃ δ’ ἄλλος ἔμικτο is elliptical: “one [man] with one [woman], another with another.” ἐκλελάθοντο (perf.) emphasizes utter forgetfulness of the journey/expedition (πορεία).

line_details.english: one man mingled with one woman, another with another; and they quite forgot the voyage,
line_details.greek: ἄλλῃ δ' ἄλλος ἔμικτο· καὶ ἐκλελάθοντο πορείης,
line_details.note: Lines 481–482: ἀποτροπίοις ἐνοπαῖς = “apotropaic cries/strains,” i.e., song that turns away (here, eros or delay). θελξίφρονι θυμῷ ἡμετέρῳ (“with our mind-bewitching heart”) presents Orpheus’ own inspired, enchanting intent as the instrument of the song; θελχθέντες (“enchanted”) picks up the effect on the crew. The εἰ μή clause gives a contrary-to-fact sense: they would have remained, had they not been charmed back to the ship.

line_details.english: had it not been that, with apotropaic strains, with our mind-bewitching heart,
line_details.greek: εἰ μὴ ἀποτροπίοις ἐνοπαῖς θελξίφρονι θυμῷ
line_details.note: Line 483: εἰρεσίη = “oarage/rowing”; μὀχθος = the toil of seafaring. ἐπεμνήσαντο = “they called to mind, bethought them of.”

line_details.english: enchanted, they went toward the black ship,
line_details.greek: ἡμετέρῳ θελχθέντες ἔβαν ποτὶ νῆα μέλαιναν,

line_details.english: yearning for the oar, and they called the toil to mind.
line_details.greek: εἰρεσίην ποθέοντες ἐπεμνήσαντο δὲ μόχθου.

text.english: Thence into the Hellespont, along with early Dawn, a fair wind bore them, the steady Zephyros, past narrow Abydos, having Dardanian Ilion and Pitye upon the right, where too the land of Abarnias and Percote, rich in ears of corn, Aisepos floods with its silver outpourings.
text.greek: - Ἔνθεν ἐς Ἑλλήσποντον ἅμ' ἠῴους φέρεν οὖρος ἀκραὴς Ζέφυρος, στεινῆς ἀπάτερθεν Ἀβύδου, Ἴλιον Δαρδανίην, Πιτύην τ' ἐπὶ δέξι' ἔχοντας, οὗ καὶ Ἀβαρνιάδος Περκώτης τ' εὔσταχυν αἶαν ἀργυρέαις Αἴσηπος ἐπικλύζει προχοῇσιν.

line_details.english: Thence into the Hellespont, along with early Dawn, a fair wind bore them,
line_details.greek: - Ἔνθεν ἐς Ἑλλήσποντον ἅμ' ἠῴους φέρεν οὖρος
line_details.note: οὖρος is a technical term for a “fair” or favorable sailing wind; ἠῴους (“with early Dawn”) marks the time of departure in elevated diction.

line_details.english: the steady Zephyros, past narrow Abydos,
line_details.greek: ἀκραὴς Ζέφυρος, στεινῆς ἀπάτερθεν Ἀβύδου,
line_details.note: ἀκραὴς with Zephyros is rendered “steady”; the adjective can mean “untempered, sheer, keen,” of a wind blowing full. στεινῆς Ἀβύδου (“narrow Abydos”) evokes the strait at Sestos–Abydos; ἀπάτερθεν is taken idiomatically as “past/from beyond.”

line_details.english: having Dardanian Ilion and Pitye upon the right,
line_details.greek: Ἴλιον Δαρδανίην, Πιτύην τ' ἐπὶ δέξι' ἔχοντας,
line_details.note: ἐπὶ δέξι’ = “on the right (hand),” i.e., to starboard as they sail; Πιτύη is Pitye/Pityeia on the Troad coast.

line_details.english: where too the land of Abarnias and Percote, rich in ears of corn,
line_details.greek: οὗ καὶ Ἀβαρνιάδος Περκώτης τ' εὔσταχυν αἶαν
line_details.note: Ἀβαρνιάδος likely refers to the district of Abarnis (a promontory/region near Lampsacus); Περκώτη (Percote) is a Troad town. εὔσταχυν = “rich in ears (of grain),” i.e., very fertile.

line_details.english: Aisepos floods with its silver outpourings.
line_details.greek: ἀργυρέαις Αἴσηπος ἐπικλύζει προχοῇσιν.
line_details.note: Αἴσηπος (Aisepos) is the Troad river (cf. Il. 2.825); ἀργυρέαις προχοῇσιν = “with silver outpourings/streams,” a conventional epithet for bright, shining waters. ἐπικλύζει = “floods/overflows,” here of irrigating the fertile plain.

text.english: And straightway, leaping forward, the much-speaking Argo sped.
text.greek: Αἶψα δ' ἐπιθρώσκουσα θέεν πολυηγόρος Ἀργώ.

line_details.english: And straightway, leaping forward, the much-speaking Argo sped.
line_details.greek: Αἶψα δ' ἐπιθρώσκουσα θέεν πολυηγόρος Ἀργώ.
line_details.note: πολυηγόρος (‘much-speaking’) likely alludes to Argo’s oracular Dodonaean beam; some take it as ‘much-spoken-of’. θέεν is augmentless imperfect 3 sg of θέω, used of ships ‘to speed’; ἐπιθρώσκουσα = ‘leaping forward.’

text.english: But when we had beached her upon the sands, then Tiphys the steersman of the barque, and the illustrious son of Aison, together with the other Minyae, to gray-eyed Tritogeneia set up, having lifted, a heavy stone; and there the Nymphs by the Artacian spring make fair waters overflow; because, thanks to her, as they voyaged over the broad Hellespont, a fair-weather calm met them within the inner recess, nor did they cast to earth their well-curved anchors, being smitten by waves beneath wintry blasts.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ψαμάθοισιν ἐκέλσαμεν, ἐν δ' ἄρα Τῖφυς ἰθύντωρ ἀκάτοιο, καὶ ἀγλαὸς Αἴσονος υἱός, σύν τ' ἄλλοι Μινύαι γλαυκώπιδι Τριτογενείῃ θῆκαν ἀείραντες βριθὺν λίθον, ἔνθα δὲ νύμφαι κρήνῃ ὑπ' Ἀρτακίῃ καλὰ νάματα πλημμύρουσιν· οὕνεκά οἱ πλώουσιν ἀνὰ πλατὺν Ἑλλήσποντον εὔδιος ἀντεβόλησε μυχοῦ ἔντοσθε γαλήνη, οὐδ' εἰς γαῖαν ἔριψαν ἐϋγνάμπτους ἀγκύρας, κύμασι θεινόμενοι ὑπὸ χειμερίαισιν ἀήταις.

line_details.english: But when we had beached her upon the sands, then Tiphys
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ψαμάθοισιν ἐκέλσαμεν, ἐν δ' ἄρα Τῖφυς
line_details.note: ἐκέλσαμεν (from the verb κελλάω/κελλ-) means “to run a ship aground, beach”; ψαμάθοισιν = “on the sands.”

line_details.english: the steersman of the barque, and the illustrious son of Aison,
line_details.greek: ἰθύντωρ ἀκάτοιο, καὶ ἀγλαὸς Αἴσονος υἱός,
line_details.note: ἰθύντωρ is a technical term for “helmsman/steersman”; ἀκάτη (“barque”) is a common epic term for the Argo.

line_details.english: together with the other Minyae, to gray-eyed Tritogeneia
line_details.greek: σύν τ' ἄλλοι Μινύαι γλαυκώπιδι Τριτογενείῃ
line_details.note: γλαυκώπιδι Τριτογενείῃ is Athena (dative of recipient) with her epithet “gray‑eyed Tritogeneia.”

line_details.english: set up, having lifted, a heavy stone; and there the Nymphs
line_details.greek: θῆκαν ἀείραντες βριθὺν λίθον, ἔνθα δὲ νύμφαι
line_details.note: βριθὺν λίθον (“a heavy stone”) is best taken as a votive/dedicatory stone set up for Athena.

line_details.english: by the Artacian spring make fair waters overflow;
line_details.greek: κρήνῃ ὑπ' Ἀρτακίῃ καλὰ νάματα πλημμύρουσιν·
line_details.note: The Artacian spring (Artacia) is a famous fountain near Kyzikos on the Propontis; ὑπ’ with the dative here = “at/by.”

line_details.english: because, thanks to her, as they voyaged over the broad Hellespont,
line_details.greek: οὕνεκά οἱ πλώουσιν ἀνὰ πλατὺν Ἑλλήσποντον
line_details.note: οἱ is dative singular referring to Athena: “thanks to her/for her sake,” explaining the dedication.

line_details.english: a fair-weather calm met them within the inner recess,
line_details.greek: εὔδιος ἀντεβόλησε μυχοῦ ἔντοσθε γαλήνη,
line_details.note: μυχὸυ ἔντοσθε = “within the inmost recess,” i.e., of the harbor; εὔδιος γαλήνη (“fair‑weather calm”) is personified as “meeting” them (ἀντεβόλησε).

line_details.english: nor did they cast to earth their well-curved anchors,
line_details.greek: οὐδ' εἰς γαῖαν ἔριψαν ἐϋγνάμπτους ἀγκύρας,
line_details.note: “Cast to earth” is Homeric/epic idiom for lowering anchors to the seabed; ἐϋγνάμπτους = “well‑curved.”

line_details.english: being smitten by waves beneath wintry blasts.
line_details.greek: κύμασι θεινόμενοι ὑπὸ χειμερίαισιν ἀήταις.
line_details.note: The participle “being smitten” indicates the usual condition requiring anchors—battering waves under wintry blasts—which in this case they avoided thanks to the calm.

text.english: Here, assembling upon the jutting shingle, we prepared meals and a lodging, each of us mindful of supper.
text.greek: Ἐνθάδε προσύνοντες ἐπὶ κροκάλαις προυχούσαις δεῖπνά τε καὶ κλισίην, δόρπου μεμνήμεθ' ἕκαστοι.

line_details.english: Here, assembling upon the jutting shingle,
line_details.greek: Ἐνθάδε προσύνοντες ἐπὶ κροκάλαις προυχούσαις
line_details.note: κροκάλαις προυχούσαις: κροκάλη = rounded pebble, hence “shingle”; προυχούσαις = “projecting, jutting,” describing a pebbly spit or out-jutting beach. προσύνοντες = “assembling, coming together.”

line_details.english: we prepared meals and a lodging, each of us mindful of supper.
line_details.greek: δεῖπνά τε καὶ κλισίην, δόρπου μεμνήμεθ' ἕκαστοι.
line_details.note: δεῖπνα = “meals” (general), δόρπος = specifically the evening meal “supper”; κλισίη is Homeric for “hut/tent,” here “lodging/camp.” The syntax is slightly elliptical: μεμνήμεθ’ governs the genitive δόρπου, while “δεῖπνα τε καὶ κλισίην” are understood as what they set about/prepared.

text.english: Then indeed the hero Kyzikos came up to them as they reclined, who held sway over the Doliones, men dwelling round about.
text.greek: Δὴ τότε κεκλιμένοισιν ἐπήλυθε Κύζικος ἥρως, ὃς Δολόπων ἤνασσε περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων.

line_details.english: Then indeed the hero Kyzikos came up to them as they reclined,
line_details.greek: Δὴ τότε κεκλιμένοισιν ἐπήλυθε Κύζικος ἥρως,
line_details.note: κεκλιμένοισιν is a dative plural “to the reclining [men],” likely of the Argonauts at banquet; ἐπήλυθε carries the nuance “came upon/approached.”

line_details.english: who held sway over the Doliones, men dwelling round about.
line_details.greek: ὃς Δολόπων ἤνασσε περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων.
line_details.note: The transmitted Δολόπων (“Dolopes”) is likely corrupt; most emend to Δολιόνων (“Doliones”), the people over whom Kyzikos is king in the tradition (cf. Apollonius Rhodius 1.936–960). περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων is a Homeric-style formula meaning “of the surrounding/neighbouring men.”

text.english: the beloved son of Aineus, whom a divine among women bore to him, Eusoros’ daughter Ainippē, fair-cheeked; who by his hospitality roused all the Minyans, slaughtering fat sheep and shambling, curving-horned bulls, and wild swine; and he gave moreover red wine, and sent abundant grain for those setting sail to carry, and cloaks and rugs, and well-spun tunics.
text.greek: Αἰνῆος φίλος υἱὸς ὅν οἱ τέκε δῖα γυναικῶν Εὐσώρου θυγάτηρ Αἰνίππη καλλιπάρῃος· ὅς ῥα φιλοξενίῃ Μινύας ἐγέρηρεν ἅπαντας, σφάζων πῖά τε μῆλα καὶ εἱλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς, ἀγροτέρους τε σύας· δῶκεν δ' ἔπι οἶνον ἐρυθρόν, σῖτον δ' ἄφθονον ἧκεν ἀποπλώουσι φέρεσθαι, χλαίνας τ' ἠδὲ τάπητας, ἐϋννήτους τε χιτῶνας.

line_details.english: the beloved son of Aineus, whom a divine among women bore to him,
line_details.greek: Αἰνῆος φίλος υἱὸς ὅν οἱ τέκε δῖα γυναικῶν
line_details.note: This refers to King Cyzicus, son of Aineus; dia gynaikōn (“divine among women”) is a standard epic epithet for a noble lady.

line_details.english: Eusoros’ daughter Ainippē, fair-cheeked;
line_details.greek: Εὐσώρου θυγάτηρ Αἰνίππη καλλιπάρῃος·
line_details.note: The mother’s name appears here as Ainippē; Apollonius Rhodius gives Aenētē as the daughter of Eusoros—likely a variant tradition. “Fair‑cheeked” (kalliparēios) is a conventional epithet.

line_details.english: who by his hospitality roused all the Minyans,
line_details.greek: ὅς ῥα φιλοξενίῃ Μινύας ἐγέρηρεν ἅπαντας,
line_details.note: “Minyans” is an epic designation for the Argonauts. The verb egerēren (“roused”) conveys ‘cheered/animated’ them through acts of xenia (guest‑friendship).

line_details.english: slaughtering fat sheep and shambling, curving-horned bulls,
line_details.greek: σφάζων πῖά τε μῆλα καὶ εἱλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς,
line_details.note: eilipodes (“shambling, rolling‑gaited”) and helikas (“curving[-horned]”) are Homeric stock epithets for cattle; “bulls” renders bous in this sacrificial context.

line_details.english: and wild swine; and he gave moreover red wine,
line_details.greek: ἀγροτέρους τε σύας· δῶκεν δ' ἔπι οἶνον ἐρυθρόν,
line_details.note: agroterous syas most naturally means “wild swine” (as opposed to domesticated pigs).

line_details.english: and sent abundant grain for those setting sail to carry,
line_details.greek: σῖτον δ' ἄφθονον ἧκεν ἀποπλώουσι φέρεσθαι,
line_details.note: sitos can mean ‘grain’ or, more generally, ‘provisions’; hēken … pheresthai = ‘sent [it] to be carried’ by those setting sail.

line_details.english: and cloaks and rugs, and well-spun tunics.
line_details.greek: χλαίνας τ' ἠδὲ τάπητας, ἐϋννήτους τε χιτῶνας.
line_details.note: chlaina = cloak; tapētēs = rug/coverlet; eunnētos = ‘well‑spun/well‑woven,’ marking quality textiles.

text.english: In turn, he cherished those present because they were of like age.
text.greek: Φίλετο δ' αὖ παρεόντας ὁμηλικίης ἕνεκα σφῆς·

line_details.english: In turn, he cherished those present because they were of like age.
line_details.greek: Φίλετο δ' αὖ παρεόντας ὁμηλικίης ἕνεκα σφῆς·
line_details.note: φίλετο is the epic middle (‘was fond of, showed affection to’). ὁμηλικίης ἕνεκα σφῆς = ‘on account of their being age-mates’; σφῆς (3rd-pl. reflexive) may refer to the group collectively. δ’ αὖ conveys resumption/‘in turn’.

text.english: And indeed he took part in all-day banquets.
text.greek: καί ῥα πανημερίῃσιν ἐν εἰλαπίναισιν ὅμαρτεν.

line_details.english: And indeed he took part in all-day banquets.
line_details.greek: καί ῥα πανημερίῃσιν ἐν εἰλαπίναισιν ὅμαρτεν.
line_details.note: ὅμαρτεν is the epic aorist of ὁμαρτέω, ‘to accompany, join in’; used intransitively here with ἐν + dat. πανημερίῃσι(ν) is an adverbial dative plural, ‘throughout the whole day’. εἰλαπίναι are festive banquets.

text.english: But when the Titan was dipped in the stream of Okeanos, and the star-robed Moon brought on the black-gleaming gloom, then went forth men renowned in war, who indeed were dwelling among the northern mountains, awestruck, like unto wild beasts, like to the Titans, and akin to stalwart men, and to the Giants; for from the shoulders of each six hands shot forth.
text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε γ' Ὠκεανοῖο ῥόον βαπτίζετο Τιτάν, μήνη δ' ἀστροχίτων ἔπαγεν μελαναυγέα ὄρφνην, τῆμος ἀρηίφατοι κίον ἀνέρες, οἵ ῥα νέμοντο ἀρκτῴοις ἐν ὄρεσσι, τεθηπότες εἴκελα θηρσί Τιτᾶσι, βριαροῖς τ' ἐναλίγκιοι ἠδὲ Γίγασιν· ἓξ γὰρ χεῖρες ἑκάστῳ ἀπ' ὤμων ἀΐσσοντο.

line_details.english: But when the Titan was dipped in the stream of Okeanos,
line_details.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε γ' Ὠκεανοῖο ῥόον βαπτίζετο Τιτάν,
line_details.note: “Titan” here denotes the Sun (Helios); βαπτίζετο (“was dipped/immersed”) evokes sunset into the encircling stream of Okeanos.

line_details.english: and the star-robed Moon brought on the black-gleaming gloom,
line_details.greek: μήνη δ' ἀστροχίτων ἔπαγεν μελαναυγέα ὄρφνην,
line_details.note: μήνη is ‘Moon’ (not ‘month’) in Orphic diction; ἀστροχίτων = ‘star-robed’; μελαναυγέα ὄρφνη is an oxymoronic ‘black-gleaming gloom’; ἔπαγεν = ‘brought on.’

line_details.english: then went forth men renowned in war, who indeed were dwelling
line_details.greek: τῆμος ἀρηίφατοι κίον ἀνέρες, οἵ ῥα νέμοντο
line_details.note: ἀρηίφατοι = ‘spoken-of for Ares,’ hence ‘war-famed’; κίον is epic aorist ‘they went’; οἵ ῥα marks the relative with a slight emphatic/confirmatory nuance.

line_details.english: among the northern mountains, awestruck, like unto wild beasts,
line_details.greek: ἀρκτῴοις ἐν ὄρεσσι, τεθηπότες εἴκελα θηρσί
line_details.note: ἀρκτῴοις = ‘northern’ (lit. ‘of the Bear’); τεθηπότες = ‘awestruck, astonied’; εἴκελα θηρσί = ‘like unto wild beasts.’

line_details.english: like to the Titans, and akin to stalwart men, and to the Giants;
line_details.greek: Τιτᾶσι, βριαροῖς τ' ἐναλίγκιοι ἠδὲ Γίγασιν·
line_details.note: βριαροῖς is the adjective ‘stout/strong,’ not the proper name Briareus; ἐναλίγκιοι = ‘akin to, like unto’; the triad Titans/‘stalwart’/Giants heightens their monstrous might.

line_details.english: for from the shoulders of each six hands shot forth.
line_details.greek: ἓξ γὰρ χεῖρες ἑκάστῳ ἀπ' ὤμων ἀΐσσοντο.
line_details.note: ἀΐσσοντο = ‘shot/darted forth,’ vividly of limbs; the six-armed men recall Hundred-Handers typology but with six hands per man.

text.english: Then, when they had caught sight of them, the unconquerable kings intent on the fray, donned their warlike gear.
text.greek: Οὓς τότ' ἐσαθρήσαντες ἀμαιμάκετοι βασιλῆες, ἐς μόθον ὁρμαίνοντες ἀρήϊα τεύχε' ἔδυνον.

line_details.english: Then, when they had caught sight of them, the unconquerable kings
line_details.greek: Οὓς τότ' ἐσαθρήσαντες ἀμαιμάκετοι βασιλῆες,
line_details.note: ἐσαθρήσαντες: aorist ptc. of (εἰ)σαθρέω, “on seeing, after catching sight”; ἀμαιμάκετοι = “unconquerable, irresistible,” a conventional epic epithet. Some editions read εἰσαθρήσαντες.

line_details.english: intent on the fray, donned their warlike gear.
line_details.greek: ἐς μόθον ὁρμαίνοντες ἀρήϊα τεύχε' ἔδυνον.
line_details.note: ἐς μόθον = “into the fray, battle-throng”; ὁρμαίνοντες here “being minded/intent,” not “rushing”; ἀρήϊα (Areian) means “warlike, of Ares,” hence “warlike gear.”

text.english: And then some defended themselves with pines, and others with firs; and they fell among the Minyae through the shadow-dark mist.
text.greek: Καὶ ῥ' οἳ μὲν πευκῇσιν ἀμύνονθ' οἳ δ' ἐλάτῃσιν· ἐν δ' ἔπεσαν Μινύαισι κατὰ σκοτόεσσαν ὁμίχλην.

line_details.english: And then some defended themselves with pines, and others with firs;
line_details.greek: Καὶ ῥ' οἳ μὲν πευκῇσιν ἀμύνονθ' οἳ δ' ἐλάτῃσιν·
line_details.note: Peurkēisin / elatēisin are instrumental datives: “with pines/firs,” i.e., using weapons or cudgels of those woods (fir/pine shafts or boughs). The middle ἀμύνονθ’ means “were defending themselves/warding off [the foe].”

line_details.english: and they fell among the Minyae through the shadow-dark mist.
line_details.greek: ἐν δ' ἔπεσαν Μινύαισι κατὰ σκοτόεσσαν ὁμίχλην.
line_details.note: ἐν ἔπεσαν + dative (“fell among”) is an epic idiom for closing in combat. Minyae = the Argonauts. κατά with the accusative marks motion “through/down through” the σκοτόεσσαν ὁμίχλην (“shadow-dark mist”), a Homeric-style formula.

text.english: Those indeed, as they were rushing on, the valiant son of Zeus slew, shooting with the bow; and along with them he destroyed Kyzikos, the son of Aineus, not at all willingly, but fettered by heedlessness; for it was his doom to be subdued by Herakles.
text.greek: Οὕς τοι ἐπειγομένους κτεῖνεν Διὸς ἄλκιμος υἱός, τόξῳ ὀϊστεύων· σὺν δ' Αἰνέος ὤλεσε παῖδα Κύζικον, οὔτι ἑκὼν, ἀλλ' ἀφραδίῃσι πεδηθείς· τῷ δ' ἄρα μόρσιμον ἧεν ὑφ' Ἡρακλῆι δαμῆναι.

line_details.english: Those indeed, as they were rushing on, the valiant son of Zeus slew,
line_details.greek: Οὕς τοι ἐπειγομένους κτεῖνεν Διὸς ἄλκιμος υἱός,
line_details.note: τοι is an enclitic intensifier (“indeed”); “the son of Zeus” designates Herakles.

line_details.english: shooting with the bow; and along with them he destroyed Kyzikos, the son of Aineus,
line_details.greek: τόξῳ ὀϊστεύων· σὺν δ' Αἰνέος ὤλεσε παῖδα
line_details.note: σύν here is adverbial (“along with, in addition”); Αἰνέος is the genitive of Aineus, father of Kyzikos. The Orphic Argonautica has Herakles as Kyzikos’ slayer, differing from the more familiar Apollonian version where Jason kills him.

line_details.english: not at all willingly, but fettered by heedlessness;
line_details.greek: Κύζικον, οὔτι ἑκὼν, ἀλλ' ἀφραδίῃσι πεδηθείς·
line_details.note: ἀφραδίῃσι is a poetic plural (“acts of folly/heedlessness”); πεδηθείς (“fettered”) is metaphorical for being constrained by error.

line_details.english: for it was his doom to be subdued by Herakles.
line_details.greek: τῷ δ' ἄρα μόρσιμον ἧεν ὑφ' Ἡρακλῆι δαμῆναι.
line_details.note: μόρσιμον ἧεν is an epic idiom for “it was fated/doom had it”; δαμῆναι (aorist passive of δαμάζω) = “to be overpowered/slain,” with ὑφ’ Ἡρακλῆι marking the agent.

text.english: Straightway the Minyae stepped within the hollow ship.
text.greek: Αἶψα δέ οἱ Μινύαι κοίλης ἔντοσθεν ἔβησαν

line_details.english: Straightway the Minyae stepped within the hollow ship.
line_details.greek: Αἶψα δέ οἱ Μινύαι κοίλης ἔντοσθεν ἔβησαν
line_details.note: οἱ is an ethical dative (“for him”), likely referring to Iason; νηός completes the enjambed phrase κοίλης [νηὸς] ἔντοσθεν ἔβησαν = “went within the hollow ship.”

text.english: Well-equipped, each took his seat at the thwart.
text.greek: νηὸς τευχήρεις, ποτὶ δὲ ζυγὸν ἷζον ἕκαστος.

line_details.english: Well-equipped, each took his seat at the thwart.
line_details.greek: νηὸς τευχήρεις, ποτὶ δὲ ζυγὸν ἷζον ἕκαστος.
line_details.note: τευχήρεις = “accoutred, in full gear,” modifying the Minyae; ζυγόν is the rower’s bench (thwart). The plural ἷζον with ἕκαστος is epic usage (“they sat, each [man] ...”).

text.english: Then Tiphys from the stern raised a shout and gave the order to haul the ladder aboard the ship, and to loose the hawsers.
text.greek: Τῖφυς δὲ πρύμνηθεν ἐπήπυεν ἠδ' ἐκέλευε κλίμακα νηὸς ἔσω ἐρύσαι, καὶ πείσματα λῦσαι.

line_details.english: Then Tiphys from the stern raised a shout and gave the order
line_details.greek: Τῖφυς δὲ πρύμνηθεν ἐπήπυεν ἠδ' ἐκέλευε
line_details.note: πρύμνηθεν = “from the stern”; ἐπῆπυεν is Homeric “raised a shout”; ἐκέλευε governs the aorist infinitives that follow.

line_details.english: to haul the ladder aboard the ship, and to loose the hawsers.
line_details.greek: κλίμακα νηὸς ἔσω ἐρύσαι, καὶ πείσματα λῦσαι.
line_details.note: κλῖμαξ is the boarding-ladder/gangway; νηὸς ἔσω literally “into the ship”; πεῖσματα are mooring cables (“hawsers”); λῦσαι = “loose, cast off.”

text.english: But his hawsers would not be loosed; rather, with inescapable bonds fitted to the swift capstan they were gripped tight, holding the ship in check; and Tiphys the blameless was amazed, and speechless, the tiller-ropes of the ship Argo slipped from his hands, for he did not expect to pass over the wave.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ λύοντο κάλοι, δεσμοῖσι δ' ἀφύκτοις ὠκείης στροφάλιγγος ἀρηρότες ἐσφίγγοντο, νῆα κατείργοντες· θάμβησε δὲ Τῖφυς ἀμύμων, ἄφθογγος δέ οἱ ἧκε χερῶν οἰήϊα νηός Ἀργῴης· οὐ γάρ οἱ ἐέλπετο κῦμα περῆσαι.

line_details.english: But his hawsers would not be loosed; rather, with inescapable bonds
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ λύοντο κάλοι, δεσμοῖσι δ' ἀφύκτοις
line_details.note: κάλοι = mooring-ropes/hawsers; οἱ is a dative of interest (“for him”), i.e., for Tiphys.

line_details.english: fitted to the swift capstan they were gripped tight,
line_details.greek: ὠκείης στροφάλιγγος ἀρηρότες ἐσφίγγοντο,
line_details.note: στροφάλιγξ, literally a ‘whirler’ or ‘humming-top’, here denotes a rotating ship’s device (capstan/windlass); ἀρηρότες = ‘fitted to’; ἐσφίγγοντο = ‘were being tightened’.

line_details.english: holding the ship in check; and Tiphys the blameless was amazed,
line_details.greek: νῆα κατείργοντες· θάμβησε δὲ Τῖφυς ἀμύμων,
line_details.note: Tiphys ἀμύμων preserves the epic epithet “blameless/noble.”

line_details.english: and speechless, the tiller-ropes of the ship Argo slipped from his hands,
line_details.greek: ἄφθογγος δέ οἱ ἧκε χερῶν οἰήϊα νηός
line_details.note: οἰήϊα are the tiller-ropes (steering-gear) controlling the rudder; ἧκε = ‘let go, fell from’; Ἀργῴης is the epic genitive “of Argo.”

line_details.english: for he did not expect to pass over the wave.
line_details.greek: Ἀργῴης· οὐ γάρ οἱ ἐέλπετο κῦμα περῆσαι.
line_details.note: κῦμα περῆσαι = “to pass over/through the wave,” an idiom for clearing a dangerous swell or breaker.

text.english: For Rheia was wont to be wroth on account of the people’s din.
text.greek: Ῥείη γὰρ κοτέεσκε δεδουπότος εἵνεκα λαοῦ·

line_details.english: For Rheia was wont to be wroth on account of the people’s din.
line_details.greek: Ῥείη γὰρ κοτέεσκε δεδουπότος εἵνεκα λαοῦ·
line_details.note: Line 535: kotéeske is the iterative imperfect (“used to be angry”). Dedoupotos (gen. sg.) is the perfect participle of doupéō (“to thud, make a crashing noise”), here “the people’s din/uproar.”

text.english: But when the path of night advanced toward its midmost point, and the far-shining stars were sinking beneath the stream of Oceanos, sweet sleep stole upon the helmsman’s eyes.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε πρὸς μέσατον νυκτὸς προὔβαινεν ἀταρπός, ἄστρα τε τηλεφανῆ δῦνεν ῥόον Ὠκεανοῖο, ὄσσε κυβερνήτῃ προσεπέστιχε νήδυμος ὕπνος.

line_details.english: But when the path of night advanced toward its midmost point,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε πρὸς μέσατον νυκτὸς προὔβαινεν ἀταρπός,
line_details.note: Line 536: “Path of night” (atarpos) is a poetic periphrasis for the progress of the hours; mésaton = “midpoint.”

line_details.english: and the far-shining stars were sinking beneath the stream of Oceanos,
line_details.greek: ἄστρα τε τηλεφανῆ δῦνεν ῥόον Ὠκεανοῖο,
line_details.note: Line 537: “Far-shining” (telephanē) is a conventional epic epithet of stars; “stream of Oceanos” (rhoos Ōkeanoio) is the cosmic river into which the stars set.

line_details.english: sweet sleep stole upon the helmsman’s eyes.
line_details.greek: ὄσσε κυβερνήτῃ προσεπέστιχε νήδυμος ὕπνος.
line_details.note: Line 538: Osse is the epic dual “eyes.” Nēdymos = “sweet, balmy.” Prosepéstiche is an epic form meaning “came/stole upon,” with the dative of person (kybernētēi) and the accusative “eyes.”

text.english: But to him, as he slumbered deep, the goddess Athene, steadfast-resounding, standing close at hand, displayed true tokens beside him; and thus, calling out, she spoke a god-declaring word: “You sleep, Agniades, smitten by sweet sleep, having cast a stupor upon your eyelids; but awake, Tiphys, and summon the heroes to go to a windless shore, springing forth from the ship, where a stranger upon the sands lies bereft of life; for him perform the burial-gifts, for All-counselling Rheia enjoins these honors, and libations, to be given to those beneath the earth, and to let tears fall from your eyes, in reverence for Themis of pure rites and the table of guest-friendship; whom, though unwilling, Heracles slew by a cast through the nightly gloom, and you have angered the spirit of the goddess Rheia.” But whenever by the rites you honor the guest‑friend who has died, then straightway, having ascended Dindymon, the seat of Rhea, with holy propitiations appease the daughter of Gaia, and when you have taken up your moorings, then indeed bethink you of the voyage.” Thus having spoken, the goddess turned back again, like an arrow, hastening to heaven. And straightway his trance was scattered, and from the stern he sprang swiftly; and with a shout he roused the host, who were sleeping along the walls here and there, leaning sidelong, trembling in spirit; and at once he told to all the heroes the phantoms of the dream, speaking in a rush.
text.greek: Τῷ δὲ βαθὺ κνώσσοντι θεὰ μενέδουπος Ἀθήνη ἄγχι παρισταμένη παρ' ἐτήτυμα σήματ' ἔφαινεν· ὧδε δ' ὁμοκλήσασα θεηγόρον ἔννεπε μῦθον· - "Εὕδεις Ἀγνιάδη, γλυκερῷ βεβολημένος ὕπνῳ, κῶμα περὶ βλεφάροισι βαλών· ἀλλ' ἔγρεο Τῖφυ, κέκλεο δ' ἡρώεσσι μολεῖν ἐπὶ νήνεμον ἀκτήν, νηὸς ἄπο προθορόντας, ὅθι ξένος ἐν ψαμάθοισι κεῖται ἀποφθίμενος· τῷ οἱ κτέρεα κτερεΐξαι παμμήτειρα Ῥέη κέλεται γέρα, ἠδέ τε λοιβάς δοῦναι ὑποχθονίοις καὶ δάκρυα λειβέμεν ὄσσων, αἰδομένους Θέμιν ἀγνοτελῆ ξενίην τε τράπεζαν· ὅν ῥ' ἀέκων ἔκτεινε βαλὼν διὰ νύκτερον ὄρφνην Ἡρακλέης, θυμὸν δὲ θεᾶς ἐχολώσατε Ῥείης. Ἀλλ' ὁπόταν θεσμοῖς ξεῖνον σεβάσησθε θανόντα Δίνδυμον αὐτίκ' ἔπειτα Ῥέης ἕδος εἰσαναβάντες ἱλασμοῖς ἱεροῖς Γαίης ἀρέσασθε θύγατρα, πείσματα δ' ἀράμενοι, τότε δὴ μνώεσθε πλοοῖο." - Ὣς εἰποῦσα θεὰ πάλιν ἐτράπετ', ἶσον ὀϊστῷ οὐρανὸν ἐσσυμένη. Τοῦ δ' αὐτίκα κῶμ' ἐκεδάσθη, πρύμνης δ' ἆλτο θοῶς· ἀνέγειρε δὲ λαὸν ἀϋτῇ τοίχων ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα παρακλιδὸν ὑπνώοντας, ψυχῇ ὑποτρομέων· ἄφαρ ἡρώεσσι δ' ὀνείρου φάσματα πᾶσιν ἔειπεν, ἐπιδρομάδην ἀγορεύων.

line_details.english: But to him, as he slumbered deep, the goddess Athene, steadfast-resounding,
line_details.greek: Τῷ δὲ βαθὺ κνώσσοντι θεὰ μενέδουπος Ἀθήνη
line_details.note: Line 539: μενέδουπος is a rare/Orphic epithet; likely from μένω + δοῦπος (“enduring-din”), hence “steadfast-resounding,” suiting Athene’s warlike aspect. Some take it as ‘steadfast in counsel’ by association with μῆτις.

line_details.english: standing close at hand, displayed true tokens beside him;
line_details.greek: ἄγχι παρισταμένη παρ' ἐτήτυμα σήματ' ἔφαινεν·
line_details.note: Line 540: The phrase ἄγχι παρισταμένη marks a divine epiphany; σήματα are “true tokens,” here dream-signs.

line_details.english: and thus, calling out, she spoke a god-declaring word:
line_details.greek: ὧδε δ' ὁμοκλήσασα θεηγόρον ἔννεπε μῦθον·
line_details.note: Line 541: θεηγόρος (“god-declaring”) is rare, indicating a speech carrying divine authority/revelation.

line_details.english: “You sleep, Agniades, smitten by sweet sleep,
line_details.greek: - "Εὕδεις Ἀγνιάδη, γλυκερῷ βεβολημένος ὕπνῳ,
line_details.note: Line 542: Ἀγνιάδη = “Agniades,” the patronymic of Tiphys (son of Hagnias/Hagnis).

line_details.english: having cast a stupor upon your eyelids; but awake, Tiphys,
line_details.greek: κῶμα περὶ βλεφάροισι βαλών· ἀλλ' ἔγρεο Τῖφυ,

line_details.english: and summon the heroes to go to a windless shore,
line_details.greek: κέκλεο δ' ἡρώεσσι μολεῖν ἐπὶ νήνεμον ἀκτήν,

line_details.english: springing forth from the ship, where a stranger upon the sands
line_details.greek: νηὸς ἄπο προθορόντας, ὅθι ξένος ἐν ψαμάθοισι
line_details.note: Line 545: ξένος can mean both “stranger” and “guest-friend,” anticipating the theme of ξενία in 549.

line_details.english: lies bereft of life; for him perform the burial-gifts,
line_details.greek: κεῖται ἀποφθίμενος· τῷ οἱ κτέρεα κτερεΐξαι
line_details.note: Line 546: τῷ οἱ is an idiomatic dative construction (“for him … to him”); κτερεΐζειν = “to pay funeral honors/offer burial-gifts.”

line_details.english: for All-counselling Rheia enjoins these honors, and libations,
line_details.greek: παμμήτειρα Ῥέη κέλεται γέρα, ἠδέ τε λοιβάς
line_details.note: Line 547: παμμήτειρα (“All-counselling”) is an Orphic epithet of Rheia; γέρα here = “rites/honors” due to the dead.

line_details.english: to be given to those beneath the earth, and to let tears fall from your eyes,
line_details.greek: δοῦναι ὑποχθονίοις καὶ δάκρυα λειβέμεν ὄσσων,
line_details.note: Line 548: ὑποχθόνιοι = the chthonic powers/spirits of the dead; the libations are directed to them.

line_details.english: in reverence for Themis of pure rites and the table of guest-friendship;
line_details.greek: αἰδομένους Θέμιν ἀγνοτελῆ ξενίην τε τράπεζαν·
line_details.note: Line 549: ἀγνοτελής (“of pure rites”) is a rare epithet of Themis; ξενίη τράπεζα = “the table of guest-friendship,” emblematic of sacred hospitality (ξενία).

line_details.english: whom, though unwilling, Heracles slew by a cast through the nightly gloom,
line_details.greek: ὅν ῥ' ἀέκων ἔκτεινε βαλὼν διὰ νύκτερον ὄρφνην
line_details.note: Line 550: ἀέκων modifies Heracles (“though unwilling”); βαλών implies a hurled weapon (ellipsis of the object) cast in the night’s darkness.

line_details.english: and you have angered the spirit of the goddess Rheia.”
line_details.greek: Ἡρακλέης, θυμὸν δὲ θεᾶς ἐχολώσατε Ῥείης.
line_details.note: Line 551: ἐχολώσατε is 2nd pl., addressing the Argonauts collectively as having provoked Rheia’s wrath.

line_details.english: But whenever by the rites you honor the guest‑friend who has died,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὁπόταν θεσμοῖς ξεῖνον σεβάσησθε θανόντα
line_details.note: thesmois = ‘rites, established customs’; xeinon = ‘guest‑friend,’ not merely ‘stranger,’ referring to King Cyzicus in context.

line_details.english: then straightway, having ascended Dindymon, the seat of Rhea,
line_details.greek: Δίνδυμον αὐτίκ' ἔπειτα Ῥέης ἕδος εἰσαναβάντες
line_details.note: Dindymon: the Phrygian mountain near Cyzicus; ‘seat of Rhea’ identifies her as the Mother (Meter Dindymene).

line_details.english: with holy propitiations appease the daughter of Gaia,
line_details.greek: ἱλασμοῖς ἱεροῖς Γαίης ἀρέσασθε θύγατρα,
line_details.note: ‘daughter of Gaia’ = Rhea (daughter of Uranus and Gaia); hilasmoi = propitiatory rites.

line_details.english: and when you have taken up your moorings, then indeed bethink you of the voyage.”
line_details.greek: πείσματα δ' ἀράμενοι, τότε δὴ μνώεσθε πλοοῖο."
line_details.note: peismata = ship’s cables/moorings; aramenoi = ‘having taken up’ (i.e., weighing the moorings).

line_details.english: Thus having spoken, the goddess turned back again, like an arrow,
line_details.greek: - Ὣς εἰποῦσα θεὰ πάλιν ἐτράπετ', ἶσον ὀϊστῷ
line_details.note: Epic simile ‘like an arrow’ marks the goddess’s sudden departure.

line_details.english: hastening to heaven. And straightway his trance was scattered,
line_details.greek: οὐρανὸν ἐσσυμένη. Τοῦ δ' αὐτίκα κῶμ' ἐκεδάσθη,
line_details.note: kōma = deep sleep/trance; ‘was scattered’ renders ekedasthe (‘was dispelled’).

line_details.english: and from the stern he sprang swiftly;
line_details.greek: πρύμνης δ' ἆλτο θοῶς· ἀνέγειρε δὲ λαὸν ἀϋτῇ
line_details.note: prymnēs: he had been at the stern; alto = ‘he sprang.’

line_details.english: and with a shout he roused the host, who were sleeping along the walls here and there, leaning sidelong,
line_details.greek: τοίχων ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα παρακλιδὸν ὑπνώοντας,
line_details.note: toichōn may be city/building walls or, loosely, bulwarks; paraklidon = ‘leaning sideways, slantwise.’

line_details.english: trembling in spirit;
line_details.greek: ψυχῇ ὑποτρομέων· ἄφαρ ἡρώεσσι δ' ὀνείρου
line_details.note: psychēi hypotromeōn = ‘quivering at heart,’ i.e., emotionally shaken by the vision.

line_details.english: and at once he told to all the heroes the phantoms of the dream, speaking in a rush.
line_details.greek: φάσματα πᾶσιν ἔειπεν, ἐπιδρομάδην ἀγορεύων.
line_details.note: phasmata oneirou = ‘dream‑phantoms/apparitions’; epidromadēn = ‘in swift succession, hurriedly.’

text.english: Then they swiftly were roused, and each leapt upon the strand.
text.greek: Οἱ δὲ θοῶς ἤγερθεν, ἐπ' ᾐόνα δ' ἆλτο ἕκαστος.

line_details.english: Then they swiftly were roused, and each leapt upon the strand.
line_details.greek: Οἱ δὲ θοῶς ἤγερθεν, ἐπ' ᾐόνα δ' ἆλτο ἕκαστος.
line_details.note: ἤγερθεν is the Homeric aorist passive of ἐγείρω used intransitively (“were roused, got up”); ᾐόνα is the epic form of ἠϊών (“shore, strand,” often written ἠϊόνα); ἆλτο is 3rd singular aorist middle of ἅλλομαι, agreeing with the singular ἕκαστος (“each”).

text.english: And along the murky vault of the sky moved golden Eos, opening the risings of the East, and heaven was revealing daybreak; then the Minyan champions perceived a corpse, bespattered with blood and dust; for all about, others war-slain were lying on every side—the huge bodies of beasts.
text.greek: Ἡ δὲ κατ' ὀρφναίοιο πόλου χρυσήνιος ἠὼς ἀντολίας ἤνοιγεν, ἐδέχνυτο δ' οὐρανὸς ὄρθρον· καὶ τότ' ἀριστῆες Μινύαι νέκυν εἰσενόησαν αἵματι καὶ κονίῃ πεπαλαγμένον· ἀμφὶ γὰρ ἄλλοι δήϊοι ἀμφὶς ἔκειντο, πελώρια σώματα θηρῶν.

line_details.english: And along the murky vault of the sky moved golden Eos,
line_details.greek: Ἡ δὲ κατ' ὀρφναίοιο πόλου χρυσήνιος ἠὼς
line_details.note: χρυσήνιος is an elevated epithet (“golden”) applied to Eos; κατ’ ὀρφναίοιο πόλου suggests motion “along/across” the darkling sky.

line_details.english: opening the risings of the East, and heaven was revealing daybreak;
line_details.greek: ἀντολίας ἤνοιγεν, ἐδέχνυτο δ' οὐρανὸς ὄρθρον·
line_details.note: ἀντολίαι (plural) literally “risings,” i.e., the East/sunrise; ἐδείχνυτο (middle) gives “was revealing/was showing itself.”

line_details.english: then the Minyan champions perceived a corpse,
line_details.greek: καὶ τότ' ἀριστῆες Μινύαι νέκυν εἰσενόησαν
line_details.note: ἀριστῆες Μινύαι = “the Minyan champions,” a traditional designation for the Argonauts; νέκυν = “a corpse.”

line_details.english: bespattered with blood and dust; for all about, others
line_details.greek: αἵματι καὶ κονίῃ πεπαλαγμένον· ἀμφὶ γὰρ ἄλλοι
line_details.note: πεπαλαγμένον is the perfect participle of παλάσσω, “to besmear/sprinkle,” hence “bespattered” with blood and dust.

line_details.english: war-slain were lying on every side—the huge bodies of beasts.
line_details.greek: δήϊοι ἀμφὶς ἔκειντο, πελώρια σώματα θηρῶν.
line_details.note: δήϊοι used substantively = “the war-slain”; θηρῶν is appositional, clarifying that the fallen were beasts (“the huge bodies of beasts”).

text.english: But they, standing in a ring and thronging about the king, laid Kyzikos beneath well‑smoothed slabs, and then they heaped up a tumulus and built a marker.
text.greek: - Ἀλλ' οἳ μὲν βασιλῆα περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντες Κύζικον εὐξέστοισιν ὑπὸ πλακέεσσιν ἔθηκαν, ἂν δ' ἄρα τύμβον ἔχευαν, ἐδωμήσαντο δὲ σῆμα.

line_details.english: But they, standing in a ring and thronging about the king,
line_details.greek: - Ἀλλ' οἳ μὲν βασιλῆα περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντες
line_details.note: περισταδόν … ἀμφιχυθέντες: the adverb “in a ring/on all sides” with the participle of ἀμφιχέω (“to pour around”) is a figurative hendiadys for “to throng/press about” the corpse before burial.

line_details.english: laid Kyzikos beneath well‑smoothed slabs,
line_details.greek: Κύζικον εὐξέστοισιν ὑπὸ πλακέεσσιν ἔθηκαν,
line_details.note: εὐξέστοισιν πλακέεσσιν: “well‑smoothed slabs,” i.e., flat stone cover; ἔθηκαν = “laid/placed” in the sense of interment; Κύζικον is the slain king Kyzikos.

line_details.english: and then they heaped up a tumulus and built a marker.
line_details.greek: ἂν δ' ἄρα τύμβον ἔχευαν, ἐδωμήσαντο δὲ σῆμα.
