line_details.note: ἂν δ’ ἄρα is an epic connective (“and then”); τύμβον ἔχευαν = “they heaped a barrow”; ἐδωμήσαντο (middle) = “they built,” and σῆμα denotes the grave‑marker/monument distinct from the earthen mound.

text.english: And straightway they brought the pots, and, preparing the cut victims, they sent the all‑black offerings down into the pits; but I myself propitiated the soul, pouring as libations the pots’ soothing offerings, with water and with milk, adding libations from honey‑flowing streams, and honoring it with my own hymns.
text.greek: Φιτροὺς δ' αἶψα κόμιζον, ἰδ' ἔντομα πορσύνοντες παμμέλαν' ἐν βόθροις μετεκίαθον· αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε ψυχὴν ἱλασάμην, σπένδων μειλίγματα χύτλων ὕδατί τ' ἠδὲ γάλακτι, μελισσορύτων ἀπὸ νασμῶν λοιβαῖς συμπροχέων, καὶ ἐμοῖς ὕμνοισι γεραίρων.

line_details.english: And straightway they brought the pots, and, preparing the cut victims,
line_details.greek: Φιτροὺς δ' αἶψα κόμιζον, ἰδ' ἔντομα πορσύνοντες
line_details.note: The reading Φιτροὺς is likely a corruption; most editors take χύτρους (“pots/jars”), supported by χύτλων/χύτρων in 573. πορσύνω = “busy with, prepare.”

line_details.english: they sent the all‑black offerings down into the pits; but I myself
line_details.greek: παμμέλαν' ἐν βόθροις μετεκίαθον· αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε
line_details.note: ἔντομα here = “cut/slain victims” (not “insects”): a technical term of chthonic sacrifice. παμμέλαν’ = “all‑black,” the proper color for chthonic victims; βόθροι are ritual pits for under‑earth deities; μετεκίαθον = “sent down (to the dead).”

line_details.english: propitiated the soul, pouring as libations the pots’ soothing offerings,
line_details.greek: ψυχὴν ἱλασάμην, σπένδων μειλίγματα χύτλων
line_details.note: μειλίγματα = “soothing/mollifying offerings,” standard for appeasing the dead; χύτλων is a form of χύτρων (“of pots/jars”).

line_details.english: with water and with milk, adding libations from honey‑flowing streams,
line_details.greek: ὕδατί τ' ἠδὲ γάλακτι, μελισσορύτων ἀπὸ νασμῶν
line_details.note: μελισσορύτων ἀπὸ νασμῶν is a periphrasis for honey (“honey‑flowing streams”); συμπροχέων = “pouring along with,” i.e., in addition to the water and milk.

line_details.english: and honoring it with my own hymns.
line_details.greek: λοιβαῖς συμπροχέων, καὶ ἐμοῖς ὕμνοισι γεραίρων.
line_details.note: γεραίρω = “honor,” here with hymns as part of the chthonic rite.

text.english: But Aisonides himself proclaimed a contest for all, prizes to be for his comrades at the funeral games, the gifts that Hypsipyle of Lemnos had given him to carry away.
text.greek: - Αὐτὸς δ' Αἰσονίδης προυθήκατο πᾶσιν ἄεθλον, τυμβιδίου ἐπ' ἀγῶνος ἑταίροις ἔμμεν' ἄεθλα, δῶρα τά οἱ πόρεν Ὑψιπύλη Λήμνοιο φέρεσθαι.

line_details.english: But Aisonides himself proclaimed a contest for all,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὸς δ' Αἰσονίδης προυθήκατο πᾶσιν ἄεθλον,
line_details.note: προυθήκατο (middle) = “set forth/announced/proposed.” ἄεθλον (sg.) here is best taken as “contest,” contrasting with ἄεθλα (pl.) “prizes” in the next line.

line_details.english: prizes to be for his comrades at the funeral games,
line_details.greek: τυμβιδίου ἐπ' ἀγῶνος ἑταίροις ἔμμεν' ἄεθλα,
line_details.note: τυμβιδίου ἐπ’ ἀγῶνος = “at the funeral contest/games” (lit. “on the tomb’s contest”). ἔμμεν’ = ἔμμεναι “to be.” ἑταίροις = “for the comrades (the Argonauts).”

line_details.english: the gifts that Hypsipyle of Lemnos had given him to carry away.
line_details.greek: δῶρα τά οἱ πόρεν Ὑψιπύλη Λήμνοιο φέρεσθαι.
line_details.note: δῶρα … φέρεσθαι = “gifts to bear away.” οἱ = “to him.” The line explains that the prizes were the parting gifts bestowed by Hypsipyle of Lemnos on Aisonides (Iason).

text.english: To Ankaios he gave, as the prize of wrestling, a two‑handled cup, golden and wide‑mouthed, to keep; and to Peleus he gave, as being the swifter in the footraces, by reason of his own fleetness of foot, a purple cloak, a many‑wrought work of Athena.
text.greek: Ἀγκαίῳ μὲν δῶκε πάλης γέρας ἀμφικύπελλον χρύσειον πολυχανδὲς ἔχειν· Πηλῆι δ' ἔδωκε θάσσοντι σταδίοισι, ποδωκείης ἕνεκα σφῆς χλαῖναν φοινικέην, πολυδαίδαλον ἔργον Ἀθήνης.

line_details.english: To Ankaios he gave, as the prize of wrestling, a two‑handled cup,
line_details.greek: Ἀγκαίῳ μὲν δῶκε πάλης γέρας ἀμφικύπελλον
line_details.note: ἀμφικύπελλον: the noun “cup” (δέπας/κύπελλον) is understood; the adjective denotes a two‑handled goblet and is a conventional epic epithet for prize‑cups.

line_details.english: golden and wide‑mouthed, to keep; and to Peleus he gave,
line_details.greek: χρύσειον πολυχανδὲς ἔχειν· Πηλῆι δ' ἔδωκε
line_details.note: πολυχανδές is rare and likely from χαίνω (“to gape”), hence “wide‑mouthed, capacious”; less plausibly from ἁνδάνω (“to please”). ἔχειν here = “to keep (as one’s own),” a formulaic prize expression.

line_details.english: as being the swifter in the footraces, by reason of his own fleetness of foot,
line_details.greek: θάσσοντι σταδίοισι, ποδωκείης ἕνεκα σφῆς
line_details.note: θάσσοντι σταδίοισι: literally “to him being swifter in the stadium‑races.” σφῆς is the archaic reflexive “his own,” stressing Peleus’ inherent speed (ποδωκείη = ‘fleetness of foot’).

line_details.english: a purple cloak, a many‑wrought work of Athena.
line_details.greek: χλαῖναν φοινικέην, πολυδαίδαλον ἔργον Ἀθήνης.
line_details.note: φοινικέην denotes costly purple/crimson dye; πολυδαίδαλον “much‑wrought, elaborate.” “Work of Athena” alludes to the goddess’s patronage of weaving.

text.english: But as the prize of the pankration he gave to Herakles a silver krater, all-gleaming; and for horsemanship to Kastor, a skillfully wrought adornment of golden phalerae; and for boxing he gave a very delicate tapestry to be borne away by prize-winning Polydeukes; for he had taken the glorious victory.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ παγκρατίοιο δόκεν γέρας Ἡρακλῆϊ ἀργύρεον κρητῆρα παναίολον· ἱππασίης δέ Κάστορι, χρυσείων φαλάρων πολυτεχνέα κόσμον· πυγμαχίης δὲ τάπητα λιανθέα δῶκε φέρεσθαι ἀθλοφόρῳ Πολυδεύκει· ὃ γὰρ κλυτὸν ᾔρατο νῖκος.

line_details.english: But as the prize of the pankration he gave to Herakles
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ παγκρατίοιο δόκεν γέρας Ἡρακλῆϊ
line_details.note: “παγκρατίοιο” (of the pankration): the all-in contest combining wrestling and boxing; “γέρας” is an honorific prize.

line_details.english: a silver krater, all-gleaming; and for horsemanship
line_details.greek: ἀργύρεον κρητῆρα παναίολον· ἱππασίης δέ
line_details.note: “παναίολον” from αἰόλος with pan-: ‘all-variegated, shimmering’; κρητήρ (krater) is a large mixing-bowl.

line_details.english: to Kastor, a skillfully wrought adornment of golden phalerae;
line_details.greek: Κάστορι, χρυσείων φαλάρων πολυτεχνέα κόσμον·
line_details.note: “φαλάρων” (phalerae): decorative metal discs for horse-harness; “πολυτεχνέα” = ‘much-/skillfully wrought.’

line_details.english: and for boxing he gave a very delicate tapestry to be borne away
line_details.greek: πυγμαχίης δὲ τάπητα λιανθέα δῶκε φέρεσθαι
line_details.note: “λιανθέα” is a rare epithet; probably ‘very delicate/soft’ (possibly ‘richly patterned’). “δῶκε φέρεσθαι” = ‘gave to be carried off (as a prize).’

line_details.english: by prize-winning Polydeukes; for he had taken the glorious victory.
line_details.greek: ἀθλοφόρῳ Πολυδεύκει· ὃ γὰρ κλυτὸν ᾔρατο νῖκος.
line_details.note: “ἀθλοφόρῳ” = ‘bearing off the prize’; “ᾔρατο” (‘he took up’) is idiomatic for ‘won’ a victory.

text.english: But he himself took up the well‑curved bow and the arrows, and, drawing it, he let fly a shaft, and it sped afar; then the Minyan band gave to Aisonides, for the sake of honor, weaving a rich‑blossomed wreath of the long‑leaved olive.
text.greek: Αὐτὸς δ' εὐκαμπὲς τόξον λάβεν ἠδ' ἄρ' ὀϊστούς, τεινάμενος δέ οἱ ἧκε βέλος, τὸ δ' ἀπέπτατο τηλοῦ· Δῶκε δ' ἄρ' Αἰσονίδῃ Μινύης λόχος εἵνεκα τιμῆς πλέξας εὐανθῆ στέφανον τανυφύλλου ἐλαίης.

line_details.english: But he himself took up the well‑curved bow and the arrows,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὸς δ' εὐκαμπὲς τόξον λάβεν ἠδ' ἄρ' ὀϊστούς,
line_details.note: eukampes (“well‑curved/pliant”) is a conventional bow‑epithet; autos (“he himself”) marks emphatic subject.

line_details.english: and, drawing it, he let fly a shaft, and it sped afar;
line_details.greek: τεινάμενος δέ οἱ ἧκε βέλος, τὸ δ' ἀπέπτατο τηλοῦ·
line_details.note: teinamenos (“drawing [the bowstring]”); hoi is a dative of goal/advantage (“at him/at his mark”); héke belos is a Homeric formula “let fly a shaft”; têlou (“afar”) keeps the epic adverbial tone.

line_details.english: then the Minyan band gave to Aisonides, for the sake of honor,
line_details.greek: Δῶκε δ' ἄρ' Αἰσονίδῃ Μινύης λόχος εἵνεκα τιμῆς
line_details.note: Aisonidēs (“son of Aison,” i.e., Jason) is preserved as an epic patronymic; Minyēs lochos (“the Minyan band”) refers to the Argonauts; heineka timēs = “for the sake of honor/as an honor.”

line_details.english: weaving a rich‑blossomed wreath of the long‑leaved olive.
line_details.greek: πλέξας εὐανθῆ στέφανον τανυφύλλου ἐλαίης.
line_details.note: euanthēs (“rich‑blossomed”) and tanyphyllos (“long‑leaved”) are traditional epithets applied to the olive; plexas (“weaving”) agrees with singular lochos as a collective subject.

text.english: But to me godlike Iason bestowed the meed of song, a golden sandal, indeed, with pinions outspread.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ μολπῆς γέρας ὤπασε δῖος Ἰήσων ἐμβάδα χρυσείην γε τιταινομένην πτερύγεσσι.

line_details.english: But to me godlike Iason bestowed the meed of song,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ μολπῆς γέρας ὤπασε δῖος Ἰήσων
line_details.note: γέρας (“meed, honorific portion”) is the technical term for a prize or share; μολπῆς is “of song.” ὤπασε (from ὀπάζω) = “bestowed/granted.” Αὐτὰρ is the epic adversative “but/then.”

line_details.english: a golden sandal, indeed, with pinions outspread.
line_details.greek: ἐμβάδα χρυσείην γε τιταινομένην πτερύγεσσι.
line_details.note: ἐμβάς = “sandal” (acc. sg. ἐμβάδα); the singular can function collectively in epic. τιταινομένην (from τιταίνω) means “stretched/extended,” here idiomatically “with [its] wings outspread.” πτέρυγες are “wings/winglets,” perhaps decorative flaps; the image evokes winged footwear (cf. Hermes). γε is an enclitic intensifier (“indeed”).

text.english: The combat ceased, and tidings flew within the palace.
text.greek: - Λῦτο δ' ἀγὼν, φήμη δὲ διέπτατο δώματος εἴσω

line_details.english: The combat ceased, and tidings flew within the palace.
line_details.greek: - Λῦτο δ' ἀγὼν, φήμη δὲ διέπτατο δώματος εἴσω

text.english: that Kyzikos was no more; and when his ill‑fated wedded consort heard it, tearing at her breasts she wailed shrilly; and about her neck having set a headband, she destroyed her life with a noose.
text.greek: Κυζίκου οἰχομένου· τοῦ δ' ὡς κλύε σύγγαμος αἰνή στήθεα δρυπτομένη λίγ' ἐκώκυεν· ἀμφὶ δὲ δειρῆς ἀψαμένη μήρινθα, βρόχῳ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὄλεσσε.

line_details.english: that Kyzikos was no more; and when his ill‑fated wedded consort heard it,
line_details.greek: Κυζίκου οἰχομένου· τοῦ δ' ὡς κλύε σύγγαμος αἰνή
line_details.note: οἰχομένου literally “gone,” a common euphemism for “dead.” σύγγαμος = “wedded consort.” αἰνή literally “dreadful,” here conveying the wife’s pitiable, grievous state.

line_details.english: tearing at her breasts she wailed shrilly; and about her neck
line_details.greek: στήθεα δρυπτομένη λίγ' ἐκώκυεν· ἀμφὶ δὲ δειρῆς

line_details.english: having set a headband, she destroyed her life with a noose.
line_details.greek: ἀψαμένη μήρινθα, βρόχῳ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὄλεσσε.
line_details.note: μήρινθα is a rare word, probably a woman’s headband or hair‑net, here used as an improvised ligature; cf. βρόχῳ “with a noose.” Some manuscripts vary the form (μήρινθα/μείρινθα).

text.english: And Ge, having received the tears upon her level expanse, sent forth a spring, gushing silver‑bright water, ever‑flowing, from the midst of the fountain, and the dwellers round about call it Kleite.
text.greek: Γῆ δ' ὑποδεξαμένη πλακὶ δάκρυα, πίδακος ἧκε βλύζουσ' ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδωρ κρήνης ἀπὸ μέσσης ἀέναον· Κλείτην δὲ περικτίονες καλέουσι.

line_details.english: And Ge, having received the tears upon her level expanse, sent forth a spring,
line_details.greek: Γῆ δ' ὑποδεξαμένη πλακὶ δάκρυα, πίδακος ἧκε
line_details.note: Ge is the personified Earth. plaki (dat. of plax) means “flat surface/plain.” pidax (“spring, fountain”) is archaic; the genitive with heke (“sent forth”) is epic/poetic usage for producing or emitting something.

line_details.english: gushing silver‑bright water, ever‑flowing, from the midst of the fountain,
line_details.greek: βλύζουσ' ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδωρ κρήνης ἀπὸ μέσσης
line_details.note: blyzein means “to bubble/gush.” argyroeides = “silver‑like/bright.” “from the midst of the fountain” (krēnēs apo messēs) stresses the emergence at the very center; aenaon (“ever‑flowing”) qualifies the water/spring.

line_details.english: and the dwellers round about call it Kleite.
line_details.greek: ἀέναον· Κλείτην δὲ περικτίονες καλέουσι.
line_details.note: Kleite is the eponym of the spring (cf. Kleite, wife of Kyzikos, in the Argonautic myth). periktiones is Homeric for “those dwelling round about, neighbors.”

text.english: And then indeed the kings, for a dream-oracular inquiry, went to the holy foothill and the summit-ridge of Dindymon, so that they might appease with wine-rich libations Rheia the elder-born, and avert the queen’s wrath.
text.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ βασιλῆες ὀνειροπόλον διὰ πύστιν, κνημὸν ἐπὶ ζάθεον καὶ Δίνδυμον ἀκρώρειαν, ὄφρα κε μειλίξαιντ' εὐοινίστοις ἐπὶ λοιβαῖς Ῥείην πρεσβυγενῆ, θυμὸν δ' ἀλέαιντο ἀνάσσης.

line_details.english: And then indeed the kings, for a dream-oracular inquiry,
line_details.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ βασιλῆες ὀνειροπόλον διὰ πύστιν,
line_details.note: ὀνειροπόλον διὰ πύστιν = “inquiry by means of a dream,” i.e., a dream-oracle/oneiromancy; πύστις is ‘consultation, inquiry’.

line_details.english: went to the holy foothill and the summit-ridge of Dindymon,
line_details.greek: κνημὸν ἐπὶ ζάθεον καὶ Δίνδυμον ἀκρώρειαν,
line_details.note: κνημός = ‘foothill, lower slope’; ἀκρώρεια = ‘crest/summit-ridge’. Δίνδυμον is Mount Dindymon (Dindymus), sacred to the Mother (Rheia/Cybele). ἐπὶ + acc. indicates motion onto.

line_details.english: so that they might appease with wine-rich libations
line_details.greek: ὄφρα κε μειλίξαιντ' εὐοινίστοις ἐπὶ λοιβαῖς
line_details.note: εὐοινίστος = ‘rich in wine’; λοιβαί = ‘libations’. μειλίσσω = ‘soothe/propitiate’.

line_details.english: Rheia the elder-born, and avert the queen’s wrath.
line_details.greek: Ῥείην πρεσβυγενῆ, θυμὸν δ' ἀλέαιντο ἀνάσσης.
line_details.note: πρεσβυγενής = ‘born earlier, elder-born,’ an epithet of Rheia. θυμὸν ἀλέαιντο = idiomatically ‘to avert/avoid the (angry) spirit,’ i.e., her wrath; ἀνάσση = ‘queen/mistress’ as a divine title.

text.english: But I for my part followed, and I raised the phorminx in my hands, and Argos came once more, leaving the well-wrought ship, who cut off the shoot of the long-barked fir, entwined by a withered vine, with sharp iron; and he expertly carved, by his skill, a holy cult-image, to remain steadfast forever for men yet to come; and with well-fitted stones he built a house for the Lady.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἑπόμην, φόρμιγγα δὲ χερσὶν ἄειρον, Ἄργος δ' αὖθ' ἵκανε, λιπὼν εὐεργέα νῆα, ὅσγε τανυφλοίου ἐλάτης ἀμφιπλεκὲς ἔρνος ἀμπέλου αὐαλέης ὀξεῖ ἀπέκερσε σιδήρῳ· Ξέσσε δ' ἐπισταμένως βρέτας ἱερὸν ἰδμοσύνῃσι, μίμνειν ἔμπεδον αἰὲν ἐπεσσομένοις ἀνθρώποις· λάασι δ' εὐτύκτοις δωμήσατο οἶκον ἀνάσσῃ.

line_details.english: But I for my part followed, and I raised the phorminx in my hands,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἑπόμην, φόρμιγγα δὲ χερσὶν ἄειρον,
line_details.note: phorminx: the epic lyre associated with Orpheus; ἄειρον is imperfect (“was lifting/held aloft”).

line_details.english: and Argos came once more, leaving the well-wrought ship,
line_details.greek: Ἄργος δ' αὖθ' ἵκανε, λιπὼν εὐεργέα νῆα,
line_details.note: Argos here is the craftsman, builder of the Argo; εὐεργέα means “well-wrought,” a standard epic epithet for crafted objects.

line_details.english: who cut off the shoot of the long-barked fir, entwined by a withered vine,
line_details.greek: ὅσγε τανυφλοίου ἐλάτης ἀμφιπλεκὲς ἔρνος
line_details.note: τανυφλοίος = “long-barked” (of fir); ἔρνος = “shoot/branch.” ἀμφιπλεκές governs a genitive: the shoot is “entwined by” the vine.

line_details.english: with sharp iron;
line_details.greek: ἀμπέλου αὐαλέης ὀξεῖ ἀπέκερσε σιδήρῳ·
line_details.note: “sharp iron” is the conventional periphrasis for a blade or tool; ἀπέκερσε = “cut off.”

line_details.english: and he expertly carved, by his skill, a holy cult-image,
line_details.greek: Ξέσσε δ' ἐπισταμένως βρέτας ἱερὸν ἰδμοσύνῃσι,
line_details.note: βρέτας denotes a wooden cult statue (xoanon); ἰδμοσύνῃσι = “by/with (his) skill(s), know-how.”

line_details.english: to remain steadfast forever for men yet to come;
line_details.greek: μίμνειν ἔμπεδον αἰὲν ἐπεσσομένοις ἀνθρώποις·
line_details.note: ἐπεσσομένοις = “those who will come later” (Homeric future participle); ἔμπεδον = “firm, steadfast.”

line_details.english: and with well-fitted stones he built a house for the Lady.
line_details.greek: λάασι δ' εὐτύκτοις δωμήσατο οἶκον ἀνάσσῃ.
line_details.note: οἶκον ἀνάσσῃ = “a house for the Lady,” i.e., a temple for a goddess; εὐτύκτοις λάασι = “with well-dressed stones.”

text.english: Then in their haste the Minyans (and Aisonides, far surpassing them all) fashioned an altar well-fitted with stones, upon which bull‑sacrificial libations and fair holy offerings the chieftains performed; and Rheia took delight in the libations.
text.greek: Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἐπειγόμενοι Μινύαι (μέγα δ' ἔξοχα πάντων Αἰσονίδης) λιθάκεσσιν ἀρηρότα βωμὸν ἔτευξαν ᾧ ἔπι ταυροθύτους λοιβὰς ἠδ' ἱερὰ καλά ῥέξαν ἀριστῆες· σπονδαῖσι δ' ἐτέρπετο Ῥείη.

line_details.english: Then in their haste the Minyans (and Aisonides, far surpassing them all)
line_details.greek: Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἐπειγόμενοι Μινύαι (μέγα δ' ἔξοχα πάντων
line_details.note: Aisonides is the patronymic for Iason (Jason), emphasizing his preeminence: “greatly beyond all the rest.”

line_details.english: fashioned an altar well-fitted with stones,
line_details.greek: Αἰσονίδης) λιθάκεσσιν ἀρηρότα βωμὸν ἔτευξαν
line_details.note: lithakessin arerota literally “well-joined with stones”; the phrase underscores careful stonework in the altar’s construction.

line_details.english: upon which bull‑sacrificial libations and fair holy offerings
line_details.greek: ᾧ ἔπι ταυροθύτους λοιβὰς ἠδ' ἱερὰ καλά
line_details.note: taurothytoi loibai = “libations attendant on a bull-sacrifice,” an unusual but intelligible collocation indicating libations as part of a tauric rite.

line_details.english: the chieftains performed; and Rheia took delight in the libations.
line_details.greek: ῥέξαν ἀριστῆες· σπονδαῖσι δ' ἐτέρπετο Ῥείη.
line_details.note: Rheia is transliterated (Rhea), the Mother of the Gods; note the variation between loibai and spondai, both terms for libations.

text.english: But they enjoined me to celebrate the god and to honor him, so that, upon meeting him, he might bestow a honey-sweet homecoming.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔμ' ἤνωγον κλῇσαι θεὸν ἠδὲ γερῆραι, ὄφρα κεν ἀντομένοις νόστον μελιηδέ' ὀπάσσοι.

line_details.english: But they enjoined me to celebrate the god and to honor him,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔμ' ἤνωγον κλῇσαι θεὸν ἠδὲ γερῆραι,
line_details.note: κλῇσαι is the aorist infinitive of κλείω/κλείζω “to celebrate, make famous,” not κλείω/κλῄω “to shut.” γερῆραι (from γεραίρω) means “to honor (with rites/gifts).” ἤνωγον = “they were urging/enjoining.”

line_details.english: so that, upon meeting him, he might bestow a honey-sweet homecoming.
line_details.greek: ὄφρα κεν ἀντομένοις νόστον μελιηδέ' ὀπάσσοι.
line_details.note: ὄφρα κεν + optative expresses purpose/contingency. ἀντομένοις (dat. pl.) = “to those who meet (him),” with the object (the god) understood from the previous line. ὀπάσσοι (from ὀπάζω) = “might grant/bestow.” μελιηδέ’ is the epic form of μελιηδέα (“honey-sweet”), with apocope before a vowel. νόστον = “homecoming/return.”

text.english: But when at last with sacrifices and with prayers we had supplicated, we descended to the Argo; and then Tiphys was calling the heroes from the stern; and together all in haste sat down upon the foremost benches, stepping over the bench, and made ready the oar.
text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ θυέεσσι λιταῖσί τε γουνασάμεσθα, Ἀργῴην ποτὶ νῆα κατήλθομεν· ἐν δ' ἄρα Τῖφυς ἥρωας πρύμνηθεν ἐκέκλετο· σὺν δ' ἄρα πάντες ἐσσύμενοι θώκοισιν ἐπὶ προτέροισι κάθιζον, βάντες ὑπὲρ θώκοιο, καὶ εἰρεσίης μνώοντο.

line_details.english: But when at last with sacrifices and with prayers we had supplicated,
line_details.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ θυέεσσι λιταῖσί τε γουνασάμεσθα,
line_details.note: γουνάσασθαι here = “to supplicate,” literally “to bend the knee”; θυέεσσι λιταῖσί τε is an instrumental dative, “with sacrifices and with prayers.”

line_details.english: we descended to the Argo; and then Tiphys
line_details.greek: Ἀργῴην ποτὶ νῆα κατήλθομεν· ἐν δ' ἄρα Τῖφυς
line_details.note: Ἀργῴην νῆα is taken as “the Argo,” i.e., the ship’s proper name; κατῆλθομεν “we went/descended (to).”

line_details.english: was calling the heroes from the stern; and together all
line_details.greek: ἥρωας πρύμνηθεν ἐκέκλετο· σὺν δ' ἄρα πάντες
line_details.note: Τῖφυς is the helmsman; πρύμνηθεν “from the stern”; ἐκέκλετο imperfect “was calling/summoning.”

line_details.english: in haste sat down upon the foremost benches,
line_details.greek: ἐσσύμενοι θώκοισιν ἐπὶ προτέροισι κάθιζον,
line_details.note: ἐσσύμενοι “hastening, in haste”; θώκοι are the rowers’ benches; προτέροισι “forward/foremost.”

line_details.english: stepping over the bench, and made ready the oar.
line_details.greek: βάντες ὑπὲρ θώκοιο, καὶ εἰρεσίης μνώοντο.
line_details.note: βάντες ὑπὲρ θώκοιο “stepping over the bench” (singular generic); εἰρεσίη is the epic word for “oar”; μνώοντο “were mindful of,” here “made ready/turned attention to.”

text.english: Without a word the slender hawsers were loosed from the land, and the sheets were spread, and swiftly from the peak of Dindymos bright‑veiled Rhea sent a favoring breeze.
text.greek: Ἀπροφάτως δ' ἀπὸ γῆς λεπτοὶ λύοντο κάλωες πείσματα δ' ἡπλώθη· κραιπνὸν δ' ἀπὸ Δινδύμου ἄκρης ἴκμενον οὖρον ἐφῆκε Ῥέη λιπαροκρήδεμνος.

line_details.english: Without a word the slender hawsers were loosed from the land,
line_details.greek: Ἀπροφάτως δ' ἀπὸ γῆς λεπτοὶ λύοντο κάλωες
line_details.note: ἀπροφάτως can mean “silently, without announcement”; κάλωες are mooring‑cables/hawsers; λύοντο in nautical context = “cast off.”

line_details.english: and the sheets were spread,
line_details.greek: πείσματα δ' ἡπλώθη· κραιπνὸν δ' ἀπὸ Δινδύμου ἄκρης
line_details.note: πείσματα are the sail‑sheets (ropes controlling a sail); neuter plural with singular verb ἡπλώθη is standard Greek syntax.

line_details.english: and swiftly from the peak of Dindymos bright‑veiled Rhea sent a favoring breeze.
line_details.greek: ἴκμενον οὖρον ἐφῆκε Ῥέη λιπαροκρήδεμνος.
line_details.note: κραιπνόν functions adverbially (“swiftly”); Δίνδυμος is Rhea’s mountain; ἴκμενον οὖρον is a set phrase for a fair wind; λιπαροκρήδεμνος = “bright‑/shining‑veiled.”

text.english: And we in turn offered upon the ship the honor-offerings, holy things, having wreathed an altar, for those who would come thereafter to learn, that there at Peismatie the mooring-ropes of Argo, though she was shut in, were loosed.
text.greek: Ἡμεῖς δ' αὖτ' ἐπὶ νηῒ γεράσμια πέμπομεν ἱρά, Βωμὸν ἐπιστέψαντες ἐπεσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι Πεισματίην τόθι πείσματ' ἐεργομένης λύθεν Ἀργοῦς.

line_details.english: And we in turn offered upon the ship the honor-offerings, holy things,
line_details.greek: Ἡμεῖς δ' αὖτ' ἐπὶ νηῒ γεράσμια πέμπομεν ἱρά,
line_details.note: γεράσμια ἱρά = “honor-offerings, sacred gifts”; ἐπὶ νηῒ can mean “upon/for the ship,” implying cultic honors paid to the ship itself.

line_details.english: having wreathed an altar, for those who would come thereafter to learn,
line_details.greek: Βωμὸν ἐπιστέψαντες ἐπεσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι
line_details.note: ἐπιστέψαντες = “having wreathed (with garlands)”; ἐπεσσομένοισι dat. “for those who will come later”; πυθέσθαι “to learn by inquiry,” with the content supplied in the next line.

line_details.english: that there at Peismatie the mooring-ropes of Argo, though she was shut in, were loosed.
line_details.greek: Πεισματίην τόθι πείσματ' ἐεργομένης λύθεν Ἀργοῦς.
line_details.note: Πεισματίην is best taken as a toponym (“Peismatie,” ‘the Mooring[-place]’) from πείσμα “mooring-rope,” giving an aetiology; ἐεργομένης = “shut in/held fast.” Some take πεισματίην adverbially (“as a mooring”), but the toponymic sense suits the context.

text.english: But when the blast had filled the vessel’s sails, she sped, cleaving through the briny waves of the sea, and she passed close by the borders of the land of Mysia; and straightway, racing on, she passed the outflows of Ryndakos, and made her way into fair, sandy havens, and grounded upon the beach; and, laying hand upon the forestays, they furled the sails and bound them about with thongs, and ran out a ladder onto the ground, and they themselves went ashore, eager for food and drink; and round about the wooded slope of Arganthos was visible, and the steep-cragged hillocks.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί γ' ὀθόνας ἀκάτου πλήρωσεν ἀήτης, θῦνε διαπρήσσουσ' ἁλιμυρέα κύματα πόντου, Μύσια δὲ σχεδόθεν παραμείβετο πείρατα γαίης· αἶψα δὲ Ῥυνδακίους προχοὰς ἤμειψε θέουσα, καλούς τ' ἐς λιμένας ψαμαθώδεας εἰσεπέρησε, κέλσε δ' ἐπ' αἰγιαλῷ· προτόνοις δ' ἐπὶ χεῖρα βαλόντες, ἱστία μηρύσαντο καὶ ἀμφ' ἱμᾶσιν ἔδησαν, κλίμακα δ' ἐξώκειλαν ἐπὶ χθονὸς, ἐκ δ' ἔβαν αὐτοί, σίτου καὶ πόσιος λελιημένοι· ἀμφὶ δὲ κναμός Ἀργάνθου κατέφαινε, βαθυσκόπελοί τε κολῶναι.

line_details.english: But when the blast had filled the vessel’s sails,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί γ' ὀθόνας ἀκάτου πλήρωσεν ἀήτης,
line_details.note: “akatos” is a light seagoing vessel; “aētēs” here = a driving gust/blast of wind.

line_details.english: she sped, cleaving through the briny waves of the sea,
line_details.greek: θῦνε διαπρήσσουσ' ἁλιμυρέα κύματα πόντου,

line_details.english: and she passed close by the borders of the land of Mysia;
line_details.greek: Μύσια δὲ σχεδόθεν παραμείβετο πείρατα γαίης·
line_details.note: “schedothen” = “at close range, hard by,” emphasizing proximity to Mysia’s borders.

line_details.english: and straightway, racing on, she passed the outflows of Ryndakos,
line_details.greek: αἶψα δὲ Ῥυνδακίους προχοὰς ἤμειψε θέουσα,
line_details.note: “prochoai” are a river’s mouths/outflows; “Ryndakos” (Ryndacus) is the Mysian river flowing to the Propontis.

line_details.english: and made her way into fair, sandy havens,
line_details.greek: καλούς τ' ἐς λιμένας ψαμαθώδεας εἰσεπέρησε,
line_details.note: “eiseperēse” = “forced/pressed her way into”; “psamathōdeis limenes” = sandy-bottomed/sandy havens.

line_details.english: and grounded upon the beach; and, laying hand upon the forestays,
line_details.greek: κέλσε δ' ἐπ' αἰγιαλῷ· προτόνοις δ' ἐπὶ χεῖρα βαλόντες,
line_details.note: “kellō” = to beach/run aground (of ships); “protonoi” are the forestays of the mast.

line_details.english: they furled the sails and bound them about with thongs,
line_details.greek: ἱστία μηρύσαντο καὶ ἀμφ' ἱμᾶσιν ἔδησαν,
line_details.note: “mērysanto” = reefed/furled; “himas” are lashings/thongs used to tie the sails.

line_details.english: and ran out a ladder onto the ground, and they themselves went ashore,
line_details.greek: κλίμακα δ' ἐξώκειλαν ἐπὶ χθονὸς, ἐκ δ' ἔβαν αὐτοί,
line_details.note: “exōkeilan” lit. “drove out onto land” is applied to the “klimax” (ladder), i.e., they ran out the gangplank for disembarkation.

line_details.english: eager for food and drink; and round about the wooded slope
line_details.greek: σίτου καὶ πόσιος λελιημένοι· ἀμφὶ δὲ κναμός
line_details.note: “leliēmenoi” (perf. mid.) = “being in eager desire, longing.” “knamos” denotes a wooded mountain-side/slope.

line_details.english: of Arganthos was visible, and the steep-cragged hillocks.
line_details.greek: Ἀργάνθου κατέφαινε, βαθυσκόπελοί τε κολῶναι.
line_details.note: “Arganthos” is a local Mysian height near Cyzicus; “bathyskopeloi kolōnai” = steep/crag-deep hillocks or mounded crags.

text.english: But Herakles hastened up through the wooded glens, holding his bow in his hands, and three‑barbed arrows, so that he might take game and provide supper for his comrades, either swine, or a horned heifer, or a wild goat.
text.greek: - Ἡρακλέης δ' ἠπείγετ' ἀν' ὑλήεντας ἐναύλους, τόξον ἔχων παλάμαις ἰδὲ τριγλώχινας ὀϊστούς ὄφρα κε θηρήσαιτο, πόροι δ' ἐπὶ δόρπον ἑταίροις, ἢ σύας, ἢ πόρτιν κεραὴν, ἢ ἄγριον αἶγα.

line_details.english: But Herakles hastened up through the wooded glens,
line_details.greek: - Ἡρακλέης δ' ἠπείγετ' ἀν' ὑλήεντας ἐναύλους,
line_details.note: ἐναύλους is best taken as “glens/ravines,” i.e., wooded hollows (often of stream-beds); ἀνὰ with the accusative conveys “up through.” ἠπείγετο = “made haste, pressed on.”

line_details.english: holding his bow in his hands, and three‑barbed arrows,
line_details.greek: τόξον ἔχων παλάμαις ἰδὲ τριγλώχινας ὀϊστούς
line_details.note: τριγλώχινας means “three‑barbed,” of arrowheads; παλάμαις (“with his hands”) is an epic pleonasm reinforcing the vividness of the arming detail.

line_details.english: so that he might take game and provide supper for his comrades,
line_details.greek: ὄφρα κε θηρήσαιτο, πόροι δ' ἐπὶ δόρπον ἑταίροις,
line_details.note: ὄφρα κε + optative expresses purpose (“so that he might”); πόροι is potential/optative of provision (“provide”); δόρπον is the evening meal, “supper.”

line_details.english: either swine, or a horned heifer, or a wild goat.
line_details.greek: ἢ σύας, ἢ πόρτιν κεραὴν, ἢ ἄγριον αἶγα.
line_details.note: σύας is generic “swine,” not necessarily boars; πόρτις is a “heifer” (young cow); κεραὴν = “horned”; ἄγριον αἶγα = “wild goat.”

text.english: But once he had escaped his notice, Hylas made for the ship, following in secret; yet he wandered from a crooked bypath, driven astray in the forest, and he came into the cave of the Nymphai the Limnakides; and they, when they spied him coming, a youth still godlike, restrained him, so that with them he might be immortal and ageless all his days.
text.greek: Τοῦ δ' ἀφομαρτήσαντος Ὕλας ἐξίκετο νηός λάθρα ἐπισπόμενος· σκολιῆς δ' ἀλίτησεν ἀταρποῦ ὕλῃ ἔνι πλαγχθεὶς, ἐν δὲ σπέος ἥλυθε Νυμφῶν Λιμνακίδων· αἱ δέ σφιν ἐσαθρήσασαι ἰόντα κοῦρον ἔτ' ἀντίθεον κατερύκανον, ὄφρα σὺν αὐταῖς ἀθάνατός τε πέλῃ καὶ ἀγήραος ἤματα πάντα.

line_details.english: But once he had escaped his notice, Hylas made for the ship,
line_details.greek: Τοῦ δ' ἀφομαρτήσαντος Ὕλας ἐξίκετο νηός
line_details.note: Τοῦ … ἀφομαρτήσαντος is a genitive absolute, with τοῦ most plausibly referring to Herakles (“after he had slipped from his notice”); ἐξίκετο νηός takes the genitive of goal (“reached/made for the ship”); rendering as “made for” eases the narrative sequence with the next line.

line_details.english: following in secret; yet he wandered from a crooked bypath,
line_details.greek: λάθρα ἐπισπόμενος· σκολιῆς δ' ἀλίτησεν ἀταρποῦ
line_details.note: Σκολιῆς ἀταρποῦ: ἀταρπός is a “side-track/bypath”; ἀλίτησεν here = “went astray, missed,” not “sinned.”

line_details.english: driven astray in the forest, and he came into the cave of the Nymphai
line_details.greek: ὕλῃ ἔνι πλαγχθεὶς, ἐν δὲ σπέος ἥλυθε Νυμφῶν
line_details.note: Πλαγχθείς (aor. pass. of πλάζομαι) = “driven/wandering astray”; ὕλη = “forest/wood”; σπέος is the epic word for “cave.” “Nymphai” is retained as a theonym.

line_details.english: the Limnakides; and they, when they spied him coming,
line_details.greek: Λιμνακίδων· αἱ δέ σφιν ἐσαθρήσασαι ἰόντα
line_details.note: Λιμνακίδες = “Lake-Nymphs” (of pools/marshes); ἐσαθρήσασαι = “having marked/spied”; σφιν is an ethical dative (“to them/on their part”).

line_details.english: a youth still godlike, restrained him, so that with them
line_details.greek: κοῦρον ἔτ' ἀντίθεον κατερύκανον, ὄφρα σὺν αὐταῖς
line_details.note: Κοῦρον ἔτ’ ἀντίθεον = “a youth still godlike”; κατερύκανον (aor.) = “restrained/detained.”

line_details.english: he might be immortal and ageless all his days.
line_details.greek: ἀθάνατός τε πέλῃ καὶ ἀγήραος ἤματα πάντα.
line_details.note: ὄφρα + subjunctive expresses purpose (“so that”); πέλῃ (subj. of πέλω) = “might be”; ἀγήραος = “ageless”; ἤματα πάντα is the epic idiom for “for all his days, forever.”

text.english: But when Helios was bearing his swift horses toward mid-morning, and a swift fair wind was blowing from the mountain, and it fell upon the white sails, and Tiphys was calling out to drive the ship inward and to loose the moorings from the beach; and they obeyed the helmsman’s injunctions.
text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε πρὸς μεσάτην ἠῶ φέρεν ὠκέας ἵππους Ἠέλιος, κραιπνὸς δ' ἐξ οὔρεος ἔπνεεν οὖρος, ἐν δ' ἔπεσ' ἀργενναῖς ὀθόναις, Τῖφυς δ' ἐγεγώνει νηὸς ἔσω περάαν, θινὸς δ' ἐκ πείσματα λύειν· οἳ δὲ κυβερνητῆρος ἐφημοσύναις ἐπίθοντο.

line_details.english: But when Helios was bearing his swift horses toward mid-morning,
line_details.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε πρὸς μεσάτην ἠῶ φέρεν ὠκέας ἵππους
line_details.note: πρὸς μεσάτην ἠῶ: “toward mid‑morning”; epic diction marking the time of day. Helios’ “swift horses” are the Sun’s team.

line_details.english: and a swift fair wind was blowing from the mountain,
line_details.greek: Ἠέλιος, κραιπνὸς δ' ἐξ οὔρεος ἔπνεεν οὖρος,
line_details.note: οὖρος is a “fair/favouring wind”; κραιπνός (“rapid, nimble”) qualifies the wind. ἐξ οὔρεος suggests a land-breeze descending from high ground.

line_details.english: and it fell upon the white sails, and Tiphys was calling out
line_details.greek: ἐν δ' ἔπεσ' ἀργενναῖς ὀθόναις, Τῖφυς δ' ἐγεγώνει
line_details.note: ὀθόναι are “linen cloths,” i.e., sails; ἀργενναῖς = “white, gleaming.” The subject of ἔπεσ’ (“fell upon”) is the wind.

line_details.english: to drive the ship inward and to loose the moorings from the beach;
line_details.greek: νηὸς ἔσω περάαν, θινὸς δ' ἐκ πείσματα λύειν·
line_details.note: νηὸς ἔσω περάαν: “to drive the ship inward,” i.e., out from shore into the open sea; θινός = “beach, strand”; πείσματα = “mooring-ropes, cables.” The infinitives depend on ἐγεγώνει (“was calling out [to]”).

line_details.english: and they obeyed the helmsman’s injunctions.
line_details.greek: οἳ δὲ κυβερνητῆρος ἐφημοσύναις ἐπίθοντο.
line_details.note: ἐφημοσύναις (“injunctions, directions”) is a rarer word; Tiphys is the κυβερνήτης (helmsman). ἐπίθοντο = “they obeyed, hearkened.”

text.english: And Eilatides Polyphemus was going swiftly up along the headland, so that he might swiftly summon Herakles to the ship; but he did not encounter him; for the overmastering might of Herakles was by no means fated to come to the fair‑flowing Phasis.
text.greek: Εἰλατίδης δ' ἀνὰ πρῶνα θοῶς Πολύφημος ἔβαινεν, ὄφρα κεν Ἡρακλῆα θοῶς ἐπὶ νῆα καλέσσοι· ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ ξύμβλητο· μολεῖν γάρ οἱ οὔτι πέπρωτο Φᾶσιν καλλίροον μένος ὄβριμον Ἡρακλῆος.

line_details.english: And Eilatides Polyphemus was going swiftly up along the headland,
line_details.greek: Εἰλατίδης δ' ἀνὰ πρῶνα θοῶς Πολύφημος ἔβαινεν,
line_details.note: Eilatides = “son of Eilatus/Elatus,” the Lapith Polyphemus (not the Cyclops). ἀνὰ πρῶνα (“up along the headland/slope”): πρών can mean headland or prow; here the topographical sense suits the context.

line_details.english: so that he might swiftly summon Herakles to the ship;
line_details.greek: ὄφρα κεν Ἡρακλῆα θοῶς ἐπὶ νῆα καλέσσοι·
line_details.note: No special difficulty; repetition of “swiftly” (thoōs) echoes epic diction.

line_details.english: but he did not encounter him;
line_details.greek: ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ ξύμβλητο· μολεῖν γάρ οἱ οὔτι πέπρωτο
line_details.note: ξύμβλητο is epic for “met/encountered” (aorist middle); the dative οἱ refers to Herakles as the one not encountered.

line_details.english: for the overmastering might of Herakles was by no means fated to come to the fair‑flowing Phasis.
line_details.greek: Φᾶσιν καλλίροον μένος ὄβριμον Ἡρακλῆος.
line_details.note: μολεῖν … πέπρωτο + dat. (“it was fated for him to come”): the dat. οἱ = Herakles. Φᾶσις is the river of Colchis; καλλίροος = “fair‑flowing.” μένος ὄβριμον (“overmastering might”) is a formulaic epithet of Herakles.

text.english: But on the next day we crossed to the baleful land, where Amycus ruled the over-proud Bebryces; who, not heeding the ordinance of Panomphaios Zeus, set a challenge against strangers from the peoples dwelling round about, whosoever should come to his steads and unshaken house, ordaining that they be put to the test in overweening boxing.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπηῶοι λυγρὴν ἐπεράσσαμεν αἶαν, ἔνθ' Ἄμυκος Βεβρύκεσσιν ὑπερφιάλοισιν ἄνασσεν· ὅστε Πανομφαίου Ζηνὸς θέμιν οὐκ ἀλεγίζων ἆθλον ἐπὶ ξείνοισι περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων, ὅστις ἐπὶ σταθμοὺς ἠδ' ἀστεμφῆ δόμον ἵξῃ, θήκατο, πυγμαχίης ὑπερόπλου πειρηθῆναι.

line_details.english: But on the next day we crossed to the baleful land,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπηῶοι λυγρὴν ἐπεράσσαμεν αἶαν,
line_details.note: ἐπηῶοι is an adverbial form meaning “on the next day”; λυγρὴν αἶαν (“baleful land”) foreshadows the grim encounter with Amycus.

line_details.english: where Amycus ruled the over-proud Bebryces;
line_details.greek: ἔνθ' Ἄμυκος Βεβρύκεσσιν ὑπερφιάλοισιν ἄνασσεν·
line_details.note: Bebryces: a tribe located in northwestern Asia Minor (Bithynia).

line_details.english: who, not heeding the ordinance of Panomphaios Zeus,
line_details.greek: ὅστε Πανομφαίου Ζηνὸς θέμιν οὐκ ἀλεγίζων
line_details.note: Panomphaios (“of all oracles/voices,” from pan- + omphē) is an epithet of Zeus; “ordinance” renders θέμις as divine/customary right, especially relevant to xenia (guest-right).

line_details.english: set a challenge against strangers from the peoples dwelling round about,
line_details.greek: ἆθλον ἐπὶ ξείνοισι περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων,
line_details.note: ἆθλον ἐπὶ + dat. conveys “to impose/set a challenge upon”; ξείνοι are “strangers/guests,” περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων “men dwelling round about, neighbors.”

line_details.english: whosoever should come to his steads and unshaken house,
line_details.greek: ὅστις ἐπὶ σταθμοὺς ἠδ' ἀστεμφῆ δόμον ἵξῃ,
line_details.note: σταθμοί are “steads, quarters, lodgings”; ἀστεμφής means “unshaken, firm,” a formulaic epithet for a solid house.

line_details.english: ordaining that they be put to the test in overweening boxing.
line_details.greek: θήκατο, πυγμαχίης ὑπερόπλου πειρηθῆναι.
line_details.note: θῆκατο … πειρηθῆναι = “he set/established (as rule) that they be tried”; πυγμαχίης ὑπερόπλου = “overweening/overmighty boxing,” marking the arrogant brutality of the bout (and by implication of Amycus).

text.english: Then mighty Polydeukes slew him by force, striking his head unawares with hard thongs; and the Minyans laid low the Bebrycians’ people with bronze.
text.greek: Τὸν μὲν ἄρ' ἠΐστωσε βίῃ κρατερὸς Πολυδεύκης, τύψας ἀπροφάτως κεφαλὴν σκληροῖσιν ἱμᾶσι· λαοὺς δ' αὖ Βεβρύκων Μινύαι χαλκῷ κατένηραν·

line_details.english: Then mighty Polydeukes slew him by force,
line_details.greek: Τὸν μὲν ἄρ' ἠΐστωσε βίῃ κρατερὸς Πολυδεύκης,
line_details.note: ἠΐστωσε is the aorist of ἀϊστόω “make unseen,” a poetic euphemism for “destroy/kill”; hence “slew him.” The ‘him’ is Amykos, felled by Polydeukes.

line_details.english: striking his head unawares with hard thongs;
line_details.greek: τύψας ἀπροφάτως κεφαλὴν σκληροῖσιν ἱμᾶσι·
line_details.note: ἱμᾶσι are the leather thongs used by boxers; ἀπροφάτως means “without warning, unawares.”

line_details.english: and the Minyans laid low the Bebrycians’ people with bronze.
line_details.greek: λαοὺς δ' αὖ Βεβρύκων Μινύαι χαλκῷ κατένηραν·
line_details.note: χαλκῷ (“with bronze”) = with bronze weapons; Μινύαι (Minyans) are the Argonauts. λαοὺς Βεβρύκων = “the people/hosts of the Bebrycians.”

text.english: From there we set out, and, wearied beneath the oar, we ran her aground on the deep shore by the great city of the Bithynians, hastening to the river outflows and the snow-bright woods, and, having bivouacked at eventide, we made our supper ready.
text.greek: - Ἔνθα δ' ἀφορμηθέντες, ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃ δὲ καμόντες, Βιθυνῶν μέγα ἄστυ βαθείῃ κέλσαμεν ἀκτῇ σπεύδοντες προχοαῖς ἠδ' ἐν νιφαργέσιν ὕλαις, ἕσπεροι αὐλισθέντες ἐφωπλισσάμεθα δόρπον.

line_details.english: From there we set out, and, wearied beneath the oar,
line_details.greek: - Ἔνθα δ' ἀφορμηθέντες, ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃ δὲ καμόντες,
line_details.note: εἰρεσίη = “rowing, oarage”; thus “wearied beneath the oar” (i.e., by hard rowing).

line_details.english: we ran her aground on the deep shore by the great city of the Bithynians,
line_details.greek: Βιθυνῶν μέγα ἄστυ βαθείῃ κέλσαμεν ἀκτῇ
line_details.note: κέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω “run (a ship) aground, beach.” βαθεῖα ἀκτή is “deep(-water) shore,” i.e., with deep water close in.

line_details.english: hastening to the river outflows and the snow-bright woods,
line_details.greek: σπεύδοντες προχοαῖς ἠδ' ἐν νιφαργέσιν ὕλαις,
line_details.note: προχοαί are “outflows, river-mouths/streams”; νιφαργής = “snow-bright, snow-gleaming,” a poetic epithet of the woods.

line_details.english: and, having bivouacked at eventide, we made our supper ready.
line_details.greek: ἕσπεροι αὐλισθέντες ἐφωπλισσάμεθα δόρπον.
line_details.note: ἐφωπλισσάμεθα (middle) = “we made ready (for ourselves).” ἕσπεροι is adverbial “at evening, toward dusk.”

text.english: There once the ill-wedded Phineus, in his overweening heart, blinded his two sons, and by casting them forth upon jutting rocks he set them as prey for beasts, because of women’s love-charms; but them the sons of renowned Boreas made again both unscathed and seeing, and upon Phineus they sent the ruin of grievous rancor, and they deprived him of the light of day.
text.greek: Ἔνθα ποτ' αἰνόγαμος Φινεὺς ὑπερήνορι θυμῷ δοιοὺς ἐξαλάωσε γόνους, προβλῆσί τε πέτραις θηρσὶν ἕλωρ προὔθηκε γυναίων εἵνεκα φίλτρων· τοὺς δὲ καὶ ἀσκηθεῖς καὶ ὀπωπότας αὖθις ἔτευξαν παῖδε κλυτοῦ Βορέου· Φινεῖ δέ οἱ ὤπασαν ἄτην ἀργαλέοιο κότου, φωτὸς δ' ἀπενόσφισαν αὐγάς.

line_details.english: There once the ill-wedded Phineus, in his overweening heart,
line_details.greek: Ἔνθα ποτ' αἰνόγαμος Φινεὺς ὑπερήνορι θυμῷ
line_details.note: αἰνόγαμος = “ill-wedded,” alluding to Phineus’ disastrous marriage; ὑπερήνορι θυμῷ conveys overbearing/overweening spirit rather than laudable “manliness.”

line_details.english: blinded his two sons, and by casting them forth upon jutting rocks
line_details.greek: δοιοὺς ἐξαλάωσε γόνους, προβλῆσί τε πέτραις
line_details.note: δοιοὺς = epic for “two”; ἐξαλάωσε “blinded utterly.” προβλῆσι πέτραις is an instrumental/manner dative, “by exposure on jutting rocks,” i.e., infanticidal abandonment.

line_details.english: he set them as prey for beasts, because of women’s love-charms;
line_details.greek: θηρσὶν ἕλωρ προὔθηκε γυναίων εἵνεκα φίλτρων·
line_details.note: γυναιῶν φίλτρων = “women’s love-charms/philters,” generic plural, likely referring to the manipulations of his wife; ἕλωρ θηρσί = “prey for beasts.”

line_details.english: but them the sons of renowned Boreas made again both unscathed and seeing,
line_details.greek: τοὺς δὲ καὶ ἀσκηθεῖς καὶ ὀπωπότας αὖθις ἔτευξαν
line_details.note: ἀσκηθεῖς = “unharmed, unscathed”; ὀπωπότας is the perfect participle of ὁράω (“having seen,” i.e., “seeing”), with αὖθις indicating restoration (“again”); ἔτευξαν (from τεύχω) with double predicate accusative = “made them [to be] ….”

line_details.english: and upon Phineus they sent the ruin of grievous rancor,
line_details.greek: παῖδε κλυτοῦ Βορέου· Φινεῖ δέ οἱ ὤπασαν ἄτην
line_details.note: παῖδε κλυτοῦ Βορέου = the Boreads (Zetes and Calais). ὤπασαν ἄτην ἀργαλέοιο κότου: ὀπάζω “to grant/inflict,” ἄτη “ruin/baneful delusion,” κότος a long-nursed rancor. Orphic tradition here makes the Boreads the agents of Phineus’ blinding.

line_details.english: and they deprived him of the light of day.
line_details.greek: ἀργαλέοιο κότου, φωτὸς δ' ἀπενόσφισαν αὐγάς.
line_details.note: φωτὸς αὐγὰς = “the light/rays of day” (idiom); ἀπενόσφισαν = “they deprived/robbed [him of].” This passage preserves a variant in which the Boreads punish Phineus by blinding him.

text.english: But when vehement Boreas, with whirling squalls, having snatched [them] up, rolled along through the dense thickets and woods of Bistonia, so that he might bring on baleful death and doom.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ζαμενὴς Βορέης στροφάδεσσιν ἀέλλαις ἁρπάξας ἐκύλινδε διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλας Βιστονίης, ἵνα κῆρ ὀλοὴν καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ.

line_details.english: But when vehement Boreas, with whirling squalls,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ζαμενὴς Βορέης στροφάδεσσιν ἀέλλαις
line_details.note: ζαμενής = “vehement, raging.” στροφάδεσσιν ἀέλλαις = “with whirling squalls” (dative of manner); στροφάδες here are not the Στροφάδες islands but ‘eddies/whirls.’

line_details.english: having snatched [them] up, rolled along through the dense thickets and woods
line_details.greek: ἁρπάξας ἐκύλινδε διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλας
line_details.note: The object of ἁρπάξας and ἐκύλινδε is implicit (what the wind seizes and rolls—leaves, debris, all before him). δρυμὰ … καὶ ὕλας forms a near-synonymous pair, “thickets and woods.”

line_details.english: of Bistonia, so that he might bring on baleful death and doom.
line_details.greek: Βιστονίης, ἵνα κῆρ ὀλοὴν καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ.
line_details.note: Βιστονίη = Bistonia, a Thracian land (of the Bistones). ἵνα introduces a purpose clause. κῆρ ὀλοήν καὶ πότμον is an intensifying hendiadys (“baleful death and doom”). ἐπίσπῃ (subj.) = “bring upon, draw on.”

text.english: But when we had left the lodging of the Agenorid Phineus, we came across the great gulf of the sea, near to the Kyaneai Rocks, which once my mother our own, very wise Kalliopeia, recounted to me.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Φινῆος Ἀγηνορίδαο λιπόντες αὖλιν, ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης ἐξικόμεσθα ἀγχοῦ Κυανέαις πέτραις, ἅς μοι ποτὲ μήτηρ ἡμετέρη κατέλεξε περίφρων Καλλιόπεια.

line_details.english: But when we had left the lodging of the Agenorid Phineus,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Φινῆος Ἀγηνορίδαο λιπόντες
line_details.note: “Agenorid” renders Ἀγηνορίδαο (descendant/son of Agenor); αὖλιν is “lodging/encampment,” not necessarily a palace.

line_details.english: we came across the great gulf of the sea, near to the Kyaneai Rocks,
line_details.greek: αὖλιν, ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης ἐξικόμεσθα
line_details.note: λαῖτμα is a poetic term for a yawning gulf or deep; ὑπέρ here conveys movement “across/over.”

line_details.english: which once my mother
line_details.greek: ἀγχοῦ Κυανέαις πέτραις, ἅς μοι ποτὲ μήτηρ
line_details.note: Κυανέαι πέτραι are the “Kyaneai (Dark-Bluish) Rocks,” i.e., the Symplegades/Clashing Rocks of the Bosporus; ἀγχοῦ = “near, hard by.”

line_details.english: our own, very wise Kalliopeia, recounted to me.
line_details.greek: ἡμετέρη κατέλεξε περίφρων Καλλιόπεια.
line_details.note: The narrator is Orpheus; hence “our mother” (ἡμετέρη) refers to his own mother, the Muse Kalliopeia. περίφρων is an epithet “very wise/prudent”; κατέλεξε means “recounted (in full), related.”

text.english: For there is for him no escape from woeful toil, but, hemmed in by the bright squalls of the winds, clashing they fall upon one another as they rush; and the boom reached over the sea and the broad heaven from the rending of the billow and the heaving of the sea; with the seething wave an immeasurable brine roared around.
text.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἱ ἐξυπάλυξις ὀϊζυροῖο πόνοιο, ἀλλὰ κατειρύμεναι ἀνέμων ἀργῇσιν ἀέλλαις ξυμβλῆτες πίπτουσιν ἐπ' ἀλλήλαισιν ἰοῦσαι· δοῦπός τ' ἂμ πέλαγός τε καὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἵκανεν ῥηγνυμένοιο κλύδωνος, ὀρινομένης τε θαλάσσης· κύματι παφλάζοντι περιβρέμει ἄσπετος ἅλμη.

line_details.english: For there is for him no escape from woeful toil,
line_details.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἱ ἐξυπάλυξις ὀϊζυροῖο πόνοιο,
line_details.note: ἐξυπάλυξις is a rare noun, literally “a slipping-out,” hence “escape”; ὀϊζυρός = “woeful, pitiable.”

line_details.english: but, hemmed in by the bright squalls of the winds,
line_details.greek: ἀλλὰ κατειρύμεναι ἀνέμων ἀργῇσιν ἀέλλαις
line_details.note: κατειρύμεναι (from κατειρύω) = “shut in, hemmed in”; ἀργῇσιν ἀέλλαις = “bright/white squalls.” The feminine morphology anticipates a feminine subject (sc. πέτραι).

line_details.english: clashing they fall upon one another as they rush;
line_details.greek: ξυμβλῆτες πίπτουσιν ἐπ' ἀλλήλαισιν ἰοῦσαι·
line_details.note: ξυμβλῆτες = “clashing/meeting (ones),” used substantively; with fem. dat. ἀλλήλαισιν it points to the Clashing Rocks (Symplegades) as the implied subject; ἰοῦσαι = “rushing, going.”

line_details.english: and the boom reached over the sea and the broad heaven
line_details.greek: δοῦπός τ' ἂμ πέλαγός τε καὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἵκανεν
line_details.note: δοῦπος = “boom, thud.” ἂμ here functions adverbially (“over/throughout”), so “reached over the sea and broad heaven.”

line_details.english: from the rending of the billow and the heaving of the sea;
line_details.greek: ῥηγνυμένοιο κλύδωνος, ὀρινομένης τε θαλάσσης·
line_details.note: Genitives are causal: “from/of the rending of the billow” (ῥηγνυμένοιο κλύδωνος) and “of the heaving sea” (ὀρινομένης θαλάσσης).

line_details.english: with the seething wave an immeasurable brine roared around.
line_details.greek: κύματι παφλάζοντι περιβρέμει ἄσπετος ἅλμη.
line_details.note: ἄσπετος = “unspeakable, immense”; παφλάζοντι = “seething, splashing”; περιβρέμει = “roars all around.”

text.english: But I spoke these words forth from my tongue to the Hagniades, then to look to the stern, that he might be on his guard.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ Ἀγνιάδῃ τάδ' ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα, πρύμναν ἔπειθ' ὁρόειν ὄφρ' ἂν πεφυλαγμένος εἴη.

line_details.english: But I spoke these words forth from my tongue to the Hagniades,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ Ἀγνιάδῃ τάδ' ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα,
line_details.note: “Hagniades” is the patronymic “son of Hagnias,” i.e., Tiphys the helmsman; ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα is formulaic epic diction (“spoke forth from my tongue”).

line_details.english: then to look to the stern, that he might be on his guard.
line_details.greek: πρύμναν ἔπειθ' ὁρόειν ὄφρ' ἂν πεφυλαγμένος εἴη.
line_details.note: πρύμναν ὁρόειν is a nautical idiom, “look to/mind the stern,” i.e., attend to the helm; ἔπειθ’ = ἔπειτα (“then”); ὄφρ’ ἂν … εἴη expresses purpose (“so that he might be on his guard”).

text.english: And as he listened, his dear heart grew numb, and in his breast he hid what was destined to be fulfilled for him, alone apart from the heroes; but glaukōpis Athēnē at Hērē’s promptings sent a heron to be borne to the tip of the mast’s yard‑arm; but it, in distress, kept flying, and, borne aloft beneath its wings in the inmost clefts of the rocks, it was whirled about; and they, quickly shaking on either side, crashed together and sheared off the tip of the bird’s tail, and among them there arose a futile wrangling.
text.greek: Τοῦ δὲ καὶ εἰσαΐοντος ἐπαχνώθη φίλον ἦτορ, ἐν στέρνοισι δὲ κεῦθεν, ἅ οἱ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλεν, μοῦνος ἀφ' ἡρώων· ἀλλὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη Ἥρης ἐννεσίῃσιν ἐρωδιὸν ἧκε φέρεσθαι ἄκρην ἱστοκεραῖαν· ὃ δ' ἀσχαλόων πεπότητο, πέτραις δ' ἐν μυχάταισιν ὑπὸ πτερύγεσσιν ἀερθείς δινεῖται· ταὶ δ' αἶψα κραδαινόμεναι ἑκάτερθεν σύμπεσον ἀλλήλαισι, καὶ οὐρῆς ἄκρον ἔκερσαν ὄρνιθος· περὶ δέ σφιν ἐτώσιον ἠρείσαντο.

line_details.english: And as he listened, his dear heart grew numb,
line_details.greek: Τοῦ δὲ καὶ εἰσαΐοντος ἐπαχνώθη φίλον ἦτορ,
line_details.note: ἐπαχνώθη literally “grew thick, congealed,” used metaphorically of the heart becoming numb or benumbed (with fear).

line_details.english: and in his breast he hid what was destined to be fulfilled for him,
line_details.greek: ἐν στέρνοισι δὲ κεῦθεν, ἅ οἱ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλεν,
line_details.note: The transmitted κεῦθεν is best taken as Homeric imperfect κεύθεεν “he hid/kept hidden.” ἅ οἱ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλεν = “the things that were about to be accomplished for him.”

line_details.english: alone apart from the heroes; but glaukōpis Athēnē
line_details.greek: μοῦνος ἀφ' ἡρώων· ἀλλὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
line_details.note: μοῦνος ἀφ’ ἡρώων = “alone, apart from the other heroes,” marking his secrecy.

line_details.english: at Hērē’s promptings sent a heron to be borne
line_details.greek: Ἥρης ἐννεσίῃσιν ἐρωδιὸν ἧκε φέρεσθαι
line_details.note: ἐννεσίῃσιν = “promptings, instigations.” ἧκε φέρεσθαι is Homeric for “sent to be borne (to fly).” ἐρωδιόν = “heron,” here an omen-bird (contrast Apollonius’ dove).

line_details.english: to the tip of the mast’s yard‑arm; but it, in distress, kept flying,
line_details.greek: ἄκρην ἱστοκεραῖαν· ὃ δ' ἀσχαλόων πεπότητο,
line_details.note: ἱστοκεραῖαν = “the mast’s yard‑arm” (κέρας of the ἱστός); ἀσχαλόων = “troubled, vexed, flustered.”

line_details.english: and, borne aloft beneath its wings in the inmost clefts of the rocks,
line_details.greek: πέτραις δ' ἐν μυχάταισιν ὑπὸ πτερύγεσσιν ἀερθείς
line_details.note: μυχάταισιν = “inmost recesses, clefts.” ἀερθείς = “borne aloft”; “beneath its wings” suggests the lifting air under the wings.

line_details.english: it was whirled about; and they, quickly shaking on either side,
line_details.greek: δινεῖται· ταὶ δ' αἶψα κραδαινόμεναι ἑκάτερθεν
line_details.note: ταί refers to the Clashing Rocks (Symplegades); κραδαινόμεναι = “quivering, shaking”; ἑκάτερθεν = “on either side.”

line_details.english: crashed together and sheared off the tip of the bird’s tail,
line_details.greek: σύμπεσον ἀλλήλαισι, καὶ οὐρῆς ἄκρον ἔκερσαν
line_details.note: ἔκερσαν (from κείρω) = “sheared off.” οὐρῆς ἄκρον = “the tip of the tail,” a favorable omen indicating near‑miss and thus possible safe passage.

line_details.english: and among them there arose a futile wrangling.
line_details.greek: ὄρνιθος· περὶ δέ σφιν ἐτώσιον ἠρείσαντο.
line_details.note: ἐτώσιον = “to no purpose, futile(ly).” ἠρείσαντο (mid. of ἐρίζω) = “they wrangled/contended”; σφιν = “among them,” i.e., among the heroes.

text.english: But Tiphys, when the heron had escaped grim destruction, quietly called to the heroes; and they, hearing, eagerly were furrowing the swift waves with their oars; but I with my own songs enchanted the sheer rocks; and they sprang apart from one another.
text.greek: Τῖφυς δ' ἐκπρολιπόντος ἐρωδιοῦ αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον σῖγα μὲν ἡρώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο· τοὶ δ' ἀΐοντες, ἱέμενοι θοὰ κύμαθ' ὑπειρεσίῃσι χάρασσον· αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μολπῇσι παρήπαφον ἡμετέρῃσι πέτρας ἠλιβάτους· αἱ δ' ἀλλήλων ἀπόρουσαν.

line_details.english: But Tiphys, when the heron had escaped grim destruction,
line_details.greek: Τῖφυς δ' ἐκπρολιπόντος ἐρωδιοῦ αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον
line_details.note: Genitive absolute: “ἐκπρολιπόντος ἐρωδιοῦ” = “when the heron had left behind (i.e., escaped) death.” Orphic Argonautica uses a heron, not the Apollonian dove, to test the Symplegades; “αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον” = “grim doom.”

line_details.english: quietly called to the heroes; and they, hearing,
line_details.greek: σῖγα μὲν ἡρώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο· τοὶ δ' ἀΐοντες,
line_details.note: “σῖγα” adverb “quietly, softly.” “ἐκέκλετο” middle ‘called to, summoned.’

line_details.english: eagerly were furrowing the swift waves with their oars;
line_details.greek: ἱέμενοι θοὰ κύμαθ' ὑπειρεσίῃσι χάρασσον·
line_details.note: “ὑπειρεσίῃσι” is epic for ‘oars’ (cf. εἴρεσις/ἐρετμός); “χαράσσειν κύματ’” = ‘to score/furrow the waves.’

line_details.english: but I with my own songs enchanted
line_details.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μολπῇσι παρήπαφον ἡμετέρῃσι
line_details.note: “παρήπαφον” (from παραπαφέω) ‘soothe/charm by song,’ marking Orpheus’ magical effect; “ἡμετέρῃσι μολπῇσι” = ‘with my/our songs.’

line_details.english: the sheer rocks; and they sprang apart from one another.
line_details.greek: πέτρας ἠλιβάτους· αἱ δ' ἀλλήλων ἀπόρουσαν.
line_details.note: “πέτρας ἠλιβάτους” = ‘sheer/precipitous rocks’ (epic epithet; often of cliffs); “ἀπόρουσαν” from ὀρούω with ἀπό-, ‘leapt/sprang apart,’ describing the Symplegades parting.

text.english: And the billow roared back; and the deep yielded beneath the ship, relying on our kithara, through the wondrous voice.
text.greek: Κῦμα δ' ἀνερρόχθησε· βυθὸς δ' ὑποείκαθε νηΐ, ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ, διὰ θέσκελον αὐδήν.

line_details.english: And the billow roared back; and the deep yielded beneath the ship,
line_details.greek: Κῦμα δ' ἀνερρόχθησε· βυθὸς δ' ὑποείκαθε νηΐ,
line_details.note: ἀνερρόχθησε (from the root of ῥόχθος, “roar”) conveys a wave surging/recoiling with a roar; ὑποείκαθε = “gave way/yielded,” with νηί as dative of advantage (“to/for the ship”).

line_details.english: relying on our kithara, through the wondrous voice.
line_details.greek: ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ, διὰ θέσκελον αὐδήν.
line_details.note: πίσυνος (“trusting in, relying on”) governs the dative κιθάρῃ; syntactically it most naturally modifies βυθός (“the deep”), personifying the sea as yielding in trust of Orpheus’ music. διὰ θέσκελον αὐδήν = “by means of the wondrous (divinely wrought) voice.” ἡμετέρῃ (“our”) reflects Orpheus’ self-reference.

text.english: But when indeed the noisy keel had passed by the mouth of the strait and through the Cyanean Rocks, straightway those rocks were rooted from the depths, and thereafter they remained forever steadfast.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ πορθμοῖο κατὰ στόμα καὶ διὰ πέτρας Κυανέας ἤμειψε λάλος τρόπις, αὐτίκ' ἄρ' αἵ γε βυσσόθεν ἐρριζοῦντο, καὶ ἔμπεδον αἰὲν ἔμιμνον.

line_details.english: But when indeed the noisy keel had passed by the mouth of the strait and through the Cyanean Rocks,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ πορθμοῖο κατὰ στόμα καὶ διὰ πέτρας
line_details.note: πορθμοῖο κατὰ στόμα = “by/at the mouth of the strait,” i.e., the Bosporus; Κυανέας = the Cyanean (Symplegades) Rocks. λάλος τρόπις literally “talkative keel,” a conventional metaphor for the keel resounding in the water; ἤμειψε = “passed, traversed” (of crossing a stretch).

line_details.english: straightway those rocks were rooted from the depths,
line_details.greek: Κυανέας ἤμειψε λάλος τρόπις, αὐτίκ' ἄρ' αἵ γε
line_details.note: αἵ γε refers back to the Cyanean Rocks. βυσσόθεν = “from the abyss/deep.” ἐρριζοῦντο (impf.) = “were rooted, took root,” describing their becoming fixed after the Argo’s passage (a standard motif).

line_details.english: and thereafter they remained forever steadfast.
line_details.greek: βυσσόθεν ἐρριζοῦντο, καὶ ἔμπεδον αἰὲν ἔμιμνον.
line_details.note: ἔμπεδον (“firm, steadfast”) is used adverbially; αἰὲν = “ever, forever”; ἔμιμνον = “remained.” No textual difficulty is apparent.

text.english: For thus the Moirai, heavy, spun out these things.
text.greek: Οὕτω γὰρ Μοῖραι τάδ' ἐπεκλώσαντο βαρεῖαι.

line_details.english: For thus the Moirai, heavy, spun out these things.
line_details.greek: Οὕτω γὰρ Μοῖραι τάδ' ἐπεκλώσαντο βαρεῖαι.
line_details.note: ἐπεκλῶσαντο (aor. mid. of ἐπικλώθω) uses the fate‑spinning metaphor, hence “spun out” = “ordained”; βαρεῖαι literally “heavy,” an epic epithet of the Moirai meaning grievous/stern.

text.english: And then indeed, having beforehand escaped the hard-to-avoid woes of destruction, we reached the black shore at the outflows of the Rhebanos, beyond the long island Thynias, on the far side of which the fish-rich Tembrios floods its luxuriant banks, and Sangarios too, which runs its waves upon the Euxeinos.
text.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ προφυγόντες ἀδευκέα πήματ' ὀλέθρου, Ῥηβανοῦ προχοαῖσι μέλαιν' ἐξικόμεθ' ἀκτήν, νῆσον ὑπὲρ δολιχὴν Θυνηίδα, τῆς ἀπάτερθεν Τέμβριος ἰχθυόεις θαλεραῖς πλημμύρεται ὄχθαις, Σαγγάριός θ' ὃς κύματ' ἐπιτρέχει Εὐξείνοιο.

line_details.english: And then indeed, having beforehand escaped the hard-to-avoid woes of destruction,
line_details.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ προφυγόντες ἀδευκέα πήματ' ὀλέθρου,
line_details.note: ἀδευκέα = “hard to avoid, ineluctable”; προφυγόντες conveys an anticipatory escape (“forestalling” disaster).

line_details.english: we reached the black shore at the outflows of the Rhebanos,
line_details.greek: Ῥηβανοῦ προχοαῖσι μέλαιν' ἐξικόμεθ' ἀκτήν,
line_details.note: Ῥηβανοῦ: likely the river Rhebas on the Bithynian Euxeinos coast; προχοαί = “outflows, mouths.”

line_details.english: beyond the long island Thynias, on the far side of which
line_details.greek: νῆσον ὑπὲρ δολιχὴν Θυνηίδα, τῆς ἀπάτερθεν
line_details.note: ὑπέρ here means “beyond/over against”; Θυνηίς = Thynias Island off the Bithynian coast; ἀπάτερθεν = “on the far side (of it).”

line_details.english: the fish-rich Tembrios floods its luxuriant banks,
line_details.greek: Τέμβριος ἰχθυόεις θαλεραῖς πλημμύρεται ὄχθαις,
line_details.note: Τέμβριος = the Tembris, a tributary of the Sangarios; θαλερός = “luxuriant, flourishing”; πλημμύρεται = “floods/overflows.”

line_details.english: and Sangarios too, which runs its waves upon the Euxeinos.
line_details.greek: Σαγγάριός θ' ὃς κύματ' ἐπιτρέχει Εὐξείνοιο.
line_details.note: Σαγγάριος = the Sangarios (Sangarius) River; Εὔξεινος = the Euxeinos (the Black Sea). The idiom κύματα ἐπιτρέχει means the river “runs/empties its waves upon” the sea.

text.english: But when we had driven her up upon the beach with our oars, we beached her beside the stream of Lykos, by which Lykos ruled the peoples, Lykos, eponym of the river, who took in the Minyan heroes, and made them welcome at the guest-table, and in turn he showed them friendship, by night and by day, unceasingly.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτ' ἐπ' αἰγιαλὸν ἐπενεισάμεθ' εἰρεσίῃσιν, ἀμφὶ Λύκοιο ῥέεθρον ἐκέλσαμεν, ᾧ ἔπι λαοῖς κραῖνε Λύκος ποταμοῖο φερώνυμος, ὅς ῥ' ὑπέδεκτο ἥρωας Μινύας, ξενίῃ δ' ὑπέδεκτο τραπέζη, φίλετο δ' αὖ νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συνεχὲς αἰεί.

line_details.english: But when we had driven her up upon the beach with our oars,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτ' ἐπ' αἰγιαλὸν ἐπενεισάμεθ' εἰρεσίῃσιν,
line_details.note: ἐπενεισάμεθα εἰρεσίῃσι(ν): epic idiom “to drive a ship up (to land) with the oars.”

line_details.english: we beached her beside the stream of Lykos, by which Lykos ruled the peoples,
line_details.greek: ἀμφὶ Λύκοιο ῥέεθρον ἐκέλσαμεν, ᾧ ἔπι λαοῖς
line_details.note: ἐκέλσαμεν (from κέλλω) = “we beached [the ship].” ᾧ ἔπι λαοῖς κραῖνε: epic construction with ἐπί + dat. “over/among,” and κραίνω “to rule”; thus “where Lykos ruled the peoples.” Lykos here is the Mariandynian king by the river Lykos (cf. Apollonius Rhod. 2).

line_details.english: Lykos, eponym of the river, who took in
line_details.greek: κραῖνε Λύκος ποταμοῖο φερώνυμος, ὅς ῥ' ὑπέδεκτο
line_details.note: ποταμοῖο φερώνυμος = “eponym of the river,” i.e., the river was named after Lykos (epic unaugmented imperfect κραῖνε = “was ruling”).

line_details.english: the Minyan heroes, and made them welcome at the guest-table,
line_details.greek: ἥρωας Μινύας, ξενίῃ δ' ὑπέδεκτο τραπέζη,
line_details.note: ξενίῃ … τραπέζῃ, dat. of instrument/attendant circumstance: “with a guest-table,” i.e., hospitality at table; ὑπέδεκτο repeated for emphasis (“received,” “welcomed”).

line_details.english: and in turn he showed them friendship, by night and by day, unceasingly.
line_details.greek: φίλετο δ' αὖ νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συνεχὲς αἰεί.
line_details.note: φίλετο (middle) with understood object = “he showed [them] affection/kindness.” νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα is a formula “by night and by day”; συνεχὲς αἰεί emphasizes unceasing, constant hospitality.

text.english: There too did Aisa grant that two men should perish, Idmon, Ampycides, and Tiphys the helmsman.
text.greek: Ἔνθα καὶ αἶσα παρέσχε καταφθίσθαι δύο φῶτας, Ἀμπυκίδην Ἴδμωνα, κυβερνητῆρά τε Τῖφυν.

line_details.english: There too did Aisa grant that two men should perish,
line_details.greek: Ἔνθα καὶ αἶσα παρέσχε καταφθίσθαι δύο φῶτας,
line_details.note: Aisa is the personified Fate; φῶτες is epic for “men/warriors,” and καταφθίσθαι carries the force “to perish utterly.”

line_details.english: Idmon, Ampycides, and Tiphys the helmsman.
line_details.greek: Ἀμπυκίδην Ἴδμωνα, κυβερνητῆρά τε Τῖφυν.
line_details.note: Ampycides is the patronymic “son of Ampycus,” identifying Idmon (the seer); κυβερνήτης denotes the ship’s helmsman, here Tiphys.

text.english: Of the one indeed a baneful disease settled upon his body, but the other a beast slew, a savage boar; and then for those men having heaped their tombs we poured the hoary brine, trusting in Ancaeus; for all declared him an adept in seamanship, pre‑eminent by his own expertise.
text.greek: Τοῦ μὲν δὴ κατὰ σῶμα λυγρὴ ἠρείσατο νοῦσος, τὸν δ' ἔκτεινεν θὴρ, σῦς ἄγριος· ἂν δ' ἄρα τοῖς γε τύμβους χευάμενοι πολιὴν ἐπενεισάμεθ' ἅλμην, Ἀγκαίῳ πίσυνοι· τὸν γὰρ φάσαν ἴδριν ἅπαντες ναυτιλίης σφετέρῃσι δαημοσύνῃσι κεκάσθαι.

line_details.english: Of the one indeed a baneful disease settled upon his body,
line_details.greek: Τοῦ μὲν δὴ κατὰ σῶμα λυγρὴ ἠρείσατο νοῦσος,
line_details.note: “The one … the other” refers to Tiphys (dead of disease) and Idmon (slain by a boar). ἠρείσατο (“pressed/settled upon”) with κατὰ σῶμα gives the sense “weighed down his body.”

line_details.english: but the other a beast slew, a savage boar; and then for those men
line_details.greek: τὸν δ' ἔκτεινεν θὴρ, σῦς ἄγριος· ἂν δ' ἄρα τοῖς γε
line_details.note: θὴρ, σῦς ἄγριος is appositional (“a beast, a wild boar”). The particle cluster ἂν δ’ ἄρα is epic and here merely marks narrative progression (“then indeed”), not modality.

line_details.english: having heaped their tombs we poured the hoary brine,
line_details.greek: τύμβους χευάμενοι πολιὴν ἐπενεισάμεθ' ἅλμην,
line_details.note: ἐπενεισάμεθ’ ἅλμην likely means “we poured brine upon [the tombs]” (a sailors’ libation); some take it as “we put to sea again,” but the funerary context favors libation. πολιός (“hoary, gray”) is a conventional epithet of sea-brine.

line_details.english: trusting in Ancaeus; for all declared him an adept
line_details.greek: Ἀγκαίῳ πίσυνοι· τὸν γὰρ φάσαν ἴδριν ἅπαντες
line_details.note: πίσυνοι with the dative = “trusting in, relying on.” Ἀγκαίῳ is Ancaeus, who succeeds Tiphys as helmsman.

line_details.english: in seamanship, pre‑eminent by his own expertise.
line_details.greek: ναυτιλίης σφετέρῃσι δαημοσύνῃσι κεκάσθαι.
line_details.note: ἴδρις = “adept, expert.” κεκάσθαι is the perfect infinitive of καίνυμαι (“to excel, be pre‑eminent”). σφετέρῃσι δαημοσύνῃσι (“by his own skills/know‑how”) is poetical plural.

text.english: But he grasped in his hand the rudders’ tiller‑ropes, steering the ship upon the streams of Parthenios, whom indeed they call, as his by‑name, Kallichoros, whom, you know, I mentioned in earlier words.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ πηδαλίων οἰήια λάζετο χειρί νῆα κατιθύνων ἐπὶ Παρθενίοιο ῥέεθρα, ὃν δὴ Καλλίχορόν μιν ἐπώνυμόν οἱ καλέουσιν, ὅν τοι ἐγὼ μύθοισιν ἐπὶ προτέροισιν ἔλεξα.

line_details.english: But he grasped in his hand the rudders’ tiller‑ropes,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ πηδαλίων οἰήια λάζετο χειρί
line_details.note: οἰήια are the helm- or tiller-ropes used to control the πηδάλια (steering oars/rudders). The middle λάζετο conveys deliberate seizing/grasping.

line_details.english: steering the ship upon the streams of Parthenios,
line_details.greek: νῆα κατιθύνων ἐπὶ Παρθενίοιο ῥέεθρα,
line_details.note: κατιθύνων = κατ‑ἰθύνων, “directing/steering (down/straight).” ἐπὶ with the accusative ῥέεθρα expresses motion “onto/into” the river’s currents.

line_details.english: whom indeed they call, as his by‑name, Kallichoros,
line_details.greek: ὃν δὴ Καλλίχορόν μιν ἐπώνυμόν οἱ καλέουσιν,
line_details.note: Καλλίχορον (“Fair‑Dancing”) is treated as an ἐπώνυμον (by‑name/epithet) of the river Parthenios; μιν and οἱ reflect the customary personification of a river as masculine. The exact local reference of “Kallichoros” is likely cultic/toponymic.

line_details.english: whom, you know, I mentioned in earlier words.
line_details.greek: ὅν τοι ἐγὼ μύθοισιν ἐπὶ προτέροισιν ἔλεξα.
line_details.note: τοι is an enclitic adding assurance (“you know”); the poet refers to prior mention “in earlier words.”

text.english: Thence, having coasted past a projecting headland, we came to the land of the Paphlagonians, which indeed, as she raced, Argo passed by over a great yawning deep; she reached the Karambian headland, where lie the Thermodon and the stream of Halys, striking upon the shore and drawing briny eddies.
text.greek: - Ἔνθεν ἄκραν προβλῆτα παραπλώσαντες ἔβημεν γῆν ἐπὶ Παφλαγόνων, τὴν δὴ παράμειψε θέουσα Ἀργὼ ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα· Καραμβιακὴν δ' ἵκετ' ἄκρην, ᾗ ἐνὶ Θερμώδων κεῖται Ἅλυος τε ῥέεθρον, βάλλον ἐπ' αἰγιαλὸν, δίνας ἁλιμυρέας ἕλκον.

line_details.english: Thence, having coasted past a projecting headland, we came
line_details.greek: - Ἔνθεν ἄκραν προβλῆτα παραπλώσαντες ἔβημεν
line_details.note: ἄκραν προβλῆτα = “projecting/jutting headland”; παραπλώσαντες “coasting past.” Epic ἔβημεν used idiomatically for “we came (to).”

line_details.english: to the land of the Paphlagonians, which indeed, as she raced,
line_details.greek: γῆν ἐπὶ Παφλαγόνων, τὴν δὴ παράμειψε θέουσα
line_details.note: θέουσα (“running, speeding”) is a conventional epithet of swift motion, used of the ship; τὴν refers back to γῆν (the Paphlagonian land); παραμείψε “passed by.”

line_details.english: Argo passed by over a great yawning deep; she reached the Karambian headland,
line_details.greek: Ἀργὼ ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα· Καραμβιακὴν δ' ἵκετ' ἄκρην,
line_details.note: μέγα λαῖτμα = “great yawning deep/gulf,” a Homeric term for the open sea; Καραμβιακὴ ἄκρη = the promontory of Carambis (modern Kerempe Burnu).

line_details.english: where lie the Thermodon and the stream of Halys,
line_details.greek: ᾗ ἐνὶ Θερμώδων κεῖται Ἅλυος τε ῥέεθρον,
line_details.note: κεῖται used of rivers’ situation/outlet; ῥέεθρον = “flow/stream” (poetic). The line compresses coastal geography, associating Carambis with the Thermodon and the Halys.

line_details.english: striking upon the shore and drawing briny eddies.
line_details.greek: βάλλον ἐπ' αἰγιαλὸν, δίνας ἁλιμυρέας ἕλκον.
line_details.note: βάλλον and ἕλκον are epic (unaugmented) imperfects with the rivers (Thermodon and Halys) as subject: “they strike upon the shingle and draw/drag briny eddies” where they meet the sea.

text.english: Down below, over against the Northern Bear, the waters surge up from beneath.
text.greek: Νέρθε δ' ὑποθρώσκουσι βορειάδος ἀντίον ἄρκτου

line_details.english: Down below, over against the Northern Bear, the waters surge up from beneath.
line_details.greek: Νέρθε δ' ὑποθρώσκουσι βορειάδος ἀντίον ἄρκτου
line_details.note: ὑποθρώσκουσι (“leap/spring up from beneath”) is used of the sea’s swell; the subject is implicit. βορειάδος ἀρ́κτου (“the Northern Bear”) is the constellation (Ursa Major), so “opposite the Northern Bear” means north-facing (the south shore of the Euxine faces north).

text.english: There lie the long reaches of Themiscyra of Doiantis.
text.greek: μακρὰ Θεμισκύρης Δοιαντίδος ἅψεα κεῖται·

line_details.english: There lie the long reaches of Themiscyra of Doiantis.
line_details.greek: μακρὰ Θεμισκύρης Δοιαντίδος ἅψεα κεῖται·
line_details.note: ἅψεα is a rare neuter plural (“edges, fringes, reaches”), here of coastline; neuter plural takes singular κεῖται. Θεμισκύρη (Themiscyra) is the Amazon land on the Thermodon. Δοιαντίδος is obscure: likely “of Doiantis,” an eponymic designation tied to the Amazons; the exact referent is uncertain in our text.

text.english: Hard by lie the cities of the Amazons, breakers of horses.
text.greek: ἄγχι δ' Ἀμαζονίδων δαμνίππων ἄστεα κεῖται,

line_details.english: Hard by lie the cities of the Amazons, breakers of horses.
line_details.greek: ἄγχι δ' Ἀμαζονίδων δαμνίππων ἄστεα κεῖται,
line_details.note: δαμνίππων = “horse-breaking/horse-taming,” a traditional epic epithet.

text.english: And the Chalybes, and the Tibarenian tribes, and the peoples of the Becheires, mingled together they inhabit the plain round about among the Mosynoi; and, coasting with the land to port, we ran the ship up on the beaches, where the Makroi were neighbors to the Mariandynoi.
text.greek: καὶ Χάλυβες, Τιβαρηνά τ' ἔθνη, λαοί τε Βέχειρες μίγδην ἐν Μοσύνοισι πέδον περιναιετάουσι· λαιὰ δ' ἐπιπλώσαντες ἐκέλσαμεν αἰγιαλοῖσι ἧχι τε Μάκροι ἔσαν Μαριανδύνοισιν ὅμουροι.

line_details.english: And the Chalybes, and the Tibarenian tribes, and the peoples of the Becheires,
line_details.greek: καὶ Χάλυβες, Τιβαρηνά τ' ἔθνη, λαοί τε Βέχειρες
line_details.note: Βέχειρες: obscure ethnonym; the reading is uncertain and has been variously identified (e.g., with the Byzeres). I retain the transmitted form.

line_details.english: mingled together they inhabit the plain round about among the Mosynoi;
line_details.greek: μίγδην ἐν Μοσύνοισι πέδον περιναιετάουσι·
line_details.note: Μοσύνοισι may denote the Mosynoeci (a Pontic people) or literally “in the mossynes,” their timber towers (cf. Herodotus). μίγδην = “mingled together”; περιναιετάω = “dwell around (the plain).”

line_details.english: and, coasting with the land to port, we ran the ship up on the beaches,
line_details.greek: λαιὰ δ' ἐπιπλώσαντες ἐκέλσαμεν αἰγιαλοῖσι
line_details.note: λαιὰ = “to port/with the land on the left” (nautical). ἐκέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω, “run a ship ashore”; ἐπιπλώσαντες = “coasting along.”

line_details.english: where the Makroi were neighbors to the Mariandynoi.
line_details.greek: ἧχι τε Μάκροι ἔσαν Μαριανδύνοισιν ὅμουροι.

text.english: Down below, for you, the long neck of Helike lies bent aside.
text.greek: Νέρθε δέ τοι Ἑλίκης δολιχὸς παρακέκλιται αὐχὴν

line_details.english: Down below, for you, the long neck of Helike lies bent aside.
line_details.greek: Νέρθε δέ τοι Ἑλίκης δολιχὸς παρακέκλιται αὐχὴν
line_details.note: Helike is most likely the Great Bear (Ursa Major), commonly used as a northern marker (“under Helike” = in the north). The phrase “long neck” (dolichos auchen) is unusual for the Bear; some take Helike here as a landform (a peninsula/isthmus) with a “neck.”

text.english: There, along the foothills, upon the projecting promontories, far-seen ravines encircle the inmost recess of a broad gulf; where stands the mountain of Syme and a luxuriant meadow in abundance, here is the stream of the loud‑thundering river Araxes, from which Thermodon, Phasis, and Tanais flow, where dwell the famed tribes of the Colchians, the Heniocheans, and the Araxians.
text.greek: ἔνθα δ' ὑπωρείῃσιν ἐπὶ προβλῆσι κυκλοῦνται τηλεφανεῖς αὐλῶνες ὑπὲρ μυχὸν εὐρέα κόλπου· οὗ Σύμης ὄρος ἐστὶ πολύς τ' εὐθαλὴς λειμών, ἐνθάδ' Ἀράξου ῥεῦμα μεγαβρεμέτου ποταμοῖο, ἐξ οὗ Θερμώδων Φᾶσις Τάναΐς τε ῥέουσιν, οὗ Κόλχων κλυτὰ φῦλα καὶ Ἡνιόχων καὶ Ἀραξῶν.

line_details.english: There, along the foothills, upon the projecting promontories,
line_details.greek: ἔνθα δ' ὑπωρείῃσιν ἐπὶ προβλῆσι κυκλοῦνται
line_details.note: hyporeiesin = “at/along the lower slopes,” i.e., foothills; problēsis = “projections,” here the jutting spurs or headlands.

line_details.english: far-seen ravines encircle the inmost recess of a broad gulf;
line_details.greek: τηλεφανεῖς αὐλῶνες ὑπὲρ μυχὸν εὐρέα κόλπου·
line_details.note: aulōnes are “hollows/valleys, ravines” (not “pipes”); telephaneis = “visible from afar.” hyper muchon = “over/above the innermost recess” of the gulf; kyklountai suggests they gird or ring it.

line_details.english: where stands the mountain of Syme and a luxuriant meadow in abundance,
line_details.greek: οὗ Σύμης ὄρος ἐστὶ πολύς τ' εὐθαλὴς λειμών,
line_details.note: Syme here is uncertain; it is unlikely to be the Aegean island Syme. Many take it as a local mountain/toponym in the eastern Euxine/Caucasian region.

line_details.english: here is the stream of the loud‑thundering river Araxes,
line_details.greek: ἐνθάδ' Ἀράξου ῥεῦμα μεγαβρεμέτου ποταμοῖο,
line_details.note: megabremetos = “loud‑thundering/roaring,” an epic epithet for a powerful river. Araxes is the great Armenian/Caucasian river, treated here as proximate to the Euxine’s eastern recess.

line_details.english: from which Thermodon, Phasis, and Tanais flow,
line_details.greek: ἐξ οὗ Θερμώδων Φᾶσις Τάναΐς τε ῥέουσιν,
line_details.note: The hydrology is mythic: Thermodon, Phasis, and Tanais are poetically derived from Araxes as a common source.

line_details.english: where dwell the famed tribes of the Colchians, the Heniocheans, and the Araxians.
line_details.greek: οὗ Κόλχων κλυτὰ φῦλα καὶ Ἡνιόχων καὶ Ἀραξῶν.
line_details.note: Klyta phyla = “famed tribes.” The Heniocheans (Heniokhoi) are a people of the eastern Black Sea coast (Strabo mentions them). “Araxians” renders Araxōn as an ethnicon (people of the Araxes).

text.english: Having passed it by, we sailed along the innermost havens, of the Ourians, and of the Chidnaians, the Charandaians, and the Solymi, and the folk of the Assyrians, and the rugged elbow of Sinope, and those of the Philyres and the Napatae, and the close‑packed cities of the Sapeires, and, besides these, we saw the Byzeres and the inhospitable tribes of the Sigymni.
text.greek: Ὃν παραμειβόμενοι, μυχάτοις ἐπεπλείομεν ὅρμοις Οὔρων, Χιδναίων τε, Χαρανδαίων, Σολύμων τε Ἀσσυρίων τε λεὼν, τρηχὺν δ' ἀγκῶνα Σινώπης, καὶ Φίλυρας Ναπάτας τε καὶ ἄστεα πυκνὰ Σαπείρων Βύζηράς τ' ἐπὶ τοῖσιν, ἰδ' ἄξενα φῦλα Σιγύμνων.

line_details.english: Having passed it by, we sailed along the innermost havens,
line_details.greek: Ὃν παραμειβόμενοι, μυχάτοις ἐπεπλείομεν ὅρμοις
line_details.note: μυχάτοις ὅρμοις literally “innermost moorings/anchorages,” suggesting coast‑hugging among deep inlets; ὅν (“it”) picks up a landmark named in the preceding context.

line_details.english: of the Ourians, and of the Chidnaians, the Charandaians, and the Solymi,
line_details.greek: Οὔρων, Χιδναίων τε, Χαρανδαίων, Σολύμων τε
line_details.note: A string of ethnics in the genitive dependent on ὅρμοις (“havens of …”). Οὔρων is uncertain: likely a tribal name (“Ourians”), though formally identical with the gen. pl. of οὖρος (“favorable wind”); Χιδναῖοι (from Chidna) and Χαρανδαῖοι (from Caranda) are obscure Anatolian groups; Σόλυμοι are the Solymi of Lycia.

line_details.english: and the folk of the Assyrians, and the rugged elbow of Sinope,
line_details.greek: Ἀσσυρίων τε λεὼν, τρηχὺν δ' ἀγκῶνα Σινώπης,
line_details.note: λεὼν is epic for λαός (“people”). “Assyrians” here is a broad, poetic label for eastern peoples. ἀγκών (“elbow”) is a standard term for a jutting headland; Sinope’s promontory fits the image.

line_details.english: and those of the Philyres and the Napatae, and the close‑packed cities of the Sapeires,
line_details.greek: καὶ Φίλυρας Ναπάτας τε καὶ ἄστεα πυκνὰ Σαπείρων
line_details.note: Φίλυρες and Σάπειρες (Sapeires/Sasperi) are peoples of the southern Euxine/Trans‑Colchian regions. Ναπάται likely “Glen‑dwellers” (from νάπη, “wooded vale”). The cases are compressed in epic style; many editors print different case‑forms (e.g., Φιλυρέων).

line_details.english: and, besides these, we saw the Byzeres and the inhospitable tribes of the Sigymni.
line_details.greek: Βύζηράς τ' ἐπὶ τοῖσιν, ἰδ' ἄξενα φῦλα Σιγύμνων.
line_details.note: Βύζηρες (Byzeres) and Σιγύμνοι (Sigymni) are rare ethnics; the latter recalls Herodotus’ Sigynnae. ἐπὶ τοῖσιν means “in addition to these.” ἰδ’ = εἴδομεν (“we saw”), governing the accusatives that follow; ἄξενα (“inhospitable”) echoes the epithet of the Euxine (Axenos).

text.english: And under the breaths of the wind Argo drew in close, at dawn, as Eos was coming over the boundless world, to the uttermost bounds of the Axenos, along the fair‑flowing Phasis.
text.greek: - Ἷκτο δ' ὑπὸ πνοιῇς ἀνέμου πλησίστιος Ἀργὼ ὄρθριον, ἐρχομένης ἠοῦς ἐπ' ἀπείρονα κόσμον, ἐσχατ' ἔπ' Ἀξείνου Φᾶσιν κατὰ καλλιρέεθρον.

line_details.english: And under the breaths of the wind Argo drew in close,
line_details.greek: - Ἷκτο δ' ὑπὸ πνοιῇς ἀνέμου πλησίστιος Ἀργὼ
line_details.note: πλησίστιος is used adverbially (“very near, close at hand”); some take it with a nautical nuance (“close to the wind”). Ἷκτο is the epic aorist of ἱκνέομαι (“came, reached”).

line_details.english: at dawn, as Eos was coming over the boundless world,
