text.english: But when I came into the precincts and the most holy sanctuary, upon a level stretch of ground I dug a triple‑ordered pit, and kindling‑twigs of juniper and of dry cedar, buckthorn of the sharper sort, and the much‑weeping poplars, swiftly bearing them I piled a pyre before the pit.
text.greek: - Ἡνίκα δ' εἰς σηκοὺς ἱκόμην ζάθεόν τε θεράπνην, χώρῳ ἐπὶ πλακόεντι βόθρον τρίστοιχον ὄρυξα, φιτρούς τ' ἀρκεύθοιο καὶ ἀζαλέης ἀπὸ κέδρου, ῥάμνον τ' ὀξυτέροιο, πολυκλαύτων τ' αἰγείρων, ὦκα φέρων νήησα πυρὴν ἔμπροσθε βόθροιο.

line_details.english: But when I came into the precincts and the most holy sanctuary,
line_details.greek: - Ἡνίκα δ' εἰς σηκοὺς ἱκόμην ζάθεόν τε θεράπνην,
line_details.note: σηκοί are sacred enclosures; θεράπνη denotes a shrine/cult‑seat; ζάθεος means “most holy.”

line_details.english: upon a level stretch of ground I dug a triple‑ordered pit,
line_details.greek: χώρῳ ἐπὶ πλακόεντι βόθρον τρίστοιχον ὄρυξα,
line_details.note: πλακόεντι = “level, flat.” βόθρος is a sacrificial pit for chthonic rites; τρίστοιχον “triple‑ordered/threefold,” i.e., arranged in three rows or sections.

line_details.english: and kindling‑twigs of juniper and of dry cedar,
line_details.greek: φιτρούς τ' ἀρκεύθοιο καὶ ἀζαλέης ἀπὸ κέδρου,
line_details.note: φιτρούς is a rare word for small sticks/kindling (cf. Hesychius: φίτρα = φρύγανα). ἀζαλέος = “parched, dry,” not related to the modern “azalea.”

line_details.english: buckthorn of the sharper sort, and the much‑weeping poplars,
line_details.greek: ῥάμνον τ' ὀξυτέροιο, πολυκλαύτων τ' αἰγείρων,
line_details.note: ῥάμνος = buckthorn; ὀξυτέροιο “of the sharper (more thorny) kind.” πολυκλαύτων “much‑weeping” is a traditional funerary epithet of the black poplar (aigeiros).

line_details.english: swiftly bearing them I piled a pyre before the pit.
line_details.greek: ὦκα φέρων νήησα πυρὴν ἔμπροσθε βόθροιο.
line_details.note: νήησα = “I heaped/piled,” aorist of νέω (II). ἔμπροσθε βόθροιο “before the pit” underscores the chthonic sacrificial setting.

text.english: And Mēdeia, wholly skilled, brought me many things, having taken them up from the coffers of the incense‑scented adyton.
text.greek: Πολλὰ δέ μοι φέρε πάμπαν ἐπισταμένη Μήδεια, φωριαμῶν ἀνελοῦσα θυώδεος ἐξ ἀδύτοιο.

line_details.english: And Mēdeia, wholly skilled, brought me many things,
line_details.greek: Πολλὰ δέ μοι φέρε πάμπαν ἐπισταμένη Μήδεια,
line_details.note: φέρε is the unaugmented imperfect (“she brought”); πάμπαν ἐπισταμένη = “wholly skilled” (sc. in her arts); the object is indefinite (“many things”), supplied by context.

line_details.english: having taken them up from the coffers of the incense‑scented adyton.
line_details.greek: φωριαμῶν ἀνελοῦσα θυώδεος ἐξ ἀδύτοιο.
line_details.note: φωριαμῶν = “coffers, chests” (rare/late word); ἀνελοῦσα = aorist ptc. “having taken up,” with genitive of separation; ἐξ ἀδύτοιο θυώδεος = “from the incense-scented inner shrine (adyton),” with epic genitives (-εος, -οιο).

text.english: Straightway I busied myself beneath the veils with cicatrizing plasters, and I would pile upon the pyre, and I performed cut-up offerings, having sacrificed three all-black whelps of dogs.
text.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' οὐλαοπλάσμαθ' ὑπὸ πέπλους ἐπονεύμην ἂν δὲ πυρὴν ἐπέβαλλον, ἰδ' ἔντομα θύματ' ἔρεζον, σκύμνους παμμέλανας σκυλάκων τρισσοὺς ἱερεύσας.

line_details.english: Straightway I busied myself beneath the veils with cicatrizing plasters,
line_details.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' οὐλαοπλάσμαθ' ὑπὸ πέπλους ἐπονεύμην
line_details.note: οὐλαοπλάσματα (acc. pl.) is a technical pharmaco-medical term, ‘cicatrizing plasters’ (from οὐλή ‘scar’ + πλάσσω ‘mould’), aptly used of Medea’s ointments; ἐπονεύμην (middle) = ‘I busied myself (with)’, from πονεύω ‘to toil, be active’; ὑπὸ πέπλους suggests ritual head-veiling during chthonic rites.

line_details.english: and I would pile upon the pyre, and I performed cut-up offerings,
line_details.greek: ἂν δὲ πυρὴν ἐπέβαλλον, ἰδ' ἔντομα θύματ' ἔρεζον,
line_details.note: ἄν with the imperfect ἐπέβαλλον marks iterative/habitual past (‘I would pile’). ἔντομα θύματα are ‘cut’ or ‘gashed’ offerings, a technical term in Hecatean/underworld ritual (cf. Apollonius Rhodius 3.1030–1036).

line_details.english: having sacrificed three all-black whelps of dogs.
line_details.greek: σκύμνους παμμέλανας σκυλάκων τρισσοὺς ἱερεύσας.
line_details.note: σκύμνους σκυλάκων is pleonastic (‘whelps of dogs’) to stress youthful victims; παμμέλανας ‘all-black’ is the standard color for chthonic sacrifices; τρισσούς ‘three’ suits Hekate’s triple aspect.

text.english: And with blood again I mixed chalkanthon and stroutheion, and split knekon, and in addition the loathsome psyllion, and red anchousa, and chalkimos; but then, filling the bellies of puppies, I set them in jars; and mixing galls with water, I poured [it] round about the pit, and, donning dusk-black garments and hateful bronze, striking it I summoned them; and they swiftly hearkened, bursting the wombs of the unsmiling abyss, Tisiphonē and Allecto and divine Megaera, brandishing dry-pine torches and hurling a murderous blaze.
text.greek: Αἵματι δ' αὖ χάλκανθον ἰδὲ στρούθειον ἔμιξα, κνῆκόν τε σχιστὴν, ἐπί τε ψύλλιον ἀηδὲς, ἄγχουσάν τ' ἐρυθρὴν, ἰδὲ χάλκιμον· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα νηδύας ἐμπλήσας σκυλάκων, φιτροῖσιν ἔθηκα· ὕδατι δ' αὖ μίξας χολάδας χεόμην περὶ βόθρον, ὄρφνινα θ' ἑσσάμενος φάρη καὶ ἀπεχθέα χαλκόν κρούων ἐλλισάμην· αἱ δ' ὁτραλέως ἐπάκουσαν, ῥήξασαι κενεῶνας ἀμειδήτοιο βερέθρου, Τισιφόνη τε καὶ Ἀληκτὼ καὶ δῖα Μέγαιρα, πεύκαις ἀζαλέαις φόνιον σέλας ἀΐσσουσαι.

line_details.english: And with blood again I mixed chalkanthon and stroutheion,
line_details.greek: Αἵματι δ' αὖ χάλκανθον ἰδὲ στρούθειον ἔμιξα,
line_details.note: chalkanthon = copper sulphate/blue vitriol; stroutheion (στρουθεῖον) is an obscure pharmakon (probably a plant; cf. Dioscorides), left transliterated.

line_details.english: and split knekon, and in addition the loathsome psyllion,
line_details.greek: κνῆκόν τε σχιστὴν, ἐπί τε ψύλλιον ἀηδὲς,
line_details.note: knēkon = safflower (Carthamus), a dye-plant; schistē (“split”) likely refers to a processed/flaked form. psyllion = fleawort (Plantago), noted here as “loathsome” (ἀηδές).

line_details.english: and red anchousa, and chalkimos; but then,
line_details.greek: ἄγχουσάν τ' ἐρυθρὴν, ἰδὲ χάλκιμον· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
line_details.note: anchousa (ἄγχουσα) = alkanet/alkanin-bearing root used as a red dye; chalkimos (χάλκιμον) = verdigris (copper rust).

line_details.english: filling the bellies of puppies, I set them in jars;
line_details.greek: νηδύας ἐμπλήσας σκυλάκων, φιτροῖσιν ἔθηκα·
line_details.note: “Bellies of puppies” (νηδύας σκυλάκων) are used as ritual containers in chthonic magic. φιτροῖσιν is probably a corruption of πίθροισιν (“large jars”); hence “I set them in jars.”

line_details.english: and mixing galls with water, I poured [it] round about the pit,
line_details.greek: ὕδατι δ' αὖ μίξας χολάδας χεόμην περὶ βόθρον,
line_details.note: χολάδες may mean “galls” (oak-galls) or “gall(-bladders)/bile”; either suits a harsh, chthonic libation. Translation keeps the ambiguity with “galls.”

line_details.english: and, donning dusk-black garments and hateful bronze,
line_details.greek: ὄρφνινα θ' ἑσσάμενος φάρη καὶ ἀπεχθέα χαλκόν
line_details.note: ὄρφνινα φάρη = “dusk-black garments.” ἀπεχθέα χαλκόν = “hateful bronze,” the clanging bronze used in underworld rites.

line_details.english: striking it I summoned them; and they swiftly hearkened,
line_details.greek: κρούων ἐλλισάμην· αἱ δ' ὁτραλέως ἐπάκουσαν,
line_details.note: ἐλλισάμην (“I summoned by incantation/rite”); combined with κρούων (“striking”) indicates summoning by clashing bronze.

line_details.english: bursting the wombs of the unsmiling abyss,
line_details.greek: ῥήξασαι κενεῶνας ἀμειδήτοιο βερέθρου,
line_details.note: κενεῶνας = “bellies/wombs”; βέρεθρον = “abyss, pit.” Vivid metaphor for the Furies forcing up from the underworld.

line_details.english: Tisiphonē and Allecto and divine Megaera,
line_details.greek: Τισιφόνη τε καὶ Ἀληκτὼ καὶ δῖα Μέγαιρα,
line_details.note: The three Erinyes are named; δῖα (“divine”) is conventional epic epithet, not contradicting their dread.

line_details.english: brandishing dry-pine torches and hurling a murderous blaze.
line_details.greek: πεύκαις ἀζαλέαις φόνιον σέλας ἀΐσσουσαι.
line_details.note: πεύκαις ἀζαλέαις = “dry/pared pines,” i.e., pine-wood torches; φόνιον σέλας = “murderous blaze.”

text.english: And straightway the pit burned, and the baneful fire crackled.
text.greek: Καίετο δ' αὐτίκα βόθρος, ἐσμαράγει δ' ὀλοὸν πῦρ·

line_details.english: And straightway the pit burned, and the baneful fire crackled.
line_details.greek: Καίετο δ' αὐτίκα βόθρος, ἐσμαράγει δ' ὀλοὸν πῦρ·
line_details.note: βόθρος is a ritual “pit” for chthonic offerings; ἐσμαράγει (onomatopoetic, often of clashing or roaring) here of the fire’s crackling/roar. Some witnesses have forms like ἐσμάραγε; the sense is auditory tumult.

text.english: And sooty reek was poured out, a far‑stretching smoke.
text.greek: λιγνὺς δ' αἰθαλόεσσα χύθη περιμήκετα καπνόν.

line_details.english: And sooty reek was poured out, a far‑stretching smoke.
line_details.greek: λιγνὺς δ' αἰθαλόεσσα χύθη περιμήκετα καπνόν.
line_details.note: λιγνύς αἰθαλόεσσα is a formula for thick, sooty reek; χύθη is “was poured out.” περιμήκετα modifies καπνόν (“far‑stretching/long‑drawn smoke”).

text.english: And straightway out of Aidēs, through the flame, they were roused.
text.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' ἐξ Ἀΐδαο διὰ φλογὸς ἠγέρθησαν

line_details.english: And straightway out of Aidēs, through the flame, they were roused.
line_details.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' ἐξ Ἀΐδαο διὰ φλογὸς ἠγέρθησαν
line_details.note: Aidēs is transliterated. The passive ἠγέρθησαν (“were roused”) commonly describes the summoning of the dead; διὰ φλογὸς (“through the flame”) may allude to a ritual or pyric medium. The subject is feminine plural, supplied by the epithets in the next line.

text.english: dread, wonder‑striking, ruthless, not to be looked upon.
text.greek: δειναὶ, θαμβήτειραι, ἀπηνέες, ἀπροσόρατοι.

line_details.english: dread, wonder‑striking, ruthless, not to be looked upon.
line_details.greek: δειναὶ, θαμβήτειραι, ἀπηνέες, ἀπροσόρατοι.
line_details.note: θαμβήτειραι is a rare epithet, literally “astonishment-/wonder‑causing.” ἀπροσόρατοι, from ὁράω with πρός-, means “impossible to look upon (face to face).” The cluster of feminine plurals marks unnamed dread female beings.

text.english: For she had a body of iron, her whom the Chthonians call Pandora; and in her company there came, of shifting form, triple‑headed—a baleful prodigy to behold, not to be withstood in battle—Hekate, child of Tartaros; and from her left shoulder there sprang a horse with flowing mane; and on the right there was to be seen a rabid‑eyed bitch; and in the middle she was savage in shape; and in both hands she held swords with hilts.
text.greek: Ἣ μὲν γὰρ δέμας ἔσχε σιδήρεον, ἣν καλέουσι Πανδώρην χθόνιοι· σὺν δ' αἰολόμορφος ἵκανε τρισσοκέφαλος, ἰδεῖν ὀλοὸν τέρας οὔτι δαϊκτὸν, Ταρταρόπαις Ἑκάτη· λαιοῦ δ' ἄρ' ἐπεσσύθη ὤμου ἵππος χαιτήεις· κατὰ δεξιὰ δ' ἦεν ἀθρῆσαι λυσσῶπις σκυλάκη· μέσση δ' ἔφυ ἀγριόμορφος χερσὶν δ' ἀμφοτέραις ἔχεν ἄορα κωπήεντα.

line_details.english: For she had a body of iron, her whom the Chthonians call Pandora;
line_details.greek: Ἣ μὲν γὰρ δέμας ἔσχε σιδήρεον, ἣν καλέουσι
line_details.note: “Pandora” here is a chthonic epithet/title, not necessarily the Hesiodic figure; “chthonians” means the underworld powers or denizens.

line_details.english: and in her company there came, of shifting form,
line_details.greek: Πανδώρην χθόνιοι· σὺν δ' αἰολόμορφος ἵκανε
line_details.note: aiolomorphos = “changeful/variegated in form,” highlighting Hekate’s polymorphy; “with her” likely refers back to the figure just named, Pandora.

line_details.english: triple‑headed—a baleful prodigy to behold, not to be withstood in battle—Hekate, child of Tartaros;
line_details.greek: τρισσοκέφαλος, ἰδεῖν ὀλοὸν τέρας οὔτι δαϊκτὸν,
line_details.note: oûti daiktón = “not to be fought/withstood in battle”; Tartaropais (“child of Tartaros”) is a rare Orphic epithet of Hekate, stressing her underworld origin; trissokephalos = “triple‑headed.”

line_details.english: and from her left shoulder there sprang a horse with flowing mane;
line_details.greek: Ταρταρόπαις Ἑκάτη· λαιοῦ δ' ἄρ' ἐπεσσύθη ὤμου
line_details.note: “From the left shoulder” suggests a bestial head or form projecting; epessythê conveys a sudden rush/leap forth; the horse head aligns with Hekate’s monstrous, composite aspect.

line_details.english: and on the right there was to be seen a rabid‑eyed bitch;
line_details.greek: ἵππος χαιτήεις· κατὰ δεξιὰ δ' ἦεν ἀθρῆσαι
line_details.note: skylakê is a diminutive of “dog,” but in epic may be merely stylistic; lyssôpis = “rabid‑eyed, raging‑eyed.”

line_details.english: and in the middle she was savage in shape;
line_details.greek: λυσσῶπις σκυλάκη· μέσση δ' ἔφυ ἀγριόμορφος
line_details.note: “In the middle she was savage in form” most naturally refers to the central head/form of the triple figure, left unspecified but characterized as wild/feral.

line_details.english: and in both hands she held swords with hilts.
line_details.greek: χερσὶν δ' ἀμφοτέραις ἔχεν ἄορα κωπήεντα.
line_details.note: aora kôpêenta = “swords with hilts/hafted blades” (kôpê = handle); not “oars,” despite the cognate form for “oar.”

text.english: Encircling, Pandora and Hekate were whirling round the pit, hither and thither.
text.greek: Ἐγκύκλιαι δινεῦντο περὶ βόθρον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα

line_details.english: Encircling, Pandora and Hekate were whirling round the pit, hither and thither.
line_details.greek: Ἐγκύκλιαι δινεῦντο περὶ βόθρον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
line_details.note: “Enkykliai” (fem. pl.) is taken predicatively with the two goddesses, meaning “encircling/revolving”; βόθρος is the chthonic “pit” of necromantic rites; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “hither and thither.”

text.english: And the Poinae were rushing together.
text.greek: Πανδώρη Ἑκάτη τε· συνεσσεύοντο δὲ Ποιναί.

line_details.english: And the Poinae were rushing together.
line_details.greek: Πανδώρη Ἑκάτη τε· συνεσσεύοντο δὲ Ποιναί.
line_details.note: Πανδώρη is an epic/Doric form of Pandora; some take it as an epithet (“All-giver”) potentially applied to Hekate/Earth. Ποίναι are the personified Retributions (akin to Erinyes), here as Hekate’s attendants. συνεσσεύοντο (from συν- + σεύω) = “were rushing together.”

text.english: And straightway, out from Artemis, the warder in person let fall to the ground the pine‑brands from his hands, and he fastened his eyes upon the sky.
text.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἄφαρ Ἀρτέμιδος φρουρὸν δέμας ἧκε χαμάζε πεύκας ἐκ χειρῶν, ἐς δ' οὐρανὸν ἤραρεν ὄσσε.

line_details.english: And straightway, out from Artemis, the warder in person let fall to the ground the pine‑brands from his hands,
line_details.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἄφαρ Ἀρτέμιδος φρουρὸν δέμας ἧκε χαμάζε
line_details.note: ἐκ Ἀρτέμιδος is best taken metonymically as “out from [the temple/shrine of] Artemis.” φρουρὸν δέμας, literally “a guardian body/form,” is compressed epic diction; here it denotes the temple‑guard “in person.” πεύκας likely means pine‑wood torches/brands. The syntax is abrupt but coherent in epic style.

line_details.english: and he fastened his eyes upon the sky.
line_details.greek: πεύκας ἐκ χειρῶν, ἐς δ' οὐρανὸν ἤραρεν ὄσσε.
line_details.note: ἤραρεν ὄσσε (from ἀραρίσκω) is a Homeric idiom meaning “fixed/fastened his eyes.”

text.english: And the attendant hounds were fawning, and the clasps of the silver bolts were being loosed; and the fair doors of the wide‑built wall flew open; and a secure grove came into view.
text.greek: Σαῖνον δὲ σκύλακες πρόπολοι, λύοντο δ' ὀχῆες κλείθρων ἀργυρέων, ἀνὰ δ' ἔπτατο καλὰ θύρετρα τείχεος εὐρυμενοῦς, ὑπεφαίνετο δ' ἄλσος ἐρυμνόν.

line_details.english: And the attendant hounds were fawning, and the clasps of the silver bolts were being loosed;
line_details.greek: Σαῖνον δὲ σκύλακες πρόπολοι, λύοντο δ' ὀχῆες
line_details.note: σαίνειν of dogs “fawning, wagging (the tail)”; ὀχῆες are the fastenings/holders of bolts—hence “clasps of the silver bolts.”

line_details.english: and the fair doors of the wide‑built wall flew open;
line_details.greek: κλείθρων ἀργυρέων, ἀνὰ δ' ἔπτατο καλὰ θύρετρα
line_details.note: ἔπτατο (“flew up”) is idiomatic of doors opening; θύρετρα can denote folding doors/gates; εὐρυμενής = “wide‑built, widely‑spread,” of city walls.

line_details.english: and a secure grove came into view.
line_details.greek: τείχεος εὐρυμενοῦς, ὑπεφαίνετο δ' ἄλσος ἐρυμνόν.
line_details.note: ἐρυμνός = “strong, secure, well‑defended”; for a grove it suggests an enclosed or inviolate sacred precinct rather than mere physical strength.

text.english: But I crossed the threshold; thereupon the maiden Medea, daughter of Aietes, and the glorious son of Aison, the Tyndarids too pressed on together, and Mopsus followed in company.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἔβην· τῆμος δέ τε κούρη Αἰήτεω Μήδεια καὶ Αἴσονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός, Τυνδαρίδαι τ' ἤπειγον ὁμοῦ, σὺν δ' ἕσπετο Μόψος.

line_details.english: But I crossed the threshold; thereupon the maiden
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἔβην· τῆμος δέ τε κούρη
line_details.note: Autar egōn is the epic connective “but I”; huper oudon ebin is a set phrase for “I crossed the threshold.” Tēmos means “then/thereupon.”

line_details.english: Medea, daughter of Aietes, and the glorious son of Aison,
line_details.greek: Αἰήτεω Μήδεια καὶ Αἴσονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός,
line_details.note: Aiëteō is the epic genitive “of Aietes,” functioning as a patronymic; “the glorious son of Aison” is Jason.

line_details.english: the Tyndarids too pressed on together, and Mopsus followed in company.
line_details.greek: Τυνδαρίδαι τ' ἤπειγον ὁμοῦ, σὺν δ' ἕσπετο Μόψος.
line_details.note: Ēpeigon can be transitive (“urged [someone] on”) or intransitive (“pressed on, made haste”); here rendered intransitively to fit the group subject. The Tyndarids are the Dioscuri (Castor and Polydeuces). Syn d’ hespeto (“and [he] followed in company”) uses syn adverbially with hépomai.

text.english: But when at last the lovely oak was seen from close at hand, and the platform of Zeus Xenios and the altar’s seat, there the dragon, coiled in his broad convolutions beneath it, whirling, lifted on high his head and his grim beard, and aloft he sent a baneful hiss, and the boundless Aither bellowed over it; and the trees crashed, shaken this way and that from the base, from the root; and the shadowy grove rang out.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ σχεδόθεν κατεφαίνετο φηγὸς ἐραννή, κρηπίς τε ξενίοιο Διὸς καὶ βώμιος ἕδρη, ἔνθα δράκων ὁλκοῖσιν ὑπὸ πλατέεσσιν ἑλιχθείς δινεύων ἀνάειρε κάρη βλοσυρόν τε γένειον, ἂν δ' ὀλοὸν σύριγξ' ἐπὶ δ' ἔβραχεν ἄσπετος αἰθήρ· Δένδρεα δ' ἐσμαράγησε, κραδαινόμεν' ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα πρυμνόθεν ἐκ ῥίζης· ἰάχησε δὲ σύσκιον ἄλσος.

line_details.english: But when at last the lovely oak was seen from close at hand,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ σχεδόθεν κατεφαίνετο φηγὸς ἐραννή,
line_details.note: phēgos in epic generally = “oak” (not “beech”); eranē = “lovely, gracious,” a stock epithet for trees/groves.

line_details.english: and the platform of Zeus Xenios and the altar’s seat,
line_details.greek: κρηπίς τε ξενίοιο Διὸς καὶ βώμιος ἕδρη,
line_details.note: Krēpis and hedra both denote a foundation/platform; Zeus Xenios is Zeus as protector of strangers and hospitality.

line_details.english: there the dragon, coiled in his broad convolutions beneath it,
line_details.greek: ἔνθα δράκων ὁλκοῖσιν ὑπὸ πλατέεσσιν ἑλιχθείς
line_details.note: The phrase holkoisin hypo plateessin helichtheis is compressed and much discussed: holkoi literally “drag-tracks/furrows,” here likely metaphorical of serpentine folds; platees “broad.” The translation renders the sense (“broad convolutions beneath [the oak]”).

line_details.english: whirling, lifted on high his head and his grim beard,
line_details.greek: δινεύων ἀνάειρε κάρη βλοσυρόν τε γένειον,
line_details.note: Geneion (“beard/chin”): dragons in Greek poetic diction can be ‘bearded’; thus “grim beard” preserves the epic coloring.

line_details.english: and aloft he sent a baneful hiss, and the boundless Aither bellowed over it;
line_details.greek: ἂν δ' ὀλοὸν σύριγξ' ἐπὶ δ' ἔβραχεν ἄσπετος αἰθήρ·
line_details.note: Syrinx here = “hiss” by metonymy (cf. syrygmos); some emend to syrygmon. Aspe tos = “boundless, unspeakable.” Aither is capitalized as a personified upper sky.

line_details.english: and the trees crashed, shaken this way and that
line_details.greek: Δένδρεα δ' ἐσμαράγησε, κραδαινόμεν' ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
line_details.note: Prym nothen ek rhizēs is an emphatic hendiadys, “from the very root,” underscoring the force of the shaking.

line_details.english: from the base, from the root; and the shadowy grove rang out.
line_details.greek: πρυμνόθεν ἐκ ῥίζης· ἰάχησε δὲ σύσκιον ἄλσος.
line_details.note: Suskion = “deep/shadowy” (densely shaded), standard of sacred groves.

text.english: But a tremor seized me and my comrades; apart, alone, Medeia within her breast wielded an unbending spirit; for with her palms she gathered the scrapings of baneful roots.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔμ' ἠδ' ἑτάρους τρόμος ἔλλαβε· νόσφι δὲ μούνη Μήδει' ἐνὶ στέρνοισιν ἀκαμπέα θυμὸν ἐνώμα· δρέψατο γὰρ παλάμῃσι λυγρῶν ἀποθρίσματα ῥιζῶν.

line_details.english: But a tremor seized me and my comrades; apart, alone,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔμ' ἠδ' ἑτάρους τρόμος ἔλλαβε· νόσφι δὲ μούνη
line_details.note: νόσφι δὲ μούνη is enjambed: “apart, alone” prepares the exception—namely Medeia—in the next line; ἔλλαβε (‘seized’) is a common epic formula for sudden emotion.

line_details.english: Medeia within her breast wielded an unbending spirit;
line_details.greek: Μήδει' ἐνὶ στέρνοισιν ἀκαμπέα θυμὸν ἐνώμα·
line_details.note: ἐνώμα is the aorist of νωμάω, “to wield, handle, direct”; θυμός here is the seat of resolve/courage, hence “unbending spirit.” The form Μήδει’ is elided for metrical reasons (for Μήδεια).

line_details.english: for with her palms she gathered the scrapings of baneful roots.
line_details.greek: δρέψατο γὰρ παλάμῃσι λυγρῶν ἀποθρίσματα ῥιζῶν.
line_details.note: ἀποθρίσματα ῥιζῶν are ‘scrapings/shavings of roots,’ a technical phrasing for pharmaka; λυγρός means ‘baneful, baleful.’ δρέψατο (middle) suggests deliberate, personal action—‘she plucked for herself.’

text.english: And then I fitted to the phorminx a wondrous strain, and from the hypatê of the shell I rang out a deep-resounding voice, sending it unuttered beneath my lips, in silence.
text.greek: Καὶ τότ' ἐγὼ φόρμιγγος ἐφήρμοσα θέσκελον ὀμφήν, κλάγξα δ' ἄρ' ἐξ ὑπάτης χέλυος βαρυηχέα φωνήν σιγαλέως ἄφθεγκτον ἐμοῖς ὑπὸ χείλεσι πέμπων.

line_details.english: And then I fitted to the phorminx a wondrous strain,
line_details.greek: Καὶ τότ' ἐγὼ φόρμιγγος ἐφήρμοσα θέσκελον ὀμφήν,
line_details.note: phorminx: the epic lyre; ἐφήρμοσα “fitted/attuned.” θέσκελος ὀμφή, literally “wondrous/divine voice,” here a lofty term for a musical strain (ὀμφή often means oracular ‘voice’).

line_details.english: and from the hypatê of the shell I rang out a deep-resounding voice,
line_details.greek: κλάγξα δ' ἄρ' ἐξ ὑπάτης χέλυος βαρυηχέα φωνήν
line_details.note: ὑπάτη is the technical name for the lowest (gravest) string in the ancient Greek system; χέλυς is the tortoise-shell lyre. κλάγξα conveys a ringing/pealing sound; βαρυηχέα “deep-sounding.”

line_details.english: sending it unuttered beneath my lips, in silence.
line_details.greek: σιγαλέως ἄφθεγκτον ἐμοῖς ὑπὸ χείλεσι πέμπων.
line_details.note: σιγαλέως likely = “silently” (cf. σιγηλῶς). ἄφθεγκτον “unuttered/wordless,” indicating instrumental sound without vocalization; ὑπὸ χείλεσι, “beneath my lips,” idiomatically, with the lips not speaking.

text.english: For I called upon Hypnos, lord of the gods and of all men, so that, when he came, he might lull the might of the sturdy dragon.
text.greek: Κλῇξα γὰρ ὕπνον ἄνακτα θεῶν πάντων τ' ἀνθρώπων, ὄφρα μολὼν θέλξειε μένος βριαροῖο δράκοντος.

line_details.english: For I called upon Hypnos, lord of the gods and of all men,
line_details.greek: Κλῇξα γὰρ ὕπνον ἄνακτα θεῶν πάντων τ' ἀνθρώπων,
line_details.note: κλῇξα (“I called upon”) from κλῄζω; Ὕπνος (Hypnos) is personified Sleep, here strikingly styled “lord of gods and men,” echoing and inverting the usual title of Zeus.

line_details.english: so that, when he came, he might lull the might of the sturdy dragon.
line_details.greek: ὄφρα μολὼν θέλξειε μένος βριαροῖο δράκοντος.
line_details.note: θέλξειε (“might charm/lull”) suits Hypnos’ power; μολών is the aorist participle of βλώσκω (“to come”); βριαροῖο = “sturdy, strong,” not the proper name Briareus; δράκων = “dragon/serpent.”

text.english: And swiftly he hearkened to me, and he sent the Kyteïan upon the land.
text.greek: Ῥίμφα δέ μοι ὑπάκουσε, Κυτηΐδα δ' ἧκ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν.

line_details.english: And swiftly he hearkened to me, and he sent the Kyteïan upon the land.
line_details.greek: Ῥίμφα δέ μοι ὑπάκουσε, Κυτηΐδα δ' ἧκ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν.
line_details.note: ῥίμφα = ‘swiftly, lightly’ (epic adverb). ἧκ’ = ἧκε ‘he sent.’ Κυτηΐδα is the accusative of Κυτηΐς, a gentilic ‘the Kyteïan (woman),’ i.e., Medea, so called from Cyt(a)ea in Colchis; cf. the more familiar ‘Cytaean’ epithet in other poets. The subject of the verbs is the deity previously invoked in context.

text.english: But when he had lulled to sleep the tribes of day‑long mortals, and the vehement blasts of the winds, and the billows of the sea, and the springs of ever‑flowing waters, and the streams of rivers, both wild beasts and birds, and whatever lives and crawls, lulling them to rest, he withdrew beneath his golden wings.
text.greek: Κοιμίσσας δ' ὅγε φῦλα πανημερίων ἀνθρώπων, καὶ ζαμενεῖς ἀνέμων πνοιὰς, καὶ κύματα πόντου, πηγάς τ' ἀενάων ὑδάτων, ποταμῶν τε ῥέεθρα, θῆράς τ' οἰωνούς τε, τά τε ζώει τε καὶ ἕρπει, εὐνάζων ἤμειψεν ὑπὸ χρυσέαις πτερύγεσσιν.

line_details.english: But when he had lulled to sleep the tribes of day‑long mortals,
line_details.greek: Κοιμίσσας δ' ὅγε φῦλα πανημερίων ἀνθρώπων,
line_details.note: πανημερίων (“of all-day”) suggests mortals active or toiling by day; the implied subject is Hypnos (Sleep), picked up by the winged imagery in line 1011.

line_details.english: and the vehement blasts of the winds, and the billows of the sea,
line_details.greek: καὶ ζαμενεῖς ἀνέμων πνοιὰς, καὶ κύματα πόντου,
line_details.note: ζαμενεῖς is an epic adjective meaning “vehement, violent,” modifying the wind’s “blasts” (πνοιὰς).

line_details.english: and the springs of ever‑flowing waters, and the streams of rivers,
line_details.greek: πηγάς τ' ἀενάων ὑδάτων, ποταμῶν τε ῥέεθρα,
line_details.note: ἀενάων ὑδάτων is a formulaic “ever-flowing”; the pairing πηγαί/ῥέεθρα distinguishes springs from river-currents.

line_details.english: both wild beasts and birds, and whatever lives and crawls,
line_details.greek: θῆράς τ' οἰωνούς τε, τά τε ζώει τε καὶ ἕρπει,
line_details.note: τὰ τε ζώει τε καὶ ἕρπει is a totalizing formula (“all that lives and crawls”); note the epic neuter plural with singular verb (ζώει).

line_details.english: lulling them to rest, he withdrew beneath his golden wings.
line_details.greek: εὐνάζων ἤμειψεν ὑπὸ χρυσέαις πτερύγεσσιν.
line_details.note: εὐνάζων … ἤμειψεν ὑπὸ χρυσέαις πτερύγεσσιν: “withdrew beneath his golden wings,” the wings identifying Hypnos; χρυσέαις marks divine radiance.

text.english: He reached the bloom‑laden land of the harsh Kolchians; and straightway deep slumber seized the eyes of the monstrous serpent, equal to death; and it laid its long neck about its throat, with head‑heavy scales. And dread‑fated Medeia, on seeing, was amazed, and she came, emboldening Aison’s illustrious son to grasp quickly the stump, for the golden‑woolled fleece; and, hearing, he did not disobey; but, lifting the immense hide, he made his way to the ship.
text.greek: Ἷξε δ' ὑπὸ στυφελῶν Κόλχων εὐανθέα χῶρον· κῶμα δ' ἄφαρ κατέμαρψε πελωρίου ὄσσε δράκοντος, ἰσοπαλὲς θανάτῳ· δολιχὴν δ' ἀμφ' αὐχένι δειρήν θῆκε καρηβαρέων φολίσιν· θάμβησε δ' ἰδοῦσα αἰνόποτμος Μήδεια· καὶ Αἴσονος ἀγλαὸν υἷα ἧκ' ἐπιθαρσύνουσα θοῶς πρέμνοιο λαβέσθαι κῶας χρυσεόμαλλον· ὁ δ' οὐκ ἀπίθησεν ἀκούσας· αὐτὰρ ἀειράμενος δέρας ἄπλετον ἷκτ' ἐπὶ νῆα.

line_details.english: He reached the bloom‑laden land of the harsh Kolchians;
line_details.greek: Ἷξε δ' ὑπὸ στυφελῶν Κόλχων εὐανθέα χῶρον·
line_details.note: ὑπὸ + gen. here conveys dominion/locale (“in the land of”); εὐανθής = “bloom‑laden”; στυφελός = “harsh, unyielding.”

line_details.english: and straightway deep slumber seized the eyes of the monstrous serpent,
line_details.greek: κῶμα δ' ἄφαρ κατέμαρψε πελωρίου ὄσσε δράκοντος,
line_details.note: κῶμα = deep, deathlike sleep; ὄσσε is dual (“both eyes”).

line_details.english: equal to death; and it laid its long neck about its throat,
line_details.greek: ἰσοπαλὲς θανάτῳ· δολιχὴν δ' ἀμφ' αὐχένι δειρήν
line_details.note: ἰσοπαλὲς θανάτῳ is a traditional formula for sleep’s potency; ἀμφ’ αὐχένι δειρήν (neck about the neck) vividly describes the serpent coiling upon itself.

line_details.english: with head‑heavy scales. And dread‑fated Medeia, on seeing, was amazed,
line_details.greek: θῆκε καρηβαρέων φολίσιν· θάμβησε δ' ἰδοῦσα
line_details.note: καρηβαρέων φολίσιν is instrumental (“with head‑heavy scales”), suggesting the droop of the scaly, heavy head; αἰνόποτμος is Medeia’s tragic epithet.

line_details.english: and she came, emboldening Aison’s illustrious son
line_details.greek: αἰνόποτμος Μήδεια· καὶ Αἴσονος ἀγλαὸν υἷα
line_details.note: ἧκ’ = ἦκε; “Aison’s illustrious son” is the epic periphrasis for Jason; ἐπιθαρσύνω = “to embolden, cheer on.”

line_details.english: to grasp quickly the stump, for the golden‑woolled fleece;
line_details.greek: ἧκ' ἐπιθαρσύνουσα θοῶς πρέμνοιο λαβέσθαι
line_details.note: πρέμνον = base/stump (of Ares’ oak); κῶας χρυσεόμαλλον = “golden‑woolled fleece,” with κῶας a synonym of δέρας used in the next line.

line_details.english: and, hearing, he did not disobey;
line_details.greek: κῶας χρυσεόμαλλον· ὁ δ' οὐκ ἀπίθησεν ἀκούσας·
line_details.note: οὐκ ἀπίθησεν = “did not disobey,” the epic litotes for “obeyed.”

line_details.english: but, lifting the immense hide, he made his way to the ship.
line_details.greek: αὐτὰρ ἀειράμενος δέρας ἄπλετον ἷκτ' ἐπὶ νῆα.
line_details.note: δέρας ἄπλετον = “immense hide/fleece”; ἷκτ’ ἐπὶ νῆα = “he reached the ship.”

text.english: The Minyan heroes rejoiced greatly; then indeed their hands they raised to the Immortals, who hold the broad heaven.
text.greek: - Ἥρωες Μινύαι μέγ' ἐγήθεον, ἂν δ' ἄρα χεῖρας ἀθανάτοις ἤειραν, οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν.

line_details.english: The Minyan heroes rejoiced greatly; then indeed their hands
line_details.greek: - Ἥρωες Μινύαι μέγ' ἐγήθεον, ἂν δ' ἄρα χεῖρας
line_details.note: “Minyan heroes” (Minyae) identifies the Argonauts as descendants of Minyas; ἂν δ’ ἄρα is a Homeric particle cluster meaning “then indeed”; the mention of hands anticipates the prayer gesture completed in the next line.

line_details.english: they raised to the Immortals, who hold the broad heaven.
line_details.greek: ἀθανάτοις ἤειραν, οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν.
line_details.note: “The Immortals” = the gods; οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν is a Homeric formula, “who hold the broad heaven,” characterizing the Olympians; ἤειραν (epic aorist of αἴρω) refers to the ritual raising of hands in prayer.

text.english: Thus they for their part were gazing upon the fleece; but straightway Aeëtes heard from the handmaids that Medea was gone.
text.greek: Ὣς οἳ μὲν περὶ κῶας ὀπώπεον· αἶψα δ' Αἰήτης ἀμφιπόλων ἤκουσεν ἀποιχομένην Μήδειαν.

line_details.english: Thus they for their part were gazing upon the fleece;
line_details.greek: Ὣς οἳ μὲν περὶ κῶας ὀπώπεον· αἶψα δ' Αἰήτης
line_details.note: ὀπώπεον is an epic form meaning “were gazing/beholding.” κῶας (“fleece”) here denotes the Golden Fleece; περὶ with the accusative conveys “around/about,” rendered idiomatically as “upon.”

line_details.english: but straightway Aeëtes heard from the handmaids that Medea was gone.
line_details.greek: ἀμφιπόλων ἤκουσεν ἀποιχομένην Μήδειαν.
line_details.note: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person from whom one hears (ἀμφιπόλων, “handmaids/attendants”) and an accusative + participle for the content (Μήδειαν ἀποιχομένην, “that Medea was gone/absent”).

text.english: Quickly then he bade Apsyrtos to muster the host.
text.greek: Ὦκα δ' ἄρ' Ἀψύρτῳ ἐπετέλλετο λαὸν ἀγεῖραι

line_details.english: Quickly then he bade Apsyrtos to muster the host.
line_details.greek: Ὦκα δ' ἄρ' Ἀψύρτῳ ἐπετέλλετο λαὸν ἀγεῖραι
line_details.note: Subject of ἐπετέλλετο is implicit (Aeētes in context); dative Ἀψύρτῳ marks the person commanded; λαόν rendered “host.”

text.english: and to track down the maiden, his sister by the same father.
text.greek: μαστεύειν δ' ἄρα παῖδα κασιγνήτην καὶ ὅπατρον·

line_details.english: and to track down the maiden, his sister by the same father.
line_details.greek: μαστεύειν δ' ἄρα παῖδα κασιγνήτην καὶ ὅπατρον·
line_details.note: μαστεύειν = “to track down, search out.” ὅπατρον = “of the same father” (homopatric), specifying Medea as Apsyrtos’ sister; παῖδα κασιγνήτην refers to Medea as “the maiden sister.”

text.english: but swiftly he pressed on beside the river’s mouths into an ambush of heroes, and he came upon the dread maiden.
text.greek: ἀλλά οἱ ὠκὺς ἔπειγε παρὰ προχοὰς ποταμοῖο εἰς λόχον ἡρώων, ἔκιχεν δ' ἄρα παρθένον αἰνήν.

line_details.english: but swiftly he pressed on beside the river’s mouths
line_details.greek: ἀλλά οἱ ὠκὺς ἔπειγε παρὰ προχοὰς ποταμοῖο
line_details.note: οἱ is an ethical/indirect dative (“for him”); ὠκὺς ἔπειγε is rendered intransitively as “he pressed on swiftly.” προχοαί = “outflows, mouths” of a river.

line_details.english: into an ambush of heroes, and he came upon the dread maiden.
line_details.greek: εἰς λόχον ἡρώων, ἔκιχεν δ' ἄρα παρθένον αἰνήν.
line_details.note: παρθένον αἰνήν = “dread/terrible maiden,” an elevated epithet of Medea; λόχος ἡρώων = the Argonauts’ ambush.

text.english: And Night, star-cloaked, was then passing the mid-course of her journey, and the baleful stratagem was fulfilled, and the unseen Keres of very-renowned Apsyrtos, under the compulsion of Medeia’s love; whom, when they had slain him, they released at the mouths of the river as it surged; and it bore him along with a swift blast; buffeted by eddies into the wave of the unharvested sea, he was swept past the islands which they call the Apsyrtides, but in no wise did they escape Zeus the Overseer nor the ordinances.
text.greek: Νὺξ δὲ τότ' ἀστροχίτων μέσσην παράμειβε πορείαν, Ἐκ δ' ἐτελεῖτο δόλος στυγερὸς καὶ κῆρες ἀϊδναί Μηδείης ὑπ' ἔρωτος, ἐρικλυτοῦ Ἀψύρτοιο, ὅν ῥα κατακτείναντες, ἐπὶ προχοὰς μεθέηκαν ὀρνυμένου ποταμοῖο· φέρεν δ' ὅγε πνεύματι κραιπνῷ· θεινόμενος δὲ δίναις εἰς κῦμ' ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο, κέλσεν ὑπὲρ νήσων, Ἀψυρτίδας ἃς καλέουσιν, ἀλλά οἱ οὔτι λάθον Δι' ἐπόψιον οὐδὲ θέμιστας.

line_details.english: And Night, star-cloaked, was then passing the mid-course of her journey,
line_details.greek: Νὺξ δὲ τότ' ἀστροχίτων μέσσην παράμειβε πορείαν,
line_details.note: “astrochitōn” = “star-cloaked,” a conventional epic epithet for Night; “mid-course” signals midnight.

line_details.english: and the baleful stratagem was fulfilled, and the unseen Keres
line_details.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἐτελεῖτο δόλος στυγερὸς καὶ κῆρες ἀϊδναί
line_details.note: “Keres aïdnai” are the “unseen” death-spirits; the singular verb with plural subject is a common poetic license. “stygeros” = “baleful.”

line_details.english: of very-renowned Apsyrtos, under the compulsion of Medeia’s love;
line_details.greek: Μηδείης ὑπ' ἔρωτος, ἐρικλυτοῦ Ἀψύρτοιο,
line_details.note: “hyp’ erōtos” expresses causation (“under the compulsion of love”), here Medeia’s love for Iason; “eriklytos” = “very-renowned.” The genitive “Apsyrtoio” depends on “Keres.”

line_details.english: whom, when they had slain him, they released at the mouths of the river as it surged;
line_details.greek: ὅν ῥα κατακτείναντες, ἐπὶ προχοὰς μεθέηκαν
line_details.note: “prochoai” are river-mouths/outfalls; “ornymenou potamoio” = “of the surging/rising river.” The river is unnamed; the context points to the region of the Apsyrtides.

line_details.english: and it bore him along with a swift blast;
line_details.greek: ὀρνυμένου ποταμοῖο· φέρεν δ' ὅγε πνεύματι κραιπνῷ·
line_details.note: “pneuma” (“breath, blast”) metaphorically for the driving force of the current (possibly wind-aided). The pronoun “hoge” refers back to the river.

line_details.english: buffeted by eddies into the wave of the unharvested sea,
line_details.greek: θεινόμενος δὲ δίναις εἰς κῦμ' ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο,
line_details.note: “halos atrugetoio” = “unharvested sea,” a Homeric formula; “theinomenos” = “smitten/buffeted,” of a body tossed by eddies (dīnai).

line_details.english: he was swept past the islands which they call the Apsyrtides,
line_details.greek: κέλσεν ὑπὲρ νήσων, Ἀψυρτίδας ἃς καλέουσιν,
line_details.note: “Apsyrtides” are the Apsyrtian Isles (traditionally in the northern Adriatic). The verb “kelsen” conveys being driven/swept along; the exact nuance is debated.

line_details.english: but in no wise did they escape Zeus the Overseer nor the ordinances.
line_details.greek: ἀλλά οἱ οὔτι λάθον Δι' ἐπόψιον οὐδὲ θέμιστας.
line_details.note: “Di’ epopsion” = “Zeus the Overseer/Watchful,” emphasizing divine surveillance; “themistas” = the (divine) ordinances/laws (of Themis). The line foreshadows retribution for the murderers.

text.english: But when they had gone within the ship, and from either side, of the bank they cut the mooring-ropes, and beneath the swift oarage, pressing on to sail, they clove the river not on a straight course, toward the fish-rich sea, through the wide mouth of the Phasis, we made for it; yet through a misstep we were borne far backward, ever putting back; and the cities of the Colchians were being left behind by the heedless Minyae, and murky dusk encompassed us all around.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ νηὸς μὲν ἔσω κίον, ἐκ δ' ἑκάτερθεν ὄχθης πείσματ' ἔκοψαν, ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃς δὲ θοῇσι πλεῖον ἐπειγόμενοι ποταμοῦ τάμον οὔτι κατευθύ πόντον ἐπ' ἰχθυόεντα διὰ στόμα Φάσιδος εὐρύ ἰέμεθ' ἀμπλακίῃ δ' ἐφορεύμεθα πολλὸν ὀπίσσω αἰὲν ἀναπλείοντες· ἐλείπετο δ' ἄστεα Κόλχων ἀφραδέσιν Μινύαις, σκοτερὴ δέ τε ἄμφεχεν ὄρφνη.

line_details.english: But when they had gone within the ship, and from either side,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ νηὸς μὲν ἔσω κίον, ἐκ δ' ἑκάτερθεν
line_details.note: ἔσω νηός = “aboard, within the ship”; ἑκάτερθεν ὄχθης = “from either bank,” implying river-mooring on both sides.

line_details.english: of the bank they cut the mooring-ropes, and beneath the swift oarage,
line_details.greek: ὄχθης πείσματ' ἔκοψαν, ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃς δὲ θοῇσι
line_details.note: πεῖσματα = mooring-cables; ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃς θοῇσι is an epic idiom, “under the impulse of swift oars.”

line_details.english: pressing on to sail, they clove the river not on a straight course,
line_details.greek: πλεῖον ἐπειγόμενοι ποταμοῦ τάμον οὔτι κατευθύ
line_details.note: τάμον (“clove, cut”) is a conventional verb for cutting a course through water; οὔτι κατευθὺ (“not straight”) indicates a slanting/irregular course, likely from current or steering error.

line_details.english: toward the fish-rich sea, through the wide mouth of the Phasis,
line_details.greek: πόντον ἐπ' ἰχθυόεντα διὰ στόμα Φάσιδος εὐρύ
line_details.note: Phasis = the Colchian river (modern Rioni); ἰχθυόεις πόντος is a traditional epithet, “fish-rich sea.”

line_details.english: we made for it; yet through a misstep we were borne far backward,
line_details.greek: ἰέμεθ' ἀμπλακίῃ δ' ἐφορεύμεθα πολλὸν ὀπίσσω
line_details.note: ἰέμεθ’ = “we made/hastened (toward it)”; ἀμπλακίῃ = “by an error, misjudgment”; ἐφορεύμεθα (iterative nuance) = “we kept being carried,” here “driven back,” probably by current/swell.

line_details.english: ever putting back; and the cities of the Colchians were being left behind by the heedless Minyae,
line_details.greek: αἰὲν ἀναπλείοντες· ἐλείπετο δ' ἄστεα Κόλχων
line_details.note: ἀναπλεῖν can mean “sail back” or “sail upstream”; ἀφραδέσιν Μινύαις is a dative of agent/instrument, “by/through the heedlessness of the Minyae” (the Argonauts).

line_details.english: and murky dusk encompassed us all around.
line_details.greek: ἀφραδέσιν Μινύαις, σκοτερὴ δέ τε ἄμφεχεν ὄρφνη.
line_details.note: ἐλείπετο (singular with neuter plural ἄστεα) is idiomatic in epic; ὄρφνη = “dusk, murk,” σκοτερὴ stressing density; ἄμφεχεν = “encompassed on all sides.”

text.english: But pressing on, we rushed along the current in heedlessness, midmost of the plain; and mortals dwell around it, the Gymnoi, the Bouonomai, and the Arkyes, field‑dwellers, the tribe of Kerketic men, and of the lordly Sindoi, who settled themselves between the Charandai and the Aulones, beside the Caucasian slope, through narrow Erytheia.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπειγόμενοι θέομεν ῥόον ἀφραδίῃσι, μεσσάτιοι πεδίοιο· βροτοὶ δέ μιν ἀμφινέμονται Γυμνοὶ Βουονόμαι τε καὶ Ἄρκυες ἀγροιῶται, Κερκετικῶν τ' ἀνδρῶν φῦλον, Σινδῶν τ' ἀγερώχων· οἳ κείσαντο μεσηγὺ Χαρανδαίων τ' αὐλώνων, Καυκάσιον παρὰ πρῶνα, διὰ στεινῆς Ἐρυθείας.

line_details.english: But pressing on, we rushed along the current in heedlessness,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπειγόμενοι θέομεν ῥόον ἀφραδίῃσι,
line_details.note: θέομεν (“we run”) is used of swift movement, often of ships; ἀφραδίῃσι is an adverbial dative, “in/through rashness, heedlessness.”

line_details.english: midmost of the plain; and mortals dwell around it,
line_details.greek: μεσσάτιοι πεδίοιο· βροτοὶ δέ μιν ἀμφινέμονται
line_details.note: μεσσάτιοι πεδίοιο modifies the action (“midmost of the plain”); μιν (“it”) most naturally refers back to ῥόον (“the stream”).

line_details.english: the Gymnoi, the Bouonomai, and the Arkyes, field‑dwellers,
line_details.greek: Γυμνοὶ Βουονόμαι τε καὶ Ἄρκυες ἀγροιῶται,
line_details.note: The ethnics are problematic: Γυμνοί may be a descriptive “the naked [people]” or an ethnonym; Βουονόμαι likely an ethnonym, perhaps related to “cow‑herders” (cf. βους + νέμω); Ἄρκυες is obscure. ἀγροιῶται = “field‑dwellers, rustics.”

line_details.english: the tribe of Kerketic men, and of the lordly Sindoi,
line_details.greek: Κερκετικῶν τ' ἀνδρῶν φῦλον, Σινδῶν τ' ἀγερώχων·
line_details.note: Κερκετικοί = the Kerketai (Cercetae) of the Euxine’s eastern shores; Σίνδοι = the Sindoi of the Maeotic region. ἀγερώχων is an epic epithet, “lordly, proud.”

line_details.english: who settled themselves between the Charandai and the Aulones,
line_details.greek: οἳ κείσαντο μεσηγὺ Χαρανδαίων τ' αὐλώνων,
line_details.note: Χαρανδαῖοι and Αὐλῶνες are usually taken as tribal names; αὐλώνων could also mean “of the ravines,” but the parallel with Χαρανδαίων favors ethnics. κείσαντο (mid.) = “they settled (themselves).”

line_details.english: beside the Caucasian slope, through narrow Erytheia.
line_details.greek: Καυκάσιον παρὰ πρῶνα, διὰ στεινῆς Ἐρυθείας.
line_details.note: Καυκάσιον πρῶνα = the slope/brow of the Caucasus. Ἐρυθεία is elsewhere the far‑western isle of Geryon; here “narrow Erytheia” likely denotes a local strait or narrow region; the toponymy is debated.

text.english: But when from the East appeared Eos, mortals-delighting Dawn, we put in at a meadow-blooming island; and there two currents with outspread floodwaters split it all around, Phasis, broad-flowing, and Saranges, ill-flowing; this one indeed flood-swollen Maiotis sends through the land to the sea, with a clanging roar, through the grass of the marsh-meadow.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτ' ἀπ' ἀντολίης ἐφάνη τερψίμβροτος ἠώς, ποιανθεῖ νήσῳ προσεκέλσαμεν· ἔνθα δὲ δισσοί χεύμασιν ἀπλώτοισι περισχίζουσι ῥέεθρα Φᾶσις τ' εὐρυμενὴς ἀκαλαρρείτης τε Σαράγγης· τόν ῥα πλημμύρουσα διὰ χθονὸς εἰς ἅλα πέμπει Μαιῶτις καναχηδὸν, ἑλειονόμου διὰ ποίης.

line_details.english: But when from the East appeared Eos, mortals-delighting Dawn,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτ' ἀπ' ἀντολίης ἐφάνη τερψίμβροτος ἠώς,
line_details.note: ἀντολίη = “the East, the Orient”; τερψίμβροτος is a traditional epithet (“delighting mortals”) of Eos (Dawn).

line_details.english: we put in at a meadow-blooming island; and there two
line_details.greek: ποιανθεῖ νήσῳ προσεκέλσαμεν· ἔνθα δὲ δισσοί
line_details.note: ποιανθεῖ (“meadow-blooming”), a poetic compound from πόα (“grass”) + ἄνθος (“flower”); προσεκέλσαμεν is a nautical “put in/made landfall.”

line_details.english: currents with outspread floodwaters split it all around,
line_details.greek: χεύμασιν ἀπλώτοισι περισχίζουσι ῥέεθρα
line_details.note: χεῦμα (“outpouring, flood”) + ἀπλώτος (“spread out, outspread”); the object of περισχίζουσι (“split round about”) is the island, understood from the previous line.

line_details.english: Phasis, broad-flowing, and Saranges, ill-flowing;
line_details.greek: Φᾶσις τ' εὐρυμενὴς ἀκαλαρρείτης τε Σαράγγης·
line_details.note: εὐρυμενής here rendered “broad-flowing” (lit. “widely spread”); ἀκαλαρρείτης is rare, literally “not fair-flowing,” hence “ill-flowing,” perhaps hinting at turbid or unruly flow.

line_details.english: this one indeed flood-swollen Maiotis sends through the land to the sea,
line_details.greek: τόν ῥα πλημμύρουσα διὰ χθονὸς εἰς ἅλα πέμπει
line_details.note: Μαιῶτις is the Maeotis (Sea of Azov) personified; τόν likely refers to the nearer river (Saranges). The poet’s geography imagines Maeotis sending its waters “through the land” toward the sea.

line_details.english: with a clanging roar, through the grass of the marsh-meadow.
line_details.greek: Μαιῶτις καναχηδὸν, ἑλειονόμου διὰ ποίης.
line_details.note: καναχηδόν = “with a clanging/roaring din”; ἑλειονόμου (“marsh-pastured/marsh-meadow”), a rare compound; hence “through the grass of the marsh-meadow.”

text.english: And then beneath the oar-stroke we sailed through night and day.
text.greek: Καὶ τόθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃ πλέομεν διὰ νύκτα καὶ ἦμαρ·

line_details.english: And then beneath the oar-stroke we sailed through night and day.
line_details.greek: Καὶ τόθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃ πλέομεν διὰ νύκτα καὶ ἦμαρ·
line_details.note: ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃ = “under the oarage,” a conventional epic idiom for rowing; διὰ νύκτα καὶ ἦμαρ = “through night and day,” i.e., continuously.

text.english: And by its two mouths, in the three‑part sea, we reached the Bosporus, lying midmost of the sea, where once the cattle‑rustling Titan sitting astride a mighty bull, cleft the strait of the sea.
text.greek: δισσαῖς δ' ἐν τριμόροισι Βοὸς πόρον ἐξικόμεσθα λίμνης ὄντα μεσηγὺ, βοοκλόπος οὗποτε Τιτάν ταύρῳ ἐφεζόμενος βριαρῷ πόρον ἔσχισε λίμνης.

line_details.english: And by its two mouths, in the three‑part sea, we reached the Bosporus,
line_details.greek: δισσαῖς δ' ἐν τριμόροισι Βοὸς πόρον ἐξικόμεσθα
line_details.note: δισσαῖς ἐν τριμόροισι: the dative is elliptical, most naturally supplying “mouths” (στόμασιν). The “three‑part sea” is the connected basins of Pontus–Propontis–Aegean; λίμνη (“lake”) is epic for “sea.”

line_details.english: lying midmost of the sea, where once the cattle‑rustling Titan
line_details.greek: λίμνης ὄντα μεσηγὺ, βοοκλόπος οὗποτε Τιτάν
line_details.note: βοοκλόπος Τιτάν: “Titan” is a divine title (often of Helios), but the scene evokes bovine crossing lore at the Bosporus (etymologically “Cow’s Ford,” linked to Io). The epithet “cattle‑rustling” is striking and has prompted varying identifications (Zeus in bovine myth, Helios, etc.); the line likely conflates such traditions.

line_details.english: sitting astride a mighty bull, cleft the strait of the sea.
line_details.greek: ταύρῳ ἐφεζόμενος βριαρῷ πόρον ἔσχισε λίμνης.
line_details.note: πόρος (“ford, passage”) here = “strait.” ἐφεζόμενος with the dative = “sitting upon, astride.”

text.english: And then, toiling all day long with the oars, we first reached the soft‑robed Maeotae; and the nation of the Geloni, and the boundless tribes of the Deep‑robed, and the Sauromatae, the Getae, the Gymnaei, and the Kekryphae, and the grim‑eyed Arimaspians—much‑afflicted peoples of men— in whose land folk dwell around the Maeotic lake.
text.greek: Καί ῥα πανημερίῃσι πονεύμενοι εἰρεσίῃσι, Μαιώτας πρώτους ἀφικάνομεν ἁβροχίτωνας· ἠδὲ Γελωνὸν ἔθνος, Βαθυχαίτων τ' ἄπλετα φῦλα, Σαυρομάτας τε, Γέτας καὶ Γυμναίους Κέκρυφάς τε ἀρσωπάς τ' Ἀρίμασπας, ἔθνη πολυπήμονα λαῶν ὧν περιναιετάει ἐν γῇ Μαιώτιδα λίμνην.

line_details.english: And then, toiling all day long with the oars,
line_details.greek: Καί ῥα πανημερίῃσι πονεύμενοι εἰρεσίῃσι,
line_details.note: εἰρεσίαι (“oars”) is a poetic term; πανημερίῃσι is an instrumental dative, “throughout whole days.”

line_details.english: we first reached the soft‑robed Maeotae;
line_details.greek: Μαιώτας πρώτους ἀφικάνομεν ἁβροχίτωνας·
line_details.note: The Maeotae dwell by Lake Maeotis (the Sea of Azov). ἁβροχίτωνες “soft‑/luxury‑robed” is an epic epithet.

line_details.english: and the nation of the Geloni, and the boundless tribes of the Deep‑robed,
line_details.greek: ἠδὲ Γελωνὸν ἔθνος, Βαθυχαίτων τ' ἄπλετα φῦλα,
line_details.note: Βαθυχαίτων may be an ethnicon (“Bathychaitones”) or an epithet meaning “deep-/long‑robed” applied to the tribes; the reference is uncertain.

line_details.english: and the Sauromatae, the Getae, the Gymnaei, and the Kekryphae,
line_details.greek: Σαυρομάτας τε, Γέτας καὶ Γυμναίους Κέκρυφάς τε
line_details.note: Κεκρυφάς is an obscure ethnicon; the form recalls κέκρυφα(λη), a woman’s hair‑net, and many consider the reading uncertain.

line_details.english: and the grim‑eyed Arimaspians—much‑afflicted peoples of men—
line_details.greek: ἀρσωπάς τ' Ἀρίμασπας, ἔθνη πολυπήμονα λαῶν
line_details.note: ἀρσωπάς is likely corrupt; many emend to ἀγριωπάς “grim‑eyed,” fitting the Arimaspians (mythic one‑eyed Scythian people). ἔθνη πολυπήμονα λαῶν = “much‑afflicted peoples of men.”

line_details.english: in whose land folk dwell around the Maeotic lake.
line_details.greek: ὧν περιναιετάει ἐν γῇ Μαιώτιδα λίμνην.
line_details.note: Syntax: περιναιετάει with accusative Μαιώτιδα λίμνην conveys “is inhabited around the Maeotic lake” in their land; Lake Maeotis = the Sea of Azov.

text.english: But when indeed the Immortals granted them an ungrudged passage, and at the last we traversed the water of the deep, (along low banks it belches sheer destruction, driven with a roar; and a boundless woodland clatters and at the Arctic boundaries it goes toward Okeanos); by it then, snatched along, through the mouth went Argo.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μὲν τοῖσι δύην ἀμέγαρτον ἔθηκαν ἀθάνατοι, πύματον δὲ βυθοῦ διαμείψαμεν ὕδωρ, (ὄχθῃσι χθαμαλῇσιν ἀποβλύει αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον, ῥοίζῳ ἐλαυνομένη· καναχεῖ δέ τοι ἄσπετος ὕλη ἀρκτῴοις περάτεσσιν ἐπέρχεται Ὠκεανόνδε)· τῷ ῥα τόθ' ἁρπαχθεῖσα διὰ στόματος κίεν Ἀργώ.

line_details.english: But when indeed the Immortals granted them an ungrudged passage,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μὲν τοῖσι δύην ἀμέγαρτον ἔθηκαν
line_details.note: δύην ἀμέγαρτον is difficult. δύη usually means “distress,” but here most take it (by context and from δύω ‘enter, pass through’) as “a passage/way,” with ἀμέγαρτος (‘ungrudged, freely granted’) describing divine favor—thus “an ungrudged passage.” Some have suspected corruption, but the sense “the gods granted them an unhindered way” suits the context.

line_details.english: and at the last we traversed the water of the deep,
line_details.greek: ἀθάνατοι, πύματον δὲ βυθοῦ διαμείψαμεν ὕδωρ,
line_details.note: πύματον (‘last, final’) suggests the final reach of waters before the transition to the stream leading to Okeanos. Note the narrator’s first-person plural, consistent with Orpheus’ voice in this poem.

line_details.english: (along low banks it belches sheer destruction,
line_details.greek: (ὄχθῃσι χθαμαλῇσιν ἀποβλύει αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον,
line_details.note: The subject is the powerful stream just below; ἀποβλύει (‘spouts, belches forth’) and αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον (“sheer ruin”) depict a destructive outflow along low banks.

line_details.english: driven with a roar; and a boundless woodland clatters
line_details.greek: ῥοίζῳ ἐλαυνομένη· καναχεῖ δέ τοι ἄσπετος ὕλη
line_details.note: ῥοίζος is the rushing roar of water; καναχεῖ (“clatters, rings”) is onomatopoetic. ἄσπετος (“boundless, unspeakable”) is epic hyperbole for an immense forest swept along.

line_details.english: and at the Arctic boundaries it goes toward Okeanos);
line_details.greek: ἀρκτῴοις περάτεσσιν ἐπέρχεται Ὠκεανόνδε)·
line_details.note: ἀρκτῴοις περάτεσσιν (“at the northern boundaries,” i.e., under the Bear/Arctos) reflects mythic northern geography; Ὠκεανό(ν)δε (with -δε) means “toward Okeanos.” The river is often identified by commentators with a northern world-river (e.g., Eridanus or Tanais) in mythic cartography.

line_details.english: by it then, snatched along, through the mouth went Argo.
line_details.greek: τῷ ῥα τόθ' ἁρπαχθεῖσα διὰ στόματος κίεν Ἀργώ.
line_details.note: τῷ refers to the stream just described; διὰ στόματος is “through the (river’s) mouth.” ἁρπαχθεῖσα conveys being seized/swept by the current.

text.english: Nine nights and days, toiling, we left behind, here and there, the unknown tribes of mortals, the race of the Paktoi and the Arkteioi, and the lordly Lelioi, and the bow-bearing Scythians, faithful attendants of Ares; and the man-eating Taurians, who carry unsmiling sacrificial implements at Mounychia, and the krater is in want of mortal blood; and then the Hyperboreans, the Nomads, and the Caspian nation.
text.greek: Ἐννέα μὲν νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα μοχθίζοντες λείπομεν ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα βροτῶν ἀγνώσια φῦλα, Πακτῶν Αρκτείων τε γένος, Λελίων τ' ἀγερώχων, τοξοφόρους τε Σκύθας, Ἄρεος πιστοὺς θεράποντας· Ταύρους τ' ἀνδροφάγους, οἳ ἀμειδέα θύσθλα φέρουσι Μουνυχίῃ, βροτέῳ δ' ἐπιδεύεται αἵματι κρητήρ· ἂν δ' ἄρ' Ὑπερβορέους, Νομάδας καὶ Κάσπιον ἔθνος.

line_details.english: Nine nights and days, toiling,
line_details.greek: Ἐννέα μὲν νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα μοχθίζοντες
line_details.note: μὲν is lightly contrastive; the syntax continues into the following lines with the main verb at 1072.

line_details.english: we left behind, here and there, the unknown tribes of mortals,
line_details.greek: λείπομεν ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα βροτῶν ἀγνώσια φῦλα,
line_details.note: ἀγνώσια φῦλα: “unknown tribes,” i.e., peoples unfamiliar to Greeks; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “here and there, hither and thither.”

line_details.english: the race of the Paktoi and the Arkteioi, and the lordly Lelioi,
line_details.greek: Πακτῶν Αρκτείων τε γένος, Λελίων τ' ἀγερώχων,
line_details.note: Paktoi likely the Pactyans (Indo-Iranian region); Arkteioi are obscure/uncertain; Lelioi likewise uncertain. ἀγερώχων = “lordly, high-handed.”

line_details.english: and the bow-bearing Scythians, faithful attendants of Ares;
line_details.greek: τοξοφόρους τε Σκύθας, Ἄρεος πιστοὺς θεράποντας·
line_details.note: Scythians stereotyped in Greek ethnography as archers and devotees of war; hence “bow-bearing … attendants of Ares.”

line_details.english: and the man-eating Taurians, who carry unsmiling sacrificial implements
line_details.greek: Ταύρους τ' ἀνδροφάγους, οἳ ἀμειδέα θύσθλα φέρουσι
line_details.note: The Taurians (of the Crimea) were famed in myth for grim rites. θύσθλα are “sacrificial implements” (often a Bacchic term); ἀμειδέα = “unsmiling, grim.”

line_details.english: at Mounychia, and the krater is in want of mortal blood;
line_details.greek: Μουνυχίῃ, βροτέῳ δ' ἐπιδεύεται αἵματι κρητήρ·
line_details.note: Μουνυχίῃ may mean “at Mounychia” (the Attic sanctuary/festival of Artemis Mounychia) or “for Mounychia (Artemis).” The krater “in want of mortal blood” evokes the (reported) Taurian custom of human sacrifice to Artemis.

line_details.english: and then the Hyperboreans, the Nomads, and the Caspian nation.
line_details.greek: ἂν δ' ἄρ' Ὑπερβορέους, Νομάδας καὶ Κάσπιον ἔθνος.
line_details.note: ἂν δ’ ἄρ’ is problematic; many emend to ἔνθα/ἔπειτα δ’ ἄρ’. The line continues the ethnographic catalogue: Hyperboreans, generic “Nomads,” and a Caspian people.

text.english: But when the tenth, man-illumining Dawn appeared, we cleared the Rhipaean glens, and straightway Argo led on, rushing forward, through the narrow current; and it fell into Okeanos; they call it the Kronian, sea, the Hyperborean mortal men, and the Dead Sea.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δεκάτη ἐφάνη φαεσίμβροτος ἠώς, Ῥιπαίους αὐλῶνας ἐκέλσαμεν, ἐκ δ' ἄφαρ Ἄργώ ἆγεν ἐπιπροθέουσα διὰ στεινοῖο ῥεέθρου· ἔμπεσε δ' Ὠκεανῷ, Κρόνιον δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι, πόντον Ὑπερβόρεοι μέροπες, νεκρήν τε θάλασσαν·

line_details.english: But when the tenth, man-illumining Dawn appeared,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δεκάτη ἐφάνη φαεσίμβροτος ἠώς,

line_details.english: we cleared the Rhipaean glens, and straightway Argo
line_details.greek: Ῥιπαίους αὐλῶνας ἐκέλσαμεν, ἐκ δ' ἄφαρ Ἄργώ
line_details.note: Ῥιπαίους αὐλῶνας: the ‘Rhipaean’ glens/vales, i.e., mythical northern mountains; ἐκέλσαμεν is a nautical aorist (probably from κέλλω), here ‘we cleared/sailed out of.’

line_details.english: led on, rushing forward, through the narrow current;
line_details.greek: ἆγεν ἐπιπροθέουσα διὰ στεινοῖο ῥεέθρου·

line_details.english: and it fell into Okeanos; they call it the Kronian,
line_details.greek: ἔμπεσε δ' Ὠκεανῷ, Κρόνιον δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι,
line_details.note: ἔμπεσε (‘fell into’) is used of a stream debouching; ἑ (‘it’) refers to the sea understood; Κρόνιον (‘Kronian’) denotes the sea associated with Kronos (the far northern ocean).

line_details.english: sea, the Hyperborean mortal men, and the Dead Sea.
line_details.greek: πόντον Ὑπερβόρεοι μέροπες, νεκρήν τε θάλασσαν·
line_details.note: Μέροπες (‘meropes’) is the Homeric epithet ‘articulate-speaking’ for men; ‘Dead Sea’ here means the motionless northern ocean, not the Levantine lake.

text.english: No longer did we deem we should elude woeful destruction, unless, as she was being driven under mighty force, the ship were made to go straight for the right-hand shore, by Ankaios, who made her obey the well-planed steering-oars.
text.greek: Οὐκέτι δὲ προφυγεῖν ἐδοκεῦμεν λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον εἰ μὴ ἄρ' ὁρμαίνουσαν ὑπὸ κρατερῇφι βίηφι νῆα μολεῖν ἴθυν' ἐπὶ δεξιὸν αἰγιαλοῖο Ἀγκαῖος, ξεστοῖσι πιθήσας πηδαλίοισιν.

line_details.english: No longer did we deem we should elude woeful destruction,
line_details.greek: Οὐκέτι δὲ προφυγεῖν ἐδοκεῦμεν λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον

line_details.english: unless, as she was being driven under mighty force,
line_details.greek: εἰ μὴ ἄρ' ὁρμαίνουσαν ὑπὸ κρατερῇφι βίηφι
line_details.note: ὁρμαίνουσαν (‘pondering/hesitating’) is used by personification of the ship; ὑπὸ κρατερῇφι βίηφι likely refers to the force of the stream/current driving her.

line_details.english: the ship were made to go straight for the right-hand shore,
line_details.greek: νῆα μολεῖν ἴθυν' ἐπὶ δεξιὸν αἰγιαλοῖο

line_details.english: by Ankaios, who made her obey the well-planed steering-oars.
line_details.greek: Ἀγκαῖος, ξεστοῖσι πιθήσας πηδαλίοισιν.
line_details.note: πηδάλια are steering-oars (not a fixed sternpost rudder); ξεστοῖσι = ‘well-planed/polished,’ marking fine craftsmanship.

text.english: She leapt up, exerting her strength with both hands.
text.greek: Ἣ δ' ἔθορεν δισσαῖσι βιησαμένη παλάμῃσιν.

line_details.english: She leapt up, exerting her strength with both hands.
line_details.greek: Ἣ δ' ἔθορεν δισσαῖσι βιησαμένη παλάμῃσιν.
line_details.note: βιησαμένη is the middle participle of βιάζομαι (“to use force, strain”), here expressing manner; δισσαῖσι παλάμῃσιν is an instrumental dative, “with both hands.” ἔθορεν is the aorist of θρῴσκω (“to spring, leap”).

text.english: But when at last we were overcome by the toilsome oars, our hands could hold out no longer, and, grieving in our dear heart, having twined our forearms, we propped our brows upon them, letting the sweat cool; and our heart was sorely pressed by hunger.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ μογερῇσιν ἐδαμνάμεθ' εἰρεσίῃσι, χεῖρες δ' οὐκέτ' ἔμιμνον, ἀκηχέμενοι δὲ φίλον κῆρ πήχεας ἀμπλέξαντες, ἐνηρείσαντο μέτωπα, ἱδρῶ ἀποψύχοντε· κέαρ δ' ἐπετείρετο λιμῷ.

line_details.english: But when at last we were overcome by the toilsome oars,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ μογερῇσιν ἐδαμνάμεθ' εἰρεσίῃσι,
line_details.note: μογερῇσιν (dat. pl. of μογερός, “toilsome, wretched”) modifies εἰρεσίῃσι (“oars”) in an instrumental dative; ἐδαμνάμεθ’ (“we were overcome/worn down”) conveys exhaustion from rowing.

line_details.english: our hands could hold out no longer, and, grieving in our dear heart,
line_details.greek: χεῖρες δ' οὐκέτ' ἔμιμνον, ἀκηχέμενοι δὲ φίλον κῆρ

line_details.english: having twined our forearms, we propped our brows upon them,
line_details.greek: πήχεας ἀμπλέξαντες, ἐνηρείσαντο μέτωπα,
line_details.note: πήχεας = “forearms”; ἐνηρείσαντο is the aorist middle of (ἐν-)ἐρείδω, “to press/lean,” with an understood object of support (“upon them,” i.e., the folded arms).

line_details.english: letting the sweat cool; and our heart was sorely pressed by hunger.
line_details.greek: ἱδρῶ ἀποψύχοντε· κέαρ δ' ἐπετείρετο λιμῷ.
line_details.note: ἱδρῶ ἀποψύχοντε = “cooling (off) the sweat,” a compressed expression; ἐπετείρετο (from ἐπιτείρω) “was pressed/oppressed” takes the dative λιμῷ (“by hunger”).

text.english: But Ankaios leapt forth and roused all the others, the heroes, coaxing them with gentle words.
text.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' ἐξᾶλτο, καὶ ἄλλους πάντας ὄτρυνεν ἥρωας, μαλακοῖσι παραιφάμενος ἐπέεσσιν·

line_details.english: But Ankaios leapt forth and roused all the others,
line_details.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' ἐξᾶλτο, καὶ ἄλλους πάντας ὄτρυνεν

line_details.english: the heroes, coaxing them with gentle words.
line_details.greek: ἥρωας, μαλακοῖσι παραιφάμενος ἐπέεσσιν·
line_details.note: “παραιφάμενος” conveys soothing/coaxing persuasion; hence “coaxing … with gentle words.”

text.english: And when then, with many-twisted cables, toward the shoal they went, over the bulwarks seaward they lightly cast their nimble ankles, and quickly they made fast with the many-twisted cables, from the lofty stern, casting a long mooring-rope, and Argos and Ankaios too gave the word to take the lead; and the heroes straightway, running along the strand, were dragging her in haste; and the sea-faring ship followed with them, cleaving wet ways beside the polished pebbles.
text.greek: Οἳ δ' ἐπεὶ οὖν τέναγός τε πολυστρέπτοισι κάλωσι βάντες ὑπὲρ τοίχων ἅλαδε σφυρὰ κοῦφα βάλοντο, ὦκα δ' ἄρ' ἀρτήσαντο πολυστρέπτοισι κάλωσι, πρύμνης ἐξ ὑπάτης, δολιχὴν μήρινθα βαλόντες Ἄργος τ' Ἀγκαῖός τε καὶ ἀρχὰς δῶκαν ἑλέσθαι· ἡρώων τοὶ δ' αἶψα δι' αἰγιαλοῖο θέοντες σῦρον ἐπειγόμενοι· σὺν δ' ἕσπετο ποντοπόρος νηῦς, τέμνουσ' ὑγρὰ κέλευθα παρὰ ξεστοῖς κροκάλοισιν.

line_details.english: And when then, with many-twisted cables, toward the shoal
line_details.greek: Οἳ δ' ἐπεὶ οὖν τέναγός τε πολυστρέπτοισι κάλωσι
line_details.note: τέναγος is a rare term for “shoal/lagoon” and the syntax is enjambed; it is taken adverbially with the following participle (“going toward/into the shoal”).

line_details.english: they went, over the bulwarks seaward they lightly cast their nimble ankles,
line_details.greek: βάντες ὑπὲρ τοίχων ἅλαδε σφυρὰ κοῦφα βάλοντο,
line_details.note: σφυρά “ankles”: σφυρά κοῦφα βάλONTO is idiomatic for leaping lightly down; hence “lightly cast their nimble ankles.”

line_details.english: and quickly they made fast with the many-twisted cables,
line_details.greek: ὦκα δ' ἄρ' ἀρτήσαντο πολυστρέπτοισι κάλωσι,

line_details.english: from the lofty stern, casting a long mooring-rope,
line_details.greek: πρύμνης ἐξ ὑπάτης, δολιχὴν μήρινθα βαλόντες
line_details.note: μήρινθα is a nautical term for a mooring-rope/cable; ἐξ ὑπάτης “from the lofty [part]” refers to the raised stern.

line_details.english: and Argos and Ankaios too gave the word to take the lead;
line_details.greek: Ἄργος τ' Ἀγκαῖός τε καὶ ἀρχὰς δῶκαν ἑλέσθαι·
line_details.note: Ἀρχὰς δῶκαν ἑλέσθαι is an idiom, “gave the word to begin/to take the lead,” here the signal to start the haul.

line_details.english: and the heroes straightway, running along the strand,
line_details.greek: ἡρώων τοὶ δ' αἶψα δι' αἰγιαλοῖο θέοντες

line_details.english: were dragging her in haste; and the sea-faring ship followed with them,
line_details.greek: σῦρον ἐπειγόμενοι· σὺν δ' ἕσπετο ποντοπόρος νηῦς,

line_details.english: cleaving wet ways beside the polished pebbles.
line_details.greek: τέμνουσ' ὑγρὰ κέλευθα παρὰ ξεστοῖς κροκάλοισιν.
line_details.note: “ὑγρὰ κέλευθα” (lit. “wet ways”) is an epic expression for the paths cut through water; “ξεστοῖς κροκάλοισιν” are smoothed/polished beach-pebbles.

text.english: For no shrilling fair wind beneath the blasts of close‑packed winds stirred that sea for them; the sea was mute, there where lies the uttermost water of Helike and Tethys.
text.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἱ λιγὺς οὖρος ὑπὸ πνοιῇσιν ὄρινε βυκτάων ἀνέμων κείνην ἅλα· κωφὰ δὲ πόντος κεῖθ' οὗπέρ θ' Ἑλίκης καὶ Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ.

line_details.english: For no shrilling fair wind beneath the blasts
line_details.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἱ λιγὺς οὖρος ὑπὸ πνοιῇσιν ὄρινε
line_details.note: λιγὺς οὖρος = “shrilling/shrill fair wind”; οἱ is a dative of reference (“for them,” i.e., the Argonauts). ὑπὸ πνοιῇσιν βυκτάων ἀνέμων is instrumental (“beneath/by the blasts of close‑packed winds”), emphasizing that no breeze at all stirred the water.

line_details.english: of close‑packed winds stirred that sea for them; the sea was mute,
line_details.greek: βυκτάων ἀνέμων κείνην ἅλα· κωφὰ δὲ πόντος
line_details.note: κωφὰ (“deaf”) is a conventional metaphor for a dead calm, hence “mute.” Note that κείνην ἅλα (“that sea”) is the object carried over from the previous line’s ὄρινε (“stirred”).

line_details.english: there where lies the uttermost water of Helike and Tethys.
line_details.greek: κεῖθ' οὗπέρ θ' Ἑλίκης καὶ Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ.
line_details.note: Helike = the Great Bear (Ursa Major); Tethys = the personified Ocean. ἔσχατον ὕδωρ (“uttermost water”) evokes the world-encircling Ocean at the limits of the sea, a Homeric-style cosmographic periphrasis.

text.english: But when the sixth dawn, light-bringing to mortals, had come, we reached a nation opulent and wealthy, of the Makrobioi, who indeed live many years, twelve thousand months of centuries’ span, while the moon is waxing, outside all hardships; but when they fulfil the fated portion of the month, in the sweet sleep of death they meet their end; nor are livelihood and the works of mortals a care to them, but amid grassy meadows they graze honey-sweet pasture, beneath ambrosial dew, drawing forth divine drink, all alike resplendent in lovely coeval youth; and a gentle calm ever nods upon their brows for children and for parents alike, upon heart and upon mind, to do what is due and to utter prudent words.
text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ἕκτη φαεσίμβροτος ἤλυθεν ἠώς, ἔθνος ἐς ἀφνειὸν καὶ πλούσιον ἐξικόμεσθα Μακροβίων, οἳ δὴ πολέας ζώουσ' ἐνιαυτούς, δώδεκα χιλιάδας μηνῶν ἑκατονταετήρων πληθούσης μήνης χαλεπῶν ἔκτοσθεν ἁπάντων· αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μηνὸς τὸ πεπρωμένον ἐξανύσωσιν, ὕπνῳ ὑπὸ γλυκερῷ θανάτου μάρπτουσι τελευτήν· Οὐ δ' ἄρα τοῖσι μέλει βίοτος καὶ ἔργ' ἀνθρώπων, ποίαις δ' ἐν μεσάταις μελιηδέα φορβὰ νέμονται ἕρσῃ ὑπ' ἀμβροσίῃ θεῖον ποτὸν ἐξαρύοντες, πάντες ὁμῶς στίλβοντες ὁμηλικίην ἐρατεινήν· Μειλιχίη δέ τοι αἰὲν ἐπ' ὀφρύσι νεῦσε γαλήνη παίδεσιν ἠδὲ τοκεῦσιν, ἐπὶ φρεσὶν ἠδὲ νόοιο, αἴσιμά τε ῥέζειν πεπνυμένα τ' ἐξαγορεύειν.

line_details.english: But when the sixth dawn, light-bringing to mortals, had come,
line_details.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ἕκτη φαεσίμβροτος ἤλυθεν ἠώς,
line_details.note: φαεσίμβροτος (“light-bringing to mortals”) is a traditional epic epithet of Dawn (ἠώς).

line_details.english: we reached a nation opulent and wealthy,
line_details.greek: ἔθνος ἐς ἀφνειὸν καὶ πλούσιον ἐξικόμεσθα

line_details.english: of the Makrobioi, who indeed live many years,
line_details.greek: Μακροβίων, οἳ δὴ πολέας ζώουσ' ἐνιαυτούς,
line_details.note: Μακροβίων is the ethnonym “Long-lived,” known from Greek ethnographic lore (cf. Herodotus).

line_details.english: twelve thousand months of centuries’ span,
line_details.greek: δώδεκα χιλιάδας μηνῶν ἑκατονταετήρων
line_details.note: The phrase δώδεκα χιλιάδας μηνῶν ἑκατονταετήρων is notoriously compact: either “twelve thousand months” (≈ 1000 years), with ἑκατονταετήρων (“of centuries”) underscoring the centuried span, or hyperbolically “hundred-year months.” The translation takes it as months amounting to centuries.

line_details.english: while the moon is waxing, outside all hardships;
line_details.greek: πληθούσης μήνης χαλεπῶν ἔκτοσθεν ἁπάντων·
line_details.note: μήνη here is best taken as “moon” (not merely “month”): πληθούσης μήνης = “as the moon waxes,” a lunar measure of their painless life.

line_details.english: but when they fulfil the fated portion of the month,
line_details.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μηνὸς τὸ πεπρωμένον ἐξανύσωσιν,
line_details.note: τὸ πεπρωμένον (“the fated/allotted [portion]”) continues the temporal imagery; μηνός keeps the lunar/monthly register.

line_details.english: in the sweet sleep of death they meet their end;
line_details.greek: ὕπνῳ ὑπὸ γλυκερῷ θανάτου μάρπτουσι τελευτήν·
line_details.note: μάρπτουσι τελευτήν (“they seize/meet their end”) renders an idiom; “sweet sleep of death” is an epic euphemism for dying gently.

line_details.english: nor are livelihood and the works of mortals a care to them,
line_details.greek: Οὐ δ' ἄρα τοῖσι μέλει βίοτος καὶ ἔργ' ἀνθρώπων,

line_details.english: but amid grassy meadows they graze honey-sweet pasture,
line_details.greek: ποίαις δ' ἐν μεσάταις μελιηδέα φορβὰ νέμονται
line_details.note: νέμονται with φορβή (“graze pasture”) is literal but applied to these blissful mortals; ποίαις μεσάταις = “meadows in the midst,” i.e., lush central meads.

line_details.english: beneath ambrosial dew, drawing forth divine drink,
line_details.greek: ἕρσῃ ὑπ' ἀμβροσίῃ θεῖον ποτὸν ἐξαρύοντες,
line_details.note: ἕρση ἀμβροσία (“ambrosial dew”) evokes paradisal sustenance; θεῖον ποτόν (“divine drink”) recalls, without naming, the fare of the blessed.

line_details.english: all alike resplendent in lovely coeval youth;
line_details.greek: πάντες ὁμῶς στίλβοντες ὁμηλικίην ἐρατεινήν·
line_details.note: ὁμηλικίη (“coeval age”) suggests ageless, equal prime for all; στἰλβοντες (“shining”) marks ideal beauty.

line_details.english: and a gentle calm ever nods upon their brows
line_details.greek: Μειλιχίη δέ τοι αἰὲν ἐπ' ὀφρύσι νεῦσε γαλήνη
line_details.note: Μειλιχίη γαλήνη is a personified “gentle calm”; νεῦσε ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι (“nods upon the brows”) = “rests/abides upon their faces,” an epic turn.

line_details.english: for children and for parents alike, upon heart and upon mind,
line_details.greek: παίδεσιν ἠδὲ τοκεῦσιν, ἐπὶ φρεσὶν ἠδὲ νόοιο,
line_details.note: The double expression ἐπὶ φρεσὶν ἠδὲ νόοιο (mixed dative/genitive) jointly denotes the inner faculties (heart/mind).

line_details.english: to do what is due and to utter prudent words.
line_details.greek: αἴσιμά τε ῥέζειν πεπνυμένα τ' ἐξαγορεύειν.
line_details.note: αἴσιμα = “what is fitting/right (according to due order/fate)”; πεπνυμένα = “prudent, sage”; ἐξαγορεύειν = “to speak out plainly/declare.”

text.english: And those we passed by in a body, to the strand, treading with our feet.
text.greek: - Καὶ τοὺς μέν ῥ' ἀθρόους παραμείβομεν, αἰγιαλόνδε

line_details.english: And those we passed by in a body, to the strand, treading with our feet.
line_details.greek: - Καὶ τοὺς μέν ῥ' ἀθρόους παραμείβομεν, αἰγιαλόνδε
line_details.note: ἀθρόους can be taken adverbially (“altogether”) or as qualifying τούς (“those [standing] in a mass”); the antecedent is from the prior context. αἰγιαλόνδε is the Homeric allative “to the strand.” ποσσὶν ἐπιστείβοντες literally “pressing with the feet,” likely of towing/hauling the ship along the shore.

text.english: then to the Cimmerians, bringing the swift ship, we came, who alone are without a share in the radiance of fire-roaring Helios.
text.greek: ποσσὶν ἐπιστείβοντες· ἔπειτα δὲ Κιμμερίοισι νῆα θοὴν ἐπάγοντες ἱκάνομεν, οἵ ῥά τε μοῦνοι αἴγλης ἄμμοροί εἰσι πυριβρόμου ἠελίοιο.

line_details.english: then to the Cimmerians,
line_details.greek: ποσσὶν ἐπιστείβοντες· ἔπειτα δὲ Κιμμερίοισι
line_details.note: Κιμμερίοισι (dat. pl.) “to the Cimmerians,” the sunless people of Od. 11; the dative of goal is completed by ἱκάνομεν in the next line.

line_details.english: bringing the swift ship, we came,
line_details.greek: νῆα θοὴν ἐπάγοντες ἱκάνομεν, οἵ ῥά τε μοῦνοι
line_details.note: ἐπάγοντες (“bringing along/toward”) is a technical verb for towing or beaching a ship; nuance retained in the translation.

line_details.english: who alone are without a share in the radiance of fire-roaring Helios.
line_details.greek: αἴγλης ἄμμοροί εἰσι πυριβρόμου ἠελίοιο.
line_details.note: αἴγλης ἄμμοροι = “without a share of radiance” (genitive with ἄμμορος). πυριβρόμου ἠελίοιο is an Orphic-style epithet, “fire-roaring Helios,” preserving the theonym Helios.

text.english: For indeed the Rhipaean mountain and the Calpian neck shut out the dawns; and huge Phlegra leans over, casting a nearer shadow on the noonday air.
text.greek: Ἐν μὲν γὰρ Ῥίπαιον ὄρος καὶ Κάλπιος αὐχήν ἀντολίας εἴργουσιν ἐπικέκλιται δὲ πελώρη ἆσσον ἐπισκιάουσα μεσημβρινὸν ἠέρα Φλέγρη·

line_details.english: For indeed the Rhipaean mountain and the Calpian neck
line_details.greek: Ἐν μὲν γὰρ Ῥίπαιον ὄρος καὶ Κάλπιος αὐχήν
line_details.note: Ῥίπαιον ὄρος (Rhipaean mountain) is the mythic northern range; Κάλπιος αὐχήν (“Calpian neck”) refers to Calpe (the Rock of Gibraltar), here imagined as a ridge/neck. The juxtaposition is part of a poetic, non‑literal world‑geography.

line_details.english: shut out the dawns; and huge Phlegra leans over,
line_details.greek: ἀντολίας εἴργουσιν ἐπικέκλιται δὲ πελώρη
line_details.note: ἀντολίας (plural) = “sunrises/dawns.” πελώρη (“huge, monstrous”) modifies Φλέγρη (Phlegra), a toponym with mythic resonance; ἐπικέκλιται “leans over/overhangs.”

line_details.english: casting a nearer shadow on the noonday air.
line_details.greek: ἆσσον ἐπισκιάουσα μεσημβρινὸν ἠέρα Φλέγρη·
line_details.note: ἆσσον “nearer, more closely”; ἐπισκιάουσα “overshadowing.” μεσημβρινὸν ἠέρα “the noonday/southern air,” a poetic way to mark the south.

text.english: In turn the sky‑pointing Alps hide the clear light from those mortal men, and a mist ever lies upon them.
text.greek: δείελον αὖ κρύπτουσι φάος ταναηκέες Ἄλπεις κείνοισιν μερόπεσσιν, ἀχλὺς δ' ἐπικέκλιται αἰεί,

line_details.english: In turn the sky‑pointing Alps hide the clear light
line_details.greek: δείελον αὖ κρύπτουσι φάος ταναηκέες Ἄλπεις
line_details.note: ταναηκέες “sky‑pointing, long‑peaked.” δείελον φάος “clear/bright daylight.”

line_details.english: from those mortal men, and a mist ever lies upon them.
line_details.greek: κείνοισιν μερόπεσσιν, ἀχλὺς δ' ἐπικέκλιται αἰεί,
line_details.note: κείνοισιν μερόπεσσιν “for those mortal men” (meropes = humans). The antecedent of “them” (regions/inhabitants) is deliberately broad; ἀχλὺς ἐπικέκλιται “a mist lies/hangs over.”

text.english: Thence, setting out with hurrying feet, we reached a rugged elbow and a windless shore, where indeed a river, murmuring with deep eddies, runs, the gold‑flowing Acheron, through a chill land, pouring forth silver‑bright water; and a dusky lake receives it; and by the river‑banks the luxuriant trees resound, close upon which the fruit lies heavy, by nights and by days, unceasingly, forever.
text.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἀφορμηθέντες ἐπειγομένοισι πόδεσσιν ἵξομεν ἀγκῶνα στυφελὸν καὶ νήνεμον ἀκτήν, ἔνθα περ ἀμβλύζων ποταμὸς δίναισι βαθείαις θείει χρυσορόας Ἀχέρων κρυεροῦ διὰ χώρου, ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδος προρέων, λίμνη τε κελαινή ἀνδέχεται· παταγεῖ δὲ παρ' ὄχθαισιν ποταμοῖο δένδρεα τηλεθάοντα ποτὶ σχεδὸν οἷσιν καρπός βέβριθε νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συννεχὲς αἰεί.

line_details.english: Thence, setting out with hurrying feet,
line_details.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἀφορμηθέντες ἐπειγομένοισι πόδεσσιν
line_details.note: ἀφορμηθέντες “setting out, taking departure”; ἐπειγομένοισι πόδεσσιν “with hurrying/pressed feet,” a Homeric‑style instrumental dative.

line_details.english: we reached a rugged elbow and a windless shore,
line_details.greek: ἵξομεν ἀγκῶνα στυφελὸν καὶ νήνεμον ἀκτήν,
line_details.note: ἀγκών “elbow,” a common metaphor for a projecting headland; στυφελός “harsh, rugged”; νήνεμος ἀκτή “windless shore.”

line_details.english: where indeed a river, murmuring with deep eddies,
line_details.greek: ἔνθα περ ἀμβλύζων ποταμὸς δίναισι βαθείαις
line_details.note: ἀμβλύζων is onomatopoetic, often of a dull/muffled plashing or murmuring; “with deep eddies” (δίναισι βαθείαις) explains the sound.

line_details.english: runs, the gold‑flowing Acheron, through a chill land,
line_details.greek: θείει χρυσορόας Ἀχέρων κρυεροῦ διὰ χώρου,
line_details.note: θείει “runs, speeds.” χρυσορόας Ἀχέρων “gold‑flowing Acheron” is striking and unusual for Acheron (more typical of Pactolus); likely an ornamental color‑epithet or a transferred trait. κρυεροῦ διὰ χώρου “through a chill land.”

line_details.english: pouring forth silver‑bright water; and a dusky lake
line_details.greek: ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδος προρέων, λίμνη τε κελαινή
line_details.note: ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδος “silver‑like water,” i.e., silvery in appearance; λίμνη κελαινὴ “dusky/dark lake,” plausibly the Acherousian lake.

line_details.english: receives it; and by the river‑banks the luxuriant trees resound,
line_details.greek: ἀνδέχεται· παταγεῖ δὲ παρ' ὄχθαισιν ποταμοῖο
line_details.note: παταγεῖ (from παταγέω) “clatters, resounds,” here of trees along the bank, taking plural δένδρεα as subject with singular verb (epic convention).

line_details.english: close upon which the fruit lies heavy,
line_details.greek: δένδρεα τηλεθάοντα ποτὶ σχεδὸν οἷσιν καρπός
line_details.note: τηλεθάοντα “luxuriant, flourishing.” ποτὶ σχεδόν “close upon/near at hand.” οἷσιν dative of relation: “close upon which (trees) the fruit….” βέβριθε (perf.) “has weighed [them] down/is heavy.”

line_details.english: by nights and by days, unceasingly, forever.
line_details.greek: βέβριθε νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συννεχὲς αἰεί.
line_details.note: νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συννεχές αἰεί piles adverbs for epic emphasis: “by night and by day, continuously, always.”

text.english: And around it low-lying and well-pastured Hermione is girt with walls along her well-built streets.
text.greek: Ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ χθαμαλή τε καὶ εὔβοτος Ἑρμιονεία τείχεσιν ἠρήρεισται ἐϋκτιμέναις ἐπ' ἀγυιαῖς.

line_details.english: And around it low-lying and well-pastured Hermione
line_details.greek: Ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ χθαμαλή τε καὶ εὔβοτος Ἑρμιονεία
line_details.note: Ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ = “around it,” with the dative pronoun referring to a previously mentioned locale; χθαμαλή “low-lying,” εὔβοτος “rich in pasture.” Ἑρμιονεία = Hermione (city/territory in Argolis); epic form varies (cf. Ἑρμιονείη).

line_details.english: is girt with walls along her well-built streets.
line_details.greek: τείχεσιν ἠρήρεισται ἐϋκτιμέναις ἐπ' ἀγυιαῖς.
line_details.note: ἠρήρεισται (perf. pass. 3 sg. of ἀραρίσκω) “has been fitted/fastened,” hence “is girt” with τείχεσιν “walls.” ἐπ’ ἀγυιαῖς ἐϋκτιμέναις = “along the well-built streets” (the adjective agrees with ἀγυιαῖς, not with τείχεσιν).

text.english: And there dwell the races of the most righteous men, for whom, once they have perished, a single ship has been made ready in sufficiency, and again their souls passed across to Acheron from the hollow ferry-boat; and near to it are cities, and the unbreakable gates of Aidēs and the district of Dreams.
text.greek: Ἐν δὲ γένη ζώουσι δικαιοτάτων ἀνθρώπων οἷσιν ἀποφθιμένοισιν ἅλις ναῦς ἴα τέτυκται, καὶ δ' αὖ αἱ ψυχαὶ μετεκίαθον εἰς Ἀχέροντα πορθμίδος ἐκ γλαφυρῆς· σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ εἰσὶ πόληες ἄρρηκτοί τ' Ἀίδαο πύλαι καὶ δῆμος ὀνείρων.

line_details.english: And there dwell the races of the most righteous men,
line_details.greek: Ἐν δὲ γένη ζώουσι δικαιοτάτων ἀνθρώπων
