line_details.note: “There” (En de) points back to the locale just described in context; gēnē = “races/tribes,” retaining epic diction.

line_details.english: for whom, once they have perished, a single ship has been made ready in sufficiency,
line_details.greek: οἷσιν ἀποφθιμένοισιν ἅλις ναῦς ἴα τέτυκται,
line_details.note: ἅλις is transmitted here; it can be taken adverbially “enough, in sufficiency,” yielding the sense that “one ship suffices” (sc. the ferry). Many take ἅλις as ἁλί (“at sea”), but the context of Acheron and the ferry favors the adverbial reading. ναῦς ἴα emphasizes “a single ship,” and τέτυκται (perf. mid.) = “has been fashioned/is ready.”

line_details.english: and again their souls passed across to Acheron
line_details.greek: καὶ δ' αὖ αἱ ψυχαὶ μετεκίαθον εἰς Ἀχέροντα
line_details.note: μετεκίαθον (aor.) = “went across/went after,” of souls moving toward/over Acheron (the underworld river).

line_details.english: from the hollow ferry-boat; and near to it are cities,
line_details.greek: πορθμίδος ἐκ γλαφυρῆς· σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ εἰσὶ πόληες
line_details.note: πορθμίδος is the ferry-boat (not the ferryman; cf. πορθμεύς). γλαφυρῆς = “hollow,” standard epic epithet for boats. οἱ is dative referring to Acheron: “near to it.” πόληες is epic for πόλεις.

line_details.english: and the unbreakable gates of Aidēs and the district of Dreams.
line_details.greek: ἄρρηκτοί τ' Ἀίδαο πύλαι καὶ δῆμος ὀνείρων.
line_details.note: ἄρρηκτοι “unbreakable” (of the gates of Aidēs). δῆμος ὀνείρων = the “district/domain of Dreams,” with δῆμος used in a topographical sense rather than “people.”

text.english: But when indeed even the city of these men and the ways of the people we had brought to the full measure of heavy doom by their own infatuation, we went our way, then indeed Ankaios made for the ship; and straightway he bade all the comrades, wearied, to embark together.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ καὶ τῶνδε πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα λαῶν σφῇ ἄτῃ βαρὺν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες ἔβημεν, δή ῥα τότ' Ἀγκαῖος νηὸς κίεν· αἶψα δὲ πάντας εἰσβαίνειν ἐκέλευσε κεκμηότας ἄμμιγ' ἑταίρους.

line_details.english: But when indeed even the city of these men and the ways of the people
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ καὶ τῶνδε πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα λαῶν
line_details.note: ἤθεα (“ways, customs, habits”) of a people; τῶνδε refers deictically to the group just encountered.

line_details.english: we had brought to the full measure of heavy doom by their own infatuation, we went our way,
line_details.greek: σφῇ ἄτῃ βαρὺν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες ἔβημεν,
line_details.note: σφῇ ἄτῃ is an instrumental dative (“by their own infatuation/delusion”). βαρὺν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες is a compressed epic idiom, “bringing heavy doom to fulfillment”; the translation expands the sense to avoid the double accusative with πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα.

line_details.english: then indeed Ankaios made for the ship; and straightway
line_details.greek: δή ῥα τότ' Ἀγκαῖος νηὸς κίεν· αἶψα δὲ πάντας
line_details.note: νηὸς κίεν is Homeric for “went to the ship,” with the genitive after a verb of motion indicating goal.

line_details.english: he bade all the comrades, wearied, to embark together.
line_details.greek: εἰσβαίνειν ἐκέλευσε κεκμηότας ἄμμιγ' ἑταίρους.
line_details.note: ἄμμιγ’ (for ἅμμιγα) is an adverb “together”; κεκμηότας (perf. part.) has present force, “wearied, spent.”

text.english: And to them he indeed addressed gentle words: “Endure, friends, the toil; for now indeed I expect that no mean wind will arise, for already I behold the keen Zephyros that makes one shiver; nor without a sign does the water of Okeanos gurgle among the sands.” But swiftly raise the mast at the mid‑thwart, and loose the sails from the forestays; and, bringing out the gear, lash them firm, expertly, casting them along the bulwarks on either side.” So they set about each his several tasks; and from the hollow ship the Tomarian oak, booming, cried aloud, that which once Pallas had fitted beneath Argive adze‑strokes.
text.greek: Τοὺς ὅγε καὶ μύθοισι προσηύδα μειλιχίοισι· - "Τλῆτε φίλοι τὸν μόχθον· ἐπεὶ νύ τοι οὔτι χέρειον ἔλπομαι ἀνστήσεσθαι· ἐπιφρίσσοντα γὰρ ἤδη ἀκραῆ ζέφυρον καταδέρκομαι· οὐδ' ἀτέκμαρτον ὕδωρ Ὠκεανοῦ κελαρύζεται ἐν ψαμάθοισιν. Ἀλλὰ θοῶς ἱστὸν μὲν ἀναστήσασθε μεσόδμῃ λύσατε δὲ προτόνων ὀθόνας· ἐκ δ' ὅπλα χέοντες σφίγξατ' ἐπισταμένως, τοίχων ἑκάτερθε βαλόντες." - Ὣς οἳ μὲν τὰ ἕκαστα πονήατο· ἐκ δ' ἄρα κοίλης νηὸς ἐπιβρομέουσα Τομαριὰς ἔκλαγε φηγός, ἥν ποθ' ὑπ' Ἀργῴαισι τομαῖς ἡρμόσσατο Παλλάς.

line_details.english: And to them he indeed addressed gentle words:
line_details.greek: Τοὺς ὅγε καὶ μύθοισι προσηύδα μειλιχίοισι·
line_details.note: ὅγε (“he indeed”) gives emphatic focus to the subject; μειλιχίοις μύθοισι is a traditional epic formula for “soothing/gentle words.”

line_details.english: “Endure, friends, the toil; for now indeed I expect that no mean wind will arise,
line_details.greek: - "Τλῆτε φίλοι τὸν μόχθον· ἐπεὶ νύ τοι οὔτι χέρειον
line_details.note: οὔτι χέρειον (‘by no means inferior/worse’) has an understood subject, i.e., a breeze/wind; ἀνστήσεσθαι is the epic form of ‘to rise’ (of winds).

line_details.english: for already I behold the keen Zephyros that makes one shiver;
line_details.greek: ἔλπομαι ἀνστήσεσθαι· ἐπιφρίσσοντα γὰρ ἤδη
line_details.note: ἐπιφρίσσοντα means ‘causing to bristle/ruffle’ (of wind on skin or sea); ἀκραῆ = ‘piercing/keen’; καταδέρκομαι = ‘I behold.’ Zephyros is the West Wind.

line_details.english: nor without a sign
line_details.greek: ἀκραῆ ζέφυρον καταδέρκομαι· οὐδ' ἀτέκμαρτον
line_details.note: ἀτέκμαρτον means ‘without a token/sign’ (τέκμαρ). The phrase signals that the following phenomenon is an omen of wind.

line_details.english: does the water of Okeanos gurgle among the sands.”
line_details.greek: ὕδωρ Ὠκεανοῦ κελαρύζεται ἐν ψαμάθοισιν.
line_details.note: κελαρύζεται (‘gurgles, babbles’) of water among sands evokes surf-sounds as a portent; Ὠκεανός is transliterated as Okeanos.

line_details.english: But swiftly raise the mast at the mid‑thwart,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλὰ θοῶς ἱστὸν μὲν ἀναστήσασθε μεσόδμῃ
line_details.note: μεσόδμῃ = “at the mid‑thwart” (the central bench/midships). Epic nautical term for the mast‑step location.

line_details.english: and loose the sails from the forestays; and, bringing out the gear,
line_details.greek: λύσατε δὲ προτόνων ὀθόνας· ἐκ δ' ὅπλα χέοντες
line_details.note: πρότονοι are the forestays; ὀθόνες = “sail‑cloths,” here the stay‑sails. λύσατε can mean “loosen/unfurl” depending on context.

line_details.english: lash them firm, expertly, casting them along the bulwarks on either side.”
line_details.greek: σφίγξατ' ἐπισταμένως, τοίχων ἑκάτερθε βαλόντες."
line_details.note: ὅπλα here likely “gear, tackle” (not weapons); σφίγγειν = “make fast, lash”; τοῖχοι = the ship’s sides/bulwarks.

line_details.english: So they set about each his several tasks; and from the hollow
line_details.greek: - Ὣς οἳ μὲν τὰ ἕκαστα πονήατο· ἐκ δ' ἄρα κοίλης
line_details.note: Formulaic: “each his several tasks.” οἳ μὲν marks their part of the action.

line_details.english: ship the Tomarian oak, booming, cried aloud,
line_details.greek: νηὸς ἐπιβρομέουσα Τομαριὰς ἔκλαγε φηγός,
line_details.note: Τομαριὰς = “of Tomaros,” i.e., the Dodonaean oak. ἐπιβρομέουσα = “booming, thunder‑sounding,” of a portentous cry.

line_details.english: that which once Pallas had fitted beneath Argive adze‑strokes.
line_details.greek: ἥν ποθ' ὑπ' Ἀργῴαισι τομαῖς ἡρμόσσατο Παλλάς.
line_details.note: ἥν … ἡρμώσσατο: the famous speaking timber from Dodona that Pallas (Athena) fitted into Argo. ὑπ’ Ἀργῴαισι τομαῖς = “beneath Argive cuttings,” i.e., under the strokes of the Argive adze.

text.english: Thus she spoke (and wonder encompassed the minds of all); Alas for me! Would that I had perished, shattered asunder, among the Cyanean Rocks and in the inhospitable surge; then even now, through the ignorance of kings, I would be unheard of, I would be bearing a nameless name; for now ever the Erinnys of Apsyrtos’ kindred blood—blood that was shed— follows with tardy foot; and indeed Atê loves ruin upon ruin.
text.greek: Ὧδε δ' ἔφη (θάμβος δὲ περὶ φρένας ἵκετο πάντας)· - "Ὤ μοι ἐγὼν, ὄφελόν με διαρραισθεῖσαν ὀλέσθαι Κυανέαις πέτραισιν ἐν ἀξείνῳ τε κλύδωνι· ἦ καὶ νῦν ἀνάπυστον ἀϊδρείῃ βασιλήων νώνυμνον φορέεσκον· ἐπεὶ νῦν αἰεὶ Ἐριννύς αἵματος ἐμφύλοιο δεδουπότος Ἀψύρτοιο ὑστερόπους ἕπεται· στέργει δὲ τοι ἄτη ἐπ' ἄτην.

line_details.english: Thus she spoke (and wonder encompassed the minds of all);
line_details.greek: Ὧδε δ' ἔφη (θάμβος δὲ περὶ φρένας ἵκετο πάντας)·
line_details.note: ἔφη is gender-indeterminate; the context (Medea) motivates “she.” θάμβος = awe/wonder “around the mind.”

line_details.english: Alas for me! Would that I had perished, shattered asunder,
line_details.greek: - "Ὤ μοι ἐγὼν, ὄφελόν με διαρραισθεῖσαν ὀλέσθαι
line_details.note: διαρραισθεῖσαν (aor. pass. ptcp., fem.) “smashed/torn asunder,” with με as object; the image anticipates being crushed between the rocks.

line_details.english: among the Cyanean Rocks and in the inhospitable surge;
line_details.greek: Κυανέαις πέτραισιν ἐν ἀξείνῳ τε κλύδωνι·
line_details.note: Κυανέαι πέτραι = the Symplegades; ἀξείνου κλύδων = the “inhospitable” surge, i.e., the Pontos (Euxine).

line_details.english: then even now, through the ignorance of kings, I would be unheard of,
line_details.greek: ἦ καὶ νῦν ἀνάπυστον ἀϊδρείῃ βασιλήων
line_details.note: ἀνάπυστον in the MSS is difficult beside νώνυμνον; many emend to ἄπυστον (“unheard of”). Translation follows the sense “unknown/unheard of.” βασιλῆες likely refers to ruling powers (e.g., Aeetes and others).

line_details.english: I would be bearing a nameless name; for now ever the Erinnys
line_details.greek: νώνυμνον φορέεσκον· ἐπεὶ νῦν αἰεὶ Ἐριννύς
line_details.note: νώνυμνον “nameless”; φορέεσκον is iterative (“I should be wont to bear”). Ἐριννύς (sing.) functions as the avenging Fury.

line_details.english: of Apsyrtos’ kindred blood—blood that was shed—
line_details.greek: αἵματος ἐμφύλοιο δεδουπότος Ἀψύρτοιο
line_details.note: δεδουπότος is textually problematic; sense demands “of blood that was shed/spilled.” ἐμφύλιος = “of kindred.” Ἀψύρτος (Apsyrtos) in the genitive.

line_details.english: follows with tardy foot; and indeed Atê loves ruin upon ruin.
line_details.greek: ὑστερόπους ἕπεται· στέργει δὲ τοι ἄτη ἐπ' ἄτην.
line_details.note: ὑστερόπους “late-footed” (of avengers who come late but surely). Ἄτη (Atê) personified as Ruin; στέργει = “loves/affects,” hence “Atê loves to heap ruin upon ruin.”

text.english: For now indeed for the baleful and silvery wickedness I shall exact vengeance from the Iernian islands, if I come nearer.
text.greek: Νῦν γὰρ δὴ λυγρῆς τε καὶ ἀργεννῆς κακότητος τίσομαι ἂν νήσοισιν Ἰερνίσιν ἆσσον ἵκωμαι.

line_details.english: For now indeed for the baleful and silvery wickedness
line_details.greek: Νῦν γὰρ δὴ λυγρῆς τε καὶ ἀργεννῆς κακότητος
line_details.note: ἀργεννῆς (lit. “silvery, silver‑white”) modifying κακότητος is an unusual collocation; it may be purely color-epithetic (“bright/white wickedness”) or an allusion to the ‘evil of silver’ (greed). Some have suspected an emendation to ἀργυρῆς (“of silver”). λυγρός = “baleful, grievous.”

line_details.english: I shall exact vengeance from the Iernian islands, if I come nearer.
line_details.greek: τίσομαι ἂν νήσοισιν Ἰερνίσιν ἆσσον ἵκωμαι .
line_details.note: τίσομαι takes the dative of the party punished (νήσοισιν). ἂν with the subjunctive ἵκωμαι gives a future‑more‑vivid condition (“if I come nearer”). Ἰερνίσιν (‘Iernian’) refers to the western isles, commonly identified with Ierne (Ireland) or the British Isles.

text.english: For unless you, by turning me in at the holy headlands, the gulf within the land and the unharvested sea you will reach—otherwise I should go out upon the Atlantic sea.” Thus having spoken, she checked her voice; and the spirit of the Minyae grew numb through and through, whether indeed they were about to incur grievous destruction, on account of the love-charms for Jason.
text.greek: Εἰ μὴ γάρ μ' ἱερῇσιν ἐπιγνάμψαντες ἄκρῃσι κόλπον ἔσω γαίης τε καὶ ἀτρυγέτοιο θαλάσσης ἵξεσθ', ἂμ πέλαγος Ἀτλαντικὸν ἐκτὸς ἵκωμαι." - Ὣς εἰποῦσ' αὐδὴν κατερήτυεν· ἐν δ' ἄρα θυμός παχνώθη Μινύαισι διαμπερὲς, εἴτ' ἄρ' ἔμελλον σχήσειν λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον, Ἰάσονος εἵνεκα φίλτρων.

line_details.english: For unless you, by turning me in at the holy headlands,
line_details.greek: Εἰ μὴ γάρ μ' ἱερῇσιν ἐπιγνάμψαντες ἄκρῃσι
line_details.note: ἐπιγνάμψαντες ἄκρῃσι: a nautical turn “to bear in toward/round the headlands.” The object μ’ (“me”) is the ship (ναῦς), here personified as speaking (cf. the Dodonaean beam). ἱεραῖσιν ἄκρῃσι likely alludes to the “sacred” promontories at the mouth of the Mediterranean (commonly identified with the Pillars of Heracles).

line_details.english: the gulf within the land and the unharvested sea
line_details.greek: κόλπον ἔσω γαίης τε καὶ ἀτρυγέτοιο θαλάσσης
line_details.note: κόλπος “gulf, bosom” = the enclosed sea; γαίης τε καὶ ἀτρυγέτοιο θαλάσσης “of land and the unharvested sea” describes the Mediterranean as an inner basin. ἀτρύγετος is the traditional epic epithet of the sea (“unharvested,” i.e., fruitless).

line_details.english: you will reach—otherwise I should go out upon the Atlantic sea.”
line_details.greek: ἵξεσθ', ἂμ πέλαγος Ἀτλαντικὸν ἐκτὸς ἵκωμαι."
line_details.note: ἵξεσθ’ belongs with the protasis (“unless … you reach”). ἂμ is textually awkward; many understand it as ἅμ’ (“at once”) or take it adverbially with the following clause. Sense: if they fail to turn in at the capes, the ship will head “outside” (ἐκτός) into the Atlantic. “Atlantic sea” renders πέλαγος Ἀτλαντικόν.

line_details.english: Thus having spoken, she checked her voice;
line_details.greek: - Ὣς εἰποῦσ' αὐδὴν κατερήτυεν· ἐν δ' ἄρα θυμός

line_details.english: and the spirit of the Minyae grew numb through and through, whether indeed they were about
line_details.greek: παχνώθη Μινύαισι διαμπερὲς, εἴτ' ἄρ' ἔμελλον
line_details.note: παχνώθη θυμός: metaphorical “the heart/spirits froze,” i.e., were seized with dread. διαμπερές “through and through, entirely.”

line_details.english: to incur grievous destruction, on account of the love-charms for Jason.
line_details.greek: σχήσειν λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον, Ἰάσονος εἵνεκα φίλτρων.
line_details.note: σχήσειν (fut. inf.) with ἔμελλον: “were about to incur/meet.” φίλτρα are love-charms/philtra; “on account of the love-charms for Jason” likely points to the dangerous consequences of Medea’s passion instigated for Jason.

text.english: Much did they debate in their shrewd minds, whether they should make her perish and cast her as spoil for the fishes, dire‑speaking Medea, and so turn aside the Erinys, had not the far‑famed son of Aison swiftly perceived it, and then, in supplication, checked the spirit of each.
text.greek: Πολλὰ δὲ μερμήριζον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσιν, ἤ μιν ἀποφθίσωσι καὶ ἰχθύσι κύρμα βάλωσιν αἰνολέχην Μήδειαν, ἀποστρέψωσι δ' Ἐριννύν, εἰ μὴ ἄρ' ὀξὺ νόησε περικλυτὸς Αἴσονος υἱός, καὶ τότε λισσόμενος θυμὸν κατερήτυ' ἑκάστου.

line_details.english: Much did they debate in their shrewd minds,
line_details.greek: Πολλὰ δὲ μερμήριζον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσιν,
line_details.note: πευκαλίμῃσιν ("shrewd, prudent") is a Homeric-style epithet modifying phrenes (“minds”); μερμηρίζω conveys anxious, deep deliberation.

line_details.english: whether they should make her perish and cast her as spoil for the fishes,
line_details.greek: ἤ μιν ἀποφθίσωσι καὶ ἰχθύσι κύρμα βάλωσιν
line_details.note: ἀποφθίσσωσι (“destroy utterly”) and κῦρμα (“spoil, prey”) are strong, epic terms; the image is of making her a carcass for fish.

line_details.english: dire‑speaking Medea, and so turn aside the Erinys,
line_details.greek: αἰνολέχην Μήδειαν, ἀποστρέψωσι δ' Ἐριννύν,
line_details.note: αἰνολέχην (“dire‑speaking”) is a rare compound epithet of Medea; Ἐριννύς (Erinys) in the singular personifies vengeance/blood‑guilt; ἀποστρέφω here = “avert, turn aside.”

line_details.english: had not the far‑famed son of Aison swiftly perceived it,
line_details.greek: εἰ μὴ ἄρ' ὀξὺ νόησε περικλυτὸς Αἴσονος υἱός,
line_details.note: περικλυτός (“far‑famed”) is a standard heroic epithet; νόησε has an implicit object (“their counsel/intent”).

line_details.english: and then, in supplication, checked the spirit of each.
line_details.greek: καὶ τότε λισσόμενος θυμὸν κατερήτυ' ἑκάστου.
line_details.note: λισσόμενος (“beseeching, in supplication”); κατερήτυ’ is the epic contracted imperfect of κατερήτυε (“was restraining/checked”); θυμός = “spirit, heart.”

text.english: But when they heard Argo’s truth-speaking voice, they took their seats swiftly by the thole-pins and grasped the oars.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τ' Ἀργοῦς ἐτυμηγόρον ἔκλυον αὐδήν ἧντο παρὰ σκαλμοῖσι θοῶς, λάζοντο δ' ἐρετμά.

line_details.english: But when they heard Argo’s truth-speaking voice,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τ' Ἀργοῦς ἐτυμηγόρον ἔκλυον αὐδήν
line_details.note: ἐτυμηγόρον (“truth-speaking”) evokes Argo’s prophetic voice, traditionally from the Dodonaean oak built into her prow; αὐδή is the ship’s audible “voice.”

line_details.english: they took their seats swiftly by the thole-pins and grasped the oars.
line_details.greek: ἧντο παρὰ σκαλμοῖσι θοῶς, λάζοντο δ' ἐρετμά.
line_details.note: σκαλμοῖσι are the thole-pins (oar-pivots); ἧντο is the epic inceptive “sat down,” and λάζοντο (middle) “took hold (for themselves),” here of the oars.

text.english: But Ankaios skillfully kept the steering-oars taut.
text.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' οἴακας ἐπισταμένως ἐτίταινε·

line_details.english: But Ankaios skillfully kept the steering-oars taut.
line_details.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' οἴακας ἐπισταμένως ἐτίταινε·
line_details.note: oïakes = the stern ‘steering-oars’ (tillers); ἐτίταινε ‘was straining/keeping taut.’ Ankaios is the helmsman (in many traditions succeeding Tiphys).

text.english: And the ship was passing along beside the island Iernis, and astern of her there came headlong, with a crash, a murky, shuddering squall, and it bellied the sails; and straightway the ship sped over the wet swell, and then no one any longer hoped to draw breath again from destruction, for the twelfth Early-born Dawn was coming on.
text.greek: Πὰρ δ' ἄρα νῆσον ἄμειβεν Ἰερνίδα, καί οἱ ὄπισθεν ἷκτο καταΐγδην δνοφερὴ τρομέουσα θύελλα, ἐν δ' ὀθόνας κόλπωσε· θέεν δ' ἄφαρ ὑγρὸν ἐπ' οἶδμα νηῦς· οὐ δή τις ἐσαῦθις ἀναπνεύσεσθαι ὀλέθρου ἤλπετο· δωδεκάτη γὰρ ἐπήϊεν ἠριγένεια.

line_details.english: And the ship was passing along beside the island Iernis, and astern of her
line_details.greek: Πὰρ δ' ἄρα νῆσον ἄμειβεν Ἰερνίδα, καί οἱ ὄπισθεν
line_details.note: Ἰερνίδα = ‘Iernis,’ commonly identified with Ireland; παρὰ νῆσον ἄμειβεν ‘was coasting past the island.’ οἱ ὄπισθεν = ‘astern (behind her/him),’ here rendered as ‘astern of her.’

line_details.english: there came headlong, with a crash, a murky, shuddering squall,
line_details.greek: ἷκτο καταΐγδην δνοφερὴ τρομέουσα θύελλα,
line_details.note: καταΐγδην is an adverb ‘headlong, with a crash’; δνοφερή ‘murky, gloomy’; τρομέουσα ‘shuddering/trembling,’ modifying θύελλα ‘squall.’

line_details.english: and it bellied the sails; and straightway the ship sped over the wet swell,
line_details.greek: ἐν δ' ὀθόνας κόλπωσε· θέεν δ' ἄφαρ ὑγρὸν ἐπ' οἶδμα
line_details.note: ὀθόνες ‘sails’; κολπόω of wind ‘to belly’ (make a pouch of) the sails; θέεν ‘sped, ran.’

line_details.english: and then no one any longer hoped to draw breath again from destruction,
line_details.greek: νηῦς· οὐ δή τις ἐσαῦθις ἀναπνεύσεσθαι ὀλέθρου
line_details.note: ἐσαῦθις ‘again/any more’; ἀναπνεῦσαι ὀλέθρου is an idiom ‘to recover breath from destruction,’ i.e., to escape death.

line_details.english: for the twelfth Early-born Dawn was coming on.
line_details.greek: ἤλπετο· δωδεκάτη γὰρ ἐπήϊεν ἠριγένεια.
line_details.note: ἠριγένεια is the fixed epithet of Eos (Dawn), ‘Early-born’; thus ‘the twelfth dawn.’ The goddess is implicit though not named.

text.english: Nor did anyone know within his own heart where indeed we were, save that at the uttermost bounds of turbid‑flowing Okeanos Lynceus perceived (for he was far‑sighted) a pine‑clad island, and the broad halls of the Queen Demeter; and about it in turn a great cloud stood wreathed.
text.greek: Οὐδέ τις ἔγνω ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, οὗ ποτ' ἄρ' ἐσμέν, εἰ μὴ ἐσχατιαῖς ἀκαλαρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο Λυγκεὺς εἰσενόησεν (ὁ γὰρ τηλωπὸν ὄπωπε) νῆσον πευκήεσσαν, ἰδ' εὐρέα δώματ' ἀνάσσης Δήμητρος· περὶ δ' αὖτε μέγα νέφος ἐστεφάνωται.

line_details.english: Nor did anyone know within his own heart where indeed we were,
line_details.greek: Οὐδέ τις ἔγνω ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, οὗ ποτ' ἄρ' ἐσμέν,
line_details.note: ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσίν is the epic plural “in their own hearts/minds”; οὗ ποτ’ ἄρ’ intensifies “where indeed/at all.”

line_details.english: save that at the uttermost bounds of turbid‑flowing Okeanos
line_details.greek: εἰ μὴ ἐσχατιαῖς ἀκαλαρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο
line_details.note: ἐσχατιαῖς = “outermost borders.” The epithet ἀκαλαρρόου is rare/uncertain; taken here as “not fair‑flowing,” hence “turbid‑flowing,” of Okeanos (transliterated).

line_details.english: Lynceus perceived (for he was far‑sighted)
line_details.greek: Λυγκεὺς εἰσενόησεν (ὁ γὰρ τηλωπὸν ὄπωπε)
line_details.note: τηλωπὸν ὄπωπε is a perfect with stative sense, “he possessed far‑seeing sight”; Lynceus is traditionally famed for extraordinary vision.

line_details.english: a pine‑clad island, and the broad halls of the Queen
line_details.greek: νῆσον πευκήεσσαν, ἰδ' εὐρέα δώματ' ἀνάσσης
line_details.note: πευκήεσσαν is a Homeric‑type adjective “pine‑clad”; ἀνάσσης = “Lady/Queen,” anticipating the naming of Demeter in the next verse; ἰδ’ = καὶ ἴδε (“and [he] saw”).

line_details.english: Demeter; and about it in turn a great cloud stood wreathed.
line_details.greek: Δήμητρος· περὶ δ' αὖτε μέγα νέφος ἐστεφάνωται.
line_details.note: ἐστεφάνωται (perfect middle) has a stative value, “is/stood wreathed.” The referent of “it” (island or halls) is ambiguous; αὖτε = “in turn/again.”

text.english: Of which you have heard the whole tale, O Musaeus, wise of mind, how once Phersēphonē, plucking tender blossoms with her hands, unawares, with her kinswomen, through the wide and great grove.
text.greek: - Ὧν πέρι μῦθον ἅπαντ' ἔκλυες, Μουσαῖε δαΐφρον, ὥς ποτε Φερσεφόνην τέρεν' ἄνθεα χερσὶ δρέπουσαν ἐξάπαφον συνόμαιμοι ἀν' εὐρύ τε καὶ μέγα ἄλσος.

line_details.english: Of which you have heard the whole tale, O Musaeus, wise of mind,
line_details.greek: - Ὧν πέρι μῦθον ἅπαντ' ἔκλυες, Μουσαῖε δαΐφρον,
line_details.note: δαΐφρον is vocative of δαΐφρων (“wise-minded”); Μουσαῖε is direct address. μῦθον ἅπαντ’ ἔκλυες = “you have heard the entire story.”

line_details.english: how once Phersēphonē, plucking tender blossoms with her hands,
line_details.greek: ὥς ποτε Φερσεφόνην τέρεν' ἄνθεα χερσὶ δρέπουσαν
line_details.note: Φερσεφόνην is an Orphic/epic form; here transliterated as Phersēphonē. τέρεν’ (< τερενά) “tender”; δρέπουσαν “plucking.”

line_details.english: unawares, with her kinswomen, through the wide and great grove.
line_details.greek: ἐξάπαφον συνόμαιμοι ἀν' εὐρύ τε καὶ μέγα ἄλσος.
line_details.note: ἐξάπαφον = “suddenly, unawares.” συνόμαιμοι likely stands for dat. pl. συνομαίμοισιν (“with her kinswomen/peers”); many editors so emend. ἀνὰ with acc. = “through(out).” The syntax continues beyond this line.

text.english: But thereafter, when Ploteus, having yoked the dark-maned horses, set the maiden aboard by a daimōn’s allotment, and, having snatched her, he bore her through the wave of the unharvested sea.
text.greek: αὐτὰρ ἔπειθ' ὥς μιν Πλωτεὺς, κυανότριχας ἵππους ζευξάμενος, κούρην ἐπεβήσατο δαίμονος αἴσῃ, ἁρπάξας δ' ἔφερεν διὰ κύματος ἀτρυγέτοιο.

line_details.english: But thereafter, when Ploteus, having yoked the dark-maned horses,
line_details.greek: αὐτὰρ ἔπειθ' ὥς μιν Πλωτεὺς, κυανότριχας ἵππους
line_details.note: Ploteus (Πλωτεύς) is likely an epithet of Poseidon (“the Seafarer”); the “dark‑maned horses” are his sea-horses drawing the chariot.

line_details.english: set the maiden aboard by a daimōn’s allotment,
line_details.greek: ζευξάμενος, κούρην ἐπεβήσατο δαίμονος αἴσῃ,
line_details.note: ἐπεβήσατο with accusative (κούρην) is unusual; it can imply either sexual “mounted” or, more contextually here, “set [her] aboard/on” the chariot implied by the yoked horses. δαίμονος αἴσῃ = “by a daimōn’s allotment,” i.e., by fate.

line_details.english: and, having snatched her, he bore her through the wave of the unharvested sea.
line_details.greek: ἁρπάξας δ' ἔφερεν διὰ κύματος ἀτρυγέτοιο.
line_details.note: ἀτρυγέτος (“unharvested”) is the conventional epic epithet of the sea; ἁρπάζω underscores violent abduction. διὰ κύματος = “through the wave.”

text.english: Then indeed I forbade us to put back, as we bore in under sail, to the island’s surf and its gleaming abodes, where no one of mortal men draws near with a ship.
text.greek: Δὴ τότ' ἐγὼν ἀπόειπον ἐπιπλώοντα νέεσθαι νήσου ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνα καὶ αἰγλήεντα τέρεμνα, ἐνθ' οὔτις σὺν νηῒ πάρα μερόπων ἀνθρώπων.

line_details.english: Then indeed I forbade us to put back, as we bore in under sail,
line_details.greek: Δὴ τότ' ἐγὼν ἀπόειπον ἐπιπλώοντα νέεσθαι
line_details.note: ἀπόειπον + infinitive = “forbid/renounce (to do).” The participle ἐπιπλώοντα is adverbial (“as we were bearing in/under way”); the subject of the infinitive νέεσθαι is understood from context (“we”).

line_details.english: to the island’s surf and its gleaming abodes,
line_details.greek: νήσου ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνα καὶ αἰγλήεντα τέρεμνα,
line_details.note: ῥηγμῖνα = “breakers, surf” (the shore-line). τέρεμνα is a Homeric word for “abodes/haunts,” often of nymphs; αἰγλήεντα = “gleaming, bright.” Some traditions read τέρμνα; τέρεμνα suits the Homeric usage (cf. Od. 13).

line_details.english: where no one of mortal men draws near with a ship.
line_details.greek: ἐνθ' οὔτις σὺν νηῒ πάρα μερόπων ἀνθρώπων.
line_details.note: σὺν νηῒ πάρα is an epic idiom for “come near/approach with a ship.” μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is the conventional epic periphrasis for “mortals.”

text.english: For it has no harbor, no refuge for the double‑curved ships, but rather a sheer rock, lofty, has sprung up all around, and it bears fair gifts that satisfy desire.
text.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἵ ἐστὶ λιμὴν νηῶν ὀχὸς ἀμφιελισσῶν, ἀλλά γε ἠλίβατος πέτρη περὶ πάντα πέφυκεν ὑψηλή· τά τε καλὰ φύει μενοεικέα δῶρα.

line_details.english: For it has no harbor, no refuge for the double‑curved ships,
line_details.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἵ ἐστὶ λιμὴν νηῶν ὀχὸς ἀμφιελισσῶν,
line_details.note: λιμὴν … ὄχος: literally “harbor, a stay/support (for ships),” hence “refuge”; the dative οἵ is possessive (“for it”); ἀμφιελισσῶν is the conventional ship‑epithet meaning “double‑curved.”

line_details.english: but rather a sheer rock, lofty, has sprung up all around,
line_details.greek: ἀλλά γε ἠλίβατος πέτρη περὶ πάντα πέφυκεν
line_details.note: ἠλίβατος = “steep, sheer, hard of access”; πέφυκεν “has grown/stands by nature”; περὶ πάντα “on all sides.”

line_details.english: and it bears fair gifts that satisfy desire.
line_details.greek: ὑψηλή· τά τε καλὰ φύει μενοεικέα δῶρα.
line_details.note: The subject of φύει (“bears/produces”) is the place understood; δῶρα “gifts” denotes the land’s produce; μενοεικέα = “desire‑satisfying,” a Homeric epithet.

text.english: And then the helmsman Ankaios of the dark‑prowed ship did not disobey, and straightway he ran up, springing to his feet, dipping the left‑hand steering‑oar beneath; and then he persuaded her not to go straight on, but held her, as she raced, to starboard.
text.greek: Καὶ τότ' ἄρ' οὐκ ἀπίθησε νεὼς κυανοπρώροιο ἰθύντωρ Ἀγκαῖος, ἀνέτρεχε δ' αἶψ' ἀνορούων, σκαιὸν ὑπεγκλίνας οἰήϊον· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἔπειθε μή τι κατευθὺ περᾶν, ἐπὶ δέξια δ' εἶργε θέουσαν.

line_details.english: And then the helmsman Ankaios of the dark‑prowed ship did not disobey,
line_details.greek: Καὶ τότ' ἄρ' οὐκ ἀπίθησε νεὼς κυανοπρώροιο
line_details.note: "ithyntor" (ἰθύντωρ) is a technical term for the steersman, lit. “straightener.” "kyanoproros" (κυανοπρώροιο) = “dark-/blue‑prowed,” a conventional epic epithet of ships; the verb “did not disobey” implies heeding a prior command.

line_details.english: and straightway he ran up, springing to his feet,
line_details.greek: ἰθύντωρ Ἀγκαῖος, ἀνέτρεχε δ' αἶψ' ἀνορούων,
line_details.note: The collocation ἀνέτρεχε … ἀνορούων (“ran up … leaping up”) is pleonastic for vivid sudden movement.

line_details.english: dipping the left‑hand steering‑oar beneath; and then he persuaded her
line_details.greek: σκαιὸν ὑπεγκλίνας οἰήϊον· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἔπειθε
line_details.note: "oieiion" (οἰήϊον) = the steering‑oar/rudder; "skaios" (σκαιός) = left/port. ὑπεγκλίνας (“bending under”) is nautical: ‘dipping/bringing the rudder under’ to alter course. ἔπειθε (“he persuaded [her]”) anthropomorphizes the ship, i.e., ‘brought her to obey the helm.’

line_details.english: not to go straight on, but held her, as she raced, to starboard.
line_details.greek: μή τι κατευθὺ περᾶν, ἐπὶ δέξια δ' εἶργε θέουσαν.
line_details.note: κατευθύ = ‘straight (ahead)’; ἐπὶ δέξια = ‘to the right,’ i.e., to starboard. εἶργε θέουσαν = ‘held/kept her as she raced,’ combining restraint with speed.

text.english: And on the third day we came to the house of Kirkê, to the Lingaian mainland and the sea‑wreathed precincts; and then upon the beaches we beached her, grieving at heart, and we made fast the moorings to the rocks; and forth Jason dispatched from the ship trusty comrades to go, seeking whether any among mortals upon the boundless earth dwells there, and that they might learn the city and the ways of the people.
text.greek: - Ἤματι δὲ τριτάτῳ Κίρκης δόμον ἐξικόμεσθα Λιγκαῖον ποτὶ χέρσον ἁλιστεφέας τε θεράπνας· καὶ τότ' ἄρ' αἰγιαλοῖσιν ἐκέλσαμεν ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ, πείσματα δ' ἐν πέτρῃσιν ἐδήσαμεν· ἐκ δ' ἄρ' Ἰήσων νηὸς ἀποπροέηκε μολεῖν ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους, διζομένος εἴ τίς σφε βροτῶν ἐπ' ἀπείρονα γαῖαν ναιετάει, γνῷεν δὲ πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα λαῶν.

line_details.english: And on the third day we came to the house of Kirkê,
line_details.greek: - Ἤματι δὲ τριτάτῳ Κίρκης δόμον ἐξικόμεσθα

line_details.english: to the Lingaian mainland and the sea‑wreathed precincts;
line_details.greek: Λιγκαῖον ποτὶ χέρσον ἁλιστεφέας τε θεράπνας·
line_details.note: Λιγκαῖον (Lingaion) is an obscure toponym; many take it as a local designation of Kirkê’s island (Aeaea), though some suspect textual corruption. θεράπνας here means “abodes/precincts,” and ἁλιστεφέας literally “sea‑wreathed/sea‑garlanded.”

line_details.english: and then upon the beaches we beached her, grieving at heart,
line_details.greek: καὶ τότ' ἄρ' αἰγιαλοῖσιν ἐκέλσαμεν ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ,
line_details.note: ἐκέλσαμεν is the technical nautical verb from κέλλω, “to run a ship aground, beach.”

line_details.english: and we made fast the moorings to the rocks; and forth Jason
line_details.greek: πείσματα δ' ἐν πέτρῃσιν ἐδήσαμεν· ἐκ δ' ἄρ' Ἰήσων
line_details.note: πείσματα are “moorings/warp‑cables,” a nautical term; ἐδήσαμεν = “we bound/made fast.”

line_details.english: dispatched from the ship trusty comrades to go,
line_details.greek: νηὸς ἀποπροέηκε μολεῖν ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους,
line_details.note: ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is the epic formula “trusty (or loyal) comrades.”

line_details.english: seeking whether any among mortals upon the boundless earth
line_details.greek: διζομένος εἴ τίς σφε βροτῶν ἐπ' ἀπείρονα γαῖαν
line_details.note: σφε is the enclitic 3rd‑person pronoun used pleonastically/adverbially in epic (“there/for them”); ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν is the formula “upon the boundless earth.”

line_details.english: dwells there, and that they might learn the city and the ways of the people.
line_details.greek: ναιετάει, γνῷεν δὲ πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα λαῶν.
line_details.note: ἤθεα are the “customs/ways” (habits, usages) of the inhabitants; λαῶν (plural) is generic for “people/folk.”

text.english: But straightway there met them, as they came on face to face, a maiden, the full sister of great‑hearted Aiētes, daughter of Hēlios; and they call her Kirke, her mother Asteropē, and far‑shining Hyperiōn.
text.greek: Τοῖς δ' ἄφαρ ὠμάρτησε καταντίον ἐρχομένοισι κούρη ὁμογνήτη μεγαλόφρονος Αἰήταο, Ἠελίου θυγάτηρ· Κίρκην δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι μήτηρ Ἀστερόπη καὶ τηλεφανὴς Ὑπερίων.

line_details.english: But straightway there met them, as they came on face to face,
line_details.greek: Τοῖς δ' ἄφαρ ὠμάρτησε καταντίον ἐρχομένοισι
line_details.note: ōmārtēse is the aorist of homarteō in the sense “to meet, encounter” (not “to err”); katanion with the participle erchomenoisi conveys “as they came opposite/face to face.”

line_details.english: a maiden, the full sister of great‑hearted Aiētes,
line_details.greek: κούρη ὁμογνήτη μεγαλόφρονος Αἰήταο,
line_details.note: homognētē means “born of the same parents,” hence “full sister.”

line_details.english: daughter of Hēlios; and they call her Kirke,
line_details.greek: Ἠελίου θυγάτηρ· Κίρκην δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι
line_details.note: kiklēskousi is the impersonal epic “they call,” i.e., “men call her.”

line_details.english: her mother Asteropē, and far‑shining Hyperiōn.
line_details.greek: μήτηρ Ἀστερόπη καὶ τηλεφανὴς Ὑπερίων.
line_details.note: The line is elliptical in apposition: “her mother [was] Asteropē, and far‑shining Hyperiōn [her father].” Hyperiōn here functions as a name/title of Hēlios (cf. “Hēlios Hyperiōn”). Asteropē is a variant mother for Kirke (elsewhere Perseis); telephanēs is the epic epithet “far‑shining.”

text.english: She then swiftly came down upon the ship; and then all of them marveled as they gazed; for from her head the tresses were wafted, like fiery rays; her fair faces gleamed, and a smokeless flame beamed forth.
text.greek: Ἥ ῥα θοῶς ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθεν· ἐκ δ' ἄρα πάντες θάμβεον εἰσορόωντες· ἀπὸ κρατὸς γὰρ ἔθειραι πυρσαῖς ἀκτίνεσσιν ἀλίγκιοι ἠώρηντο· στίλβε δὲ καλὰ πρόσωπα, φλογὸς δ' ἀπέλαμπεν ἀϋτμή.

line_details.english: She then swiftly came down upon the ship; and then all of them
line_details.greek: Ἥ ῥα θοῶς ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθεν· ἐκ δ' ἄρα πάντες
line_details.note: ἐκ δ’ ἄρα πάντες is elliptical in Greek (often ‘up from their seats’ is understood); I render simply ‘and then all of them’ to preserve the enjambment.

line_details.english: marveled as they gazed; for from her head the tresses
line_details.greek: θάμβεον εἰσορόωντες· ἀπὸ κρατὸς γὰρ ἔθειραι
line_details.note: No special difficulties.

line_details.english: were wafted, like fiery rays;
line_details.greek: πυρσαῖς ἀκτίνεσσιν ἀλίγκιοι ἠώρηντο·
line_details.note: ἠώρηντο (‘were wafted, hung suspended’) suggests a floating or streaming motion; πυρσαῖς means ‘fiery, ruddy’.

line_details.english: her fair faces gleamed, and a smokeless flame beamed forth.
line_details.greek: στίλβε δὲ καλὰ πρόσωπα, φλογὸς δ' ἀπέλαμπεν ἀϋτμή.
line_details.note: Plural ‘faces’ alludes to Hekate’s triple visage in this scene. The phrase φλογὸς δ’ ἀπέλαμπεν ἀϋτμή is syntactically compressed; I translate idiomatically as ‘a smokeless flame beamed forth’ (taking φλογός as a genitive of source/description).

text.english: But when he had beheld Medea with his eyes, (veiled in linen, and with a fine veil she had drawn about her cheeks, ashamed; for beneath her bosom a greenish pallor had distressed her).
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Μήδειαν ἐσέδρακεν ὀφθαλμοῖσι, (λῖτι καλυπτομένην, ἑανῷ δ' ἀμφέσχε παρειάς αἰδομένη· χλωρὸν γὰρ ὑπὸ στέρνοις ἀκάχητο).

line_details.english: But when he had beheld Medea with his eyes,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Μήδειαν ἐσέδρακεν ὀφθαλμοῖσι,
line_details.note: ἐσέδρακεν is an epic form from δέρκομαι (“to behold”); ὀφθαλμοῖσι is an instrumental dative (“with his eyes”).

line_details.english: (veiled in linen, and with a fine veil she had drawn about her cheeks,
line_details.greek: (λῖτι καλυπτομένην, ἑανῷ δ' ἀμφέσχε παρειάς
line_details.note: λῖτι is difficult; generally taken as the dative of λῖτον (“linen [garment/veil]”), hence “veiled in linen.” Many editors consider emendation to λίνῳ. ἑανῷ (“fine, thin,” esp. of clothing); ἀμφέσχε is from ἀμφέχω (“to wrap about”).

line_details.english: ashamed; for beneath her bosom a greenish pallor had distressed her).
line_details.greek: αἰδομένη· χλωρὸν γὰρ ὑπὸ στέρνοις ἀκάχητο).
line_details.note: αἰδομένη = “being modest/ashamed.” χλωρόν denotes the pale/greenish hue of fear; δέος (“fear”) is effectively understood. ἀκάχητο is the pluperfect of ἀκάχημαι (“to be distressed”); the subject is Medea understood, and “beneath her bosom” conveys the seat of emotion (the heart).

text.english: Then, pitying her, Kirke addressed her and spoke: “O wretched one, what sort of fate has Kypris now bestowed on you? For the very deeds for which you come have not escaped notice, as you make for our island—all in vain—on account of your aged father and your brother, whom in dreadful wise you slew; for I do not think you will draw any nearer to your native lands, even if you attempt to heal your transgressions by purificatory rites, not until you wash off the defilement by divine cleansings, through the lore of Orpheus, beside the pebbly shore of Malea.” For it is not the custom of our house to receive propitiants, for you are bespattered with such gore; But straightway I, with ready heart, will send provisions, food and luscious wine for you to have, and along with them much meat.” So speaking, she flew back again; and in the middle of the ship there lay the gear prepared for a banquet and for drink.
text.greek: Ἣν τότ' ἐποικτείρουσα προσηύδανε καὶ φάτο Κίρκη· - "Ὦ δειλὴ, τί νύ τοι τοίην Κύπρις ὤπασε μοῖραν; Οὐ γάρ τοι λελάθεσθε, ἅπερ ῥέξαντες ἱκνεῖσθε νῆσον ἐφ' ἡμετέρην πανετώσιον οὕνεκα πατρός γηραιοῦ κάσιός τε, τὸν ἐκπάγλως· ὀλέσαντες, οὐδὲ γὰρ ὔμμε πάτρῃσιν οἴομαι ἆσσον ἱκέσθαι, εἰ ἐν ἀναγνίστοισιν ἀλιτροσύναις ἀκέοντες, μέσφ' ὅταν ἐκνίψησθε μύσος θείοισι καθαρμοῖς Ὀρφέως ἰδμοσύνῃσι παρὰ κροκάλοισι Μαλείης. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἡμετέροιο δόμου θέμις ἐστιν ἱκέσθαι προστροπίους· τοίῳ γε λύθρῳ πεπαλαγμένοι ἐστέ· Ἀλλά μιν αὐτίκ' ἐγὼ πρόφρων ξυνήϊα πέμψω σῖτον καὶ μέθυ λαρὸν ἔχειν, σὺν δὲ κρέα πολλά." - Ὣς εἰποῦσ', ἄψορρος ἀπέπτατο· νηῒ δὲ μέσσῃ δαιτός τ' ἠδὲ ποτοῖο τετυγμένα τεύχε' ἔκειτο.

line_details.english: Then, pitying her, Kirke addressed her and spoke:
line_details.greek: Ἣν τότ' ἐποικτείρουσα προσηύδανε καὶ φάτο Κίρκη·
line_details.note: “Her” refers to Medea; Kirke (Circe) is the speaker.

line_details.english: “O wretched one, what sort of fate has Kypris now bestowed on you?
line_details.greek: - "Ὦ δειλὴ, τί νύ τοι τοίην Κύπρις ὤπασε μοῖραν;

line_details.english: For the very deeds for which you come have not escaped notice,
line_details.greek: Οὐ γάρ τοι λελάθεσθε, ἅπερ ῥέξαντες ἱκνεῖσθε
line_details.note: λελάθεσθε (“have escaped notice”): the sense is that their deeds are known; ἅπερ ῥέξαντες ἱκνεῖσθε “the very things for which you come.”

line_details.english: as you make for our island—all in vain—on account of your aged father
line_details.greek: νῆσον ἐφ' ἡμετέρην πανετώσιον οὕνεκα πατρός
line_details.note: πανετώσιον is likely from ἐτώσιος (“vain, fruitless”): hence “all in vain,” i.e., coming to Kirke’s island will not avail them without proper rites.

line_details.english: and your brother, whom in dreadful wise you slew;
line_details.greek: γηραιοῦ κάσιός τε, τὸν ἐκπάγλως· ὀλέσαντες,
line_details.note: κάσιος is an epic form for “brother”; τὸν functions as a quasi-relative (“whom”); ἐκπάλως intensifies (“terribly, dreadfully”); the reference is to Apsyrtos/Apsyrtus.

line_details.english: for I do not think you will draw any nearer to your native lands,
line_details.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ὔμμε πάτρῃσιν οἴομαι ἆσσον ἱκέσθαι,

line_details.english: even if you attempt to heal your transgressions by purificatory rites,
line_details.greek: εἰ ἐν ἀναγνίστοισιν ἀλιτροσύναις ἀκέοντες,
line_details.note: ἀναγνίστοισιν is a rare/technical term; probably from (ἁ)γνίζω “to purify,” meaning “purificatory.” Some take it as “unrecognized/illegitimate,” but the contrast with the next line’s “divine purifications” suggests ordinary rites versus divinely sanctioned ones.

line_details.english: not until you wash off the defilement by divine cleansings,
line_details.greek: μέσφ' ὅταν ἐκνίψησθε μύσος θείοισι καθαρμοῖς
line_details.note: μῦσος “pollution” (of kin-murder); καθαρμοί are technical “purifications/expiations.”

line_details.english: through the lore of Orpheus, beside the pebbly shore of Malea.”
line_details.greek: Ὀρφέως ἰδμοσύνῃσι παρὰ κροκάλοισι Μαλείης.
line_details.note: κροκάλοι “pebbles, shingle”; Malea is Cape Malea in Laconia; ἰδμοσύναις “expert knowledge, lore”: Orpheus’ specialized ritual knowledge effects the purification near Malea.

line_details.english: For it is not the custom of our house to receive propitiants,
line_details.greek: Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἡμετέροιο δόμου θέμις ἐστιν ἱκέσθαι
line_details.note: θέμις ἐστιν = “it is the (sacred) custom/right.” προστροπίους (acc. pl.) is used substantively: “those seeking propitiation,” i.e., suppliants for expiation; accusative functions as the subject of the infinitive ἱκέσθαι.

line_details.english: for you are bespattered with such gore;
line_details.greek: προστροπίους· τοίῳ γε λύθρῳ πεπαλαγμένοι ἐστέ·
line_details.note: λύθρον is “blood-filth, gore,” often signaling ritual miasma; πεπαλαγμένοι = “spattered, besmeared.”

line_details.english: But straightway I, with ready heart, will send provisions,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλά μιν αὐτίκ' ἐγὼ πρόφρων ξυνήϊα πέμψω
line_details.note: ξυνήϊα = “provisions, ship’s stores”; πρόφρων = “with ready goodwill.” The enclitic μιν is an anticipatory/pleonastic object, effectively pointing ahead to the supplies to be sent.

line_details.english: food and luscious wine for you to have, and along with them much meat.”
line_details.greek: σῖτον καὶ μέθυ λαρὸν ἔχειν, σὺν δὲ κρέα πολλά."
line_details.note: λάρον (laron) = “delicious, luscious” (of wine). ἔχειν is epexegetic (“for you to have”), with the beneficiary understood (sc. ὑμῖν).

line_details.english: So speaking, she flew back again; and in the middle of the ship
line_details.greek: - Ὣς εἰποῦσ', ἄψορρος ἀπέπτατο· νηῒ δὲ μέσσῃ
line_details.note: ἄψορρος = “back again”; ἀπέπτατο (“flew off”) hints at a divine or winged figure’s departure.

line_details.english: there lay the gear prepared for a banquet and for drink.
line_details.greek: δαιτός τ' ἠδὲ ποτοῖο τετυγμένα τεύχε' ἔκειτο.
line_details.note: τεύχεα here = “gear/implements” (not arms): the made-ready paraphernalia of feasting and drinking; τετυγμένα = “prepared, made ready.”

text.english: And then, as we were pressing on, there sped a clear, favoring blast of wind.
text.greek: Ἂν δ' ἄρ' ἐπειγομένοισι θέεν λιγὺς οὖρος ἀήτης·

line_details.english: And then, as we were pressing on, there sped a clear, favoring blast of wind.
line_details.greek: Ἂν δ' ἄρ' ἐπειγομένοισι θέεν λιγὺς οὖρος ἀήτης·
line_details.note: ἐπειγομένοις is a dative of attendant circumstance (“as we were hurrying”); θέεν is epic imperfect 3sg of ‘run’ (here “sped”); λιγύς applied to wind means “clear/keen”; οὖρος = a fair/favoring wind; ἀήτης = “blast, gust,” not the proper name Aiētes.

text.english: And then, having loosed the moorings from that island, cleaving the wave through the mouth of Tartessos, we came, and we made landfall at the Pillars of Herakles.
text.greek: καὶ τότε λυσάμενοι κείνης ἀπὸ πείσματα νήσου, κῦμα διαπρήσσοντες ἀνὰ στόμα Ταρτησσοῖο ἱκόμεθα, στήλαισι δ' ἐκέλσαμεν Ἡρακλεῆος.

line_details.english: And then, having loosed the moorings from that island,
line_details.greek: καὶ τότε λυσάμενοι κείνης ἀπὸ πείσματα νήσου,
line_details.note: πείσματα are the ship’s moorings/cables; λύεσθαι πείσματα is a set phrase for casting off from shore.

line_details.english: cleaving the wave through the mouth of Tartessos,
line_details.greek: κῦμα διαπρήσσοντες ἀνὰ στόμα Ταρτησσοῖο
line_details.note: διαπρήσσειν = “cleave, make one’s way through (the sea)”; ἀνὰ στόμα “through/up along the mouth.” Ταρτησσός (Tartessos) is the far‑western river/region (often the Guadalquivir); the “mouth” may poetically denote either the river’s outlet or, more broadly, the western straits.

line_details.english: we came, and we made landfall at the Pillars of Herakles.
line_details.greek: ἱκόμεθα, στήλαισι δ' ἐκέλσαμεν Ἡρακλεῆος.
line_details.note: ἐκέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω “to bring/put in (a ship),” here with dative of place: “made landfall at.” The στῆλαι Ἡρακλέους are the “Pillars of Herakles,” i.e., the promontories at the Straits of Gibraltar.

text.english: Around the sacred headlands of lord Dionysos we tarried at eventide; for the spirit was in want of a feast.
text.greek: Ἄκραις δ' ἀμφ' ἱεραῖσι Διωνύσοιο ἄνακτος μίμνομεν ἑσπέριοι· δαιτὸς γὰρ ἐδεύετο θυμός.

line_details.english: Around the sacred headlands of lord Dionysos
line_details.greek: Ἄκραις δ' ἀμφ' ἱεραῖσι Διωνύσοιο ἄνακτος
line_details.note: Ἄκραις (dat. pl.) = “headlands, promontories”; ἀμφί with the dative is epic “around/at.” Διονύσοιο ἄνακτος = “of lord Dionysos.”

line_details.english: we tarried at eventide; for the spirit was in want of a feast.
line_details.greek: μίμνομεν ἑσπέριοι· δαιτὸς γὰρ ἐδεύετο θυμός.
line_details.note: ἑσπέριοι is used adverbially, “toward evening/at eventide” (not “western”). θυμός + ἐδεύετο δαιτός is an epic idiom for hunger: “the spirit/heart was in need of a feast.”

text.english: Then at the eastern risings the light‑bearing radiance rose, and at dawn with our oar‑blades we furrowed the glaucous brine, and we reached the Sardinian deep, and the gulfs of the Latins, the isles of Ausonia, and we came to the Tyrrhenian coasts; but when we made for Lilybaion’s resounding strait, and we held our course to the three‑cornered island, of Enkelados, then the Aetnaean flame held their eager rush in check, indeed then over the prow the baleful water closed about, from below; and from the inmost deep Kharybdis roared with a bubbling wave, and it reached to the sail’s very tip.
text.greek: Τῆμος δ' ἀντολίαισιν ἐγείρετο φωσφόρος αἴγλη, ὄρθριοι εἰρεσίῃς γλαυκὴν ἐχαράξαμεν ἅλμην, Σαρδῶον δ' ἱκόμεσθα βυθὸν, κόλπους τε Λατίνων, νήσους τ' Αὐσονίας, Τυρρηνὰς δ' ἱκόμεθ' ἀκτάς· Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Λιλύβαιον ἐπέσχομεν ἠχέτα πορθμὸν, Τριγλώχινά τε νῆσον ἐπέσχομεν, Ἐγκελάδοιο Αἰτναίη φλόξ σφιν ἄρ' ἐρήτυεν μεμαῶτας, δὴ τόθ' ὑπὲρ πρώρης ὀλοὸν περιέζεεν ὕδωρ νειόθεν, ἐκ μυχάτου δὲ βυθοῦ ῥοίβδησε Χάρυβδις κύματι καχλάζοντι, καὶ ἱστίον ἄκρον ἵκανε.

line_details.english: Then at the eastern risings the light‑bearing radiance rose,
line_details.greek: Τῆμος δ' ἀντολίαισιν ἐγείρετο φωσφόρος αἴγλη,
line_details.note: ἀντολίαισιν (“eastern risings”) = dawn; φωσφόρος αἴγλη “light‑bearing radiance” may allude to Phōsphoros (the Morning Star).

line_details.english: and at dawn with our oar‑blades we furrowed the glaucous brine,
line_details.greek: ὄρθριοι εἰρεσίῃς γλαυκὴν ἐχαράξαμεν ἅλμην,
line_details.note: εἰρεσίῃς = “oar‑blades”; γλαυκή “glaucous,” the grey‑blue of the sea; ἅλμη “brine.”

line_details.english: and we reached the Sardinian deep, and the gulfs of the Latins,
line_details.greek: Σαρδῶον δ' ἱκόμεσθα βυθὸν, κόλπους τε Λατίνων,
line_details.note: Σαρδῶον βυθόν = the sea off Sardinia; “Latins” = inhabitants of Latium (central west Italy).

line_details.english: the isles of Ausonia, and we came to the Tyrrhenian coasts;
line_details.greek: νήσους τ' Αὐσονίας, Τυρρηνὰς δ' ἱκόμεθ' ἀκτάς·
line_details.note: Αὐσονία is a poetic name for Italy; “Tyrrhenian coasts” = the western Italian littoral.

line_details.english: but when we made for Lilybaion’s resounding strait,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Λιλύβαιον ἐπέσχομεν ἠχέτα πορθμὸν,
line_details.note: Λιλύβαιον (Lilybaion) is the W tip of Sicily; πορθμός “strait/sound”; the geography anticipates the Messina strait and is not precise.

line_details.english: and we held our course to the three‑cornered island, of Enkelados,
line_details.greek: Τριγλώχινά τε νῆσον ἐπέσχομεν, Ἐγκελάδοιο
line_details.note: τριγλώχινα “three‑cornered,” a standard epithet of Sicily; Enkelados (Encelados) is the Giant pinned beneath Aitna (Etna).

line_details.english: then the Aetnaean flame held their eager rush in check,
line_details.greek: Αἰτναίη φλόξ σφιν ἄρ' ἐρήτυεν μεμαῶτας,
line_details.note: σφιν (“them”) has an ambiguous antecedent; it likely refers to violent forces (e.g., convulsions/winds/waves) checked by Enkelados’ Aetnaean fire; ἐρήτυεν “held back,” μεμαῶτας “eager, impetuous.”

line_details.english: indeed then over the prow the baleful water closed about,
line_details.greek: δὴ τόθ' ὑπὲρ πρώρης ὀλοὸν περιέζεεν ὕδωρ
line_details.note: περιέζεεν “closed about/encircled”; ὀλοόν “baleful, deadly.”

line_details.english: from below; and from the inmost deep Kharybdis roared
line_details.greek: νειόθεν, ἐκ μυχάτου δὲ βυθοῦ ῥοίβδησε Χάρυβδις
line_details.note: μυχάτου βυθοῦ “the inmost depth”; ῥοΐβδησε is onomatopoetic (“roared/whirred”); Kharybdis is the whirlpool in the Messina strait.

line_details.english: with a bubbling wave, and it reached to the sail’s very tip.
line_details.greek: κύματι καχλάζοντι, καὶ ἱστίον ἄκρον ἵκανε.
line_details.note: κύματι καχλάζοντι “with a bubbling/foaming wave”; ἵκανε “reached”; the subject is the surge raised by Kharybdis, reaching the sail’s peak.

text.english: But then the current held the ship fast there for him, nor did it allow her to run right forward, nor straightway to spring back astern, but upon the hollow, baleful deep she was whirled round and round.
text.greek: Νῆα δ' ἄρ' αὐτόθι οἱ κατέχεν ῥόος, οὐδέ μιν εἴα προπροθέειν, οὐδ' αὐτίκ' ἀναρρώσεσθαι ὀπίσσω, κοίλῳ ἔπὶ λυγρῷ δὲ περιστροφάδην ἀλάλητο.

line_details.english: But then the current held the ship fast there for him, nor did it allow her
line_details.greek: Νῆα δ' ἄρ' αὐτόθι οἱ κατέχεν ῥόος, οὐδέ μιν εἴα
line_details.note: oî is an ethical/interest dative (“for him,” likely the helmsman/Jason) and may be left untranslated in English; mín refers to the ship (fem.).

line_details.english: to run right forward, nor straightway to spring back astern,
line_details.greek: προπροθέειν, οὐδ' αὐτίκ' ἀναρρώσεσθαι ὀπίσσω,
line_details.note: proprothéein is an intensive “to run/dart right forward.” anar­rṓsesthai opíssō here means “to spring back astern/backwards”; the future infinitive after “did not allow” is acceptable epic idiom of prevented action.

line_details.english: but upon the hollow, baleful deep she was whirled round and round.
line_details.greek: κοίλῳ ἔπὶ λυγρῷ δὲ περιστροφάδην ἀλάλητο.
line_details.note: koílō(i) … lyg­rō(i) likely with an understood póntō(i) (“upon the hollow, baleful sea”); peristrophádēn = “in whirling fashion, round and round.” alálēto is the imperfect middle of aláomai, “was being driven/whirled about.”

text.english: Indeed, all too soon would Argo have sunk down beneath the deeps, if the eldest daughter of the Old Man of the Sea, who longed to behold Peleus, her husband of broad might, had not, gentle, come forth from the deep and warded off destruction from the Argoan galley, and drawn it out from beneath the mud.
text.greek: Ἦ τάχα καὶ δύσεσθ' Ἀργὼ κατὰ βένθε' ἔμελλεν εἰ μὴ πρεσβίστη θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος εὐρυβίην Πηλῆα πόσιν λελίητο ἰδέσθαι, μειλιχίη δ' ἐκδῦτο βυθοῦ καὶ ῥύσσατ' ὀλέθρου Ἀργῴαν ἄκατον, καὶ ὑπ' ἰλύος ἐξεσάωσε.

line_details.english: Indeed, all too soon would Argo have sunk down beneath the deeps,
line_details.greek: Ἦ τάχα καὶ δύσεσθ' Ἀργὼ κατὰ βένθε' ἔμελλεν
line_details.note: δύσεσθ’ = δύσεσθαι with elision; ἔμελλεν + infinitive with εἰ μὴ expresses the averted counterfactual “would have… if not.” βένθε’ = βένθεα “the depths” (of the sea).

line_details.english: if the eldest daughter of the Old Man of the Sea,
line_details.greek: εἰ μὴ πρεσβίστη θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος
line_details.note: ἁλίοιο γέροντος “Old Man of the Sea” is the traditional epithet of Nereus (also of Proteus in Homer); here the daughter is Thetis. πρεσβίστη may mean “eldest” or “most venerable.”

line_details.english: who longed to behold Peleus, her husband of broad might,
line_details.greek: εὐρυβίην Πηλῆα πόσιν λελίητο ἰδέσθαι,
line_details.note: λελίητο (perfect of λιλαίομαι) “was eager/longed.” εὐρυβίην is difficult; it is best taken as an epithet “of broad might” applied to Peleus by sense (“Peleus of broad might”). The form is irregular, and some emend to εὐρύβιον, but the transmitted sense is clear.

line_details.english: had not, gentle, come forth from the deep and warded off destruction
line_details.greek: μειλιχίη δ' ἐκδῦτο βυθοῦ καὶ ῥύσσατ' ὀλέθρου
line_details.note: μειλιχίη “gentle, kindly” as an epic epithet of a Nereid. ἐκδῦτο (middle) “came forth/emerged” from the depths.

line_details.english: from the Argoan galley, and drawn it out from beneath the mud.
line_details.greek: Ἀργῴαν ἄκατον, καὶ ὑπ' ἰλύος ἐξεσάωσε.
line_details.note: ἄκατος denotes a light, swift galley; here “the Argoan galley.” ἐξεσάωσε “drew out, saved from.” ἰλύς “mud,” implying the ship had grounded on shoals.

text.english: Then indeed at that time we who were sailing checked our course, not very far off, by a projecting crag; and overhead a rock, broken sheer, overarching with smooth ledges, forces the sea inward, and within beneath the grim wave makes a hollow roar.
text.greek: - Δὴ τότε οἱ πλώοντες ἐπέσχομεν οὐ μάλα τηλοῦ προβλῆτα σκόπελον· πέτρη δ' ἐφύπερθεν ἀπορρώξ λισσοῖς χηραμόνεσσιν ἐπιθρώσκουσα βιᾶται πόντον ἔσω, χαροπὸν δ' ἄρ' ὑποβρέμει ἔνδοθι κῦμα.

line_details.english: Then indeed at that time we who were sailing checked our course, not very far off,
line_details.greek: - Δὴ τότε οἱ πλώοντες ἐπέσχομεν οὐ μάλα τηλοῦ
line_details.note: ἐπέσχομεν has a nautical sense: “to heave to, check one’s way.” The object (the crag) is supplied by the next line.

line_details.english: by a projecting crag; and overhead a rock, broken sheer,
line_details.greek: προβλῆτα σκόπελον· πέτρη δ' ἐφύπερθεν ἀπορρώξ
line_details.note: ἐφύπερθεν = “overhead/above”; ἀπορρώξ = “sheer, precipitous.” The subject for the following participle and verb is πέτρη (“rock”).

line_details.english: overarching with smooth ledges, forces the sea inward,
line_details.greek: λισσοῖς χηραμόνεσσιν ἐπιθρώσκουσα βιᾶται
line_details.note: χηραμόνεσσιν is a rare/uncertain word; likely “rock-shelves/ledges.” I render “smooth ledges.” The participle ἐπιθρώσκουσα (“leaping upon”) is used metaphorically of an overhanging/overarching rock.

line_details.english: and within beneath the grim wave makes a hollow roar.
line_details.greek: πόντον ἔσω, χαροπὸν δ' ἄρ' ὑποβρέμει ἔνδοθι κῦμα.
line_details.note: χαροπός applied to the wave conveys a grim, grey-gleaming aspect; ὑποβρέμει = “to rumble with a muffled/hollow roar,” suited to a sea-cave.

text.english: There, seated, they sing forth a clear‑toned voice.
text.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἐφεζόμεναι λιγυρὴν ὄπα γηρύουσι

line_details.english: There, seated, they sing forth a clear‑toned voice.
line_details.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἐφεζόμεναι λιγυρὴν ὄπα γηρύουσι
line_details.note: The subject (“they”) is supplied from the next line’s κοῦραι, here the Sirens; γηρύουσι conveys “utter/sing,” and λιγυρὴν ὄπα is an epic formula for a clear, piercing voice.

text.english: maidens; and by the hearing of mortals they bewitch them to be unreturning.
text.greek: κοῦραι, ἀνοστήτους δὲ βροτῶν θέλγουσιν ἀκουᾷ.

line_details.english: maidens; and by the hearing of mortals they bewitch them to be unreturning.
line_details.greek: κοῦραι, ἀνοστήτους δὲ βροτῶν θέλγουσιν ἀκουᾷ.
line_details.note: ἀνοστήτους (“unreturning”) echoes νόστος (homecoming): the Sirens’ song prevents return. ἀκουᾷ is the dative of ἀκοή (“hearing”), used instrumentally (“by/through the hearing”); hence the sense “they bewitch mortals by the very act of listening.”

text.english: Then indeed the hearing of the Seirenes’ song proved welcome to the Minyae.
text.greek: Δὴ τότε Μινύαισιν ἐφήνδανε πύστις ἀοιδῆς

line_details.english: Then indeed the hearing of the Seirenes’ song proved welcome to the Minyae.
line_details.greek: Δὴ τότε Μινύαισιν ἐφήνδανε πύστις ἀοιδῆς
line_details.note: πύστις means “hearing, report, knowledge”; here “the hearing (of the song)” suits the context. Minyae = the Argonauts.

text.english: Nor were they about to sail past the baneful voice, but from their hands they let the oars fall; and Ankaios was steering toward a jutting headland, had I not, shaking the phorminx in my hands, blended my mother’s delightful adornment of song.
text.greek: Σειρήνων· οὐδέ σφι παραπλώσεσθαι ἔμελλον φθογγὴν οὐλομένην, χειρῶν δέ οἱ ἧκαν ἐρετμά· Ἀγκαῖος δ' ἴθυνεν ἐπὶ προβλῆτα κολωνόν εἰ μὴ ἐγὼ φόρμιγγα τιτηνάμενος παλάμῃσι μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἐκέρασσ' εὐτερπέα κόσμον ἀοιδῆς.

line_details.english: Nor were they about to sail past the baneful voice,
line_details.greek: Σειρήνων· οὐδέ σφι παραπλώσεσθαι ἔμελλον
line_details.note: παραπλῶσθαι (“sail past/by”) with φθογγή (“voice, sound”) is striking and metonymic; οὐλομένην is the epic “baneful, accursed.”

line_details.english: but from their hands they let the oars fall;
line_details.greek: φθογγὴν οὐλομένην, χειρῶν δέ οἱ ἧκαν ἐρετμά·
line_details.note: χειρῶν … ἧκαν ἐρετμά = “they let the oars go from their hands.” The enclitic οἱ is an ethic dative (“on them/for them”), not essential to English.

line_details.english: and Ankaios was steering toward a jutting headland,
line_details.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' ἴθυνεν ἐπὶ προβλῆτα κολωνόν
line_details.note: προβλῆτα κολωνόν = “projecting/jutting hill,” i.e., a promontory; ἴθυνεν “was steering straight (toward).” Ankaios is the helmsman.

line_details.english: had I not, shaking the phorminx in my hands,
line_details.greek: εἰ μὴ ἐγὼ φόρμιγγα τιτηνάμενος παλάμῃσι
line_details.note: φόρμιγξ (phorminx) is the epic lyre; τιτηνάμενος “shaking, brandishing,” a conventional performance verb for striking up song.

line_details.english: blended my mother’s delightful adornment of song.
line_details.greek: μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἐκέρασσ' εὐτερπέα κόσμον ἀοιδῆς.
line_details.note: ἐκέρασσ’ (“I blended/mingled”) uses the musical metaphor of mixing strains; κόσμος ἀοιδῆς “order/adornment of song.” μητρὸς ἐμῆς refers to Orpheus’ mother (the Muse Kalliope) as the source of his song.

text.english: And he sang, ringing clear, through a wondrous hymn, how once they contended for the storm‑footed horses: Zeus Hypsibremetes and Pontios Ennosigaios; but Kyanochaites, angered with father Zeus, smote the Lyctonian land with his golden trident and in an instant scattered it over the boundless sea, to be islands in the sea; these they named Sardō and Euboia, and, besides, windy Kypros.
text.greek: - Ἤειδον δὲ λιγὺ κλάζων διὰ θέσκελον ὕμνον, ὥς ποτέ οἱ δήρισσαν ἀελλοπόδων ὑπὲρ ἵππων· Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης καὶ πόντιος Ἐννοσίγαιος· Αὐτὰρ Κυανοχαῖτα χολωσάμενος Διὶ πατρί τύψεν Λυκτονίην γαίην χρυσῆνι τριαίνῃ καί ῥ' ἀΐγδην ἐσκέδασεν κατ' ἀπείρονα πόντον, νήσους εἰναλίας ἔμεναι· τάς ῥ' ἐξονόμηναν Σαρδώ τ' Εὔβοιάν τ' ἐπὶ δὲ Κύπρον ἠνεμόεσσαν

line_details.english: And he sang, ringing clear, through a wondrous hymn,
line_details.greek: - Ἤειδον δὲ λιγὺ κλάζων διὰ θέσκελον ὕμνον,
line_details.note: theskelos = “wondrous, god‑wrought”; ligy klazōn = “ringing/shrilling clearly.”

line_details.english: how once they contended for the storm‑footed horses:
line_details.greek: ὥς ποτέ οἱ δήρισσαν ἀελλοπόδων ὑπὲρ ἵππων·
line_details.note: aellopodōn = “storm‑footed,” an epic epithet of swift horses; dērissan = “contended/struggled.”

line_details.english: Zeus Hypsibremetes and Pontios Ennosigaios;
line_details.greek: Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης καὶ πόντιος Ἐννοσίγαιος·
line_details.note: Ennosigaios is a cultic name of Poseidon (“Earth‑shaker”); Pontios = “of the sea.” Hypsibremetes = “High‑Thunderer,” epithet of Zeus (kept in transliteration).

line_details.english: but Kyanochaites, angered with father Zeus,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ Κυανοχαῖτα χολωσάμενος Διὶ πατρί
line_details.note: Kyanochaites (“dark‑blue‑haired”) is an epithet of Poseidon; Diì patri = “with/at father Zeus.”

line_details.english: smote the Lyctonian land with his golden trident
line_details.greek: τύψεν Λυκτονίην γαίην χρυσῆνι τριαίνῃ
line_details.note: Lyctonian = of Lyktos in Crete; the golden trident is Poseidon’s weapon.

line_details.english: and in an instant scattered it over the boundless sea,
line_details.greek: καί ῥ' ἀΐγδην ἐσκέδασεν κατ' ἀπείρονα πόντον,
line_details.note: aïgdēn = “at once, in an instant.”

line_details.english: to be islands in the sea; these they named
line_details.greek: νήσους εἰναλίας ἔμεναι· τάς ῥ' ἐξονόμηναν
line_details.note: einalias = “of the sea”; exonomēnan = “they named (by name),” impersonal/indefinite subject.

line_details.english: Sardō and Euboia, and, besides, windy Kypros.
line_details.greek: Σαρδώ τ' Εὔβοιάν τ' ἐπὶ δὲ Κύπρον ἠνεμόεσσαν
line_details.note: Toponyms: Sardō = Sardinia; Euboia = Euboea; Kypros = Cyprus; anemoeassan = “windy.”

text.english: Then, as he was playing the phorminx, from the snowy crag the Sirens were astonished, and they hushed their own song; and the one cast the lotos‑reeds away, the other the tortoise‑shell from her hands.
text.greek: Δὴ τότε φορμίζοντος, ἀπὸ σκοπέλου νιφόεντος Σειρῆνες θάμβησαν, ἑὴν δ' ἄμπαυσαν ἀοιδήν· Καί ῥ' ἡ μὲν λωτοὺς, ἡ δ' αὖ χέλυν ἔκβαλε χειρῶν.

line_details.english: Then, as he was playing the phorminx, from the snowy crag
line_details.greek: Δὴ τότε φορμίζοντος, ἀπὸ σκοπέλου νιφόεντος
line_details.note: phorminx = early lyre; skopelos niphōn = “snow‑white/snowy crag.”

line_details.english: the Sirens were astonished, and they hushed their own song;
line_details.greek: Σειρῆνες θάμβησαν, ἑὴν δ' ἄμπαυσαν ἀοιδήν·

line_details.english: and the one cast the lotos‑reeds away, the other the tortoise‑shell from her hands.
line_details.greek: Καί ῥ' ἡ μὲν λωτοὺς, ἡ δ' αὖ χέλυν ἔκβαλε χειρῶν.
line_details.note: lotos here is the lotos‑reed used as a wind instrument, not the flower; chelys is the tortoise‑shell lyre.

text.english: Terribly they groaned, when the baleful doom of allotted death was advancing, and from the cleft’s utmost edge they themselves hurled down into the bottom of the brine-roaring sea, and for rocks they exchanged their body and their overweening form.
text.greek: Δεινὰ δ' ἀνεστονάχησαν, ἐπεὶ πότμος ἤϊε λυγρός μοιριδίου θανάτοιο· σφέας δ' ἀπὸ ῥωγάδος ἄκρης ἐς βυθὸν δίσκευσαν ἁλιρροθίοιο θαλάσσης, πέτραις δ' ἠλλάξαντο δέμας μορφήν θ' ὑπέροπλον.

line_details.english: Terribly they groaned, when the baleful doom of allotted death was advancing,
line_details.greek: Δεινὰ δ' ἀνεστονάχησαν, ἐπεὶ πότμος ἤϊε λυγρός
line_details.note: Subject = the Sirens (context): ἐπεὶ πότμος ἤϊε (“when doom was going/approaching”) is an epic idiom; λυγρός = “baleful, woeful.” μοιριδίου (sc. θανάτοιο) = “allotted by Moira, fated.”

line_details.english: and from the cleft’s utmost edge they themselves
line_details.greek: μοιριδίου θανάτοιο· σφέας δ' ἀπὸ ῥωγάδος ἄκρης
line_details.note: ῥωγάς = a rift/cleft in rock; hence “cleft’s utmost edge.” σφέας used reflexively = “themselves.”

line_details.english: hurled down into the bottom of the brine-roaring sea,
line_details.greek: ἐς βυθὸν δίσκευσαν ἁλιρροθίοιο θαλάσσης,
line_details.note: δίσκευσαν (from δισκεύω) literally “they discused,” i.e., “flung [themselves] like a discus,” hence “hurled down.” ἁλιρροθίος = “brine-roaring” (of the sea’s surge).

line_details.english: and for rocks they exchanged their body and their overweening form.
line_details.greek: πέτραις δ' ἠλλάξαντο δέμας μορφήν θ' ὑπέροπλον.
line_details.note: ἠλλάξαντο with acc. + dat. = “they exchanged [X] for [Y],” used for metamorphosis: here, body/form for rocks. ὑπέροπλος = “overweening, presumptuous,” not “well-armed.” This line reflects the myth that the Sirens, defeated, cast themselves into the sea and became rocks.

text.english: But when, speeding on, she had passed beyond this doom as well, Argō reached the sea’s swell and a bay, her rigging along the forestays filled with swift winds, she came to deep Kerkyra, which the Phaeacians inhabited, skilled in oar-craft and in sea-wandering travel, and for them, by his injunctions, the ordinances Alkinoos, most just of kings, was wont to ordain.
text.greek: - Αὐταρ ἐπεὶ καὶ τόνδε πότμον παράμειψε θέουσα Ἀργὼ, κῦμα δὲ πόντου καὶ κόλπον ἵκανε, λαιψηροῖς πλήθουσα κατὰ προτόνων ἀνέμοισι, Κέρκυραν βαθέην ἐξίκετο, τήν σφιν ἔναιον ἴδριες εἰρεσίης καὶ ἁλιπλάγκτοιο πορείης Φαίηκες· τοῖσιν δ' ἄρ' ἐφημοσύναισι θέμιστας Ἀλκίνοος κραίνεσκε δικαιότατος βασιλήων.

line_details.english: But when, speeding on, she had passed beyond this doom as well,
line_details.greek: - Αὐταρ ἐπεὶ καὶ τόνδε πότμον παράμειψε θέουσα
line_details.note: παράμειψε πότμον (“passed beyond doom”) is an epic idiom meaning effectively “escaped that peril”; θεοῦσα is a feminine participle (“speeding”) agreeing with Argō.

line_details.english: Argō reached the sea’s swell and a bay,
line_details.greek: Ἀργὼ, κῦμα δὲ πόντου καὶ κόλπον ἵκανε,
line_details.note: κῦμα πόντου καὶ κόλπον is likely a hendiadys contrasting open water and a sheltered inlet (“swell … and a bay”).

line_details.english: her rigging along the forestays filled with swift winds,
line_details.greek: λαιψηροῖς πλήθουσα κατὰ προτόνων ἀνέμοισι,
line_details.note: πρότονοι are the forestays/shrouds; πλήθουσα ἀνέμοισι implies the sails/gear are swelling with wind, though “sail” is not explicitly named.

line_details.english: she came to deep Kerkyra, which the Phaeacians inhabited,
line_details.greek: Κέρκυραν βαθέην ἐξίκετο, τήν σφιν ἔναιον
line_details.note: βαθεῖα (“deep”) likely = “deep‑harbored”/“sea‑deep.” σφιν is an ethical dative (“for their part/there”), here best rendered idiomatically as “which … [they] inhabited.”

line_details.english: skilled in oar-craft and in sea-wandering travel,
line_details.greek: ἴδριες εἰρεσίης καὶ ἁλιπλάγκτοιο πορείης
line_details.note: εἰρεσία = “oarage, rowing”; ἁλιπλάνκτος = “sea‑wandering, roving by sea.” ἴδριες = “skilled, adept.”

line_details.english: and for them, by his injunctions, the ordinances
line_details.greek: Φαίηκες· τοῖσιν δ' ἄρ' ἐφημοσύναισι θέμιστας
line_details.note: ἐφημοσύναι = “injunctions/behests,” a rarer term for authoritative proclamations; θέμιστες are traditional ordinances/judgments.

line_details.english: Alkinoos, most just of kings, was wont to ordain.
line_details.greek: Ἀλκίνοος κραίνεσκε δικαιότατος βασιλήων.
line_details.note: κραίνεσκε (iterative imperfect) conveys habitual action, “was wont to ordain”; δικαιότατος βασιλῆων is a Homeric‑style superlative formula. The king’s name is given in Greek transliteration (Alkinoos).

text.english: And having made fast the hawsers, we made ready to offer sacred rites to Zeus Panomphaios and to Apollon Epaktios.
text.greek: Πείσματα δ' ἁψάμενοι πορσύνομεν ἱερὰ θέσθαι Ζηνὶ πανομφαίῳ καὶ ἐπακτίῳ Ἀπόλλωνι.

line_details.english: And having made fast the hawsers, we made ready to offer sacred rites
line_details.greek: Πείσματα δ' ἁψάμενοι πορσύνομεν ἱερὰ θέσθαι
line_details.note: πείσματα = mooring-ropes/hawsers; πορσύνω with infinitive and ἱερὰ θέσθαι is an idiom for preparing to perform/offer sacrifices.

line_details.english: to Zeus Panomphaios and to Apollon Epaktios.
line_details.greek: Ζηνὶ πανομφαίῳ καὶ ἐπακτίῳ Ἀπόλλωνι.
line_details.note: πανομφαῖος literally “of all-oracles”/“all-voiced,” a traditional epithet of Zeus; ἐπακτίος means “of the shore/landing,” a cult title; divine names are transliterated.

text.english: Then indeed, being urged on, they were borne along beneath the oars, in countless ships—the mighty company of Aeëtes, of Colchians and Erraunians, of Charandaians and Solymoi— seeking the Minyae, until they should bring Medeia into the sight of her father Aeëtes, and that he might exact requital for their own reckless outrages—the slaying of her brother.
text.greek: - Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃσιν ἐπειγόμενοι φορέοντο νηυσὶν ἀπειρεσίαις βριαρὸς λόχος Αἰήταο Κόλχων Ἐρραύνων τε, Χαρανδαίων Σολύμων τε διζόμενος Μινύας, τόφρ' ἂν Μήδειαν ἄγοιντο ὄψιν ἐς Αἰήταο πατρὸς, τίσειε δ' ἀμοιβάς σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἀδελφειοῦ κταμένοιο.

line_details.english: Then indeed, being urged on, they were borne along beneath the oars,
line_details.greek: - Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃσιν ἐπειγόμενοι φορέοντο
line_details.note: ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃσιν (“beneath the oars”) is a Homeric formula for a ship being driven by rowing; the subject (the band) is supplied by the next line.

line_details.english: in countless ships—the mighty company of Aeëtes,
line_details.greek: νηυσὶν ἀπειρεσίαις βριαρὸς λόχος Αἰήταο

line_details.english: of Colchians and Erraunians, of Charandaians and Solymoi—
line_details.greek: Κόλχων Ἐρραύνων τε, Χαρανδαίων Σολύμων τε
line_details.note: The ethnonyms Erraunians and Charandaians are obscure; forms and identifications vary in the tradition. Solymoi are the Solymi of Lycia/Asia Minor.

line_details.english: seeking the Minyae, until they should bring Medeia
line_details.greek: διζόμενος Μινύας, τόφρ' ἂν Μήδειαν ἄγοιντο
line_details.note: διζόμενος (“seeking”) is singular, agreeing with the collective “band” (λόχος); τόφρ’ ἄν with optative (ἄγοιντο) expresses “until” with anticipated outcome.

line_details.english: into the sight of her father Aeëtes, and that he might exact requital
line_details.greek: ὄψιν ἐς Αἰήταο πατρὸς, τίσειε δ' ἀμοιβάς
line_details.note: Subject of τίσειε (“exact requital”) is Aeëtes; ὄψιν ἐς means “into the sight/presence.”

line_details.english: for their own reckless outrages—the slaying of her brother.
line_details.greek: σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἀδελφειοῦ κταμένοιο.
line_details.note: ἀδελφειοῦ κταμενοῖο (“of a slain brother”) most naturally refers to Apsyrtos, Medeia’s brother; the possessor is left implicit. σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν is the Odyssean “by/for their own reckless outrages.”

text.english: But when indeed they drew nearer to the innermost recess of the hollow haven, straightway the heralds went to the house of Alkinoos, Medeia’s knees gave way, and fear blanched her cheeks, lest he, having seized her unwilling, might send her back to her own house, the king of the Phaiakians, and the deeds might be bruited abroad.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ κοίλου λιμένας μυχῷ ἆσσον ἵκοντο, αἶψα δ' ἄρ' Ἀλκινόοιο δόμον κήρυκες ἔβαινον, Μηδείης λύτο γοῦνα, δέος δ' ὤχριε παρειάς, μή οἱ ἑλὼν ἀέκουσαν ἑὸν πέμψειε δόμονδε Φαιήκων βασιλεὺς, ἀνάπυστά τε ἔργα γένηται.

line_details.english: But when indeed they drew nearer to the innermost recess of the hollow haven,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ κοίλου λιμένας μυχῷ ἆσσον ἵκοντο,
line_details.note: κοίλου λιμένας μυχῷ is syntactically awkward: one expects a genitive with μυχῷ (e.g., λιμένος) or agreement of κοίλου with λιμένας (κοίλους). Many editors emend to κοίλου λιμένος μυχῷ (“to the recess of the hollow harbor”).

line_details.english: straightway the heralds went to the house of Alkinoos,
line_details.greek: αἶψα δ' ἄρ' Ἀλκινόοιο δόμον κήρυκες ἔβαινον,

line_details.english: Medeia’s knees gave way, and fear blanched her cheeks,
line_details.greek: Μηδείης λύτο γοῦνα, δέος δ' ὤχριε παρειάς,
line_details.note: λύτο γοῦνα (“her knees were loosed”) is a Homeric idiom for weakness from fear; ὤχριε means “grew pale.”

line_details.english: lest he, having seized her unwilling, might send her back to her own house,
line_details.greek: μή οἱ ἑλὼν ἀέκουσαν ἑὸν πέμψειε δόμονδε
line_details.note: μή + optative (πέμψειε, γένηται) marks a feared outcome in past narrative. The dative οἱ is dativus incommodi (“to her hurt”). ἑὸν δόμονδε means “to her own house,” i.e., back to her paternal home in Colchis.

line_details.english: the king of the Phaiakians, and the deeds might be bruited abroad.
line_details.greek: Φαιήκων βασιλεὺς, ἀνάπυστά τε ἔργα γένηται.
line_details.note: Φαιήκων βασιλεύς stands in apposition, supplying the subject of the feared action. ἀνάπυστα (“noised abroad, notorious”) has Homeric coloring; ἔργα likely refers to the Argonauts’ deeds becoming common report.

text.english: But Moira, whose mind brings things to fulfillment, did not nod assent to these things for him, not until upon the halls of Pelias a baneful destruction and upon the ruler himself Jason should bring an evil doom.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ τάδε μοῖρα τελεσσίνοος κατένευσε, πρὶν δή τοι Πελίαο δόμοις ἔπι λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον αὐτῷ τε κρείοντι φέροι κακὸν οἶτον Ἰήσων.

line_details.english: But Moira, whose mind brings things to fulfillment, did not nod assent to these things for him,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ τάδε μοῖρα τελεσσίνοος κατένευσε,
line_details.note: τελεσσίνοος (of Moira): literally “fulfilling-minded”; κατένευσε preserves the epic image of divine assent by a nod. I take Moira here as the personified goddess (hence capitalization).

line_details.english: not until upon the halls of Pelias a baneful destruction
line_details.greek: πρὶν δή τοι Πελίαο δόμοις ἔπι λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον
line_details.note: τοι is an enclitic particle without direct English equivalent; ἐπὶ with the dative (“upon/against”) marks hostile direction; λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον is a formulaic “baneful destruction.”

line_details.english: and upon the ruler himself Jason should bring an evil doom.
line_details.greek: αὐτῷ τε κρείοντι φέροι κακὸν οἶτον Ἰήσων.
line_details.note: φέροι is optative in a πρίν-clause, hence “until … should bring”; κρείων (“ruler, lord”) in the dative goes with ἐπὶ understood; οἶτος is “doom, lot,” rendered here as “evil doom.”

text.english: But when indeed she heard the voice of the harsh king, Arete, rosy‑armed—and Alkinoos, godlike— Alkinoos straightway gave orders to the heralds to bring the contested maiden from the stout ship, and for her own father to exact the penalty for her transgressions; but Arete, the far‑famed queen, pitied her, and, gently addressing her own husband, spoke thus: "Surely it is no welcome thing to thrust aside their companionship, but rather to spread the couch and unloose love from its torch." For Dionaean Aphrodite is very wroth with them, with men and with women, whosoever shall contrive these deeds.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ βασιλῆος ἀπηνέος ἔκλυεν αὐδήν Ἀρήτη ῥοδόπηχυς, ἰδ' Ἀλκίνοος θεοειδής, Ἀλκίνοος μέν ῥ' ὦκ' ἐπετέλλετο κηρύκεσσι, κούρην ἀμφήριστον ἄγειν ἀπὸ νηὸς ἐρυμνῆς, πατρί θ' ἑῷ τίσεσθαι δίκην ἀλιτημοσυνάων, Ἀρήτη δ' ᾤκτειρεν ἀγακλειτὴ βασίλεια, μείλιχα παρφαμένη δὲ τὸν ὃν πόσιν, ὠδ' ἀγόρευεν· - "Οὐ μὲν δὴ φίλον ἐστὶν ἀπό ῥ' ὤσασθαι ὅμιλον Λέκτρα τε στορέσαι, λῦσαί τ' ἐκ πυρσὸν ἔρωτος. Θυμαίνει μάλα γάρ σφι Διωναίη Ἀφροδίτη ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξὶν, ὅτις τάδε μήσεται ἔργα.

line_details.english: But when indeed she heard the voice of the harsh king,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ βασιλῆος ἀπηνέος ἔκλυεν αὐδήν
line_details.note: “the harsh king” is most naturally Aeetes; his “voice” denotes the demand conveyed by the Colchian envoys.

line_details.english: Arete, rosy‑armed—and Alkinoos, godlike—
line_details.greek: Ἀρήτη ῥοδόπηχυς, ἰδ' Ἀλκίνοος θεοειδής,
line_details.note: ῥοδόπηχυς (“rosy‑armed”) is a Homeric‑style epithet; θεοειδής (“godlike”) marks Alkinoos’ noble appearance.

line_details.english: Alkinoos straightway gave orders to the heralds
line_details.greek: Ἀλκίνοος μέν ῥ' ὦκ' ἐπετέλλετο κηρύκεσσι,
line_details.note: No special difficulty.

line_details.english: to bring the contested maiden from the stout ship,
line_details.greek: κούρην ἀμφήριστον ἄγειν ἀπὸ νηὸς ἐρυμνῆς,
line_details.note: ἀμφήριστος means “contested, disputed,” often of a prize; here of the maiden (Medea) claimed by both sides. ἐρυμνός of a ship = “stout, well‑defended.”

line_details.english: and for her own father to exact the penalty for her transgressions;
line_details.greek: πατρί θ' ἑῷ τίσεσθαι δίκην ἀλιτημοσυνάων,
line_details.note: τίσασθαι δίκην is middle “to exact the penalty”; the subject is the father (πατρὶ ἑῷ), not the maiden. Hence “for her own father to exact the penalty.”

line_details.english: but Arete, the far‑famed queen, pitied her,
line_details.greek: Ἀρήτη δ' ᾤκτειρεν ἀγακλειτὴ βασίλεια,
line_details.note: No special difficulty.

line_details.english: and, gently addressing her own husband, spoke thus:
line_details.greek: μείλιχα παρφαμένη δὲ τὸν ὃν πόσιν, ὠδ' ἀγόρευεν·
line_details.note: παρφαμένη (“speaking gently/soothingly”) is a Homeric verb of soft address.

line_details.english: "Surely it is no welcome thing to thrust aside their companionship,
line_details.greek: - "Οὐ μὲν δὴ φίλον ἐστὶν ἀπό ῥ' ὤσασθαι ὅμιλον
line_details.note: ὅμιλος here is taken as “companionship, consorting” (from ὁμιλέω), i.e., the couple’s union; οὐ μὲν δὴ marks the disfavored course (to separate them).

line_details.english: but rather to spread the couch and unloose love from its torch."
line_details.greek: Λέκτρα τε στορέσαι, λῦσαί τ' ἐκ πυρσὸν ἔρωτος.
line_details.note: The “torch” evokes both the fire of Eros and the marriage‑torch; λύσαι … ἔρωτα conveys allaying love’s fire through consummation. “but rather” renders the implied contrast with the preceding clause.

line_details.english: For Dionaean Aphrodite is very wroth with them,
line_details.greek: Θυμαίνει μάλα γάρ σφι Διωναίη Ἀφροδίτη
line_details.note: θυμαίνει = “is wroth, rages,” governing the dative (σφι, enclitic 3rd pl. “with/against them”); Διωναίη = “Dionaean,” i.e., of Dione, an epic epithet of Aphrodite.

line_details.english: with men and with women, whosoever shall contrive these deeds.
line_details.greek: ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξὶν, ὅτις τάδε μήσεται ἔργα.
line_details.note: ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξίν = dative of persons affected, “with/against men and women (alike)”; ὅτις functions as an indefinite relative (“whosoever”); μήσεται is future middle of μήδομαι (“devise, contrive”); τάδε ἔργα = “these deeds,” deictic to the preceding context.

text.english: But if she be a maiden and comes unsullied, let her go to her father’s house and to the haunts of the Colchians; but if, with bridal converse and having reclined upon the couch, she has disgraced her maidenhood, let her own husband take her to himself.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' εἰ μὲν κούρη πέλεται καὶ ἄχραντος ἱκάνει, οἰχέσθω πατρός τε δόμον καὶ ἐς ἤθεα Κόλχων· εἰ δέ κε νυμφιδίοις ὀάροις λέκτρῳ τε κλιθεῖσα παρθενίην ᾔσχυνεν, ἑὸς πόσις ἄμμιν ἀγέσθω."

line_details.english: But if she be a maiden and comes unsullied,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' εἰ μὲν κούρη πέλεται καὶ ἄχραντος ἱκάνει,
line_details.note: ἄχραντος = “undefiled,” with possible sexual and ritual overtones.

line_details.english: let her go to her father’s house and to the haunts of the Colchians;
line_details.greek: οἰχέσθω πατρός τε δόμον καὶ ἐς ἤθεα Κόλχων·
line_details.note: ἤθεα literally “haunts, abodes”; here = the homeland/realms of the Colchians.

line_details.english: but if, with bridal converse and having reclined upon the couch,
line_details.greek: εἰ δέ κε νυμφιδίοις ὀάροις λέκτρῳ τε κλιθεῖσα
line_details.note: νυμφιδίοις ὀάροις = “nuptial/bridal talk,” i.e., intimate wooing; κλιθεῖσα (aor. pass. part. of κλίνω) = “having reclined/lay down.”

line_details.english: she has disgraced her maidenhood, let her own husband take her to himself.
line_details.greek: παρθενίην ᾔσχυνεν, ἑὸς πόσις ἄμμιν ἀγέσθω."
line_details.note: παρθενίην ᾔσχυνεν = “put shame upon maidenhood”; ἄμμιν is an ethical dative (“for us/as far as we are concerned”), and ἀγέσθω (middle) = “let him take [her] for himself (as wife).”

text.english: Thus she spoke; and the word came over the mind of Alcinous; and thus all these things were destined to be brought to completion.
text.greek: - Ὣς ἔφατ'· Ἀλκινόῳ δὲ περὶ φρένας ἤλυθε μῦθος· Καί ῥ' οὕτω τάδε πάντα τελευτήσεσθαι ἔμελλεν.

line_details.english: Thus she spoke; and the word came over the mind of Alcinous;
line_details.greek: - Ὣς ἔφατ'· Ἀλκινόῳ δὲ περὶ φρένας ἤλυθε μῦθος·
line_details.note: περὶ φρένας ἤλυθε μῦθος is an idiom meaning “the word/thought came over (occupied) his mind,” i.e., it found favor; the speaker just above is likely Arete.

line_details.english: and thus all these things were destined to be brought to completion.
line_details.greek: Καί ῥ' οὕτω τάδε πάντα τελευτήσεσθαι ἔμελλεν.
