line_details.note: τελευτᾶν here = “to come to fulfillment/consummation, be accomplished.”

text.english: But the counsel of Minyas did not escape her; for straightway Hêrê in the guise of a handmaid, swiftly spoke and nodded assent, springing upon the ship, what the lords were contriving for him.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ βουλὴ Μινύας λάθεν· αἶψα γὰρ Ἥρη δμωῒ δέμας εἰκυῖα, θοῶς φάτο καὶ κατένευσε, νηὸς ἔπι προθοροῦσα, τά οἱ μήτιον ἄνακτες.

line_details.english: But the counsel of Minyas did not escape her; for straightway Hêrê
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ βουλὴ Μινύας λάθεν· αἶψα γὰρ Ἥρη
line_details.note: “Minyas” is a patronymic designation for Jason (a Minyan). The dative οἱ = “to her,” i.e., Hêrê; λάθεν + dative = “escaped [one’s] notice.”

line_details.english: in the guise of a handmaid, swiftly spoke and nodded assent,
line_details.greek: δμωῒ δέμας εἰκυῖα, θοῶς φάτο καὶ κατένευσε,

line_details.english: springing upon the ship, what the lords were contriving for him.
line_details.greek: νηὸς ἔπι προθοροῦσα, τά οἱ μήτιον ἄνακτες.
line_details.note: νηὸς is the genitive of ναῦς “ship” used with ἐπί (“upon”). μήτιον is the epic 3rd pl. of μητιάω “devise, contrive.” ἄνακτες “lords” likely refers to human rulers/princes; οἱ = “for him” (Jason).

text.english: Then indeed Medeia made ready the bridal bed at the uttermost stern, and round about they strewed ground-bedding, spreading the Golden Fleece about her.
text.greek: Δὴ τότε Μηδείη θαλάμων πορσύνετο λέκτρον πρύμνῃ ἐπ' ἀκροτάτῃ, περὶ δ' ἐστορέσαντο χαμεύνας, ἀμφ' αὐτῇ χρύσειον ἐφαπλώσαντες ἄωτον.

line_details.english: Then indeed Medeia made ready the bridal bed
line_details.greek: Δὴ τότε Μηδείη θαλάμων πορσύνετο λέκτρον
line_details.note: θαλάμων (gen. pl.) is the epic idiom for “of the (bridal) chamber”; hence the idiomatic “bridal bed.” πορσύνετο (mid.) = “made ready.”

line_details.english: at the uttermost stern, and round about they strewed ground-bedding,
line_details.greek: πρύμνῃ ἐπ' ἀκροτάτῃ, περὶ δ' ἐστορέσαντο χαμεύνας,
line_details.note: χαμεῦνας = “ground-beds,” bedding laid on the floor/deck; subject of ἐστορέσαντο is implicit “they” (the comrades/attendants). πρύμνῃ ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτῃ specifies the very stern of the ship.

line_details.english: spreading the Golden Fleece about her.
line_details.greek: ἀμφ' αὐτῇ χρύσειον ἐφαπλώσαντες ἄωτον.
line_details.note: χρύσειον ἄωτον literally “the golden choicest (wool),” i.e., the Golden Fleece, used here as a coverlet; ἐφαπλώσαντες = “spreading over,” with ἀμφ’ αὐτῇ (“about her”) indicating the enveloping placement.

text.english: But when they had hung the oxhides upon the spear-shafts, and the gear as well, and had veiled the reverend work of wedlock, then she parted with the maidenly blossom, dread-wedded Medea, amid ill-omened wedding-songs.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δοράτεσσιν ἐπαρτήσαντο βοείας, τεύχεά τε, κρύπτον τε γάμων αἰδέσσιμον ἔργον, καὶ τότε παρθενίης νοσφίζετο κούριον ἄνθος αἰνόγαμος Μήδεια δυσαινήτοις ὑμεναίοις.

line_details.english: But when they had hung the oxhides upon the spear-shafts,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δοράτεσσιν ἐπαρτήσαντο βοείας,
line_details.note: doratessin (“upon spear-shafts,” dat. pl. of doru) + boeias (“oxhide”) likely describes makeshift screens or a tent hung on spear-shafts.

line_details.english: and the gear as well, and had veiled the reverend work of wedlock,
line_details.greek: τεύχεά τε, κρύπτον τε γάμων αἰδέσσιμον ἔργον,
line_details.note: aidesimon ergon (“reverend/modest work”) is a euphemism for the consummation of marriage; krypton underscores privacy/modesty.

line_details.english: then she parted with the maidenly blossom,
line_details.greek: καὶ τότε παρθενίης νοσφίζετο κούριον ἄνθος
line_details.note: nosphizeto (middle) = “was separated from/parted with”; kourion anthos is the stock phrase “maidenly/virginal bloom.”

line_details.english: dread-wedded Medea, amid ill-omened wedding-songs.
line_details.greek: αἰνόγαμος Μήδεια δυσαινήτοις ὑμεναίοις.
line_details.note: ainogamos (“dread-/baleful-wedded”) foreshadows Medea’s tragic marriage; dysainētois (“ill-omened/ill-praised”) modifies hymenaiois, the wedding songs (with implicit reference to the god Hymenaios).

text.english: But when they came into the presence of the blameless king, the Kolchians and the Minyae, and each party spoke, Aisonides won the decision to lead Medeia as his wife, by Alkinous; and they swiftly loosed the ship’s moorings, then, beneath the oars, the much-spoken-of Argo sped, cleaving her course through the gulf of Ambrakia; There—what shall I proclaim to you, Mousaios, god-born, all that they suffered, together with the Minyae, as the gusts drove them toward the Syrtis, or how they won deliverance from a sea-wandering voyage; and what pains they suffered in Crete, enduring, as they kept watch against the bronze triple-giant, until we came, who would not permit them to come within the harbors.
text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ βασιλῆος ἀμύμονος ὄψιν ἵκοντο Κόλχοι καὶ Μινύαι, καὶ ἐμυθήσαντο ἕκαστοι, ἐκ δ' ἔλαχ' Αἰσονίδης ἄλοχον Μήδειαν ἄγεσθαι Ἀλκινόου, τοὶ δ' ὦκα λύοντ' ἐκ πείσματα νηός δὴ τόθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃσι θέεν πολυηγόρος Ἀργώ, Ἀμπρακίου κόλποιο διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθα· - Ἔνθα τί τοι, Μουσαῖε θεηγενὲς, ἐξαγορεύσω ὅσσα πάθον Μινύαισιν ὁμοῦ ποτὶ Σύρτιν ἀήταις ἢ πῶς ἐξεσάωθεν ἁλιπλάγκτοιο πορείης· ὅσσα τ' ἄρ' ἐν Κρήτῃ πάθον ἄλγεα τετληῶτες, χάλκειον τριγίγαντα δοκεύμενοι ὄφρ' ἱκόμεσθα, ὅς ῥά οἱ οὐκ εἴα λιμένων ἔντοσθεν ἱκέσθαι.

line_details.english: But when they came into the presence of the blameless king,
line_details.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ βασιλῆος ἀμύμονος ὄψιν ἵκοντο
line_details.note: ὄψιν ἵκοντο = “came into the presence/sight (of).” ἀμύμονος is a traditional epic epithet, “blameless.”

line_details.english: the Kolchians and the Minyae, and each party spoke,
line_details.greek: Κόλχοι καὶ Μινύαι, καὶ ἐμυθήσαντο ἕκαστοι,
line_details.note: ἐμυθήσαντο: middle, “made speeches/pleaded their case.” Each side presents its claim before the king.

line_details.english: Aisonides won the decision to lead Medeia as his wife,
line_details.greek: ἐκ δ' ἔλαχ' Αἰσονίδης ἄλοχον Μήδειαν ἄγεσθαι
line_details.note: ἐκ δ’ ἔλαχ’ … ἄγεσθαι: “won by lot/award to take [her] as wife.” Refers to Alkinous’s arbitration that Medeia remain with Aisonides if already a wife.

line_details.english: by Alkinous; and they swiftly loosed the ship’s moorings,
line_details.greek: Ἀλκινόου, τοὶ δ' ὦκα λύοντ' ἐκ πείσματα νηός
line_details.note: Ἀλκινόου is genitive of agent (“by Alkinous”). πείσματα = “fastenings, moorings” of the ship.

line_details.english: then, beneath the oars, the much-spoken-of Argo sped,
line_details.greek: δὴ τόθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃσι θέεν πολυηγόρος Ἀργώ,
line_details.note: πολυήγορος is rare; likely “much-spoken-of,” i.e., celebrated in story. ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃσι = “beneath the oars,” epic locution for rowing speed.

line_details.english: cleaving her course through the gulf of Ambrakia;
line_details.greek: Ἀμπρακίου κόλποιο διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθα·
line_details.note: Ἀμπρακίου κόλπος = the Ambracian Gulf (NW Greece). διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθα = “pressing/cleaving her course.”

line_details.english: There—what shall I proclaim to you, Mousaios, god-born,
line_details.greek: - Ἔνθα τί τοι, Μουσαῖε θεηγενὲς, ἐξαγορεύσω
line_details.note: Apostrophe to Mousaios (Μουσαῖε), called θεηγενές “god-born.” ἐξαγορεύω = “proclaim/declare publicly.”

line_details.english: all that they suffered, together with the Minyae, as the gusts drove them toward the Syrtis,
line_details.greek: ὅσσα πάθον Μινύαισιν ὁμοῦ ποτὶ Σύρτιν ἀήταις
line_details.note: ἀήταις (dat.) = “by gusts/squalls”; ποτὶ Σύρτιν = “toward the Syrtis,” the dangerous Libyan shallows; ὁμοῦ = “together (with).”

line_details.english: or how they won deliverance from a sea-wandering voyage;
line_details.greek: ἢ πῶς ἐξεσάωθεν ἁλιπλάγκτοιο πορείης·
line_details.note: ἐξεσάωθεν = “escaped alive, won deliverance.” ἁλιπλάγκτος πορείη = “sea-wandering/sea-tossed voyage.”

line_details.english: and what pains they suffered in Crete, enduring,
line_details.greek: ὅσσα τ' ἄρ' ἐν Κρήτῃ πάθον ἄλγεα τετληῶτες,
line_details.note: τετληῶτες = “enduring, steadfast,” participle with concessive nuance (“though enduring”) or descriptive.

line_details.english: as they kept watch against the bronze triple-giant, until we came,
line_details.greek: χάλκειον τριγίγαντα δοκεύμενοι ὄφρ' ἱκόμεσθα,
line_details.note: χάλκειον τριγίγαντα refers to Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete. τριγίγαντα is a crux; often taken as “triple-/thrice-giant,” perhaps alluding to his thrice-daily circuit of the island; some have proposed emendations. δοκεύειν = “keep watch/lie in wait against.” ὄφρ’ ἱκόμεσθα = “until we came/arrived.”

line_details.english: who would not permit them to come within the harbors.
line_details.greek: ὅς ῥά οἱ οὐκ εἴα λιμένων ἔντοσθεν ἱκέσθαι.
line_details.note: οἱ (dat.) = “for them,” dative of disadvantage. λιμένων ἔντοσθεν = “inside the harbors.” οὐκ εἴα = “would not allow.”

text.english: And as we were hemmed in by the heavy-sounding wave of the sea, and straightway weighed down by dark-blue clouds, we hoped the swift ship might reach the Melainian crags; but Paian, the Far-shooter, ever close at hand, from rugged Delos sent forth a shaft, and by it revealed one of the Midmost Sporades; and thereafter all call it Kranae— —so the neighboring folk name the island.
text.greek: Ἠδ' ὡς στεινόμενοι βαρυηχέϊ κύματι πόντου ῥίμφα τε κυανέῃσι βαρυνόμενοι νεφέλῃσιν, ἠλπόμεθα σκοπέλοισι Μελαινείοισιν ἱκέσθαι νῆα θοήν· Παιὰν δ' ἄρ' ἑκηβόλος ἀγχόθεν αἰέν, Δήλου ἀπὸ κραναῆς ἧκεν βέλος, ἐκ δ' ἀνέφηνε Μεσσατίων Σποράδων· Κρανάην δέ ἑ πάντες ὀπίσσω νῆσον ἐπικλήσκουσι περικτίονες ἄνθρωποι.

line_details.english: And as we were hemmed in by the heavy-sounding wave of the sea,
line_details.greek: Ἠδ' ὡς στεινόμενοι βαρυηχέϊ κύματι πόντου
line_details.note: στεινόμενοι = “hemmed in, in straits”; βαρυηχέϊ (“heavy-sounding”) is an epic compound epithet of the surf.

line_details.english: and straightway weighed down by dark-blue clouds,
line_details.greek: ῥίμφα τε κυανέῃσι βαρυνόμενοι νεφέλῃσιν,
line_details.note: ῥίμφα = “straightway, swiftly”; κυανέῃσι (“blue-black”) evokes storm-clouds.

line_details.english: we hoped the swift ship might reach the Melainian crags;
line_details.greek: ἠλπόμεθα σκοπέλοισι Μελαινείοισιν ἱκέσθαι
line_details.note: νῆα θοὴν functions as the accusative subject of the infinitive ἱκέσθαι (“we hoped the swift ship would reach…”). Μελαινείοισι σκοπέλοισι probably means “the Black Rocks,” a toponym of uncertain identification.

line_details.english: but Paian, the Far-shooter, ever close at hand,
line_details.greek: νῆα θοήν· Παιὰν δ' ἄρ' ἑκηβόλος ἀγχόθεν αἰέν,
line_details.note: Παιὰν ἑκηβόλος = Apollo (Paian, the Far-shooter); ἀγχόθεν αἰέν = “ever at hand,” stressing his ready aid.

line_details.english: from rugged Delos sent forth a shaft, and by it revealed
line_details.greek: Δήλου ἀπὸ κραναῆς ἧκεν βέλος, ἐκ δ' ἀνέφηνε
line_details.note: ἧκεν βέλος = “sent a shaft,” a poetic sign/omen; Δήλου … κραναῆς = “rugged Delos,” a conventional epithet (kranaē = rocky).

line_details.english: one of the Midmost Sporades; and thereafter all call it Kranae—
line_details.greek: Μεσσατίων Σποράδων· Κρανάην δέ ἑ πάντες ὀπίσσω
line_details.note: Μεσσατίων Σποράδων = “the Midmost Sporades,” i.e., the central group of the scattered Aegean isles. ἑ = “it” (the island revealed). Κρανάην (“Kranae”) is a toponym meaning “Rocky.”

line_details.english: —so the neighboring folk name the island.
line_details.greek: νῆσον ἐπικλήσκουσι περικτίονες ἄνθρωποι.
line_details.note: περικτίονες ἄνθρωποι = “the neighboring folk/dwellers”; ἐπικλήσκουσι = “call by name.”

text.english: But it was not themis for him to destroy Aisonides outright from out of the sea.
text.greek: - Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ θέμις ἔσκε διαμπερὲς ἐξ ἁλὸς ἔρξαι

line_details.english: But it was not themis for him to destroy Aisonides outright from out of the sea.
line_details.greek: - Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ θέμις ἔσκε διαμπερὲς ἐξ ἁλὸς ἔρξαι
line_details.note: θέμις = divine right/law; διαμπερές = ‘utterly, outright.’ The infinitive ἔρξαι with personal object (Αἰσονίδην) is elliptical (‘to do [harm] to’ = ‘destroy’). ἐξ ἁλός may mean ‘at sea’ or ‘after [he had come] out of the sea’; the sense is that such destruction was not lawful. Subject ‘he’ is supplied from 1362 (Hyperion).

text.english: For he was bearing the ransom, and baleful Fate leapt back behind.
text.greek: Αἰσονίδην· περὶ γάρ ῥα λύτρον φέρεν· ἆλτο δ' ὀπίσσω

line_details.english: For he was bearing the ransom, and baleful Fate leapt back behind.
line_details.greek: Αἰσονίδην· περὶ γάρ ῥα λύτρον φέρεν· ἆλτο δ' ὀπίσσω
line_details.note: λύτρον = ransom, expiatory payment/blood‑price; the subject ‘he’ is Aisonides (Jason), who bears expiation, hence Moira withdraws (ἆλτο δ’ ὀπίσσω).

text.english: For Hyperion was wroth with forethought.
text.greek: Μοῖρ' ὀλοή· κότεεν γὰρ ἐπιφραδέως Ὑπερίων.

line_details.english: For Hyperion was wroth with forethought.
line_details.greek: Μοῖρ' ὀλοή· κότεεν γὰρ ἐπιφραδέως Ὑπερίων.
line_details.note: Υπερίων = Hyperion (Helios). ἐπιφραδέως = ‘with deliberation/forethought,’ implying controlled, knowing anger that respects the ransom and themis.

text.english: But when under oars we reached the Malean headlands, by Kirkē’s counsels we were on the point of casting off the curses of Aietes and the sin‑avenging Erinys; then indeed I, for the Minyans, performed holy expiatory offerings of purification, and I appeased Gaiēochos Ennosigaios, to grant those hastening home a return and the sight of their sweet parents.
text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃς Μαλεώτιδας ἱκόμεθ' ἄκρας, Κίρκης ἐννεσίῃσιν ἀπορρίψεσθαι ἔμελλον ἀρὰς Αἰήτεω καὶ ἠλιτόποινον Ἐριννύν· δὴ τότ' ἐγὼ Μινύαισιν ἐφ' ἱερὰ λύτρα καθαρμῶν ῥέξα, καὶ ἐλλισάμην Γαιήοχον Ἐννοσίγαιον νόστον ἐπειγομένοις δόμεναι γλυκερούς τε τοκῆας.

line_details.english: But when under oars we reached the Malean headlands,
line_details.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃς Μαλεώτιδας ἱκόμεθ' ἄκρας,
line_details.note: “under oars” (hyp’ eiresiēs) is an epic idiom for traveling by rowing; “Malean headlands” refers to Cape Malea (Laconia).

line_details.english: by Kirkē’s counsels we were on the point of casting off
line_details.greek: Κίρκης ἐννεσίῃσιν ἀπορρίψεσθαι ἔμελλον
line_details.note: ennesiē = “counsel”; aporripsesthai “to cast off, rid oneself (of).” The sense is purification following Kirkē’s advice.

line_details.english: the curses of Aietes and the sin‑avenging Erinys;
line_details.greek: ἀρὰς Αἰήτεω καὶ ἠλιτόποινον Ἐριννύν·
line_details.note: ēlitopoinos = “sin‑avenging,” from alitē “offense/sin”; singular Erinys as the personified avenger (blood‑guilt).

line_details.english: then indeed I, for the Minyans, performed holy expiatory offerings of purification,
line_details.greek: δὴ τότ' ἐγὼ Μινύαισιν ἐφ' ἱερὰ λύτρα καθαρμῶν
line_details.note: hierà lýtra katharmōn = “sacred ransom‑offerings of purification,” i.e., expiatory rites to remove miasma; epi with acc. expresses “for, on behalf of.”

line_details.english: and I appeased Gaiēochos Ennosigaios,
line_details.greek: ῥέξα, καὶ ἐλλισάμην Γαιήοχον Ἐννοσίγαιον
line_details.note: ellisamen (ἐλλισάμην) = “I appeased/propitiated,” a rarer verb; Gaiēochos Ennosigaios are epithets of Poseidon (“Earth‑holder, Earth‑shaker”).

line_details.english: to grant those hastening home a return and the sight of their sweet parents.
line_details.greek: νόστον ἐπειγομένοις δόμεναι γλυκερούς τε τοκῆας.
line_details.note: domenai is the epic infinitive for dounai “to grant”; the addition “the sight of” renders the idiom with “sweet parents,” i.e., safe return to them; epeigomenois is a dative of advantage “for those eager for home.”

text.english: And they, as they sailed toward well-built Iolkos, were offering sacrifice; but I came to windy Tainaron, so that I might perform cut-offerings for the very-glorious kings who indeed hold the keys of the nether pits.
text.greek: - Καί ῥ' οἳ μὲν πλώοντες ἐϋκτιμένην ἐπ' Ἰωλκόν θῦνον· ἐγὼ δ' ἱκόμην ἐπὶ Ταίναρον ἠνεμόεντα, ὄφρα κεν ἔντομα ῥέξω ἀγακλειτοῖς βασιλεῦσιν οἵ τ' ἄρα νερτερίων βερέθρων κληῗδας ἔχουσιν.

line_details.english: And they, as they sailed toward well-built Iolkos,
line_details.greek: - Καί ῥ' οἳ μὲν πλώοντες ἐϋκτιμένην ἐπ' Ἰωλκόν
line_details.note: The verb θῦνον (“were offering sacrifice”) in the next line governs this clause: sense = “as they sailed to well-built Iolkos, they offered sacrifice.”

line_details.english: were offering sacrifice; but I came to windy Tainaron,
line_details.greek: θῦνον· ἐγὼ δ' ἱκόμην ἐπὶ Ταίναρον ἠνεμόεντα,
line_details.note: Tainaron (Taenarum), the windy cape in Laconia, was famed as an entrance to Hades.

line_details.english: so that I might perform cut-offerings for the very-glorious kings
line_details.greek: ὄφρα κεν ἔντομα ῥέξω ἀγακλειτοῖς βασιλεῦσιν
line_details.note: ἔντομα ῥέξω is a technical phrase for chthonic rites performed by incision/slaughter (with blood offered into a pit); the “very-glorious kings” are the underworld pair, Plouton (Aïdoneus) and Persephone.

line_details.english: who indeed hold the keys of the nether pits.
line_details.greek: οἵ τ' ἄρα νερτερίων βερέθρων κληῗδας ἔχουσιν.
line_details.note: “Keys of the nether pits” (νερτερίων βερέθρων κληῖδες) evokes sovereign control over access to the Underworld.

text.english: Thence, setting out, I sped to snow‑clad Thrace, to the land of Leibethra, to my fatherland; and I entered the far‑famed cave, where my mother bore me in the marriage‑bed of great‑hearted Oiagros.
text.greek: Ἔνθεν δ' ὁρμηθεὶς ἐσύθην χιονώδεα Θρῄκην Λειβήθρων ἐς χῶρον, ἐμὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν· ἄντρον δ' εἰσεπέρησα περικλυτὸν, ἔνθα με μήτηρ γείνατ' ἐνὶ λέκτροις μεγαλήτορος Οἰάγροιο.

line_details.english: Thence, setting out, I sped to snow‑clad Thrace,
line_details.greek: Ἔνθεν δ' ὁρμηθεὶς ἐσύθην χιονώδεα Θρῄκην
line_details.note: ἐσύθην is the intransitive aorist (passive in form) of σεύω, “I sped/rushed”; ὁρμηθείς “setting out.” χιονῶδεα is a Homeric-style epithet, “snow‑clad,” for Thrace.

line_details.english: to the land of Leibethra, to my fatherland;
line_details.greek: Λειβήθρων ἐς χῶρον, ἐμὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
line_details.note: Λειβήθρων is genitive plural with ἐς χῶρον (“to the land/region of Leibethra”), a Pierian/Thracian site associated with Orpheus. The double ἐς echoes the motion toward place and homeland (πατρὶς γαῖα).

line_details.english: and I entered the far‑famed cave, where my mother
line_details.greek: ἄντρον δ' εἰσεπέρησα περικλυτὸν, ἔνθα με μήτηρ
line_details.note: εἰσεπέρησα is an epic aorist of περάω (“to pass into/through”), here “I entered.” περικλυτόν = “far‑famed.” The ἄντρον is the specific cave at Leibethra tied to Orphic lore.

line_details.english: bore me in the marriage‑bed of great‑hearted Oiagros.
line_details.greek: γείνατ' ἐνὶ λέκτροις μεγαλήτορος Οἰάγροιο.
line_details.note: λέκτροις denotes the marriage‑bed; μεγαλήτωρ is a standard heroic epithet. Οἰάγροιο = Oiagros, traditionally Orpheus’ Thracian father; the unnamed mother is Kalliope in the usual myth.
